Although Dropout results in a non-smooth energy landscape lacking formal convergence assurances, the discretized Hamiltonian demonstrates strong empirical effectiveness. Our method enables reliable estimation of predictive accuracy and yields improved generalization, particularly for challenging test cases.

Predicting urban ride-hailing demand is a vital yet complex component of building intelligent transportation systems. Accurate demand forecasts enable more efficient vehicle deployment and better platform dispatching. Traditional deep learning approaches that do not utilize external structured data often rely on hybrid models combining CNNs and RNNs, leveraging extensive pixel-level labeled data. However, these methods face significant challenges due to sparse spatial data and limited ability to capture long-term temporal dependencies. To overcome these hurdles, we introduce a novel virtual graph modeling technique aimed at highlighting key demand areas, alongside a new Deep Multi-View Spatiotemporal Virtual Graph Neural Network (DMVST-VGNN). This model enhances the learning of spatial dynamics and long-range temporal dependencies by integrating a 1D Convolutional Neural Network, a Multi Graph Attention Neural Network, and a Transformer layer—corresponding to short-term temporal patterns, spatial relationships, and long-term temporal trends, respectively. We validate our approach with experiments on two large-scale datasets from New York City across fine-grained prediction scenarios. The results demonstrate that DMVST-VGNN outperforms existing methods, showcasing its effectiveness and superiority in citywide ride-hailing demand forecasting.

High-quality education is a fundamental cornerstone for building a more sustainable future. The recent COVID-19 pandemic has accelerated the adoption of online education, enabling students and teachers to engage in learning and teaching from their homes. Concurrently, online learning platforms now facilitate the collection and analysis of vast amounts of educational data, paving the way for enhanced intelligent educational services. Knowledge Tracing (KT), which focuses on tracking students' evolving understanding, plays a vital role in supporting these intelligent systems. Consequently, this emerging field has garnered increasing research interest, leading to significant advancements. In this review, we introduce a novel technical taxonomy of existing KT models and systematically present an overview of these approaches. We also discuss various KT model variants developed to more accurately reflect the comprehensive learning process, examining them across three stages: before, during, and after learning. Additionally, we highlight key applications of KT across different educational contexts and conclude by outlining promising avenues for future research in this rapidly evolving domain.

Understanding formation mechanisms is essential for analyzing complex networks, yet extracting them from observations remains difficult. Typically, in real-world scenarios, only the final graph is available, not the detailed construction process, and these observed graphs often display intricate structural features. In this study, we introduce GraphOpt, an end-to-end framework that simultaneously learns an implicit model of how graphs are formed and uncovers the underlying optimization process as a latent objective function. This learned objective can explain the structural properties of observed graphs and can be transferred to other graphs within the same domain. GraphOpt conceptualizes link creation as a sequential decision-making process and employs a maximum entropy inverse reinforcement learning approach to solve it. Additionally, it features a novel continuous latent action space that enhances scalability. Empirical results show that GraphOpt identifies a latent objective that generalizes across graphs with varying characteristics. It also learns a robust stochastic policy that yields competitive link prediction results without explicit training for this task and facilitates the generation of graphs with properties resembling those of the observed graphs.

Although recent advancements have improved image denoising using CNNs, the complexity and depth of these architectures still limit their practical deployment. Simpler, more computationally efficient methods like BM3D continue to be favored, especially in environments with limited resources. In this research, we explore whether compact neural networks can achieve results comparable to BM3D in denoising images affected by additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN). We design networks with just two hidden layers, experimenting with various neuron models and layer widths to compare their performance against BM3D across different noise intensities. Our findings clearly demonstrate that the emerging self-organized operational neural network variant based on a generative neuron model (Self-ONNs) not only outperforms traditional CNNs but also delivers results competitive with BM3D, significantly exceeding its performance at higher noise levels.

For autonomous agents, executing a suboptimal policy can be costly or even hazardous. Therefore, it is important to estimate lower bounds on policy performance with confidence intervals without actually deploying the policy. Current exact high-confidence off-policy evaluation techniques that rely on importance sampling demand large amounts of data to produce tight bounds. Existing model-based approaches are limited to discrete state spaces. Given that exact bounds are often computationally infeasible across many domains, we accept approximate bounds that offer less stringent safety guarantees but are more data-efficient. In this work, we introduce two bootstrapping off-policy evaluation methods utilizing learned Markov Decision Process (MDP) transition models to estimate lower confidence bounds on policy performance with limited data, applicable to both continuous and discrete state spaces. To account for potential biases introduced by the model, we derive a theoretical upper bound on model bias when the transition function is estimated from independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) trajectories. This provides insights into the conditions under which model-based methods may exhibit high bias. We also conduct empirical evaluations of our proposed methods, analyzing the scenarios in which various bootstrapping off-policy confidence interval techniques succeed or fail.

Understanding the links between images and covariates is a fundamental goal in medical imaging research. To address this image response regression challenge, we introduce a novel nonparametric method within the framework of spatially varying coefficient models, where the spatially varying functions are modeled using deep neural networks. Our approach improves upon existing methods by explicitly incorporating spatial smoothness and subject heterogeneity, offering clear interpretability and exceptional flexibility in modeling complex associations. A central feature of our strategy is to consider each image voxel as an individual effective sample. This approach helps mitigate the common issue of limited sample sizes in medical imaging studies and enhances the robustness and reproducibility of the results. We focus on a broad class of piecewise smooth functions, proving estimation and variable selection consistency, along with deriving asymptotic error bounds. The effectiveness of our method is demonstrated through comprehensive simulation studies and further validated through analyses of two functional magnetic resonance imaging datasets.

Neural network-based machine learning techniques are delivering impressive outcomes across numerous fields. Typically, training these models necessitates large, representative datasets, which are often crowdsourced and may include sensitive data. It is crucial to ensure that the models do not disclose private information contained in these datasets. To achieve this, we introduce novel algorithmic methods for learning and provide an enhanced analysis of privacy expenses within the differential privacy framework. Our implementation and experimental results show that it is possible to train deep neural networks with non-convex objectives while maintaining a modest privacy budget, all without significantly increasing software complexity, training time, or compromising model performance.

In 2021, the Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory hosted an internal competition to develop artificial intelligence (AI) agents capable of excelling at the cooperative card game Hanabi. The agents were assessed based on their performance in partnership with human players they had never encountered before. This report describes the development of the winning agent, which achieved an average human-player score of 16.5—surpassing the current best benchmarks for human-AI Hanabi collaboration. The winning solution involved observing and accurately modeling the decision-making process of the author, followed by training with a behavioral clone of their gameplay. Remarkably, the agent uncovered a human-compatible play style by initially mimicking human decisions and then experimenting with variations on this approach, resulting in improved scores against human partners. This work provides an in-depth analysis of the design and implementation of this human-friendly Hanabi teammate, exploring the concept of human-complementary strategies and discussing their potential to enhance AI applications within human-machine teams.

We introduce Bayesian extensions to two nonparametric regression techniques: kernel regression and mutual \(k\)-nearest neighbor regression. These extensions are grounded in Gaussian process models, enabling the derivation of probability distributions for target value estimates and providing a systematic framework for hyperparameter selection. We demonstrate that, asymptotically, the proposed Bayesian methods converge to their respective traditional counterparts—kernel and mutual \(k\)-nearest neighbor regression. Simulations on both synthetic and real-world datasets indicate that our methods effectively select appropriate hyperparameters and perform as well as or better than the original methods.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) have achieved remarkable success across numerous tasks, largely thanks to large-scale, meticulously annotated datasets. However, the process of labeling such extensive data is often costly and prone to errors, leading to noisy labels that can compromise annotation quality. Training on datasets with noisy labels can significantly impair a model’s generalization ability. Existing approaches typically involve complex training procedures or incur high computational costs for only marginal gains. In this paper, we introduce Temporal Calibrated Regularization (TCR), a method that leverages both the original labels and the predictions from the previous epoch to help DNNs retain simple learned patterns with minimal additional overhead. Through comprehensive experiments across various neural network architectures and datasets, we demonstrate that TCR consistently improves the robustness of DNNs against label noise.

We present Binacox, a novel prognostic approach designed to identify multiple cut-points within features in a multivariate context featuring numerous continuous variables. This method leverages the Cox model framework, integrating one-hot encoding with the binarsity penalty—combining total-variation regularization and an additional linear constraint—to facilitate both feature selection and cut-point detection. We establish original nonasymptotic oracle inequalities for predictive accuracy, measured via the Kullback-Leibler divergence, and for estimation, demonstrating a rapid rate of convergence. The effectiveness of Binacox is thoroughly evaluated through extensive Monte Carlo simulations and validated on three publicly available genetic cancer datasets. On these high-dimensional datasets, our approach markedly surpasses existing state-of-the-art survival models in risk prediction performance, as measured by the C-index, while also achieving computational speeds several orders of magnitude faster. Moreover, Binacox offers enhanced interpretability from a clinical standpoint by automatically identifying critical cut-points in relevant variables.

Recent advancements in fairness within machine learning have primarily focused on how to define, measure, and promote "fair" outcomes. However, less consideration has been given to the ethical principles that underpin these efforts. One such perspective is consequentialism, which fundamentally asserts that outcomes are the primary concern. Although consequentialism presents its own challenges—such as difficulties in decision-making due to uncertainty, subjectivity, and the complexities of aggregating outcomes—it still offers a compelling framework for critically evaluating current research on fairness in machine learning. Additionally, it highlights key tradeoffs, including who should be considered, the advantages and disadvantages of implementing policies, and the importance of long-term implications. In this paper, we offer a consequentialist critique of prevalent fairness definitions in machine learning and explore how consequentialism can inform the field from a machine learning standpoint. We conclude with a broader discussion on learning processes and the role of randomization, emphasizing their significant ethical implications for automated decision-making systems.

Large-scale recommender systems are essential for identifying the most relevant items from extensive catalogs, playing a vital role in modern search and recommendation platforms. To handle the vast input space of high-cardinality categorical features, typical models learn a shared embedding space through neural networks, based on user feedback data for both queries and items. However, with millions or even billions of items, user feedback is often concentrated on only a small subset, resulting in a power-law distribution that leads to extremely sparse data for long-tail items. Drawing inspiration from recent breakthroughs in self-supervised representation learning in computer vision and natural language processing, we introduce a multi-task self-supervised learning (SSL) framework tailored for large-scale item recommendation. This framework addresses the challenge of label sparsity by enhancing the modeling of latent relationships among item features. Specifically, SSL not only enriches item representations but also serves as an effective regularizer to improve model generalization. Additionally, we propose a novel data augmentation technique that leverages feature correlations within our framework. We validated our approach on two real-world datasets containing 500 million and 1 billion training examples, respectively. The results confirm the effectiveness of SSL regularization, demonstrating superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods.

Efficient neural networks and hardware accelerators are actively being investigated to enhance DNN inference speed on edge devices. For instance, MobileNet employs depthwise separable convolution to significantly reduce latency, while systolic arrays deliver superior performance per watt. However, combining these approaches proves inefficient: the computational pattern of depthwise separable convolution is not systolic and does not leverage data reuse effectively, preventing full utilization of the systolic array's limited dataflow. In this work, we introduce FuSeConv (Fully-Separable Convolution) as a seamless replacement for depthwise separable convolution. FuSeConv extends the concept of convolution decomposition into fully separable 1D convolutions along both spatial and depth axes. This approach results in computations that are inherently systolic, enabling efficient use of the systolic array through a slightly adapted dataflow. Using FuSeConv, we attain a speed-up of 3x to 7x with MobileNet models on a 64x64 systolic array, while maintaining comparable accuracy on ImageNet. This substantial speed improvement highlights the potential of hardware-aware Neural Operator Search (NOS) alongside existing Neural Architecture Search (NAS) methods.

Over the past decade, numerous off-policy prediction learning algorithms have been introduced, yet it remains uncertain which methods achieve faster learning speeds. In this study, we empirically evaluate eleven off-policy prediction algorithms with linear function approximation across two small-scale tasks: the Rooms task and the High Variance Rooms task. These tasks are intentionally designed to challenge rapid learning. In the Rooms task, importance sampling ratios can reach as high as 2^14, occasionally dropping to 2. To mitigate the high variance stemming from these ratios, the step size must be kept small, which consequently slows the learning process. The High Variance Rooms task presents an even more extreme scenario, with the product of importance sampling ratios potentially reaching 2^14 multiplied by 25. Building on the empirical framework established by Ghiassian and Sutton (2021), we analyze the same set of algorithms and utilize their experimental methodology. The algorithms examined include Off-policy TD(λ), five Gradient-TD variants, two Emphatic-TD methods, Tree Backup(λ), Vtrace(λ), and ABTD(ζ). Our findings indicate that the performance of these algorithms is heavily influenced by the variance introduced through importance sampling ratios. The experimental results demonstrate that Tree

Tensor networks are decompositions of high-rank tensors into interconnected networks of lower-rank tensors, primarily utilized in the study of quantum many-body systems. Recently, interest in tensor networks has expanded to supervised learning, particularly for image classification tasks. In this study, we extend the capabilities of the matrix product state (MPS) tensor network—originally designed for one-dimensional vectors—to effectively handle two- and three-dimensional medical images. Our approach involves treating small patches of images as orderless, compressing their spatial details into feature dimensions, and applying MPS operations to these localized, orderless regions. These local representations are then combined hierarchically to preserve overall structural information. We introduce the locally orderless tensor network (LoTeNet) and compare its performance with existing methods across three datasets. Throughout all experiments, the LoTeNet architecture remains consistent, demonstrating that it requires fewer computational resources while achieving performance that matches or exceeds that of competing techniques.

Modern approaches to single image super-resolution (SISR) using deep neural networks focus not only on enhancing accuracy but also on developing lightweight, computationally efficient models. Recently, neural architecture search (NAS) techniques have demonstrated remarkable potential in achieving these goals. Building on this foundation, we propose a novel trilevel NAS framework that better balances various efficiency metrics with super-resolution performance. Unlike existing NAS methods, our approach conducts a more exhaustive search, resulting in an optimized, compact, and highly efficient architecture. We introduce an innovative hierarchical search space modeling that operates across three levels: network, cell, and kernel. To ensure the search process remains differentiable and efficient within this trilevel space, we utilize a novel sparsestmax technique, which adeptly generates sparse candidate distributions, facilitating more effective selection from an expanded search space. Additionally, we incorporate a sorting mechanism into the sparsestmax relaxation to enhance network-level compression. Our NAS optimization enables simultaneous search and training within a single phase, significantly reducing both search and training times. Extensive evaluations on benchmark datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms current state-of-the-art NAS approaches in terms of super-resolution quality and efficiency.

Speech sounds produced in spoken language are generated by modifying the configuration of the articulators surrounding the vocal tract. These sounds carry extensive information that can enhance our understanding of the mechanisms underlying human speech production. We introduce a novel deep neural network framework that interprets the acoustic data within variable-length sequences of vocal tract shaping during speech, as captured by real-time magnetic resonance imaging (rtMRI), and converts this information into text. Our approach integrates spatiotemporal convolutional layers, a recurrent neural network, and the connectionist temporal classification (CTC) loss, trained entirely in an end-to-end manner. Evaluated on the USC-TIMIT dataset, the model achieved a 40.6% phoneme error rate (PER) at the sentence level, significantly outperforming existing approaches. To our knowledge, this is the first study to demonstrate the recognition of complete spoken sentences based on an individual's articulatory movements captured via rtMRI video. Additionally, we conducted an analysis of how the geometry of articulation varies across different sub-regions of the vocal tract—namely, the pharyngeal, velar and dorsal, hard palate, and labial constriction areas—in relation to various emotions and gender differences. The findings suggest that distortions in these sub-regions are influenced by both emotional state and gender.

Despite the increasing demand for multilingual task-oriented dialogue systems (such as Alexa and Google Home), research in multilingual or cross-lingual contexts remains limited. To address this gap, we introduce a zero-shot approach for adapting task-oriented dialogue systems to low-resource languages. Our method begins by leveraging a small set of parallel word pairs to enhance cross-lingual word-level alignment. We then incorporate a latent variable model to handle variations in similar sentences across different languages, accounting for both imperfect alignments and linguistic differences. Experimental results demonstrate that, despite relying on significantly fewer external resources, our model outperforms current state-of-the-art approaches in natural language understanding tasks—specifically intent detection and slot filling—in zero-shot settings.

This paper, to the best of our knowledge, is the first to present physics-informed neural networks for precise estimation of AC-OPF results, along with rigorous performance guarantees. Power system operators and various other stakeholders are increasingly relying on Optimal Power Flow (OPF) algorithms for diverse applications, including planning and real-time system operations. However, solving the AC Optimal Power Flow problem in its native form is often complex due to its nonlinear and non-convex nature. While numerous approximations and relaxations have been developed, recent research has mainly focused on machine learning methods, particularly neural networks. Nonetheless, these methods have only partially incorporated the physical models during training and, more critically, have offered no assurances regarding potential constraint violations in their outputs. Our approach addresses these issues by (i) embedding the AC power flow equations directly into the neural network training process and (ii) employing rigorous techniques to identify and minimize the worst-case constraint violations across the entire input space, all while preserving prediction optimality. We demonstrate that physics-informed neural networks outperform standard neural networks in terms of accuracy and constraint adherence, and we also illustrate methods to further reduce the maximum constraint violations across all neural network models.

Distances between data points are fundamental in many machine learning applications. However, when noise contaminates the data, these distances—and consequently the models relying on them—may become less reliable, especially in high-dimensional settings. Even small effects of noise can accumulate, causing empirical nearest and furthest neighbors to deviate significantly from the true relationships. In this work, we precisely analyze these phenomena in noisy high-dimensional data using an asymptotic probabilistic framework. While it has been previously suggested that neighborhood queries lose meaning and stability when distance concentration occurs—reducing the contrast between closest and furthest neighbors—we find that this is not necessarily true. By decomposing the data into underlying ground truth and noise components, we show that, under certain conditions, the true neighborhood relations inferred from noisy data remain largely intact despite distance concentration. Our findings are supported by comprehensive empirical tests, and we present intriguing experiments demonstrating that the critical 'phase shift'—the point at which neighbors become effectively random—aligns with the phase transition associated with the data’s intrinsic dimensionality.

Monocular depth estimation is essential for 3D recognition and understanding. A primary challenge in existing methods is their insufficient utilization of structural information, resulting in inaccuracies in spatial layout, discontinuous surfaces, and unclear boundaries. In this study, we address these issues from three perspectives. First, to better capture the spatial relationships among visual features, we introduce a structure-aware neural network equipped with spatial attention modules. These modules direct the network’s focus to both global structures and local details across various feature layers. Second, we propose a global focal relative loss for pairs of points, which reinforces spatial constraints in the predictions and explicitly penalizes errors in regions with depth discontinuities, thereby maintaining sharper depth boundaries. Lastly, analyzing failure cases of previous methods, we compile a new Hard Case (HC) Depth dataset featuring challenging scenes such as complex lighting, moving objects, and tilted camera angles. This dataset is integrated into a curriculum learning strategy that gradually introduces diverse training examples, improving the model’s robustness. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach significantly surpasses current state-of-the-art methods in accuracy on the NYUDv2 dataset and exhibits superior generalization to unseen data.

Legal practitioners often navigate extensive and complex legal case proceedings. To accurately grasp the motivations behind the actions of various parties involved, it is crucial to clearly identify and interpret the segments of the documents that convey intent relevant to the case. In this paper, we present a dataset comprising 93 legal documents categorized into four case types: Murder, Land Dispute, Robbery, and Corruption. Within these documents, we annotate phrases that explicitly express intent aligned with the case category. Additionally, we provide fine-grained annotations of intent for each phrase to facilitate a more nuanced understanding of the case details. We also evaluate the performance of several transformer-based models in automating the extraction of intent phrases at both coarse and fine levels, as well as in classifying documents into the respective categories. The results indicate that our dataset poses significant challenges, particularly for fine-grained intent classification.

We analyze the underdamped Langevin diffusion when the logarithm of the target distribution is smooth and strongly concave. We introduce a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm derived from its discretization and demonstrate that it attains an \(\varepsilon\) error in 2-Wasserstein distance within \(\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{d}/\varepsilon)\) steps. This represents a noteworthy improvement over the current best rate for overdamped Langevin MCMC, which requires \(\mathcal{O}(d/\varepsilon^2)\) steps under comparable smoothness and concavity conditions. The underdamped Langevin MCMC can be interpreted as a variant of Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC), an approach known to outperform overdamped Langevin methods in various applications. We provide precise quantitative bounds that substantiate this empirical advantage.

A novel Markov chain update method leveraging a machine-learned flow-based generative model is introduced for Monte Carlo sampling in lattice field theories. This generative model can be trained to generate samples that approximate the target Boltzmann distribution dictated by the lattice action of the theory under investigation. Systematic training of the model leads to reductions in autocorrelation times within the Markov chain, even in parameter regions where conventional Markov chain Monte Carlo methods suffer from critical slowing down. Additionally, the model can be trained without prior samples from the target distribution. The proposed approach is evaluated against Hybrid Monte Carlo (HMC) and local Metropolis algorithms in the context of two-dimensional \(\phi^4\) theory.

In multi-label classification tasks, each instance is associated with multiple labels simultaneously. Leveraging the relationships among these labels can lead to more accurate models. These label correlations can be examined at various levels, such as pairwise relationships or higher-order interactions. While higher-order correlations offer a more comprehensive understanding, they are often more computationally intensive and pose scalability challenges. This study focuses on exploiting high-order label correlations within subsets of labels through a supervised learning classifier system (UCS). To achieve this, the label powerset (LP) strategy is implemented, along with a prediction aggregation method that combines outputs within the relevant label set for unseen instances, enhancing the LP approach's ability to handle previously unencountered label combinations. Performance is evaluated using exact match ratio and Hamming loss metrics, with an analysis of the expected fitness values for classifiers based on these measures. Additionally, a complexity analysis of the proposed algorithm is presented. Experimental comparisons with other well-known LP-based methods across multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate the competitive performance of the proposed approach.

We investigate a variation of the multi-armed bandit problem in which side information, specifically bounds on the mean reward of each arm, is available. We introduce a novel algorithm called Global Under-Explore (GLUE), which leverages these mean bounds to construct pseudo-variances for each arm. These pseudo-variances then guide the exploration strategy, balancing exploration and exploitation effectively. Our analysis of GLUE demonstrates regret bounds that are always at least as favorable as those of the traditional UCB algorithm. Additionally, we establish that GLUE surpasses existing regret guarantees in structured bandit settings, supported by both theoretical proofs and empirical evaluations. Lastly, we explore an application in adaptive intervention learning, where prior data—often confounded by unmeasured variables—can still yield meaningful mean bounds. These bounds can be inferred from such logs and used to enhance the learning process. Our approach is validated through semi-synthetic experiments based on real-world datasets, confirming its practical efficacy.

Amid growing interest in Machine Learning (ML) and a supportive environment for data development, we propose an innovative approach for predicting two-dimensional physical fields based on data. Polynomial Chaos Expansion (PCE), a well-established tool within the Uncertainty Quantification (UQ) community, has traditionally served as a robust method for mapping probabilistic inputs to outputs. Recently, PCE has been tested within a purely ML framework and demonstrated performance comparable to conventional ML techniques for pointwise predictions. Its advantages include explicitness, flexibility with small training datasets, and integration within a probabilistic framework. Concurrently, Dimensionality Reduction (DR) techniques are increasingly employed for pattern recognition and data compression, especially as data quality improves. This study highlights the effectiveness of Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD) for building statistical predictive models. Both POD and PCE have proven their value within their respective domains. The primary objective of this paper is to integrate these methods for field measurement-based forecasting. The outlined approach also facilitates data analysis. Additionally, the paper addresses several challenges associated with multidimensional field measurements, such as limited data availability. The combined POD-PCE methodology offers a promising avenue for advanced field prediction and analysis.

Critical environments such as military and defense operations, aviation user-technology interactions, and assessments of hardware or software intuitiveness all demand evaluation of the mental workload imposed on users during specific tasks. This assessment is essential to identify ways to optimize tasks and operations, thereby reducing cognitive strain and enabling users to operate systems more efficiently and with less difficulty. It is important to recognize that a task deemed simple by one user may be challenging for another; understanding this variability requires a user-centered approach. We propose to measure mental workload (MWL) experienced by an operator performing information-intensive tasks, providing insights into task complexity from the user's perspective. In this study, we have developed an experimental setup that simulates contemporary workload conditions encountered during everyday tasks. Our approach involves automatically assessing perceived task complexity through analysis of electroencephalogram (EEG) data collected during operation. Several critical steps are involved in this process, including...

Low-bit width neural networks have been widely investigated for deployment on edge devices to minimize computational demands. Prior methods primarily rely on gradient-based optimization within a two-stage train-and-compress framework or integrate gradient quantization directly into the training process. These strategies often necessitate high-performance hardware during training and typically require storing full-precision weights alongside their quantized counterparts. In this study, we propose approaches that leverage direct combinatorial optimization for risk minimization with binary weights, which can be transformed into a non-monotone submodular maximization problem under specific conditions. We utilize approximation algorithms tailored for both single-layer and multi-layer neural networks. For linear models, our method operates with a time complexity of $\mathcal{O}(nd)$, where $n$ denotes the number of samples and $d$ the data dimension. We demonstrate that combining greedy coordinate descent with our novel optimization technique yields competitive accuracy in binary classification tasks.

Predictive modeling has increasingly incorporated flexible yet complex techniques such as neural networks and ensemble methods— including stacking, boosting, and bagging. These approaches typically involve a large number of parameters or hyperparameters, a trade-off for their adaptability. However, this abundance of parameters often makes models difficult to interpret. This paper introduces a cohesive set of explanation tools for predictive models, commonly referred to as black boxes. Each explainer functions as a technique for probing and understanding these models. The methods are model-agnostic, meaning they can extract meaningful insights from any predictive algorithm regardless of its internal architecture. Each explainer targets a specific aspect of a model: some assist in breaking down individual predictions, others are better suited for assessing overall performance, and some elucidate variable importance and conditional responses. Every explainer described here can be applied to a single model or multiple models simultaneously. When multiple models are involved, they can be compared to highlight their respective strengths and weaknesses, providing valuable insights for model validation. These explainers are implemented within the DALEX package for R and are based on a consistent, standardized framework.

Voice conversion (VC) involves transforming the timbre, accent, and tonal qualities of a source speaker's voice into those of another while maintaining the original linguistic content. Despite advances, VC remains particularly challenging in one-shot scenarios. Auto-encoder-based VC approaches aim to separate speaker identity from speech content without prior knowledge of the target speaker, thereby enabling generalization to unseen voices. This disentanglement is typically achieved through techniques such as vector quantization (VQ), adversarial training, or instance normalization (IN). However, imperfect separation can negatively impact the naturalness and clarity of the synthesized speech. In this study, we enhance audio quality by incorporating the U-Net architecture into an auto-encoder-based VC framework. We observe that effectively utilizing U-Net requires a robust information bottleneck, which can be facilitated through VQ of the latent representations. Both objective metrics and subjective listening tests indicate that our proposed approach excels in producing natural-sounding speech with high speaker similarity.

Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) have recently gained prominence in the Deep Learning community for their ability to quantify uncertainty in classification tasks. They are widely applied across various fields, including astrophysics and autonomous driving. Unlike traditional neural networks that rely on point estimates for weights, BNNs incorporate a prior distribution over the weights, facilitating the estimation of both aleatoric (data-related) and epistemic (model-related) uncertainties. A specific variant of BNN, known as Monte Carlo Dropout (MC Dropout), models weights with a Bernoulli distribution through the use of Dropout techniques. Various approaches have been proposed to optimize the dropout rate, such as employing a variational framework. In this paper, we introduce a novel method called "Dropout Regulation" (DR), which dynamically adjusts the dropout rate during training through a control mechanism inspired by automation systems. DR enables accurate uncertainty estimation comparable to state-of-the-art techniques, while maintaining simplicity and ease of implementation.

Machine learning methods have become increasingly prominent in astronomical research, demonstrating high accuracy in object classification within image datasets. In this study, we utilize archival data from the Faint Images of the Radio Sky at Twenty Centimeters (FIRST) survey to categorize radio galaxies into four classes: Fanaroff-Riley Class I (FRI), Fanaroff-Riley Class II (FRII), Bent-Tailed (BENT), and Compact (COMPT). Our approach is based on Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), featuring an architecture with three parallel convolutional blocks that are integrated and followed by two fully connected layers for final classification. When tested on an independent dataset, our model achieved an average precision, recall, and F1 score of 96% across the targeted classes. The most effective data augmentation techniques included rotations, horizontal and vertical flips, and increasing brightness. Conversely, shifts, zooming, and decreasing brightness negatively impacted model performance. These results demonstrate that the proposed model can efficiently and accurately distinguish among various morphological classes of radio galaxies.

Open book question answering (OpenBookQA) is a form of natural language question answering (NLQA) that involves providing answers based on a predefined set of open book facts and general knowledge about a topic. Recently, the OpenBookQA challenge has been introduced to advance research in this area. Unlike typical NLQA tasks focused mainly on linguistic comprehension, OpenBookQA demands more profound reasoning that combines understanding language with leveraging common knowledge. In this paper, we explore question answering on the OpenBookQA dataset by integrating cutting-edge language models with abductive information retrieval, information gain-based re-ranking, passage selection, and weighted scoring methods. Our approach achieves a 72.0% accuracy, representing an 11.6% improvement over the existing best results.

Skew-Gaussian processes (SkewGPs) extend the multivariate Unified Skew-Normal distributions from finite-dimensional vectors to functions, offering a more general and flexible modeling approach than Gaussian processes by capturing asymmetric distributions. In recent work, we demonstrated that SkewGPs are conjugate to the probit likelihood, enabling exact posterior computations for non-parametric binary classification and preference learning. In this study, we further develop these insights by proving that SkewGPs are conjugate not only with the normal and affine probit likelihoods but also with their product, broadening the scope of this conjugacy. This advancement allows us to (i) address classification, preference modeling, as well as numeric, ordinal regression, and mixed problems within a unified framework; (ii) derive closed-form expressions for the resulting posterior distributions. Empirical results show that our SkewGP-based framework outperforms traditional Gaussian processes in active learning and Bayesian (constrained) optimization tasks—both crucial in experimental design and data science.

We introduce a robust method for addressing review-level sentiment classification by leveraging sentence-level polarity correction. Our approach involves assessing the consistency of sentence polarities within each product review prior to applying machine learning algorithms. Sentences exhibiting conflicting polarities are discarded, while those with aligned sentiments are utilized to train advanced classifiers. This polarity correction strategy enhances performance across various product review categories, surpassing baseline models that lack such correction. Experimental evaluations demonstrate an average F-measure of 82% across four distinct product review domains.

We introduce the multiplicative recurrent neural network as a comprehensive framework for modeling compositional meaning in language and assess its effectiveness in fine-grained sentiment analysis. By establishing a link to earlier matrix-space models for compositionality, we demonstrate that these models are specific instances of the broader multiplicative recurrent network. Our experimental results indicate that these models perform on par with or surpass Elman-type additive recurrent neural networks and outperform matrix-space models on a well-known sentiment analysis dataset. Additionally, they deliver comparable performance to structural deep models on the newly released Stanford Sentiment Treebank, all without requiring the construction of parse trees.

Data privacy is a critical concern for embodied agents capable of perceiving their surroundings, communicating with humans, and operating in real-world settings. While assisting humans with various tasks, these agents may access and process sensitive information, including household layouts and individual activities. In this study, we present a privacy-preserving approach to embodied agent learning for Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN), where an agent navigates indoor environments based on natural language instructions. We treat each house as a local client that only shares local updates with a central cloud server and other clients, without revealing raw data. To safeguard privacy during both training and initial exploration phases, we introduce a novel federated vision-and-language navigation (FedVLN) framework. Specifically, we design a decentralized training method that confines each client’s data to local model updates, and a federated pre-exploration technique that performs partial model aggregation to enhance the model’s ability to handle unseen environments. Extensive experiments on the R2R and RxR datasets demonstrate that our FedVLN framework enables decentralized VLN models to achieve performance comparable to centralized training while maintaining privacy of observed environments. Moreover, federated pre-exploration significantly surpasses centralized pre-exploration results, all while safeguarding the privacy of unseen environments.

Gaussian variational approximation is a widely used approach for estimating posterior distributions in Bayesian inference, particularly in high-dimensional and large-scale data scenarios. To balance computational efficiency with the ability to model variable correlations, previous research has introduced a low-rank plus diagonal structure for the Gaussian covariance matrix. For specific Bayesian learning problems, ensuring the uniqueness of the solution often involves imposing strict constraints on the parameterized covariance matrix, which can lead to issues during optimization. In this paper, we address this challenge by exploring two specialized covariance structures constrained by the Stiefel and Grassmann manifolds, respectively, to facilitate the optimization process within these factorization frameworks. To accelerate updates with minimal hyperparameter tuning, we develop two novel Riemannian stochastic gradient descent algorithms and compare their performance with existing manifold optimization techniques. Besides resolving the identification problem, our simulation and empirical results demonstrate that the proposed methods achieve competitive accuracy and comparable convergence speeds in both high-dimensional and large-scale learning tasks.

ABC-Boost is a recent family of boosting algorithms designed for multi-class classification, leveraging the widely used sum-to-zero constraint. Implementing ABC-Boost requires selecting a base class at each boosting iteration. Previous approaches relied on an exhaustive search method to determine the base class, which proved to be computationally expensive. Despite demonstrating strong performance across various datasets with implementations like ABC-Mart and ABC-LogitBoost, the exhaustive search becomes impractical for large-scale data. To address this issue, this paper introduces a heuristic that incorporates Gaps when selecting the base class during training. Specifically, instead of updating the base class at every step, it is only revised every G boosting iterations (with G=1 corresponding to prior methods). We evaluate this approach on large datasets such as Covertype and Poker, as well as on moderate-sized datasets. The preliminary results are very promising: even with G=100 or higher, there is virtually no reduction in test accuracy on large datasets, and on moderate datasets, accuracy remains stable when G is between 20 and 50. With this heuristic, ABC-Boost shows great potential as a practical and effective tool for accurate multi-class classification.

Currently, many scientific and industrial domains face a growing demand for estimating treatment effects and resolving causal inquiries. Central to addressing these challenges is the abundance of observational data and effective methods for utilizing it. In this paper, we introduce a novel neural network-based model designed to predict potential outcomes and propensity scores. Our approach leverages not only covariates but also the outcomes of neighboring instances within the training dataset. Experimental results demonstrate that our model outperforms existing leading methods in accurately estimating treatment effects.

Pauli spin blockade (PSB) serves as a valuable tool for initializing and reading out spin qubits, even at higher temperatures, though its identification can be challenging. In this work, we introduce a machine learning algorithm designed to automatically detect PSB from charge transport measurements. To overcome the limited availability of experimental PSB data, the algorithm is trained on simulated datasets and validated across multiple devices. We applied this method to a silicon field-effect transistor and achieved an accuracy of 96% on various test devices, demonstrating its robustness against device-to-device variations. This approach holds promise for broad application across diverse quantum dot systems.

This paper addresses fairness concerns in unsupervised outlier detection. Conventional algorithms, lacking explicit fairness considerations, may unintentionally embed and perpetuate statistical biases present in data, leading to societal issues. To mitigate such unfairness and provide a fair set of potential outliers, we introduce Deep Clustering based Fair Outlier Detection (DCFOD). This approach aims to learn effective representations that maximize utility while ensuring the learned features are invariant across sensitive attribute subgroups. Recognizing the intertwined relationship between clustering and outlier detection, our method employs deep clustering to uncover the underlying cluster structure and identify outliers. Simultaneously, adversarial training is used to remove sensitive attribute patterns, promoting fairness. Technically, we develop an instance-level weighted representation learning strategy that enhances the integration of deep clustering and outlier detection. A dynamic weight module emphasizes the importance of probable inliers and reduces the influence of outliers. Extensive experiments on eight datasets, benchmarking against 17 outlier detection methods, demonstrate that our DCFOD consistently outperforms others in both outlier detection accuracy and fairness measures.

This letter presents our preliminary work on employing deep neural networks (DNNs) for the identification of wireless communication scenarios within multi-path fading channels. We have examined six different channel scenarios based on the COST 207 channel model. Our results show a 100% identification accuracy when the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) exceeds 20 dB, while an average accuracy of 88.4% was achieved across SNRs ranging from 0 dB to 40 dB. The proposed approach has been tested under fast time-varying conditions that closely mimic real-world wireless multi-path fading channels, demonstrating its practical feasibility for scenario identification in real-world applications.

Noisy labels are an unavoidable challenge in the machine learning community, often leading to degraded classifier performance by causing overfitting to incorrect labels. Traditional approaches to handle noisy labels typically modify the classifier during training, which presents two main limitations: firstly, they are not applicable to pre-trained classifiers without retraining; secondly, it is difficult to simultaneously train a classifier while mitigating the adverse effects of noisy labels. To address these issues, we introduce a novel approach called Noisy Prediction Calibration (NPC). This method employs a generative model to estimate a new transition matrix, enabling the correction of a pre-trained classifier's noisy predictions towards true labels through a post-processing step. We demonstrate that NPC is theoretically consistent with existing transition matrix-based methods and, empirically, it offers a more precise estimation of true labels even without retraining the classifier. Furthermore, NPC can be applied to any classifier trained with noisy labels, provided that the predictions and instances are accessible. Our experiments show that NPC significantly enhances classification accuracy across various baseline models on both synthetic and real-world datasets. The implementation code is available at https://github.com/BaeHeeSun/NPC.

This paper explores shape fitting challenges, $\epsilon$-coresets, and total sensitivity. Our focus is on the $(j,k)$-projective clustering problems, encompassing $k$-median/$k$-means, $k$-line clustering, $j$-subspace approximation, and the integer $(j,k)$-projective clustering problem. We establish upper bounds for the total sensitivities associated with these problems and leverage these bounds to construct $\epsilon$-coresets. By employing a dimension-reduction approach, we significantly streamline previous results concerning total sensitivity in $k$-median/$k$-means clustering, and we develop positively-weighted $\epsilon$-coresets for various forms of the $(j,k)$-projective clustering problem. Additionally, we generalize earlier findings on $\epsilon$-coresets for the integer $(j,k)$-projective clustering problem from fixed to high-dimensional settings.

The advent of big data collection and accessibility, combined with advancements in pre-trained models such as BERT and XLNET, has dramatically enhanced the predictive capabilities of modern natural language processing tasks, including text classification and generation. This progress enables organizations to offer machine learning as a service (MLaaS) by providing APIs built on fine-tuned BERT-based models. Nonetheless, these APIs have been found to carry various security and privacy risks. Previous research has highlighted vulnerabilities related to adversarial examples that exploit the security flaws of BERT-based APIs via model extraction. However, the privacy leakage risks associated with these extracted models have received less attention. Additionally, given the high capacity of BERT-based APIs, fine-tuned models are prone to overfitting, raising concerns about what sensitive information might be inferred from the extracted models—an area that remains largely unexplored. In this paper, we address these issues by introducing a practical model extraction attack that allows an adversary to steal a BERT-based API (the target or victim model) with only a limited number of queries. We also propose an attribute inference attack capable of uncovering sensitive attributes from the training data used by these APIs. Our comprehensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of these methods.

Imitation learning facilitates high-fidelity, vision-based policy acquisition within highly detailed, photorealistic environments. Despite its advantages, this approach often depends on traditional discrete-time neural models and struggles to adapt to domain shifts because it overlooks the causal relationships between the agent and its environment. In this paper, we introduce a theoretical and experimental framework for learning causal representations through continuous-time neural networks, which offer advantages over their discrete-time counterparts. We test our approach in the domain of visual control for drones across a range of challenging tasks, including short- and long-term navigation, as well as pursuing static and moving objects within photorealistic settings. Our findings show that causal continuous-time deep models can achieve robust navigation performance, outperforming advanced recurrent models that often fail in these scenarios. These models learn intricate causal control representations directly from raw visual data and are capable of scaling to a variety of tasks through imitation learning.

A key goal of Artificial Intelligence is to develop learning algorithms capable of running on general-purpose computing systems like the human brain. The Neural Turing Machine (NTM) represents a significant step toward creating such a versatile computational device. This paper presents a systematic review of the NTM. It begins with an overview of the mind-map and taxonomy of machine learning, neural networks, and Turing machines. Subsequently, it examines the NTM in detail, covering its concepts, architecture, various versions, applications, and comparative analyses. Finally, the discussion addresses existing challenges and outlines potential directions for future research.

The transferability of adversarial attacks from one model (the surrogate) to another (the victim) has long been a concern within the machine learning community. Demonstrating the ability to bypass unseen models with ease highlights the potential risks associated with adversarial exploits. In this study, we observe that current transfer attack research grants attackers an unrealistic advantage: access to the exact same training data as the victim. We introduce the first investigation into adversarial attack transferability under more realistic conditions, where neither the attacker nor the victim queries each other, and their available data may only partially overlap—either in the data used or in the classes learned. This threat model is particularly pertinent to fields such as medicine and malware detection. Under these circumstances, the success rate of attacks does not follow the expected pattern based on data or class overlap and varies depending on the dataset. This unpredictability complicates the reasoning of both attackers and defenders, thereby enriching the broader understanding of model robustness and security. Advances in affordable, high-performance IoT systems have made edge computing—processing data locally at the source—an increasingly practical approach. By reducing reliance on extensive network infrastructure and decreasing latency between edge devices and cloud servers, edge computing is especially vital for mission-critical applications. This paper examines the feasibility of image classification on IoT devices and evaluates its performance. We analyze how various factors—such as dataset size, image resolution, algorithm type and stage, and hardware specifications—impact energy consumption during image classification. Our findings reveal a strong, positive linear correlation between energy use and three key predictors: model complexity, image resolution, and dataset size. To facilitate energy consumption prediction for edge devices engaged in image classification, we explore three machine learning models—linear regression, Gaussian process, and random forests—using data from our experiments. We compare their accuracy and trade-offs, confirming that the random forest model provides the best performance, achieving R-squared values of 0.95 and 0.79 across different validation scenarios.

Knitting is a highly effective method for creating intricate three-dimensional surfaces, thanks to the inherent flexibility of interlaced yarns and recent manufacturing advancements that enable precise control of local stitch patterns. However, fully modeling knitted membranes at the yarn level is impractical for large-scale structures. To address this, we adopt a two-scale homogenization strategy, representing the membrane as a Kirchhoff-Love shell at the macro level and as Euler-Bernoulli rods at the micro level. Both the shell and rod governing equations are discretized using cubic B-spline basis functions. Our homogenization approach focuses solely on the in-plane response of the membrane. 

Solving the nonlinear microscale problem—especially considering large deformations and contact constraints—is computationally intensive and not feasible for online applications using traditional methods. To overcome this, we employ a pre-trained Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) model that quickly maps macroscale deformations to stresses. During the offline training phase, the GPR model is developed by solving the microscale problem across a comprehensive set of deformation states, sampled either uniformly or via Sobol sequences. This trained model captures the microscale's nonlinearities and anisotropic behaviors, effectively serving as a material model that predicts the membrane's response.

Some data types are only partially separable, which makes classification particularly challenging. In other words, only certain portions of the data contain useful information, while the rest do not provide any meaningful clues for distinguishing between classes. This renders the common assumption that the entire labeled dataset uniformly contributes to classification ineffective. As a result, traditional classification methods that rely on this assumption often fail under such conditions. In this research, we introduce a novel framework designed to address the classification of partially separable data types that are not amenable to standard approaches. We also propose an algorithm based on this framework, which employs an iterative clustering process to identify separable subgroups within the data. These identified subgroups are then utilized to improve classification accuracy. The effectiveness of our approach was demonstrated through experiments on a real dataset for autism screening, where it successfully distinguished children with autism from typically developing children, outperforming other methods that were unable to achieve similar results.

Human decision-making behavior exhibits considerable variability. In numerous games, individuals on average do not achieve optimal payoffs, and even after many rounds, the behavior of individual players remains heterogeneous. For example, in repeated prisoner’s dilemma games, humans often do not maximize their average rewards and display a wide range of cooperative tendencies. The underlying causes of these suboptimal outcomes are not fully understood. In this study, we demonstrate that the dynamics driven by a tendency to favor previously rewarding choices—interacting with the opponent's strategy—can account for systematic deviations from 'rationality' and also explain the diversity observed in decision behaviors. We specifically examine how choice probabilities evolve in prisoner’s dilemma scenarios where opponents employ strategies with varying levels of extortion and generosity. Our findings show that a straightforward model of human learning can capture a surprisingly broad spectrum of decision-making patterns. It successfully explains reduced cooperation in response to extortionate opponents, increased cooperation when facing generous ones, and the wide distributions of choices among players. Additionally, it predicts how individual cooperation rates change over the course of the game. We conclude that these dynamics are crucial for understanding significant aspects of human strategic behavior.

Many deep reinforcement learning algorithms incorporate inductive biases that shape the agent's objectives and its interaction with the environment. These biases manifest in various forms, such as domain knowledge and pre-tuned hyperparameters. Generally, there exists a trade-off between versatility and performance: stronger biases can accelerate learning, while weaker biases tend to foster more flexible, general algorithms. This balance is crucial because integrating such biases is not without cost—significant effort may be needed to acquire relevant domain insights or to fine-tune hyperparameters effectively. In this study, we revisit several domain-specific elements that influence the agent’s objectives and environmental interactions in typical deep reinforcement learning systems. We assess whether substituting these components with adaptive, literature-based solutions impacts performance. Our experiments reveal that, in some cases, replacing domain-specific components with adaptive alternatives results in performance declines, as expected when comparing handcrafted to more generic components. However, in other instances, adaptive solutions outperform the traditional ones. To evaluate the advantage of reducing domain-specific dependencies, we compare the learning efficiency of both systems across a different set of continuous control tasks, without further tuning. As anticipated, the system utilizing adaptive components demonstrated superior performance on

This paper addresses the challenge of modeling both narrowband and wideband speech using a unified acoustic model (AM), referred to as a mixed bandwidth AM. Our approach incorporates an auxiliary input feature that encodes bandwidth information, with bandwidth embeddings learned concurrently during acoustic model training. Experimental results demonstrate that integrating bandwidth embeddings enables the model to effectively manage the variability between narrow and wideband speech, facilitating the development of a single, robust mixed-bandwidth AM. Additionally, we introduce the use of parallel convolutional layers, each dedicated to handling either narrowband or wideband input, to better mitigate the mismatch between the two types of speech signals. The resulting system achieves a 13% relative improvement in performance on narrowband speech without any loss in accuracy for wideband speech.

We analyze an online learning-to-rank scenario where, at each iteration, an oblivious adversary presents a list of \( m \) documents related to a query, and the learner assigns scores to order these documents. Subsequently, the adversary reveals a relevance vector, and the learner updates its ranking model based on the feedback received. In this setup, feedback is limited to the relevance levels of only the top \( k \) documents in the ranked list, with \( k \ll m \). Despite this restricted feedback, the learner's performance is evaluated against the complete relevance vectors using an appropriate learning-to-rank loss function. We develop efficient algorithms tailored to well-known losses within the pointwise, pairwise, and listwise categories. Additionally, we establish that no online algorithm can achieve sublinear regret with top-1 feedback for any loss function calibrated to NDCG. Our algorithms are tested on benchmark datasets, demonstrating effective online learning of ranking functions under highly limited feedback conditions.

To address the rapid growth of state-of-the-art machine learning models—largely driven by the empirical benefits of over-parameterization—and to meet the need for fast, efficient, and privacy-preserving on-device models on resource-limited platforms, the research community has prioritized techniques such as pruning, quantization, and distillation for model compression. Aiming to streamline the adoption of a unified interface for neural network pruning in PyTorch, this work introduces the recent addition of the torch.nn.utils.prune module. This open-source module offers common pruning functionalities designed to lower the technical barriers to reducing model size and capacity at various stages—before, during, or after training. We detail the module’s user interface, explain implementation specifics, showcase example applications, and propose strategies for extending its capabilities to incorporate new pruning methods.

Analytical performance models play a crucial role in maintaining desirable service quality and deployment costs across varying conditions and workloads. Although prior research has introduced several models for traditional cloud computing paradigms, there is a noticeable gap in such models for serverless computing that can offer developers concrete performance guarantees. Additionally, most current serverless platforms still depend on developers manually specifying deployment configurations that influence both performance and cost, often without providing real-time or direct feedback. In our previous work, we developed performance models for steady-state and transient analysis of scale-per-request serverless platforms like AWS Lambda, Azure Functions, and Google Cloud Functions, enabling developers to receive immediate insights into service quality and costs. Building on this foundation, our current work focuses on creating analytical performance models tailored to modern serverless platforms that utilize concurrency levels and request rates for autoscaling decisions—examples include Knative and Google Cloud Run (a managed Knative service by Google). These models aim to assist both developers and providers in accurately predicting the performance and cost outcomes of various deployment configurations, empowering more efficient and reliable serverless application management.

We developed a liver cancer prediction model utilizing machine learning algorithms trained on epidemiological data from over 55,000 individuals collected from 2014 to the present. The model achieved its highest performance with an AUC of 0.71. Additionally, we examined the model parameters to identify the most significant risk factors influencing the prediction.

Federated learning is a decentralized framework that trains a model across numerous devices while keeping data localized on each device. This approach encounters several system-related challenges, including (i) communication bottlenecks caused by the need for many devices to upload their local updates to a central parameter server, and (ii) scalability issues arising from the vast number of devices involved in the network. These system challenges, coupled with the statistical heterogeneity of data and privacy concerns, make the development of provably efficient federated learning methodologies a critical yet complex task. In this work, we introduce FedPAQ, a communication-efficient federated learning algorithm incorporating Periodic Averaging and Quantization. FedPAQ is built around three core components: (1) periodic averaging, where local models are updated on devices and only periodically synchronized with the server; (2) partial device participation, which involves a subset of devices contributing in each training round; and (3) quantized message passing, in which edge devices compress their updates before transmission to the server. These strategies effectively tackle communication and scalability issues inherent in federated learning. Furthermore, we establish that FedPAQ attains near-optimal theoretical performance for both strongly convex and non-convex loss functions, and we empirically validate the tradeoffs between communication and computation that our approach offers.

Deep networks trained on large-scale datasets can develop transferable features that facilitate learning across multiple tasks. As these deep features evolve from being broadly applicable to becoming more specialized within the network, a key challenge in multi-task learning is leveraging the underlying task relatedness embedded in parameter tensors to enhance feature transferability across task-specific layers. This paper introduces Multilinear Relationship Networks (MRN), which uncover task relationships using innovative tensor normal priors applied to the parameter tensors of various task-specific layers within deep convolutional networks. By simultaneously learning transferable features and the multilinear relationships among tasks and features, MRN effectively addresses the issues of negative transfer in feature layers and under-transfer in classifier layers. Experimental results demonstrate that MRN achieves state-of-the-art performance across three multi-task learning benchmarks.

Our goal is to automate molecule design based on specific chemical properties. Our key contributions include a streamlined method for generating chemically valid SMILES strings by integrating a novel context-free grammar with masking techniques, ensuring validity throughout the process. Additionally, we frame molecular property optimization as a reinforcement learning problem, employing a best-of-batch policy gradient approach within a Transformer architecture. This method requires significantly fewer model steps per atom compared to previous techniques, facilitating the creation of larger molecules and surpassing existing state-of-the-art benchmarks by a substantial margin. The combination of reinforcement learning with a tailored context-free grammar and masking to enforce non-local constraints is broadly applicable to optimizing graph structures where local and non-local constraints coexist.

Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) have been extensively utilized in natural language processing and have achieved remarkable success. Conventional RNNs typically process each token in a sentence uniformly and equally, which may overlook the intricate semantic structural information inherent in sentences—knowledge that is vital for understanding natural language. Since semantic structures, such as word dependency patterns, are not explicitly parameterized, effectively capturing and utilizing this structural information poses a significant challenge. In this paper, we introduce an enhanced version of RNN called Multi-Channel RNN (MC-RNN), designed to dynamically grasp and exploit local semantic structures. Specifically, MC-RNN comprises multiple channels, each representing a distinct local dependence pattern at any given moment. An attention mechanism is integrated to combine these patterns dynamically based on semantic context at each step. We further parameterize the structural information by adaptively selecting the most suitable connection structures among channels, enabling the model to effectively capture diverse local structures and dependence patterns within sentences. To demonstrate the effectiveness of MC-RNN, we perform comprehensive experiments across key natural language processing tasks, including neural machine translation, abstractive summarization, and language modeling. The results consistently show that MC-RNN significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art systems.

With the rise of conversational assistants such as Amazon Alexa and Google Now, dialogue systems are rapidly gaining popularity, particularly within industrial environments. These systems generally comprise a Spoken Language Understanding (SLU) component, which involves two primary tasks: Intent Classification (IC) and Slot Labeling (SL). Typically, these tasks are modeled jointly to optimize performance, but this approach often results in increased model complexity and opacity. 

In this study, we first develop a framework to modularize the joint IC-SL task, enhancing the transparency of the architecture. Next, we investigate various modeling paradigms—including self-attention, convolutional, and recurrent models—and provide a comprehensive large-scale analysis across two datasets. Building upon this framework, we introduce a novel class of 'label-recurrent' models that are inherently non-recurrent but incorporate a 10-dimensional representation of label history. Our results demonstrate that these models are highly interpretable, achieve significant accuracy improvements—over 30% error reduction in SL compared to state-of-the-art methods on the Snips dataset—and are computationally efficient, with inference times twice as fast and training times reduced by two-thirds to half relative to comparable recurrent models. This advancement offers a valuable edge for deployment in critical real-world applications.

Protein secondary structure serves as a vital link between the primary amino acid sequence and the three-dimensional (tertiary) conformation. Accurate prediction of the eight-state (Q8) protein secondary structure has become essential for understanding protein function and structure in bioinformatics. Recent advances in deep learning have significantly improved the accuracy of Q8 prediction, yet there remains considerable scope for further enhancement, particularly in the eight-state classification.

In this study, we introduce PS8-Net, a novel deep convolutional neural network designed to boost the precision of eight-class secondary structure prediction. The model's input comprises a meticulously crafted feature matrix that integrates sequence-based features and profile information. Central to our architecture is the PS8 module, which employs skip connections to effectively capture long-term dependencies from deeper layers, extract local context from earlier layers, and integrate global information—collectively improving the prediction process.

Our proposed PS8-Net achieves Q8 accuracies of 76.89%, 71.94%, 76.86%, and 75.26% on the benchmark datasets CullPdb6133, CB513, CASP10, and CASP11, respectively. This architecture efficiently models the interdependencies—both local and global—among amino acids, resulting in highly accurate secondary structure predictions across all classes.

Deploying machine learning models in high-stakes environments such as healthcare requires more than just high accuracy; considerations of fairness, robustness, and interpretability are equally critical. Generalized Additive Models (GAMs) are a well-established class of interpretable models frequently used in these sensitive settings. However, they often lack the differentiability and scalability features inherent to deep learning approaches. In this paper, we introduce the neural GAM (NODE-GAM) and neural GA$^2$M (NODE-GA$^2$M), which are designed to scale efficiently and outperform traditional GAMs on large datasets, all while maintaining a level of interpretability that surpasses many ensemble and deep learning models. We provide evidence that our models uncover meaningful patterns within the data. Additionally, we show that incorporating self-supervised pre-training enhances model accuracy—a benefit not achievable with non-differentiable GAMs.

Unlike other optimality measures such as function value, the problem of identifying near-stationary points in convex optimization has received limited attention. Even in deterministic settings, the most effective method (OGM-G, developed by Kim and Fessler in 2021) has only recently been introduced. In this paper, we systematically explore algorithmic strategies for finding near-stationary points in convex finite-sum problems. Our key contributions include several novel algorithmic developments: (1) a memory-efficient version of OGM-G derived through the performance estimation problem framework (Drori and Teboulle, 2014); (2) a new accelerated SVRG variant capable of achieving rapid convergence rates for both gradient norm and function value minimization; (3) an adaptively regularized accelerated SVRG method that does not depend on prior knowledge of initial constants and attains near-optimal complexity bounds. Emphasizing simplicity and practicality, these new schemes are designed to facilitate future research and application.

In knowledge distillation, since a single, all-powerful teacher network cannot address every problem, recent research has explored the use of multiple teacher networks for knowledge transfer. However, their effectiveness is sometimes limited because immature teachers may pass along incorrect knowledge to the student network. To address this issue and leverage the strengths of multiple networks, we propose dividing the networks into two groups: teachers and students. The student group consists of immature networks that need to learn from the teachers, while the teacher group includes the well-performing networks. Additionally, our online role-changing strategy allows the top-performing networks within the student group to be promoted to the teacher group at each iteration, and vice versa. After training the teacher group using the error images of the student group to enhance their knowledge, we successfully transfer the collective knowledge from the teacher group to the student group. Our method demonstrates superior performance on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, achieving high accuracy. We also validate the versatility of our approach across various backbone architectures, including ResNet, WRN, VGG, MobileNet, and ShuffleNet.
