By applying this unified data structure, we reframe the RTLMP prediction challenge as a video forecasting task. We develop a generative adversarial network (GAN)-based video prediction model to capture the spatial and temporal relationships within historical RTLMP data and generate predictions for the upcoming hour. To enhance forecast accuracy, an autoregressive moving average (ARMA) calibration technique is employed. Notably, our method relies solely on publicly available market data, circumventing the need for sensitive system topology, model parameters, or operational specifics. Through case studies utilizing data from ISO New England (ISO-NE) and the Southwest Power Pool (SPP), we demonstrate that our model effectively learns the spatio-temporal patterns of RTLMPs and delivers precise forecasts.

Multi-label learning has garnered significant interest within the machine learning community. The problem transformation approach, Binary Relevance, simplifies multi-label tasks by converting them into multiple single-label problems. Its popularity stems from its straightforward structure and computational efficiency. However, Binary Relevance overlooks the relationships between labels, which can complicate certain tasks. This paper introduces a novel multi-label learning algorithm that also accommodates single-label classification. Based on the traditional support vector machine framework, it modifies the single decision hyperplane into two parallel hyperplanes, resulting in the Multi-Label Parallel Support Vector Machine (MLPSVM). At the conclusion of the paper, MLPSVM is evaluated against other multi-label learning methods. Experimental results demonstrate that MLPSVM performs effectively across various datasets.

Nearest neighbor techniques have gained prominence in official statistics, particularly for imputation and statistical matching tasks; they are also central to machine learning, where numerous variants have been developed. The selection of an appropriate distance measure largely depends on the nature of the variables involved. Unfortunately, few options effectively accommodate mixed-type variables, a common scenario in official statistics. The most widely used distance for handling mixed data is based on the complement of Gower's similarity coefficient, valued for its bounded range between 0 and 1 and its ability to manage missing values. However, in its standard unweighted form, the contribution of individual variables to the overall Gower distance is often unbalanced due to the differing characteristics of the variables. This article aims to address these key limitations by proposing modifications to the calculation of distances for interval and ratio-scaled variables. Simple adjustments are introduced to mitigate the influence of outliers on the scaled Manhattan distance, while more advanced techniques leveraging kernel density estimation seek to balance the contributions of various variable types. The effectiveness of these proposed modifications is assessed through performance evaluations.

Dense anchor-based object proposal techniques for scene text detection are often employed to attain high recall, resulting in notable improvements in accuracy but at the cost of extensive computational resources during searching, regression, and classification. In this paper, we introduce an anchor selection-based region proposal network (AS-RPN) that utilizes effectively chosen anchors instead of densely packed ones to generate text proposals. The centers, scales, aspect ratios, and orientations of anchors are made learnable rather than fixed, which enhances recall while significantly reducing the number of anchors required. By integrating AS-RPN into the Faster R-CNN framework, the resulting AS-RPN-based Faster R-CNN achieves performance comparable to previous state-of-the-art text detection methods on standard benchmarks such as COCO-Text, ICDAR2013, ICDAR2015, and MSRA-TD500, using only a single scale and a single model (ResNet50) during testing.

Given multiple source domains, domain generalization seeks to develop a universal model that maintains strong performance on any unseen but related target domain. In this study, we concentrate on scenarios where domain shifts are present among the class-conditional distributions across different domains. Existing methods often lack robustness when the variations in these conditional distributions for the same class are substantial. To address this, we introduce an extension of distributional robust optimization tailored to the class-conditional domain generalization challenge. Our method focuses on maximizing the worst-case classifier performance over class-conditional distributions contained within a Wasserstein ball centered at the barycenter of the source conditional distributions. Additionally, we present an iterative algorithm to automatically determine the optimal radius of these Wasserstein balls. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed framework outperforms approaches that do not incorporate domain generalization when tested on unseen target domains.

Due to information asymmetry, identifying optimal policies for Decentralized Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (Dec-POMDPs) is challenging, with complexity increasing doubly exponentially as the horizon extends. This difficulty is amplified in multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) scenarios where transition probabilities, observation kernels, and reward functions are unknown. In response, we propose a comprehensive compression framework that employs approximate shared and private state representations, enabling the construction of decentralized policies. We analyze the optimality gap when implementing dynamic programming (DP) using these approximate states, relating it to the approximation error parameters and the remaining planning steps. When the compression is perfectly accurate (error-free), our DP reduces to the conventional approach found in existing research. Our framework encompasses and extends several methods previously introduced in the literature. The findings provide valuable insights for designing practical deep-MARL architectures under the "centralized training, decentralized execution" paradigm.

Given the extensive volume of research papers in deep learning, ensuring reproducibility and adopting existing work pose significant challenges, primarily due to the scarcity of open-source implementations provided by authors. Additionally, re-implementing research models in alternative frameworks is often complex and time-consuming. To overcome these obstacles, we introduce DLPaper2Code, an innovative and extensible solution designed to extract and interpret deep learning architecture diagrams and tables from research papers, transforming them into abstract computational graphs. These graphs are then automatically converted into executable source code in both Keras and Caffe in real-time. We also develop an arXiv-like platform where the automatically generated designs are publicly accessible for approximately 5,000 papers. Users can rate and modify these designs through an intuitive drag-and-drop interface, facilitating crowdsourced improvements. To validate our approach, we constructed a synthetic dataset comprising over 216,000 valid design visualizations generated via a carefully crafted grammar. Experiments with this dataset demonstrate that our framework achieves over 93% accuracy in extracting content from flow diagrams.

The signature is an infinite graded sequence of statistics that uniquely characterizes geometric rough paths, including those with bounded variation. This concept has been effectively utilized in machine learning, primarily in low-dimensional settings. However, in high-dimensional contexts, the truncated signature transform encounters exponential growth in the number of features, posing significant challenges. To address this issue, we introduce a novel neural network model inspired by Convolutional Neural Networks. Our approach efficiently reduces the feature dimension in a data-dependent manner. Empirical experiments are conducted to demonstrate the effectiveness of our model.

Almost all models used in machine learning for prediction do not perfectly capture reality. Consequently, most learning occurs under conditions of model misspecification. In this study, we introduce a novel analysis of the generalization ability of Bayesian model averaging in the presence of model misspecification and i.i.d. data, utilizing a new class of second-order PAC-Bayes bounds. Our analysis demonstrates, in clear and intuitive terms, that Bayesian model averaging yields suboptimal generalization when the model is misspecified. Therefore, we present strong theoretical evidence indicating that Bayesian methods are not ideal for learning predictive models unless the model class is perfectly aligned with reality. Leveraging these second-order PAC-Bayes bounds, we develop a new family of Bayesian-inspired algorithms that can be implemented as variational or ensemble methods. These algorithms produce a revised posterior distribution—distinct from the traditional Bayesian posterior—that leads to a posterior predictive distribution with improved generalization performance. Experiments with Bayesian neural networks reinforce these conclusions.

Large pre-trained language models have been employed to generate code, offering a versatile interface for translating natural language specifications into programs. However, these models frequently produce outputs that violate syntactic and semantic rules of the target language, restricting their practical applicability. In this paper, we introduce Synchromesh: a framework designed to significantly enhance the reliability of pre-trained models in code generation tasks. Synchromesh consists of two key components. First, it retrieves few-shot examples from a training repository using Target Similarity Tuning (TST), a novel approach for semantic example selection. TST learns to identify utterances that describe similar target programs, even when surface-level language features differ. Next, Synchromesh supplies these examples to a pre-trained language model and generates programs through Constrained Semantic Decoding (CSD), a general method for restricting outputs to valid programs within the target language. CSD employs constraints on partial outputs to facilitate the generation of correct, complete programs without requiring re-training or fine-tuning of the language model. We evaluate our approach by synthesizing code from natural language prompts using GPT-3 and Codex across three real-world languages: SQL queries, Vega-Lite visualizations, and SMCalFlow programs. These domains exhibit complex constraints, including syntax, scope, typing, and contextual logic, which CSD effectively enforces. Our results demonstrate...

We introduce a dataset comprising high-resolution images of 13 micro-PCBs, captured from various angles and orientations relative to the camera. Each image is annotated with labels for PCB type, rotation category, and perspective category. We detail the design and findings of experiments exploring different combinations of training rotations and perspectives, analyzing their effects on test accuracy. Additionally, we assess how effectively data augmentation techniques can simulate unseen rotations and perspectives during testing. All experiments employ convolutional neural networks (CNNs), both with and without homogeneous vector capsules (HVCs), to examine the capsules' capacity to better encode the equivariance of micro-PCB sub-components. Our results indicate that models integrated with HVCs—capable of capturing equivariance among sub-components—and trained on a diverse range of perspectives, yield the highest classification accuracy for micro-PCB data.

This paper introduces a differentiable linear quadratic Model Predictive Control (MPC) framework designed for safe imitation learning. The approach incorporates an infinite-horizon cost implemented via a terminal cost function derived from the discrete-time algebraic Riccati equation (DARE), ensuring that the resultant controller guarantees closed-loop stability. A key innovation is the analytical derivation of the derivative of the DARE solution, facilitating the application of differentiation-based learning techniques. Additionally, the framework features a structured MPC optimization process: an augmented Lagrangian method maintains feasibility during training while strictly adhering to state and input constraints, and a pre-stabilizing controller ensures the accuracy of both the MPC solutions and their derivatives at each iteration. The effectiveness of this framework is validated through a series of numerical experiments.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) are increasingly employed in critical safety applications where prediction reliability is essential. Despite their outstanding predictive performance, existing DNNs lack an inherent mechanism to quantify and propagate significant input data uncertainty—an especially important feature in safety-critical contexts. This uncertainty is often epistemic, stemming from various sources such as limited knowledge of the data generation process, measurement imprecision, ignorance, and insufficient understanding of underlying physical phenomena. While recent research has primarily addressed parameter uncertainty, approaches for comprehensive, end-to-end training of DNNs that incorporate epistemic input data uncertainty remain scarce and often tailored to specific problems. In this work, we introduce a gradient-based DNN framework, termed Deep Interval Neural Network (DINN), which can quantify both input and parameter uncertainties through interval analysis. We demonstrate the effectiveness of DINN on an air pollution dataset affected by sensor uncertainty, showing that it can provide accurate, bounded estimates despite uncertain inputs.

Quick Shift is a widely used algorithm for mode detection and clustering. In this work, we establish finite-sample guarantees for its statistical consistency in accurately identifying modes and recovering clusters under mild distributional conditions. Furthermore, we leverage these findings to develop a reliable modal regression method.

GANs are renowned for their effectiveness in producing realistic images. However, their application extends to the generation of tabular data as well. In this discussion, we will review recent research articles exploring the use of tabular GANs in practice. Our approach involves augmenting the training data with GAN-generated samples to align the training distribution more closely with the test distribution. We will compare the performance of models trained on the original training set, on the training set supplemented with GAN-generated data, and on data sampled through adversarial training. Our findings suggest that leveraging GANs can be a viable strategy, especially when there is a significant imbalance between training and test data distributions.

Iconography in art is the field that examines the visual elements within artworks to identify their motifs and themes, as well as to understand how these are depicted. This area of study is actively pursued for various purposes, including interpreting meaning, tracing the origins and dissemination of representations across different times and locations, and exploring influence among artists and artworks. With the rise of digital archives containing vast collections of art images, there is now an opportunity to leverage Computer Vision technologies to analyze these images on an unprecedented scale, thereby enhancing iconography research and education. In this paper, we introduce a new dataset of paintings specifically designed for iconography classification and present both quantitative and qualitative results from applying a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) classifier to determine the iconography of artworks. Our classifier demonstrates strong performance, achieving 71.17% precision, 70.89% recall, 70.25% F1-score, and an average precision of 72.73%, particularly in identifying saints within Christian religious paintings—a challenging task due to the visual similarities among certain classes. Qualitative analysis indicates that the CNN concentrates on traditional iconic motifs that define each saint’s depiction, effectively leveraging these features to make accurate classifications.

Distant supervision (DS) is an effective approach to expanding datasets for improving relation extraction (RE) models, though it often introduces significant label noise. Existing methods utilizing attention mechanisms, reinforcement learning, or generative adversarial networks (GANs) tend to function as black boxes, offering little insight into the sample selection process for DS and exhibiting limited stability across different domains. In contrast, this work introduces a novel, model-agnostic instance sampling technique for DS based on influence functions (IF), dubbed REIF. Our approach identifies beneficial and detrimental instances within each bag by leveraging IF, enabling dynamic and targeted instance sampling. We develop an efficient influence sampling algorithm that reduces computational complexity from $\mathcal{O}(mn)$ to $\mathcal{O}(1)$ and analyze its robustness relative to the sampling function. Extensive experiments demonstrate that simply selecting favorable instances during training with REIF surpasses several complex baseline models. Additionally, we show that REIF facilitates interpretable instance selection, enhancing transparency in the sampling process.

A robust and adaptable method for structured prediction involves embedding the objects to be predicted into a (potentially infinite-dimensional) feature space via output kernels, followed by solving a regression problem within this space. To obtain a prediction in the original domain, a pre-image problem is then solved. In this framework, the embedding—linked to the chosen loss function—is established before the learning process begins. In this paper, we introduce an approach that jointly learns a finite approximation of the output embedding alongside the regression function in the new feature space. This is achieved by utilizing prior information about the outputs and exploiting previously untapped unsupervised output data, both of which are often accessible in structured prediction tasks. We demonstrate that this structured predictor is a consistent estimator and establish a bound on its excess risk. Additionally, this innovative structured prediction method significantly reduces computational complexity compared to traditional output kernel techniques. Empirical evaluations across various structured prediction scenarios show that our approach is versatile and scalable to large datasets.

Traditional neural language models often produce generic responses lacking in coherence and emotional depth. To tackle this problem, we propose a syntactically constrained, bidirectional-asynchronous framework called Emotional Conversation Generation (E-SCBA). Our model incorporates pre-selected emotion and topic keywords into the decoding process asynchronously, contrasting with most existing methods that generate replies sequentially from the first to the last word. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach enhances reply diversity and significantly improves both logical consistency and emotional expression compared to baseline models.

In the era of data science and deep learning, over-parameterized models have garnered significant attention. Empirical evidence shows that although these models, such as deep neural networks, tend to overfit training data, they often maintain low testing errors and occasionally even surpass traditional algorithms designed to prevent overfitting. The primary aim of this work is to rigorously quantify the advantages of data interpolation within the framework of the nearest neighbors (NN) algorithm. Specifically, we examine a class of interpolated weighting schemes and meticulously analyze their asymptotic performance. Our findings uncover a U-shaped relationship between performance and the degree of data interpolation, demonstrating that a modest amount of interpolation can **strictly** enhance both prediction accuracy and statistical stability compared to the optimal un-interpolated $k$-nearest neighbors algorithm. This theoretical insight supports (and anticipates) the existence of a second U-shaped curve observed in the recently identified double descent phenomenon. It is important to note that our objective is not to advocate for the use of interpolated-NN methods, but rather to provide theoretical understanding of data interpolation driven by the phenomena discussed.

Personalized medicine, a healthcare approach tailored to an individual's unique characteristics, is becoming an increasingly prominent and promising field. A key objective in personalized medicine is to identify a subgroup of patients—based on baseline covariates—that derives greater benefit from a specific targeted treatment compared to alternative options. Currently, most subgroup identification methods focus solely on enhancing treatment effects within a subgroup, often overlooking the importance of subgroup size. However, clinically meaningful subgroup learning should aim to maximize the number of patients who can safely and effectively benefit from the preferred treatment. 

In this study, we introduce an optimal subgroup selection rule (SSR) designed to maximize the number of selected patients while ensuring the mean outcome meets a pre-specified threshold of clinical significance, such as a minimum average treatment effect. We establish two equivalent theoretical formulations of the optimal SSR based on a contrast function that characterizes the interaction between treatment and covariates in influencing outcomes. Additionally, we develop a Constrained Policy Tree Search Algorithm (CAPITAL) to identify the optimal SSR within the interpretable framework of decision trees. Our method is versatile, capable of incorporating multiple constraints to penalize the inclusion of patients with negative treatment effects, and adaptable to handle time-to-event data through a restricted approach.

Graph representation learning has gained significant attention due to its broad applications in link prediction, node classification, and recommendation systems. Most embedding techniques aim to maintain specific properties of the original graph within a low-dimensional space. However, real-world graphs often exhibit multiple complex characteristics that are challenging to capture with a single method. In this study, we introduce the concept of graph representation ensemble learning and propose a novel framework for effectively combining multiple graph embedding techniques. Our analysis explores both theoretical and empirical relationships among leading embedding methods. We evaluate our approach on node classification tasks across four real-world graphs and demonstrate that ensemble methods can outperform existing state-of-the-art techniques by up to 8% in macro-F1 score. Additionally, we highlight that our approach yields even greater improvements—up to 12%—for underrepresented classes, enhancing overall classification performance.

We establish a comprehensive framework to rigorously analyze the performance guarantees of the Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm and its variant, gradient EM. Our approach is structured in two stages: first, we examine these algorithms at the population level, assuming an infinite data limit, and then we extend our results to scenarios involving finite samples. Initially, we delineate the basin of attraction for any global maximizer of the population likelihood. This is achieved through an innovative perspective that models EM updates as a perturbed likelihood ascent process, and similarly, interprets gradient EM updates as a perturbed form of standard gradient ascent. Building on this foundation, we derive non-asymptotic bounds for the EM and gradient EM algorithms when operating with a finite dataset. Our theoretical insights are applied to three classic incomplete-data problems: mixtures of Gaussians, mixtures of regressions, and linear regression with covariates missing completely at random. In each case, our results guarantee that, starting from an appropriate initial point, a modest number of EM or gradient EM iterations will, with high probability, produce an estimate close to the maximum likelihood estimate within the statistical error margin. We also include simulation studies to illustrate our theoretical findings.

Spiking neural networks (SNNs) have attracted significant attention due to their energy-efficient nature; however, the absence of scalable training algorithms has limited their practical application in machine learning. To expand their usability, researchers have extensively explored converting deep neural networks into SNNs. Nonetheless, many existing methods have not fully leveraged the spatio-temporal dynamics inherent in SNNs, resulting in inefficiencies such as increased spike counts and higher inference delays. In this study, we introduce T2FSNN, a novel approach that incorporates time-to-first-spike coding into deep SNNs by employing a kernel-based dynamic threshold and dendritic mechanisms to address these limitations. Furthermore, we implement gradient-based optimization and early firing strategies to enhance the efficiency of T2FSNN. Our experimental results demonstrate that the proposed techniques significantly reduce inference latency and spike activity—by 78% and over 99%, respectively—compared to the current state-of-the-art burst coding method on CIFAR-100.

Recent observations have highlighted the over-smoothing phenomenon in Transformer-based models across both vision and language domains. However, prior research has not thoroughly explored the root causes of this issue. In this study, we approach the problem from a graph-theoretic perspective—an area where over-smoothing was initially identified and examined. Conceptually, the self-attention matrix can be interpreted as a normalized adjacency matrix of a corresponding graph. Building on this analogy, we conduct a theoretical analysis revealing that layer normalization significantly influences the onset of over-smoothing in Transformer models. Specifically, when the standard deviation in layer normalization becomes sufficiently large, the outputs of Transformer layers tend to converge toward a low-rank subspace, leading to excessive smoothing. To mitigate this effect, we propose hierarchical fusion strategies that adaptively combine representations from various layers, thereby enhancing output diversity. Extensive experiments across diverse datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our fusion approach in alleviating over-smoothing.

In this working notes paper, we detail the participation of the IBM Research AI (Almaden) team in the 2019 ImageCLEF VQA-Med challenge. The competition involved four question-answering tasks centered on radiology images. The complexity of the challenge was heightened by the variety of imaging modalities, organs, and disease types, coupled with a limited and imbalanced training dataset. To address these challenges, we developed a modular pipeline that leveraged transfer learning and multi-task learning techniques. Our efforts culminated in the creation of a novel model named the Supporting Facts Network (SFN), which fundamentally aims to utilize information from earlier tasks to enhance performance on more difficult subsequent tasks. This strategy resulted in a notable improvement in validation scores, with an 18-point increase in F-1 score. Ultimately, we submitted four entries to the competition and achieved a seventh-place ranking.

Text classifier predictions are frequently influenced by spurious correlations—such as the association of the term "Spielberg" with positively reviewed movies, despite the fact that the term itself does not inherently carry positive sentiment. In this paper, we introduce a method to differentiate between spurious and genuine correlations in text classification tasks. We formulate this as a supervised classification problem, employing features derived from treatment effect estimators to identify spurious versus authentic correlations. Thanks to the generic nature and low dimensionality of these features, our approach performs effectively even with limited training data and can be transferred across different domains. Experiments conducted on four datasets—covering sentiment analysis and toxicity detection—demonstrate that incorporating this method into feature selection enhances the robustness of classification, as evidenced by improved worst-case accuracy on samples influenced by spurious correlations.

We introduce an innovative approach to the Register Allocation problem by employing a multi-agent hierarchical Reinforcement Learning framework. Our method accurately formalizes the constraints specific to a given instruction-set architecture, guaranteeing that the generated code maintains semantic integrity. Additionally, we design a gRPC-based framework that offers a modular and efficient compiler interface for both training and inference processes. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that our solution either matches or surpasses the performance of LLVM register allocators on Intel x86 and ARM AArch64 platforms.

Reinforcement learning (RL) has been extensively explored for enhancing sequence-generation models. Nonetheless, traditional reward functions in RL often fail to sufficiently capture semantic nuances, leading to model biases. Additionally, sparse and delayed rewards hinder efficient exploration. To address these challenges, we introduce the concept of nested-Wasserstein distance for distributional semantic alignment. Building on this, we propose a novel nested-Wasserstein self-imitation learning framework that encourages the model to leverage previously high-reward sequences, fostering better exploration and more accurate semantic matching. Our approach can be viewed as an approximate form of proximal policy optimization within Wasserstein trust regions. Experimental results across various unconditional and conditional sequence-generation tasks consistently demonstrate that our method yields superior performance.

A hybrid approach leveraging deep learning for short-term load forecasting is introduced. This strategy features a novel tree-based ensemble method called Warm-start Gradient Tree Boosting (WGTB). Existing methods typically either combine submodels of a single type, which limits their ability to exploit the diverse statistical strengths of different inference models, or simply aggregate outputs from completely different models without fully harnessing ensemble potential. Drawing inspiration from the bias-variance trade-off, WGTB is designed to address the significant differences among various inference models in terms of accuracy, volatility, and linearity. The overall approach combines four distinct inference models with varying capacities. WGTB then ensembles their outputs through a warm-start procedure that blends bagging and boosting techniques, effectively reducing both bias and variance simultaneously. The strategy is validated using two real-world datasets from the State Grid Corporation of China, each at hourly resolution. Results confirm the effectiveness of this hybrid approach, which leverages the complementary statistical strengths of low-bias and low-variance inference models.

DeepTingle is a text prediction and classification system developed using the collected works of the acclaimed gay erotica author Chuck Tingle. Unlike everyday writing assistive tools—such as predictive text, translation, and grammar checkers—that are typically trained on broad, ostensibly neutral datasets, DeepTingle is built on a highly specific, internally coherent yet externally unconventional dataset. This approach allows us to highlight and challenge the norms embedded within data-driven creative and productivity tools. Since these tools essentially serve as extensions of our cognition into technology, it is crucial to scrutinize the underlying norms they carry and, by extension, shape within us. DeepTingle is implemented as a web application utilizing LSTM networks and GloVe word embeddings, built with JavaScript and Keras-JS.

Neural networks employed for multi-interaction trajectory reconstruction currently lack the capability to quantify the uncertainty in their predictions, a feature that would greatly enhance system analysis and understanding. In this study, we extend the Factorised Neural Relational Inference model to produce both mean and standard deviation estimates for each component of the phase space vector, enabling uncertainty modeling through an appropriate loss function. We explore various loss functions, incorporating concepts from convexification and Bayesian approaches. Our findings highlight the importance of the physical interpretability of variables when assessing uncertainty and reveal the presence of problematic local minima that pose challenges during training.

Every piece of natural language is crafted in a specific style, which emerges from a complex interplay of various stylistic elements such as formality indicators, emotional tone, metaphors, and more. Achieving a comprehensive understanding of a text necessitates considering these factors, as they interrelate and co-vary in intricate ways to shape the overall style. Exploring these co-occurrence patterns offers valuable insights into stylistic language, often referred to as cross-style language understanding. In this paper, we introduce the xSLUE benchmark corpus—a resource that integrates existing datasets and includes a newly collected dataset—to facilitate sentence-level cross-style language understanding and evaluation. The benchmark encompasses texts spanning 15 distinct styles, categorized into four overarching groups: figurative, personal, affective, and interpersonal. To ensure robust assessment, we also compile a diagnostic set in which all 15 styles are annotated on the same texts. Leveraging xSLUE, we demonstrate three compelling cross-style applications involving classification, correlation analysis, and generation. Firstly, a cross-style classifier trained concurrently on multiple styles outperforms classifiers trained on individual styles, enhancing overall accuracy. Secondly, our analysis reveals that certain styles tend to co-occur strongly within human-authored texts. Lastly, we observe that combining styles with contradictory characteristics tends to produce texts that are stylistically inconsistent. We believe that our benchmark and the insights from these case studies will significantly advance the field of stylistic language research.

Deep learning has emerged as the predominant approach for analyzing and interpreting whole-slide digital pathology images (WSIs). Traditionally, it is believed that tumor regions contain the most predictive information. In this study, we introduce an unsupervised clustering-based multiple-instance learning method and apply it to develop deep learning models for predicting gene mutations using WSIs from three cancer types within The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA): colorectal cancer (CRC), lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD), and head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC). Our results demonstrate that unsupervised clustering of image patches can effectively identify informative patches, exclude non-predictive areas, and significantly enhance mutation prediction accuracy across all three cancer types compared to methods that use entire WSIs without patch selection or models focusing solely on tumor regions. Furthermore, our approach surpasses two recently published baseline algorithms that also utilize unsupervised clustering to support model predictions. This clustering-driven mutation prediction technique enables the localization of spatial regions associated with specific gene mutations through probability scores, thereby revealing the heterogeneity of predicted genotypes within the tumor microenvironment. Importantly, our findings suggest that focusing exclusively on tumor regions may not always be the most effective strategy for selecting patches to predict gene mutations, highlighting the potential benefits of incorporating diverse tissue types.

This paper addresses the challenge of retrieving videos from an unlabeled gallery based on an unseen text query. In the absence of annotations within the target gallery, we leverage a related source gallery composed of video-caption pairs, despite the domain gap between these source videos and the target collection. We introduce the task of Unsupervised Domain Adaptation for Cross-modal Video Retrieval and present a new benchmark focused on fine-grained actions. Our proposed solution is an iterative domain alignment technique that utilizes pseudo-labeling of target videos and cross-domain ranking between source and target. This method effectively adapts the embedding space to the target gallery, consistently surpassing approaches that rely solely on source data, as well as marginal and conditional alignment strategies.

An increasing number of machine learning models are being deployed in high-stakes domains such as finance and healthcare. Although these models often deliver superior performance, many function as black boxes, making their decisions difficult to interpret. Consequently, researchers are actively developing methods to elucidate these opaque models. Post hoc explanation techniques, like LIME, rely on perturbations to interpret a model after it has been trained. However, such methods are known to suffer from significant instability, which undermines their reliability and diminishes user trust. In this paper, we introduce S-LIME, a novel approach that employs a hypothesis testing framework grounded in the central limit theorem to determine the optimal number of perturbation points needed to ensure stable explanations. We validate our method through experiments on both simulated and real-world datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness.

We introduce a decentralized "local2global" framework for graph representation learning, designed to enable scalable application of any embedding method. Our approach begins by partitioning the input graph into overlapping subgraphs, or "patches," and independently training local embeddings for each patch. Subsequently, these local representations are merged into a single, globally coherent embedding by estimating the optimal set of rigid transformations that align the local patches, leveraging their overlaps through a process known as group synchronization. A key advantage of the local2global method, compared to existing approaches, is that the patches are trained independently, eliminating the need for expensive parameter synchronization during distributed training. This trait makes local2global particularly suitable for large-scale industrial settings, where the input graph may be too large to fit entirely into memory and may be stored across multiple locations. Preliminary experiments on medium-sized datasets—containing up to approximately 7,000 nodes and 200,000 edges—show promising results, with graph reconstruction accuracy comparable to that of globally trained embeddings. Ongoing work aims to extend this evaluation to larger datasets and to apply the approach to downstream tasks such as node classification and link prediction.

Deep neural network performance declines when the feature distribution in the test environment (target domain) diverges from that of the training environment (source domain). To address this issue, test-time adaptation (TTA) enables a model to adapt to the target domain without requiring access to the source dataset during testing. However, most existing TTA approaches do not incorporate explicit feature distribution alignment between source and target domains, a key aspect of unsupervised domain adaptation, because direct access to source data is not permitted in TTA settings. 

In this paper, we introduce a novel TTA technique called Covariance-Aware Feature Alignment (CAFe), which explicitly aligns source and target feature distributions during testing. CAFe achieves this without accessing source data by leveraging auxiliary feature statistics—specifically, mean and covariance matrices—pre-computed from the source domain, which are lightweight and straightforward to obtain. To enhance computational efficiency and stability, we further propose feature grouping, which partitions feature dimensions into groups based on their correlations using spectral clustering. This approach prevents covariance matrix degeneration and promotes robust alignment.

Empirical results demonstrate that CAFe significantly outperforms existing TTA methods across various scenarios involving distribution shifts.

In this expository note, we highlight an unexpected phenomenon in overparameterized linear regression, where the number of features exceeds the number of data points: there exists a regime in which increasing the number of samples leads to higher test risk for the estimator obtained via gradient descent. Essentially, more data can paradoxically impair the estimator’s performance. This counterintuitive behavior aligns with recent theoretical research on the "double-descent" phenomenon observed in linear models. Our focus is on a straightforward setting—linear regression with isotropic Gaussian covariates—to isolate and better understand this effect. It emerges from an unusual bias-variance tradeoff in the overparameterized regime: while the bias diminishes as more samples are added, the variance conversely grows.

Solving symbolic mathematics has traditionally been regarded as a domain requiring human ingenuity, involving compositional reasoning and recursive processes. However, recent research indicates that large-scale language models, such as transformers, possess a surprising universality: they can be trained as sequence-to-sequence models to tackle complex mathematical equations. These expansive transformer models typically demand vast amounts of training data to effectively generalize to unseen symbolic problems. In this paper, we propose a sample-efficient approach to address symbolic tasks by initially pretraining the transformer with language translation tasks, followed by fine-tuning on the specific symbolic mathematics challenges. Our method achieves comparable accuracy on integration tasks while requiring approximately 1.5 orders of magnitude fewer training samples than current state-of-the-art deep learning approaches for symbolic mathematics. Although the test accuracy on differential equation tasks is notably lower—due to the higher-order recursions involved that are not captured in language translation pretraining—our results vary when different language pairs are used for pretraining, revealing language biases in solving symbolic mathematics problems. Finally, we examine the robustness of the fine-tuned model under distribution shifts in symbolic math tasks, highlighting its resilience and limitations.

The process of diagnosing colorectal cancer primarily involves localizing and characterizing abnormal growths in the colon tissue, known as polyps. Despite recent advancements in deep object localization techniques, accurately identifying polyps remains difficult due to tissue similarities and the presence of numerous artifacts. Recent research has highlighted the detrimental effect of artifacts on polyp detection accuracy and has begun integrating artifact considerations into the training process. However, the potential of leveraging prior knowledge about the spatial interactions between polyps and artifacts has yet to be explored. In this study, we incorporate artifact information through a post-processing approach. Our method formulates this task as an inductive graph representation learning problem, consisting of both training and inference phases. Detected bounding boxes around polyps and artifacts are represented as nodes within a graph, connected based on a specific criterion. During training, we develop a node classifier trained with ground truth bounding boxes. During inference, this classifier analyzes a second, generated graph—constructed from predictions of polyps and artifacts produced by region proposal networks. We investigate how different connectivity schemes and artifact considerations influence our method’s performance and demonstrate that it significantly improves detection robustness.

Self-reinforcing feedback loops serve as both a cause and consequence of the over- or under-representation of certain content within interactive recommender systems. This dynamic results in inaccurate estimates of user preferences—specifically, an overestimation of frequently promoted content—and compromises the fairness of the system, which we define as providing each alternative with an equal opportunity to be presented. We analyze two models: one that explicitly accounts for, and another that neglects, the systematic and limited exposure to different options. Through simulations, we show that failing to consider these exposure limitations leads to an overestimation of promoted items and an underestimation of censored alternatives. Addressing this issue by conditioning on the actual limited exposure effectively corrects these biases.

We explore the challenge of truth discovery from opinions provided by multiple agents who may exhibit unreliability or bias. Our approach accounts for the possibility that agents’ reliabilities or biases are interconnected within the same community—defined as a group of agents sharing similar viewpoints on a specific event. Importantly, an agent may belong to different communities for different events, and these community memberships are initially unknown. We integrate social network information into our truth discovery model and employ Laplace variational inference techniques to infer agents’ reliabilities, community memberships, and event truths. To handle large-scale social networks efficiently, we also introduce a stochastic variational inference method. Through simulations and real-world data experiments, we demonstrate that our methods outperform several existing inference techniques—such as majority voting, TruthFinder, AccuSim, the Confidence-Aware Truth Discovery approach, Bayesian Classifier Combination (BCC), and Community BCC—particularly in scenarios with sparse observations.

Split-Merge MCMC (Monte Carlo Markov Chain) is a fundamental and widely used variant of MCMC for scenarios where the state encompasses an unknown number of components. It is well established that current advanced split-merge MCMC techniques do not scale effectively. Achieving rapid mixing typically requires designing smart, informative proposals to lower rejection rates. However, all known sophisticated proposals involve costly computations to generate informative transitions, making each iteration prohibitively expensive for large-scale datasets. Conversely, computationally cheap but uninformative proposals, such as simple random split-merge methods, tend to result in extremely slow convergence. This inherent tradeoff between mixing speed and per-iteration cost appears difficult to overcome. 

In this paper, we identify a promising middle ground. We exploit certain unique properties of weighted MinHash, a popular Locality Sensitive Hashing (LSH) technique, to develop a new class of split-merge proposals. These proposals are substantially more informative than random sampling while remaining computationally efficient. Our approach achieves an improved balance between convergence speed and per-iteration cost. Consequently, our proposals are approximately six times faster than state-of-the-art sampling methods on two large real-world datasets, KDDCUP and PubMed, each containing several million data points.

We introduce CLSRIL-23, a self-supervised learning-based pre-trained model for audio that captures cross-lingual speech representations across 23 Indic languages from raw audio data. Built upon wav2vec 2.0, the model employs a contrastive task applied to masked latent speech features and jointly learns quantization of these features shared among all languages. During pretraining, we analyze the language-specific loss to assess the impact of monolingual versus multilingual training. The model's effectiveness is evaluated on various downstream speech recognition tasks, revealing that multilingual pretraining consistently outperforms monolingual approaches. This improvement manifests as better phonetic encoding of languages and enhanced task performance, with a 5% reduction in Word Error Rate (WER) and a 9.5% decrease in Character Error Rate (CER) observed during fine-tuning for Hindi. All related code and models are publicly available. CLSRIL-23 has been trained on approximately 10,000 hours of audio data across 23 languages, aiming to advance speech recognition research for low-resource Indic languages. We anticipate that this self-supervised methodology will drive the development of new state-of-the-art systems in the field.

Label space expansion for multi-label classification (MLC) is a technique that transforms original label vectors into higher-dimensional codes prior to training, and then decodes these predicted codes back into label vectors during testing. This approach has been shown to enhance the effectiveness of MLC algorithms when combined with standard error-correcting codes for encoding and decoding. However, such coding schemes can be complex to implement and may not readily accommodate common application demands, such as cost-sensitive MLC, which requires adaptation to varying evaluation metrics. In this study, we introduce a simpler coding scheme based on a reference pair of label vectors that naturally incorporates cost sensitivity. Our proposed cost-sensitive reference pair encoding (CSRPE) algorithm includes cluster-based encoding, weight-driven training, and voting-based decoding—all leveraging cost information. Additionally, we utilize the cost insights embedded within CSRPE’s code space to develop a novel active learning strategy for cost-sensitive MLC. Extensive experiments confirm that CSRPE outperforms state-of-the-art methods across various MLC evaluation criteria. The results also indicate that the CSRPE-based active learning approach surpasses existing active MLC algorithms and further validates the practical advantages of CSRPE.

Sparse R-CNN is a recent, robust baseline for object detection that employs set prediction using sparse, learnable proposal boxes and features. In this work, we enhance Sparse R-CNN through two dynamic strategies. First, the original Sparse R-CNN utilizes a one-to-one label assignment scheme, leveraging the Hungarian algorithm to match each ground truth with a single positive sample. However, this rigid one-to-one matching may not be optimal for aligning learned proposals with ground truths. To improve this, we introduce Dynamic Label Assignment (DLA), which utilizes an optimal transport algorithm to assign multiple positive samples during the iterative training process. This approach gradually relaxes the matching constraints across stages, as later stages generate more refined and accurate proposals. Second, during inference, the proposal boxes and features are fixed across different images, limiting adaptability. Inspired by dynamic convolution, we propose Dynamic Proposal Generation (DPG), which dynamically assembles multiple proposal experts to produce better initial proposals—both boxes and features—for subsequent training stages. DPG enables sample-dependent proposal generation during inference. Experiments show that our method, dubbed Dynamic Sparse R-CNN, significantly enhances detection performance over the original model.

End-to-end Speech Translation (ST) models offer several advantages over traditional cascaded systems combining Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) and text Machine Translation (MT), such as reduced inference latency and minimized error propagation. Nonetheless, their performance is often constrained by limited training data, as collecting extensive parallel speech and translation transcripts poses significant challenges. Previous research has explored leveraging pre-trained components and multi-task learning to make use of weakly supervised data, including speech-to-transcript or text-to-foreign-text pairs. In this paper, we show that employing pre-trained MT or text-to-speech (TTS) synthesis models to transform weakly supervised datasets into speech-to-translation pairs can outperform multi-task learning approaches. Additionally, we demonstrate that a high-quality end-to-end ST model can be developed solely from weakly supervised data, utilizing synthetic data generated from unlabeled monolingual text or speech to enhance performance. We also address strategies to prevent overfitting to synthetic speech, supported by a detailed quantitative ablation study.

We train multi-task autoencoders on various linguistic tasks and examine the resulting hidden sentence representations. The representations undergo notable changes when translation and part-of-speech decoders are incorporated. As the number of decoders increases, the model produces more accurate clustering of sentences based on their syntactic similarity, indicating a reduction in entanglement within the representation space. To further investigate this space, we perform interpolations between sentences, resulting in intriguing pseudo-English sentences, many exhibiting recognizable syntactic structures. Finally, we highlight a fascinating characteristic of our models: the difference vector between two sentences can be added to a third sentence with similar features, effectively transforming it in a meaningful way.

Hyperbolic spaces are particularly well-suited for representing data with inherent hierarchical structures, such as tree-like datasets. However, it is often essential to align different, yet related, representations in a meaningful way. This alignment is a significant challenge in machine learning, with applications including ontology matching and cross-lingual alignment. Optimal transport (OT) methods are a natural solution for this problem, as they aim to find a transformation that maps one dataset onto another while respecting distribution constraints. In this work, we introduce a novel approach that utilizes OT on embeddings within the Poincaré model of hyperbolic spaces. Our technique leverages the gyrobarycenter mapping in Möbius gyrovector spaces. This formalism enables us to extend existing Euclidean OT-based domain adaptation methods to their hyperbolic equivalents. Empirical results demonstrate that both Euclidean and hyperbolic approaches achieve comparable performance in retrieval tasks.

Source code (Context) and its parsed abstract syntax tree (AST; Structure) are two essential, complementary representations of the same software program. Historically, machine learning model developers have primarily focused on either Structure or Context alone. We introduce a novel approach that simultaneously leverages both the Context and Structure of source code during training. Unlike previous methods, our model relies solely on language-agnostic features—namely, raw source code and attributes derived directly from the AST. This approach achieves state-of-the-art results in monolingual code summarization across five programming languages examined in this study. Additionally, we present the first multilingual code summarization model. Our findings demonstrate that training jointly on non-parallel data spanning multiple programming languages enhances performance across all individual languages, with the most significant improvements observed in low-resource languages. Notably, training on Context alone does not yield similar benefits, underscoring the importance of integrating both Structure and Context for effective code representation learning.

Meta-learning focuses on optimizing the hyperparameters of a model class or training algorithm by observing data from multiple related tasks. Building on Baxter's framework [1], we assume these tasks originate from the same task environment, characterized by a distribution over tasks and individual data distributions for each task. The statistical properties of this environment determine the degree of similarity among tasks. The objective of the meta-learner is to select hyperparameters that minimize the expected loss when training on a new task sampled from this environment. The difference between this expected loss, called the meta-population loss, and the empirical loss computed from the observed data of related tasks, known as the meta-generalization gap, serves as a measure of the meta-learner's ability to generalize. In this work, we introduce new information-theoretic bounds on the expected absolute value of the meta-generalization gap. Unlike previous approaches [2], our bounds explicitly account for the influence of task relatedness, the number of tasks, and the sample size per task. We quantify task similarity through the Kullback-Leibler (KL) and Jensen-Shannon (JS) divergences and demonstrate the effectiveness of our bounds through illustrative examples.

Person Re-Identification (Re-ID) plays a crucial role in numerous video surveillance applications. However, developing discriminative features for Re-ID remains challenging due to significant variations in the image data, such as changing human poses, lighting conditions, and viewpoints. In this paper, we introduce HAVANA, an innovative, lightweight, and extensible Hierarchical and Variation-Normalized Autoencoder designed to learn features resilient to intra-class differences. Unlike existing generative methods that attempt to eliminate variations through extensive supervised signals, HAVANA reduces intra-class discrepancies using a Variation-Normalized Autoencoder trained without additional supervision. We also propose a novel Jensen-Shannon triplet loss for effective contrastive distribution learning in Re-ID. Furthermore, we develop the Hierarchical Variation Distiller, a hierarchical Variational Autoencoder (VAE) that decomposes the latent space to explicitly model and factorize variations. To our knowledge, HAVANA is the first VAE-based framework specifically tailored for person ReID.

The effectiveness of deep machine learning in automatically delineating tumor regions has been proven for intraoperative neuronavigation through active IR-mapping utilizing the cold test. This method employs a matrix IR camera to remotely monitor the spatiotemporal distribution of surface temperature, which reflects the dynamics of local cerebral blood flow. Its advantages include being non-invasive, completely safe for both patients and medical personnel, cost-effective in terms of implementation and operation, and simple and quick to use. A significant limitation of traditional IR diagnostic techniques is the reliance on a diagnostician to define tumor boundaries, introducing substantial uncertainty and increasing the risk of diagnostic errors that are challenging to oversee. The present study demonstrates that integrating deep learning algorithms effectively addresses and eliminates this drawback.

Transfer learning offers a powerful strategy for developing predictive models that seamlessly integrate simulation and experimental data within a unified framework. This approach involves initially training a neural network on an extensive dataset of simulated results, followed by fine-tuning the model with limited experimental data to enhance its accuracy and alignment with real-world outcomes. Previously, this methodology has been applied to improve predictive models for Omega and NIF inertial confinement fusion (ICF) experiments, resulting in predictions that outperform pure simulations. In our current study, we simulate a hypothetical ICF campaign driven by transfer learning, aiming to maximize neutron yield through Bayesian optimization. The transfer learning model efficiently approaches within 5% of the theoretical maximum yield within a relatively small design space, achieving this in fewer than 20 experiments. Additionally, we show that this method outperforms conventional model calibration techniques traditionally used in ICF design, offering a more efficient pathway for optimizing experimental performance amid uncertainties.

Deep learning (DL) has become the leading approach for various medical image segmentation tasks, offering high accuracy and robustness. However, it typically relies on large quantities of manually annotated training data, which can be difficult or impossible to obtain in certain applications. Additionally, DL models often struggle with generalizing to new, out-of-sample data. Conversely, multi-atlas segmentation (MAS) achieves promising results with limited training data and exhibits strong generalizability. Integrating the precise capabilities of DL with the robust generalization of MAS into a hybrid approach is highly desirable, especially for segmentation challenges where manual labeling is scarce. Most existing research focuses on enhancing individual components of MAS using DL rather than developing a comprehensive end-to-end system aimed at improving overall segmentation accuracy. While one study has investigated this concept in binary 2D image segmentation, its applicability to multi-class 3D segmentation remains uncertain. In this work, we introduce a 3D end-to-end hybrid pipeline called Deep Label Fusion (DLF), designed to leverage the strengths of both MAS and DL. Experimental results demonstrate that DLF significantly outperforms traditional label fusion methods and the U-Net, a standard deep learning architecture, in segmenting the medial temporal region.

The Jacobian matrix (or the gradient in single-output networks) is intrinsically linked to key characteristics of neural networks, including the shape of the function landscape, the existence of stationary points, (local) Lipschitz constants, and robustness against adversarial perturbations. In this work, we introduce RecurJac, a recursive algorithm designed to efficiently compute both upper and lower bounds for each element of a neural network’s Jacobian with respect to its input, accommodating a wide variety of activation functions. As an added benefit, our method allows for the rapid estimation of a (local) Lipschitz constant, which is vital for verifying neural network robustness and ensuring stable training in generative adversarial networks (GANs). Experimental results demonstrate that the (local) Lipschitz constants derived through our approach surpass those obtained by previous methods, leading to more reliable robustness assessments. Our algorithm operates with polynomial time complexity, making it feasible to apply even to relatively large networks. Furthermore, by leveraging our Jacobian bounds, we can analyze the network’s landscape—such as identifying the presence of stationary points within a local vicinity. The source code is publicly available at \url{http://github.com/huanzhang12/RecurJac-Jacobian-bounds}.

Graph classification is a key area of research with numerous practical applications. However, in many real-world scenarios, the limited availability of labeled graphs hampers the training of robust models and increases the risk of overfitting. To tackle this challenge, we introduce two strategies leveraging contrastive self-supervised learning (CSSL) to reduce overfitting. The first strategy involves pretraining graph encoders with CSSL on abundant unlabeled graphs, eliminating the need for manual labels, followed by fine-tuning on labeled data. The second strategy incorporates a CSSL-based regularizer that enables simultaneous optimization of the supervised classification objective and the unsupervised CSSL task. For graph-based CSSL, we generate augmented versions of original graphs through a series of graph modification operations, creating new graphs from the original data. A contrastive loss function then guides the learning process by encouraging the encoder to recognize whether two augmented graphs originate from the same source graph. Experimental results across various graph classification benchmarks confirm the effectiveness of our proposed approaches.

Knowledge tracing (KT) models, such as the deep knowledge tracing (DKT) model, monitor a learner's skill development over time by analyzing their responses to related questions. However, a common limitation in many existing KT approaches is the assumption that all questions associated with a particular skill are equally indicative of the learner's ability, which does not accurately reflect real-world educational settings. To address this issue, we introduce qDKT, an enhanced version of DKT that predicts the probability of a learner answering each individual question correctly over time. First, qDKT employs graph Laplacian regularization to smooth predictions across questions within the same skill, which is especially effective when dealing with large question datasets. Second, it utilizes an initialization method inspired by the fastText algorithm, renowned for its success in various language modeling tasks. Our evaluations on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate that qDKT sets new state-of-the-art results in predicting learner performance. Consequently, qDKT serves as a straightforward yet robust baseline for developing future question-centric knowledge tracing models.

Mobile and embedded applications demand neural network-based pattern recognition systems that operate efficiently within strict computational constraints. Unlike traditional synchronous, frame-based vision systems and CNNs, asynchronous, spiking neural networks driven by event-based visual input offer low-latency responses to sparse, salient features, resulting in high runtime efficiency. However, the discrete, event-driven nature of the data poses challenges for directly training asynchronous neural networks. This paper explores the conversion of standard CNNs, trained on frame-based data, into asynchronous spiking neural networks. As a case study, we examine a CNN devised to guide a robot in following a moving target. We highlight potential issues during conversion and demonstrate how our proposed solutions reduce the classification accuracy gap to just 3% compared to the original synchronous CNN, while achieving a 12-fold reduction in computational load. Although tested on a simple task, this work marks a significant advancement toward low-power, rapid, and embedded neural network-based vision systems for robotics.

In most machine learning applications, we assess a model \( M \) on a dataset \( S \) by using a population-level metric \( F(S; M) \). Examples of such metrics include precision and recall for binary recognition, the F1 score for multi-class classification, and BLEU for language generation. Conversely, during training, the model \( M \) is optimized by minimizing a sample-specific loss \( G(S_t; M) \) at each training step \( t \), where \( S_t \) is a subset of \( S \) (often called a mini-batch). Common choices for \( G \) include cross-entropy loss, Dice loss, and sentence-level BLEU scores. A core assumption underlying this framework is that the average of the sample-level loss \( G \), taken over all possible samples, should serve as a good approximation of the population-level metric \( F \). In other words, \( \mathbb{E}[ G(S_t; M) ] \) is expected to be close to \( F(S; M) \). In this paper, we systematically examine this assumption across various NLP tasks. Our theoretical and experimental analyses reveal that some widely used sample-level loss functions \( G \) may be misaligned with the true population metric \( F \), leading to models trained to optimize \( G \) that are significantly suboptimal with respect to \( F \). We refer to this phenomenon as Simpson's bias, highlighting its deep roots in classical statistical principles.

Protein engineering aims to discover protein sequences with enhanced functionalities. Leveraging machine learning, protein sequence generation techniques can incorporate existing knowledge and experimental data to streamline this process. In this review, we spotlight recent advancements in applying machine learning to create protein sequences, with particular emphasis on the burgeoning area of deep generative approaches.

A novel message-passing (MP) approach is introduced for the matrix completion task in recommender systems. We model the problem using a (generative) factor graph framework linked to probabilistic low-rank matrix factorization. Building on this model, we present a new algorithm called IMP, designed to recover a data matrix from limited observed entries. IMP operates by first clustering the data and then performing inference through message passing. We evaluate its performance against several existing matrix completion methods using real-world collaborative filtering datasets, such as Netflix. Our findings indicate that, although many algorithms perform similarly when a large proportion of entries are known, IMP significantly outperforms others when the observed data is sparse. This advantage is especially valuable in addressing the cold-start problem commonly faced in collaborative filtering systems.

This paper addresses the challenge of large-scale multi-agent reinforcement learning. Initially, we examined the representation issue of the pairwise value function to mitigate the complexity arising from agent interactions. Next, we employed an L2-norm technique to ensure that the trivial component of the approximated value function remains bounded. Finally, our experimental results on a battle game validate the effectiveness of the proposed methodology.

Recent developments in deep learning have demonstrated notable success in medical image analysis; however, training these models typically requires extensive ground-truth annotations from human experts. Acquiring such annotations is often costly and limited, especially in medical imaging contexts. As a result, there is growing interest in developing methods that can learn from unlabeled raw data. In this study, we introduce a self-supervised learning strategy aimed at extracting rich and transferable representations from medical imaging videos without relying on any human-provided labels. Our approach is based on the premise that effective representation learning should enable the model to recognize anatomical structures within unlabeled data. To achieve this, we design anatomy-aware tasks that leverage the inherent information in the data itself, providing supervision without external annotations. Specifically, the model is tasked with restoring the correct sequence of a shuffled video clip and simultaneously predicting the geometric transformations applied to it. Experiments conducted on fetal ultrasound videos demonstrate that our method successfully learns meaningful and robust representations, which effectively transfer to downstream applications such as standard plane detection and saliency prediction.

Automated digitization of paper maps presents a complex and vital challenge for both researchers and industry professionals. As a crucial step in map digitization, semantic segmentation traditionally depends on manual visual interpretation, which is often time-consuming and inefficient. In this study, we focus on urban planning maps as a representative sample to explore the potential of employing a U-shaped fully convolutional neural network architecture for end-to-end map semantic segmentation. Experiments conducted on a test region in Tokyo’s Shibuya district show that our approach achieves a remarkable Jaccard similarity coefficient of 93.63% and an overall accuracy of 99.36%. When implemented on GPGPU platforms with cuDNN, the entire processing of the Shibuya district can be completed in less than three minutes. These results demonstrate that the proposed method is a highly accurate and efficient tool for urban planning map semantic segmentation, offering promising prospects for practical applications.

This paper primarily addresses the problem of personalized font generation through image style transfer. Its main goal is to develop a neural network framework capable of extracting and recombining the content and style of characters. This approach enables the synthesis of an entire font set using only a small number of sample characters. The study integrates various deep learning architectures, including Convolutional Neural Networks, Multi-layer Perceptrons, and Residual Networks, to identify the most effective model for capturing font character features. Experimental results demonstrate that the generated characters closely resemble real ones, as evidenced by evaluations using the Structural Similarity Index and Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio metrics.

Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) is a popular and effective technique for sampling from high-dimensional distributions in statistics and machine learning. Its second-order "leapfrog" algorithm has long been suspected to operate with complexity proportional to \(d^{1/4}\) gradient evaluations. In this work, we confirm this conjecture for strongly log-concave target distributions that meet a mild third-order regularity condition related to the input data. Our regularity criterion is less restrictive than the Lipschitz Hessian assumption, enabling us to derive faster convergence rates for a broader class of distributions than previously possible with the standard Lipschitz Hessian bound. Notably, key distributions satisfying our condition include posterior distributions in Bayesian logistic regression when the data exhibits an "incoherence" property. Compared to existing bounds, which generally scale as \(d^{1/2}\) gradient evaluations for strongly log-concave distributions, our results demonstrate a significant improvement. Additionally, simulations on synthetic datasets indicate that when the regularity condition holds, leapfrog HMC outperforms alternative methods in both accuracy and gradient evaluation efficiency.

Recent advances in Super-Resolution for medical imaging have leveraged deep learning techniques like Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to produce perceptually convincing single-image Super-Resolution. However, these methods typically struggle to adapt to different scale factors, requiring separate neural networks for each integer scale, which leads to high storage requirements and energy consumption. A recent study introduced a novel meta-learning approach utilizing a Weight Prediction Network, enabling Super-Resolution across arbitrary scale factors with a single neural network. In this work, we present a new model that integrates this meta-learning technique with SRGAN, a leading GAN-based architecture, to deliver high-fidelity, arbitrary-scale Super-Resolution tailored for medical images. Using our network to perform various magnifications on images from the Multimodal Brain Tumor Segmentation Challenge (BraTS) dataset, we demonstrate an improvement of up to 20% in SSIM scores over traditional interpolation methods, while maintaining strong generalizability to brain MRI images. Our results indicate consistent performance across different scales and competitive accuracy compared to state-of-the-art methods such as EDSR, with the added advantage of being fifty times smaller. Combining efficiency, robustness, and versatility, this approach has the potential to establish a new foundation for scalable, high-quality Super-Resolution in medical imaging.

The orthogonal Haar scattering transform is a deep neural network that is constructed through a hierarchy of simple operations such as additions, subtractions, and absolute values applied to pairs of coefficients. It offers a straightforward mathematical framework for unsupervised learning in deep networks. By implementing non-linear contractions tailored for classification, it uses an unsupervised pair-matching algorithm with polynomial complexity. When applied to graph data, a structured Haar scattering captures permutation-invariant representations of connected point groups. If the graph’s connectivity is unknown, unsupervised Haar pair learning can reliably estimate the connected dyadic groups of points. Experimental results demonstrate its effectiveness in classifying image datasets arranged on regular grids or graphs, regardless of whether the connectivity is known or needs to be inferred.

Normalization techniques are fundamental components of the deep learning toolkit, enhancing training speed and stability while reducing reliance on meticulously adjusted learning rate schedules. However, when dealing with multi-modal data distributions, the performance of batch normalization (BN)—arguably the most widely used normalization method—diminishes. To address this, we introduce a more versatile approach: by extending normalization beyond a single mean and variance, our method dynamically identifies modes within the data and normalizes samples that exhibit shared characteristics accordingly. Experimental results on various single-task and multi-task datasets demonstrate that our approach surpasses BN and other common normalization methods in effectiveness.

Variable screening serves as a rapid dimension reduction technique to aid high-dimensional feature selection. As an initial filtering step, it identifies a manageable subset of candidate variables for subsequent refinement through more precise feature selection, ultimately leading to the final model. The effectiveness of variable screening hinges on its computational speed and its capacity to significantly reduce the variable count without excluding key predictors. When the number of variables \( p \) substantially exceeds the sample size \( n \), variable screening becomes especially vital because: 1) Faster feature selection algorithms are required; 2) Conditions that ensure selection consistency may no longer be valid. This paper examines a class of linear screening methods and develops a consistency framework for these techniques. In particular, we demonstrate that the restricted diagonally dominant (RDD) condition is both necessary and sufficient for strong screening consistency. We provide concrete examples, showing that two methods—SIS and HOLP—are strongly screening consistent (under certain additional constraints) with high probability when \( n > O\left( (\rho s + \sigma / \tau)^2 \log p \right) \) under random design setups. Furthermore, we explore the relationship between the RDD condition and the irrepresentable condition, highlighting some limitations of SIS.

This study introduces PatchNet, an automated hierarchical deep learning tool designed to classify patches by analyzing features from commit messages and code modifications. Unlike existing deep learning models for source code, PatchNet employs a deep hierarchical architecture that reflects the inherent hierarchical and sequential nature of code changes. It offers multiple configurable parameters to customize the training process. The effectiveness of PatchNet was demonstrated through its application in automatically identifying stable-relevant patches within the Linux kernel, and it shows promise for automating other software engineering tasks involving patch classification.
