The findings suggest that AutoML models can indeed excel in complex classification scenarios, particularly in datasets characterized by less discriminative features, overlapping class distributions, or pronounced non-linearity. 

However, implementing AutoML in real-world phishing detection faces certain challenges. Currently, AutoML frameworks primarily support supervised classification tasks, requiring labeled datasets, which can be costly and time-consuming to produce. Additionally, these models lack the capability for incremental updates, posing limitations for adapting to evolving threats. This highlights that expertise in domain-specific knowledge remains crucial for addressing these challenges effectively.

We examine the challenge of reconstructing a partially observed high-rank matrix whose columns follow a nonlinear structure, such as a union of subspaces, an algebraic variety, or clustered groups. The problem is approached by formulating the recovery as a rank minimization of a nonlinear feature map applied to the original matrix, which we approximate through a constrained non-convex optimization framework on the Grassmann manifold. We introduce two algorithmic strategies: one based on Riemannian optimization and the other utilizing an alternating minimization approach, each with both first- and second-order variants. These algorithms come with rigorous theoretical guarantees; notably, for the alternating minimization method, we prove global convergence and establish worst-case complexity bounds. Furthermore, leveraging the Kurdyka-Lojasiewicz property, we demonstrate that the alternating minimization converges to a unique limit point. Extensive numerical experiments illustrate the effectiveness of our methods in recovering union of subspaces and clustering tasks under both entry sampling and dense Gaussian sampling scenarios. Our approaches are competitive with existing methods, with the Riemannian second-order algorithms achieving particularly high accuracy in matrix recovery.

We present an algorithm for completing an order-$m$ symmetric low-rank tensor from its multilinear entries, achieving a runtime approximately proportional to the total number of tensor entries. This tensor completion method is then utilized to address the problem of learning mixtures of product distributions over the hypercube, leading to novel algorithmic insights. When the centers of the product distribution are linearly independent, our approach enables the recovery of distributions with up to $\Omega(n)$ centers in polynomial time and with polynomial sample complexity. In the general scenario, we can recover distributions with up to $\tilde\Omega(n)$ centers within quasi-polynomial time, thereby resolving an open question posed by Feldman et al. (SIAM J. Comput.) for distributions characterized by incoherent bias vectors. The core of our algorithm relies on iteratively applying a low-rank matrix completion technique designed for matrices with adversarially missing entries.

Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) serve as aerial base stations that relay time-sensitive data packets from IoT devices to the nearby terrestrial base station (TBS). Efficient scheduling of these packets in UAV-relayed IoT networks is a complex challenge, as it involves two key steps: (i) sampling packets generated at IoT devices by UAVs (hop 1), and (ii) forwarding the sampled packets from UAVs to the TBS (hop 2). To address this, we introduce Age-of-Information (AoI) scheduling algorithms tailored for two-hop UAV-relayed IoT networks. 

Our first contribution is a low-complexity AoI scheduler named MAF-MAD, which combines the Maximum AoI First (MAF) policy for selecting IoT devices at the UAVs (hop 1) with the Maximum AoI Difference (MAD) policy for updating sampled packets to the TBS (hop 2). We demonstrate that MAF-MAD is optimal under ideal conditions, such as lossless wireless channels and generate-at-will traffic from IoT devices. 

For more realistic scenarios involving lossy channels and variable traffic patterns, we propose a deep reinforcement learning-based scheduler utilizing Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO). Simulation results indicate that this PPO-based scheduler consistently outperforms other approaches—including MAF-MAD, MAF, and round-robin—in diverse practical conditions.

Deep learning has revolutionized our ability to solve complex problems, achieving feats that were unimaginable just a few decades ago. However, alongside its numerous benefits, it also presents risks to society. One prominent issue is the rise of deep fakes—synthetic media that convincingly mimic real images or videos. With the advent of user-friendly smartphone applications, anyone can generate and distribute such false content, posing a serious threat to the integrity of online information. Although deep fakes produced by neural networks can appear indistinguishable from genuine media, they often leave subtle spatial and temporal signatures that can be detected upon analysis. These signatures, invisible to the human eye, can be identified using specialized neural networks trained for deep fake detection. In this paper, we examine several cutting-edge neural network models—namely MesoNet, ResNet-50, VGG-19, and Xception Net—and compare their effectiveness in identifying manipulated media to address this pressing challenge.

Effective weight initialization is essential for the successful training and rapid convergence of deep neural networks (DNNs). Traditionally, research in this area has concentrated on balancing the variance of weights within each layer to ensure stability in two key aspects: (i) the forward propagation of input data through the network and (ii) the backward propagation of loss gradients. However, this common heuristic overlooks the dependencies among gradients across different layers and primarily addresses only first-order effects. In this paper, we introduce a novel initialization strategy grounded in a comprehensive assessment of the overall curvature of the weight landscape across layers, achieved by estimating and regulating the norm of their Hessian matrix. Our method offers a more systematic approach and encompasses previous results related to DNN activation functions such as smooth activations, dropout, and ReLU. Experimental evaluations on Word2Vec and image classification benchmarks like MNIST and CIFAR demonstrate that monitoring the Hessian norm serves as a valuable diagnostic tool, enabling more precise and theoretically grounded weight initialization.

While various approaches are available to address specific types of distribution shift—such as label shift caused by adversarial attacks or domain shift—the problem of jointly addressing these shifts remains unsolved. In our investigation of a combined distribution shift involving both adversarial and domain-specific perturbations, we demonstrate that the joint shift leads to worse model performance than either shift alone. Additionally, we find that using a similar domain for training can impair performance more than utilizing a dissimilar domain. To mitigate this decline, we explore perturbation sets inspired by input and parameter space constraints and employ a meta-learning approach using hypernetworks to adapt model parameters based on test-time inputs, aiming to restore performance.

A crucial element of human intelligence is the ability to communicate knowledge concisely. Despite their predictive capabilities, many existing machine learning models function as black boxes, making it challenging for humans to extract meaningful insights. Focusing on sequential decision-making, we have developed a novel machine learning algorithm that presents insights to humans as clear, interpretable "tips." Our method selects the tip that most effectively narrows the performance gap between human users and the optimal policy. We assess our approach through a series of randomized controlled user studies in which participants manage a virtual kitchen. The results demonstrate that the tips generated by our algorithm can substantially enhance human performance compared to intuitive baseline strategies. Additionally, we share empirical findings that can guide the development of algorithms for human-AI interactions. For example, we observe that participants do not passively follow our tips; instead, they incorporate them with their own experience to uncover new strategies for improving their performance.

A significant challenge in deep learning is ensuring the privacy and security of neural networks (NNs). Historically, these concerns have been addressed independently. However, the relationship between privacy-preserving training techniques and model robustness remains poorly understood. This study experimentally investigates how training with Differential Privacy (DP), a common privacy protection method, influences a model's vulnerability to various adversarial attacks. The findings indicate that models trained with DP tend to be less robust than their non-private equivalents. Moreover, adversarial examples are more transferable between DP models than between private and non-private models. In-depth analysis reveals notable differences in gradients between DP and non-DP models. Importantly, this work is the first to identify that improper parameter selection in DP training can induce gradient masking, which may misleadingly suggest a false sense of security.

Society increasingly depends on algorithms such as classifiers for critical decision-making, underscoring the importance of ethical assurances like fairness. Fairness is often characterized by ensuring that certain statistics of a classifier remain approximately equal across protected groups within a population. This paper reviews existing fairness approaches and uses these insights to develop algorithmic strategies that embed fairness into genetic programming for classification tasks. We introduce two key ideas: first, integrating a fairness objective into a multi-objective optimization framework; second, modifying lexicase selection to dynamically define test cases over intersections of protected groups. We explain why lexicase selection is particularly suited to encouraging models to perform well across numerous subgroups—potentially infinitely many—over which fairness is sought. Using a recent genetic programming methodology, we construct models for four datasets where fairness constraints are crucial, and compare their performance against previous methods that employ game-theoretic solutions. Our evaluation focuses on the ability to produce Pareto-optimal trade-offs between subgroup fairness and accuracy. The results indicate that genetic programming approaches, especially random search techniques, are highly effective for this purpose.

We examine the notion that the act of writing can be viewed as an effort to maximize one's expected utility. To illustrate this concept concretely, we focus on the societally significant decisions made by the United States Supreme Court. Building on extensive prior research in quantitative political science, we establish a framework for empirically analyzing justices' decisions and their connection to the texts involved. Our model incorporates texts authored by amici curiae ("friends of the court" who are separate from the litigants) seeking to influence the ruling, and we explicitly represent their objectives within a random utility framework. We highlight the advantages of this methodology, including enhanced accuracy in predicting votes and the capacity to conduct counterfactual analyses.

Pathologist-defined labels are considered the gold standard for histopathological datasets, despite known issues with consistency in certain tasks. To date, several datasets documenting mitotic figures have been developed and utilized to train promising deep learning algorithms. However, evaluating the robustness of these algorithms and the reproducibility of their methods requires testing across multiple independent datasets. Currently, the impact of different labeling approaches across these datasets remains unclear. To address this, we introduce an alternative set of labels for the images within the auxiliary mitosis dataset from the TUPAC16 challenge. In addition to manual screening of mitotic figures, we employed a novel, algorithm-assisted labeling method designed to reduce the likelihood of missing rare mitotic figures. All candidate mitotic figures were independently reviewed by two pathologists. This new, publicly available label set includes 1,999 confirmed mitotic figures—representing a 28.80% increase—and encompasses 10,483 labels of cells with high similarity to mitotic figures, categorized as hard examples. Our analysis revealed a significant improvement in F₁ scores when comparing the original label set (0.549) to the new set (0.735) using a standard deep learning object detection model. Models trained on this alternative dataset demonstrated higher confidence levels, indicating enhanced detection performance.

Understanding the properties of large-scale graphs through sampling has long been a fundamental challenge in statistical network analysis, dating back to early pioneering efforts by Goodman \cite{Goodman1949} and Frank \cite{Frank1978}. In this work, we revisit a problem originally posed by Frank \cite{Frank1978}: estimating the number of connected components in a large graph using a subgraph sampling approach. In this method, a random subset of vertices is selected, and the induced subgraph is observed. The core question we explore is whether precise estimation is possible in the \emph{sublinear} regime, where only a negligible fraction of the vertices are sampled. We find that such estimation is impossible if the original graph permits high-degree vertices or contains long induced cycles. Conversely, for the class of chordal graphs—characterized by the absence of induced cycles of length four or more—we identify the optimal sample complexity within constant factors and develop linear-time estimators that meet these bounds with provable guarantees. This work broadens the scope beyond previous studies, which primarily focused on unbiased estimators and specific graph families like forests or cliques. Our approach hinges on the combinatorial properties inherent to chordal graphs and leverages identities related to induced subgraph counts. These elements are instrumental not only in constructing the estimators but also in their theoretical analysis, underpinning key proofs in our results.

Automatic speech recognition systems typically utilize spectral-based features such as Mel-Frequency Cepstral Coefficients (MFCC) or Perceptual Linear Prediction (PLP). These features are derived from prior knowledge related to speech perception and production. Recently, convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have demonstrated the ability to estimate phoneme conditional probabilities through a fully data-driven approach, directly using raw temporal speech signals as input. This approach has been shown to achieve comparable or superior performance to traditional HMM/ANN systems in phoneme recognition and large-scale continuous speech recognition tasks, while requiring fewer parameters. Building on these findings, we explore the implementation of a simple linear classifier within the CNN-based framework. In this setup, the network learns linearly separable features directly from raw speech. Our results indicate that such a system attains performance comparable to or better than that of multi-layer perceptron (MLP) systems utilizing cepstral-based features as input.

Computing approximate nearest neighbors in high-dimensional spaces is a fundamental challenge in large-scale data mining, with broad applications in machine learning and data science. One of the most effective and widely used techniques for approximate nearest neighbor search is locality-sensitive hashing (LSH). In this study, we focus on developing LSH schemes tailored for distance measures between probability distributions, specifically for f-divergences and their extensions to quantify mutual information loss. We first introduce a versatile framework for designing LSH schemes for f-divergence-based distance functions and construct specific schemes for the generalized Jensen-Shannon divergence and triangular discrimination within this framework. Additionally, we establish a two-sided approximation of the generalized Jensen-Shannon divergence using the Hellinger distance, which may have independent significance. Furthermore, we propose a general approach to reduce the task of creating LSH schemes for Krein kernels—which can be represented as the difference of two positive definite kernels—to the problem of maximum inner product search. We demonstrate this method by applying it to mutual information loss, highlighting its relevance in important areas such as model compression.

Representation learning for knowledge graphs (KGs) has traditionally focused on straightforward link prediction tasks. In this study, we tackle a more complex challenge: predicting answers to conjunctive queries containing multiple missing entities. We introduce Bi-Directional Query Embedding (BIQE), a novel approach that employs models based on bi-directional attention mechanisms to embed conjunctive queries. Unlike previous methods, our bidirectional self-attention captures interactions among all components of a query graph effectively. Additionally, we present a new dataset designed for conjunctive query answer prediction and demonstrate through experiments that BIQE substantially surpasses existing state-of-the-art baselines.

Selecting an appropriate approximate posterior distribution is a fundamental challenge in variational inference. Typically, many variational inference applications utilize simple families of posterior approximations, such as mean-field or other structured forms, to enable efficient computation. However, this simplification often compromises the accuracy of the resulting inferences. To address this limitation, we propose a novel method for defining flexible, highly complex, and scalable approximate posteriors. Our approach employs normalizing flows—transformations that convert a straightforward initial distribution into a more intricate one through a sequence of invertible mappings. By viewing normalizing flows in this way, we introduce classifications of both finite and infinitesimal flows, offering a unified framework for constructing expressive posterior approximations. We demonstrate that leveraging the theoretical benefits of closely matching the true posterior, combined with the scalability of amortized methods, leads to significant improvements in both the performance and applicability of variational inference.

Policy gradient methods are a popular category of model-free reinforcement learning algorithms that utilize a state-dependent baseline to mitigate the variance of gradient estimators. Recent research has extended this concept by incorporating both state and action into the baseline, claiming that such an approach substantially reduces variance and enhances sample efficiency without biasing the gradient estimates. To investigate these claims, we analyze the variance of the policy gradient estimator by decomposition and conduct numerical experiments, revealing that learned state-action-dependent baselines do not actually decrease variance compared to purely state-dependent baselines in standard benchmark environments. We validate these findings by examining the open-source implementations associated with the previous studies, discovering that subtle implementation choices lead to deviations from the published methods and account for the empirical performance gains previously reported. Additionally, our variance analysis identifies opportunities for improvement, which we illustrate through a straightforward modification to the typical value function parameterization, resulting in notable performance improvements.

Although computer vision has gained significant prominence in computer science over the past decade, its application within engineering design research remains limited. Existing datasets and technological advancements enable researchers to capture and access a vast number of observations and video files, but the analysis of this wealth of data has become a bottleneck. To address this challenge, this study explores the use of machine learning, specifically object detection techniques, to facilitate the analysis of physical prototypes. Utilizing a substantial dataset comprising 5,950 images of 850 digitally cataloged physical prototypes from early-stage development projects, the authors examine potential applications for processing this data. They retrained two established object detection models—one from the TensorFlow Object Detection API and another from Darknet—using custom images of physical prototypes. The study presents a proof-of-concept involving four trained models: two designed to identify wood-based sheet materials and two aimed at detecting microcontroller-containing samples. These models are evaluated through standard object detection metrics, and the discussion considers the broader applicability of such models within engineering design research. The results demonstrate that the models can effectively classify material types and prototype features, highlighting their potential as valuable tools in design analysis.

A synergistic strategy combining device, circuit, and neural network architecture optimization was employed to mitigate performance degradation caused by junction temperature variations in a Fe-FinFET-based artificial neural network. We established that the digital nature of the binarized neural network—where the "0" state is deeply embedded in the subthreshold region and the "1" state resides in strong inversion—is essential for ensuring robust DNN inference. Using a purely software-based binary neural network (BNN) with a 96.1% accuracy on the MNIST handwritten digit dataset as a reference, the Fe-FinFET-based BNN (considering device-to-device variations at 300 K) achieved 95.7% inference accuracy. While a nonbinary neural network exhibited significant accuracy loss due to temperature fluctuations, the optimized Fe-FinFET-based BNN demonstrated remarkable resilience to temperature changes, maintaining at least 95.2% accuracy across a broad temperature range from -233K to 398K after gate stack and bias adjustments. For temperatures exceeding 398K, reprogramming the device conductance was necessary to restore optimal performance.

This research explores the potential of using phonological features in text-to-speech systems to produce both native and non-native speech in English and Mandarin. We developed a mapping framework converting ARPABET and pinyin into SAMPA and SAMPA-SC, which were then translated into phonological features. Our goal was to determine if this approach could effectively generate authentic native, non-native, and code-switched speech in both languages. Two experiments were conducted—one with a small dataset and another with a larger one. The findings indicate that phonological features are a viable input for TTS systems, though additional work is needed to enhance model accuracy. Moreover, the accented speech generated by these models offers valuable insights into second language acquisition processes.

Federated learning (FL) is an innovative machine learning approach that enables model training without consolidating data at a central repository. Traditionally, most FL research focuses on a centralized setup, where a single server coordinates numerous devices to iteratively develop the model. However, this centralized structure faces scalability challenges as the number of devices increases, mainly due to strict communication and bandwidth limitations. To overcome these limitations, this paper introduces a ConFederated Learning (CFL) framework. In CFL, multiple servers are employed, each managing its own subset of devices, similar to the conventional FL paradigm. Importantly, these servers collaborate in a decentralized manner, allowing for more efficient utilization of the dispersed data across the network. We design an Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) algorithm tailored for CFL. This algorithm incorporates a random scheduling strategy that selectively activates a subset of devices at each iteration, significantly reducing the communication burden associated with data uploads. Theoretical insights are provided to validate the effectiveness of our approach, and numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed method reliably converges.

Regularization techniques are commonly used in deep neural networks (DNNs) to mitigate overfitting. When it comes to penalty-based regularization methods for DNNs, convex penalties are often preferred due to their favorable optimization guarantees. Recent theoretical advancements have demonstrated that nonconvex penalties, which meet specific regularity criteria, can also achieve strong performance when optimized with standard algorithms. In this study, we explore both novel and existing nonconvex penalties for DNN regularization. We offer theoretical justifications for the newly proposed penalties and evaluate their effectiveness, alongside existing ones, through DNN analyses across seven datasets.

The Bayesian approach offers promising solutions to key challenges in deep neural networks, such as poor calibration and data inefficiency. However, applying Bayesian inference to large neural networks often necessitates restrictive approximations. In this study, we demonstrate that performing inference on a small subset of model weights is sufficient to achieve accurate predictive posteriors, with the remaining weights treated as point estimates. This subnetwork inference method allows us to utilize more expressive, otherwise intractable, posterior approximations over these selected weights. Specifically, we implement a subnetwork linearized Laplace technique as a straightforward and scalable Bayesian deep learning approach: we first find a MAP estimate of all weights, then infer a full-covariance Gaussian posterior over a chosen subnetwork using the linearized Laplace approximation. We introduce a subnetwork selection strategy designed to preserve the model’s predictive uncertainty as much as possible. Empirical results show that our method outperforms ensembles and less expressive posterior approximations applied to entire networks. The subnetwork (linearized) Laplace method is available within the Laplace PyTorch library at https://github.com/AlexImmer/Laplace.

In recent years, the increasing size of neural networks has spurred extensive research into compression methods to address the limitations of large models. These efforts are primarily categorized into three main groups: Knowledge Distillation, Pruning, and Quantization. Despite steady progress in this area, the practical adoption and commercial deployment of these techniques have lagged behind. To bridge this gap, we introduce KD-Lib, an open-source PyTorch library offering modular, state-of-the-art implementations of algorithms from all three categories, built atop multiple abstraction layers. KD-Lib is designed to be model- and algorithm-agnostic, with enhanced support for hyperparameter tuning via Optuna and comprehensive logging and monitoring through TensorBoard. The library is available at https://github.com/SforAiDl/KD_Lib.

AI systems have become integral to a broad spectrum of financial services, playing an increasingly vital role in critical decision-making processes. This escalation underscores the growing importance of compliance and robust model governance. Traditional governance methods, originally designed for conventional financial applications and modeling techniques, often fall short when applied to AI due to fundamental differences such as inherent uncertainty and the absence of explicit programming. Managing AI models typically involves intricate review procedures and a heavy reliance on manual interventions, leading to challenges related to effectiveness, cost, complexity, and operational speed. Additionally, the rapid escalation in AI model complexity raises concerns about the sustainability of current governance approaches. This paper examines the key challenges associated with AI model governance within the financial sector. As part of our perspective, we propose a comprehensive system-level framework aimed at enhancing self-regulation, robustness, and compliance. This framework seeks to unlock potential solutions through greater automation and the integration of monitoring, management, and mitigation functions. Moreover, it offers improved capabilities for model governance and risk management, ensuring better oversight of model risks throughout the deployment lifecycle.

In our current era characterized by extensive catalogs, tools for large-scale statistical analysis, such as machine learning, play a crucial role. An illustrative example is the Sloan Moving Object Catalog (MOC), which provides astrometric and photometric data for all moving objects within the Sloan survey area. A notable advantage of this telescope is its use of five filters, enabling taxonomic analysis of asteroids through their color properties. However, until now, the variation in asteroid colors caused by changes in the phase angle has not been considered. In this study, we address this gap by utilizing absolute magnitudes for classification purposes. Our goal is to develop a new asteroid taxonomic classification framework based on magnitude data that remains robust against phase angle-induced variations. We selected 9,481 asteroids with computed absolute magnitudes in Hg, Hi, and Hz bands, derived from the Sloan MOC using the HG12 system, and used these to determine their absolute colors. For taxonomy classification, we employed an unsupervised machine learning method called fuzzy C-means, which is particularly effective for soft clustering of datasets where

Graph generative models represent a rapidly evolving area within machine learning. As new models with increasing complexity continue to emerge, establishing a rigorous method for evaluating and comparing them becomes essential. In this paper, we outline key criteria for a meaningful comparison metric and review the current landscape, which largely depends on the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD). We systematically examine MMD's effectiveness in comparing graph generative models, identifying potential challenges and common pitfalls encountered by researchers. Through detailed analysis of MMD’s behavior on synthetically perturbed graphs and recent graph generative models, we propose strategies to address these issues. Our findings are distilled into practical recommendations to guide researchers in effectively evaluating graph generative models.

The traditional backpropagation algorithm, which has been instrumental in training deep neural networks, has driven much of the success in deep learning. Nonetheless, its reliance on sequential backward updates and non-local computations poses significant challenges for large-scale parallelization and diverges from the mechanisms observed in biological learning systems. Inspired by neuroscience, alternative learning algorithms such as predictive coding leverage local computations, offering promising avenues to overcome these limitations and push beyond existing deep learning paradigms. Originally conceptualized as a model of cortical information processing in theoretical neuroscience, recent advancements have transformed predictive coding into a versatile, general-purpose training algorithm that operates solely through local computations. In this survey, we examine key contributions that support this perspective, highlighting the strong theoretical links between predictive coding and backpropagation. We also explore the multiple benefits of predictive coding models over traditional backpropagation-trained networks, including their enhanced flexibility—they can serve as classifiers, generators, and associative memories simultaneously—and their ability to be applied on arbitrary graph structures. Lastly, we review empirical benchmarks comparing predictive coding networks to standard machine learning tasks, emphasizing its potential advantages and applications.

Federated learning has become a promising and highly distributed approach for training comprehensive deep models across numerous edge devices, all while keeping users' private data securely on their local devices. In this study, motivated by the goals of promoting fairness among users and enhancing robustness against malicious threats, we conceptualize federated learning as a multi-objective optimization problem and introduce a novel algorithm, FedMGDA+. This algorithm is designed to reliably converge to Pareto stationary solutions. FedMGDA+ is straightforward to implement, requires tuning fewer hyperparameters, and ensures that the performance of individual users is preserved without compromise. We analyze and validate the convergence characteristics of FedMGDA+ and explore its relationships with existing methods. Extensive testing on various datasets demonstrates that FedMGDA+ performs favorably when compared to current state-of-the-art approaches.

Many real-world data streams tend to change frequently and in a nonstationary manner. However, most deep learning approaches train neural networks on fixed datasets, which often results in significant performance drops when dataset shifts occur. Since annotating or inspecting newly streamed data manually is typically impractical, there is a need for a method to measure model drift in an unsupervised manner at inference time. In this paper, we introduce a novel approach for estimating model drift by leveraging statistics from batch normalization layers applied to unlabeled test data. To mitigate the impact of sampling errors in streamed inputs, we incorporate low-rank approximation techniques for each representational layer. Our method proves effective not only in detecting dataset shifts but also in selecting the most suitable model from a pool of candidates—such as multiple models in a model zoo or different training trajectories—without supervision. Additionally, we validate the robustness of our approach by comparing model drift scores across various network architectures.

Bayesian inference challenges often involve sampling or approximating high-dimensional probability distributions. This paper concentrates on the recently developed Stein variational gradient descent (SVGD) method, a class of algorithms that utilize iterative steepest descent steps within a reproducing kernel Hilbert space framework. This approach naturally results in interacting particle systems, whose mean-field limit can be interpreted as a gradient flow on the space of probability measures endowed with a specific geometric structure. We exploit this perspective to better understand the convergence behavior of SVGD, with particular emphasis on selecting an appropriate positive definite kernel function. Our analysis suggests considering certain nondifferentiable kernels with tailored tail behavior. Numerical experiments demonstrate that these choices can lead to substantial improvements in performance.

Existing spatial object recommendation methods typically treat objects uniformly during ranking, overlooking their inherent heterogeneity arising from varying levels of spatial granularity. For instance, one user might prefer suggestions for a specific region, such as Manhattan, while another might be interested in a particular venue like a restaurant. Moreover, user preferences can fluctuate at different stages of data exploration. In this paper, we explore methods to support top-k spatial object recommendations across multiple levels of spatial granularity, accommodating diverse POIs such as cities, suburbs, or buildings. To address this challenge, we introduce a POI tree structure that models the spatial containment relationships among POIs. We also propose a novel multi-task learning framework called MPR (Multi-level POI Recommendation), where each task is designed to identify the top-k POIs at a specific spatial granularity. Each task comprises two subtasks: (i) attribute-based representation learning, which derives feature embeddings for users and POIs based on their profiles; and (ii) interaction-based representation learning, which incorporates user-POI interaction data. Additionally, MPR offers interpretability by providing explanations for its recommendation choices.

Given the widespread use of smartphones and wearable devices today, mobile health (mHealth) technologies hold great potential to positively impact individual health outcomes. Current decision-making approaches in mHealth often rely on idealized assumptions, either considering users as completely uniform or entirely distinct. In reality, users may resemble some but not all others. To address this, we introduce a novel group-driven reinforcement learning framework for mHealth. Our goal is to facilitate information sharing among similar users, thereby transforming limited user data into more effective RL policies. Specifically, we utilize K-means clustering to group users based on the similarity of their trajectory data, and then develop a shared RL policy for each group. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art RL methods in the mHealth domain.

Normalization techniques are crucial for facilitating efficient and often more effective training of deep neural networks. Unlike traditional approaches that explicitly normalize activations, we propose introducing an additional loss term. This term incentivizes the activations' variance to remain stable across different mini-batches, preventing significant fluctuations. Our analysis shows that this encourages activations to cluster around a few distinct modes. Furthermore, when input data originates from a mixture of two Gaussians, our loss function either merges these components or separates them optimally in the LDA sense, depending on their prior probabilities. Additionally, we establish a connection between this regularization term and the batch normalization method, offering a new perspective on its regularization effects. Experimental results reveal that our approach enhances accuracy compared to batch normalization in both convolutional neural networks and fully connected architectures.

Deep learning has gained widespread popularity in recent years, largely driven by advances in high-performance computing devices such as GPUs. However, deploying these deep models on end-user devices, smartphones, or embedded systems with limited resources presents significant challenges. To address this, we introduce a novel lightweight deep learning module called LPRNet, which utilizes low-rank pointwise residual (LPR) convolution. The core idea of LPRNet is to employ low-rank approximation within pointwise convolution to significantly reduce the module's size, while retaining depthwise convolutions as residual components to correct potential inaccuracies introduced by the low-rank approximation. This approach is especially important when the reduction in rank compromises the convolutional process. We demonstrate our design by substituting modules with matching input-output dimensions in MobileNet and ShuffleNetv2. Experimental results on visual recognition tasks such as image classification and face alignment on popular benchmarks show that LPRNet delivers competitive performance while substantially decreasing FLOPs and memory requirements compared to existing state-of-the-art models focused on model compression.

Adversarial training enhances the training dataset by adding perturbations to bolster robustness against worst-case disturbances. However, this often results in a rise in standard error on unaltered test samples. Previous explanations for this tradeoff assumed that no predictor within the hypothesis class exhibits simultaneously low standard and robust errors. In this study, we precisely analyze how augmentation impacts standard error in linear regression, particularly when the optimal linear predictor achieves zero error both standard and robust. We demonstrate that standard error can increase even when the augmented perturbations consist of noiseless data from the optimal predictor. Furthermore, we establish that the recently introduced robust self-training (RST) estimator effectively reduces robust error without compromising standard error in noiseless linear regression. Empirical results on neural networks show that RST, combined with various adversarial training techniques, enhances both standard and robust errors across scenarios involving random rotations, adversarial rotations, and adversarial \(\ell_\infty\) perturbations on CIFAR-10.

This paper introduces Principal Trade-off Analysis (PTA), a decomposition technique similar to Principal Component Analysis (PCA), that enables representing any game as a weighted combination of simple, continuous R-P-S (rock-paper-scissors-like) games. When applied to empirically derived tournament graphs, PTA yields a series of embeddings into orthogonal two-dimensional feature spaces, capturing independent strategic trade-offs. Each of these trade-offs corresponds to a mode of cyclic competition. Like PCA, PTA offers optimal low-rank approximations of tournament graphs, which can be truncated to achieve simplified representations. The complexity of cyclic competition can be measured by counting the number of significant cyclic modes. We demonstrate PTA through applications to two games: Blotto and Pokemon. The resulting two-dimensional disc game representations are highly suitable for visualization and are straightforward to interpret. In the case of Blotto, PTA uncovers game symmetries and highlights strategic trade-offs associated with different winning strategies. For Pokemon, PTA embeddings reveal clusters that align with Pokemon types—an intrinsic design feature that introduces cyclic trade-offs within the game.

Owing to the remarkable success of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) in processing graph-structured data, a variety of GNN-based approaches have been developed to leverage knowledge graphs (KGs). In this study, we analyze key factors underlying existing GNN methods by examining exemplar models through the perspective of propagation paths. We observe that while the answer entity may be proximal to the queried node, the information dependency often spans a long distance. Consequently, enhancing reasoning capabilities involves exploring extended propagation paths. However, detecting such long-range dependencies in KGs is challenging due to the exponential growth in involved entities. To address this, we propose learning an adaptive propagation path that selectively filters out irrelevant entities while retaining promising targets during the propagation process. First, we introduce an incremental sampling mechanism designed to preserve both nearby and promising target entities. Second, we develop a learning-based sampling distribution to efficiently identify targets with fewer involved entities, enabling GNNs to delve deeper and capture long-range dependencies. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach is both efficient and achieves state-of-the-art performance in both transductive and inductive reasoning scenarios, leveraging deeper propagation for improved results.

Inspired by the recent achievements of deep learning across various fields, data-driven design of metamaterials has become a promising approach to harness the potential of multiscale architectures. Nonetheless, current model-focused methods often lack robust strategies for generating high-quality data. Relying on space-filling designs in shape descriptor space, existing metamaterial datasets tend to exhibit property distributions that are either highly skewed or misaligned with the specific design objectives. To address these challenges, we introduce t-METASET: an intelligent framework for task-aware data acquisition aimed at creating more effective datasets. Our approach tackles a common yet frequently overlooked scenario in early-stage design: starting with a large, uncharacterized shape library (~10,000 shapes) with no property evaluations. The core concept involves utilizing a data-driven shape descriptor learned through generative models, fitting a sparse regressor as an initial predictor, and employing diversity metrics to guide data collection toward regions that support the achievement of design goals. We evaluate t-METASET across three hypothetical deployment scenarios—general use, task-specific use, and customizable application—using two large-scale, shape-only mechanical metamaterial datasets as testbeds. The results demonstrate that t-METASET can incrementally build task-relevant datasets, enhancing the flexibility of general design representations and paving the way for future advancements in the field.

Domain adaptation (DA) and domain generalization (DG) have become prominent solutions to address the issue of domain shift, where the data distributions of source and target domains differ. Unlike DA, which leverages target domain data during training, DG poses a greater challenge by requiring models to generalize to completely unseen target domains without any access to target data during training. While current leading approaches predominantly utilize adversarial techniques, their application to DG remains limited. Additionally, these methods often overlook the advantages of correlation alignment, which has been shown to significantly reduce domain discrepancy. In this work, we introduce a correlation-aware adversarial framework for both DA and DG, wherein feature representations from source and target data are aligned through correlation-based methods combined with adversarial learning. Integrating the correlation alignment module enhances the model’s ability to become more domain-invariant, especially in unsupervised settings with unlabeled target data, thus more effectively minimizing domain differences. Extensive experiments on standard benchmark datasets demonstrate that our approach achieves superior, state-of-the-art performance.

The processes of agent creation and removal in cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) remain insufficiently explored areas of research. Many current MARL algorithms assume a fixed number of agents throughout an experiment. However, in real-world scenarios, agents may cease operation before their teammates, raising the challenge of credit assignment for such early terminations. Specifically, the issue involves propagating the rewards earned by surviving agents back to those that have terminated, a problem we term Posthumous Credit Assignment. Existing approaches often address this by placing terminated agents into an absorbing state until the entire group concludes, allowing algorithms and APIs to handle these agents without modification. Nonetheless, this method introduces practical concerns related to training efficiency and resource consumption. In this study, we first show that in a toy supervised learning setting with a fully connected network, the sample complexity increases with the number of absorbing states, whereas attention mechanisms demonstrate greater robustness to input size variability. Subsequently, we propose a novel architecture for an existing advanced MARL algorithm that replaces the fully connected layer with attention mechanisms, eliminating the need for absorbing states.

Deciphering behavior, perception, or cognitive states directly from neural signals holds significant promise for brain-computer interface development and advances in systems neuroscience. Over the past decade, deep learning has emerged as the leading approach across numerous machine learning applications, from speech recognition to image segmentation. Its success in various fields has sparked a new wave of innovative applications within neuroscience. In this review, we examine deep learning methods for neural decoding, highlighting different neural recording techniques—from spike trains to EEG—and how they are processed by various architectures to extract meaningful features. We also discuss how these techniques have been used to predict common outputs such as movement, speech, and visual perception, emphasizing the role of pretrained deep networks as priors for complex decoding tasks like reconstructing speech or images. Overall, deep learning has proven to be a powerful tool for enhancing both the accuracy and adaptability of neural decoding, and we identify key areas for future research and development.

We investigate the bandit problem in which each arm is linked to a stationary phi-mixing process, resulting in dependent rewards. This setting raises the challenge of approximating independence by selectively ignoring certain reward observations. As we will demonstrate, addressing this problem involves balancing exploration, exploitation, and the pursuit of independence. To this end, we introduce a UCB-based strategy accompanied by a comprehensive regret analysis for scenarios where the size of independence blocks—i.e., the rewards that are ignored—is fixed. Moreover, we go beyond this by proposing an algorithm capable of estimating the optimal size of these blocks directly from the data. Finally, we extend our analysis to the restless case, where all mixing processes evolve concurrently over time, adding another layer of complexity to the problem.

We present a methodology for optimizing control policies in a large linear particle accelerator through deep reinforcement learning integrated with a high-fidelity physics simulation. The system features an AI controller employing deep neural networks to represent the state and action spaces, learning optimal strategies from reward signals generated by the physics engine. In this study, we focus exclusively on managing a small segment of the accelerator. Initial findings demonstrate that our approach can surpass human performance in controlling particle beam current and distribution. The overarching aim of this research is to drastically cut down tuning times—by several orders of magnitude—and move toward near-autonomous operation of such facilities.

How can we develop a universal approach to select the most appropriate samples for training a classifier, especially when prior information is scarce? Active learning serves as an iterative optimization process that is crucial for building a refined training set to enhance classification accuracy across various domains such as text analysis, image recognition, and social network modeling. Although integrating the representativeness and informativeness of samples has shown promise in active sampling, current state-of-the-art methods often perform well only under specific data conditions. This raises the question: can we unify these two sampling criteria without relying on assumptions about the data? 

In this paper, we introduce a comprehensive active learning framework that effectively combines both criteria. Drawing inspiration from a two-sample discrepancy problem, we design triple measures to ensure that selected query samples are both representative of the unlabeled data and diverse relative to the labeled data. These measures are flexible and can be constructed using any suitable similarity metric. Additionally, an uncertainty measure is incorporated to assess the informativeness of samples, which can be implemented through various techniques. 

Building on this framework, we propose a practical active learning algorithm that leverages a radial basis function approach, providing a robust method for sample selection without imposing restrictive assumptions on the data.

We introduce a distributed cubic-regularized Newton algorithm designed for large-scale convex optimization across networked systems. This approach relies solely on local computations and communications, making it well-suited for federated learning scenarios with arbitrary network structures. Under the assumption that the objective function is convex with Lipschitz continuous gradients and Hessians, we establish a convergence rate of \( O(k^{-3}) \), where \( k \) denotes the number of iterations. Additionally, we derive bounds on the communication complexity per iteration that depend on the network topology. Numerical experiments are presented to confirm the validity of our theoretical findings.

Despite the rapid advancements of deep neural networks (DNNs) in recent years, their susceptibility to adversarial threats remains a significant concern. Malicious backdoors can be embedded into models through contaminating the training data, aiming to cause incorrect predictions whenever a specific trigger is present during inference. To address these risks, numerous detection and defense strategies have been developed. However, most existing approaches depend on access to poisoned training data or the internal details of the model (white-box access), which are often unavailable in real-world scenarios. 

In this work, we introduce a black-box backdoor detection (B3D) method that relies solely on query access to the model to identify backdoor infections. Our approach employs a gradient-free optimization technique to reverse-engineer potential triggers for each class, thereby facilitating the detection of backdoor attacks. Beyond detection, we also propose a straightforward method to ensure reliable model predictions once a backdoor presence is suspected. Extensive experiments conducted across hundreds of DNN models trained on multiple datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in black-box settings, successfully defending against various types of backdoor threats.

Given a set of data points lying within the convex hull of certain vertices, a fundamental challenge in data analysis and machine learning is to accurately identify these vertices amidst noise. Numerous algorithms have been designed under the premise that each vertex has at least one neighboring data point; two prominent examples are Vertex Component Analysis (VCA) and the Successive Projection Algorithm (SPA). This premise is referred to as the pure-pixel assumption in blind hyperspectral unmixing and as the separability assumption in nonnegative matrix factorization. Recently, Bhattacharyya and Kannan (ACM-SIAM Symposium on Discrete Algorithms, 2020) introduced an algorithm called ALLS (Approximate Learning of a Latent Simplex), which assumes that each vertex has multiple nearby data points. Under this assumption, ALLS exhibits greater probabilistic robustness to noise compared to methods relying solely on the separability assumption. Inspired by ALLS, this paper introduces smoothed versions of VCA and SPA—namely, Smoothed VCA (SVCA) and Smoothed SPA (SSPA)—which extend the original algorithms by assuming the existence of several neighboring data points for each vertex. We demonstrate the superior performance of SVCA and SSPA over VCA, SPA, and ALLS through experiments on synthetic datasets and real-world data.

Functional connectivity (FC) has emerged as a key approach for understanding brain functions by analyzing interactions within brain networks and elucidating how these interactions give rise to cognition. Traditionally, FC is characterized by statistical correlations between activity in different brain regions. However, such correlations only reveal spatial relationships without indicating causal influences among regions. Therefore, investigating causal relationships is essential. Directed acyclic graph (DAG) models have been employed in recent FC studies to infer causality but often face challenges due to limited sample sizes and high-dimensional data involving numerous variables, which lead to computational difficulties and convergence issues. Moreover, identifying DAG structures is generally NP-hard, complicating the modeling process. To address these challenges, we introduce a $\psi$-learning integrated linear non-Gaussian acyclic model ($\psi$-LiNGAM). This approach leverages the association-based $\psi$-learning method to enhance causal inference, particularly in high-dimensional settings. Our simulation studies reveal that the proposed method outperforms several existing techniques in both robustness and accuracy regarding graph structure detection and causal directionality. We further applied this method to resting-state fMRI (rsfMRI) data sourced from publicly available datasets.

Autoencoders produce latent representations of input data. Recent research has demonstrated that they can also estimate the probability density functions of these inputs. This ability enables the application of Bayesian decision theory. When latent models are obtained for each class or specific points in a parameter estimation space, likelihood functions for these classes or points can be effectively estimated. We illustrate how an ensemble of autoencoders addresses the recognition problem: each autoencoder models its own context, with a latent vector representing input data within that context. Sharing latent spaces among autoencoders introduces a crucial advantage—the capacity to distinguish between 'treatment' (the input data) and 'context' (the autoencoder's specific model). This separation allows the input information to be processed through multiple autoencoders, enhancing recognition capabilities. Two key and highly valuable outcomes of this work are: a mechanism suggesting a pathway to form abstract concepts, and a method to reduce the dataset size during training. These findings are validated by experimental results discussed in the article.

Most learning-based segmentation techniques rely heavily on large volumes of high-quality labeled training data. In this paper, we introduce a novel segmentation model that can be trained with minimal supervision, including semi- or completely unsupervised approaches. Specifically, in the unsupervised scenario, we reformulate the Active Contour Without Edges (ACWE) framework by parameterizing it with a convolutional neural network (ConvNet), and we optimize its parameters through a self-supervised learning process. In the semi-supervised case, we incorporate auxiliary ground truth segmentations during training. Our results demonstrate that this approach enables rapid, high-precision bone segmentation in single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) images.

Recent studies have demonstrated that knowledge distillation effectively reduces network size while enhancing generalization capabilities. For instance, a large, pre-trained teacher network can serve as a foundation to bootstrap a student model that ultimately surpasses the teacher in environments with limited labels. Despite these promising results, the underlying reasons for this success remain somewhat unclear—specifically, what improvements the student model gains. To explore this, we employ two non-linear, low-dimensional embedding techniques—t-SNE and IVIS—to visualize the representation spaces across various network layers. We conduct extensive experiments varying architectural parameters and distillation strategies. The visualizations and associated metrics reveal that distillation encourages the network to develop a more compact and discriminative representation space early on, resulting in higher accuracy compared to the non-distilled counterpart.

We introduce an innovative approach to address the type inference challenge in dynamic languages. Our method aims to integrate \emph{logical} constraints—precise, deterministic information derived from the type system—with \emph{natural} constraints—probabilistic, uncertain insights about types gleaned from sources such as identifier names. To realize this integration, we propose a probabilistic type inference framework that marries logical reasoning with machine learning: logical constraints are extracted directly from the program, while a deep learning model predicts types based on superficial code features that are statistically linked to specific types. The key novelty of our approach lies in enforcing that predictions from the learning component adhere to logical constraints, achieved by reformulating the logical inference task into a continuous optimization problem. We have developed a tool named OptTyper, designed to infer missing types in TypeScript files. OptTyper seamlessly combines a continuous interpretation of logical constraints—obtained through traditional static analysis—with natural constraints learned by a deep neural network that captures naming conventions from extensive code repositories. Our evaluation demonstrates that integrating logical and natural constraints significantly outperforms methods relying on either source alone, achieving a notable 4\% improvement in inference accuracy.

mlpack is an open-source C++ library dedicated to machine learning, prioritizing speed and adaptability. Since its launch in 2007, it has expanded into a comprehensive project encompassing a wide range of algorithms, from traditional methods like decision trees and logistic regression to state-of-the-art techniques such as deep neural networks and the latest cutting-edge approaches not available in other libraries. Renowned for its high performance, benchmarks demonstrate that mlpack often surpasses other libraries in speed for comparable algorithms. The library benefits from an active global community of contributors, including members from PUST. This brief paper outlines the objectives and architecture of mlpack, explains how the open-source community collaborates, and provides a simple example of using mlpack to solve a basic data science task.

Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) have been effectively utilized in a range of sequential decision-making tasks, natural language processing, and time-series forecasting. Typically, these networks are trained using back-propagation through time (BPTT), a process that becomes computationally intensive as the length of dependencies and the number of hidden units increase. To mitigate training time, recent approaches have incorporated extreme learning machines (ELMs) into RNN training, achieving speedups of up to 99% in certain scenarios. Thanks to their non-iterative nature, ELMs can be parallelized more efficiently than BPTT, potentially enabling even greater acceleration. In this paper, we introduce \opt, an advanced parallel RNN training algorithm based on ELM principles. \opt leverages GPU shared memory and parallel QR factorization techniques to efficiently obtain optimal solutions. We provide a theoretical analysis of \opt~across six RNN architectures, including LSTM and GRU, and evaluate its performance on ten time-series prediction tasks. The results demonstrate that \opt~can deliver up to 845 times faster training than its sequential version and reduces training time by up to 20 times compared to parallel BPTT.

We investigate how permutation symmetries in overparameterized multi-layer neural networks give rise to `symmetry-induced' critical points. Assuming a network with \(L\) layers, each of minimal widths \(r_1^*, \ldots, r_{L-1}^*\), attains a zero-loss minimum at \(r_1^* \cdots r_{L-1}^*\) isolated points, which are permutations of one another. We demonstrate that adding a single neuron to each layer suffices to unify these discrete minima into a continuous manifold. In particular, for a two-layer overparameterized network with width \(r^* + h =: m\), we explicitly characterize the manifold of global minima: it comprises \(T(r^*, m)\) affine subspaces, each of dimension at least \(h\), interconnected with one another. For a network of width \(m\), we identify the quantity \(G(r, m)\), representing the count of affine subspaces containing only symmetry-induced critical points related to those of a smaller network with width \(r < r^*\). Through combinatorial analysis, we derive closed-form expressions for \(T\) and \(G\), revealing that in the mildly overparameterized regime (small \(h\)), the number of symmetry-induced critical subspaces surpasses the number of affine subspaces comprising the global minima manifold; this relationship reverses in the heavily overparameterized regime.

Variational autoencoders (VAEs) are widely used generative models for discrete data. However, when equipped with flexible decoders, they often tend to overlook the latent representations. In this paper, we introduce a VAE variant with a deterministic decoder (DD-VAE) tailored for sequential data, which selects the highest-scoring tokens instead of sampling. This deterministic decoding process depends solely on the latent codes to generate diverse outputs, leading to a more structured learned manifold. To realize DD-VAE, we develop a novel class of proposal distributions with bounded support and derive the Kullback-Leibler divergence for Gaussian and uniform priors. Additionally, we explore a continuous relaxation of the deterministic decoding objective and examine how reconstruction accuracy relates to relaxation parameters. We evaluate DD-VAE across multiple datasets, including applications in molecular generation and optimization tasks.

High-dimensional and incomplete (HDI) data are commonly encountered in diverse industrial scenarios characterized by intricate interactions among numerous nodes, which are typically non-negative to reflect the inherent nature of node relationships. A Non-negative Latent Factor (NLF) model effectively extracts intrinsic features from such data. Nonetheless, existing NLF models rely on static divergence metrics, such as Euclidean distance or α-β divergence, to formulate their learning objectives, limiting their ability to accurately model HDI data across different domains. To overcome this limitation, this study proposes an Adaptive Divergence-based Non-negative Latent Factor (ADNLF) model, built on three key concepts: (a) extending the objective function using the α-β divergence to enhance its capacity to represent various HDI datasets; (b) introducing a non-negative bridging function to seamlessly connect the optimization variables with the output latent factors, ensuring the non-negativity constraints are maintained consistently; and (c) enabling the divergence parameters to adapt dynamically through particle swarm optimization, thereby promoting flexible divergence measures within the learning process for improved scalability. Extensive experiments conducted on four real-world HDI datasets demonstrate that, compared to leading NLF models, the ADNLF approach achieves substantially higher accuracy in estimating missing data, while also offering efficient computational performance.

In this paper, we introduce a learning-based methodology for assessing argument acceptability across various abstract argumentation semantics. Specifically, we develop an Argumentation Graph Neural Network (AGNN) that trains a message-passing mechanism to estimate the probability of an argument being accepted. Experimental results reveal that the AGNN nearly perfectly predicts argument acceptability under different semantics and scales effectively to larger argumentation frameworks. Additionally, analysis of the message-passing behavior indicates that the AGNN internalizes fundamental principles of argument semantics as documented in existing literature, enabling it to be trained for predicting extensions under diverse semantics. We demonstrate how this can be extended to multi-extension semantics by leveraging AGNNs to guide a straightforward search process. Our code is available at https://github.com/DennisCraandijk/DL-Abstract-Argumentation.

Quantization and Knowledge Distillation (KD) techniques are extensively employed to decrease the memory footprint and power usage of deep neural networks (DNNs), particularly for resource-limited edge devices. While combining these methods holds significant promise for meeting such constraints, it can sometimes fall short of expectations. This is primarily because the regularization effect of KD further reduces the already diminished representational capacity of a quantized model. To overcome this limitation, we introduce Quantization-aware Knowledge Distillation (QKD), a method that harmonizes quantization and KD across three carefully designed phases. The first, Self-studying (SS), involves fine-tuning a low-precision, quantized student network without KD to establish a solid starting point. The second, Co-studying (CS), focuses on training a teacher model to enhance its compatibility with quantization, making it more effective than a fixed teacher. The final phase, Tutoring (TU), transfers knowledge from this optimized teacher to the student. We thoroughly test our approach on the ImageNet and CIFAR-10/100 datasets, including ablation studies on networks utilizing both standard and depthwise-separable convolutions. Our QKD method surpasses current state-of-the-art approaches, achieving a 1.3% accuracy improvement on ResNet-18 with W4A4 quantization and a 2.6% gain on MobileNetV2 with W4A4. Furthermore, QKD can restore full-precision accuracy at low-bit quantization levels, reaching W3A3 for ResNet and W6A6 for MobileNetV2.

Modern e-commerce catalogs encompass millions of products, each accompanied by textual and visual information essential for efficient search and browsing. A particularly challenging category is books, where the "author name" field often presents significant difficulties. Books authored by a particular individual, such as F. Scott Fitzgerald, may be listed under various names due to abbreviations, spelling differences, or typographical errors. To address this issue at scale, we have developed an integrated system that combines open data sources on books with advanced machine learning techniques rooted in deep learning for natural language processing. Specifically, we utilize Siamese neural networks to identify approximate matches with known author names and employ sequence-to-sequence models to correct author name entries. Our approach was tested on product data from Rakuten France, an e-commerce platform, achieving a top proposal accuracy of 72% in normalizing author names.

Today, synthesized speech is widespread due to the rise of virtual assistants, user-friendly tools for creating and editing speech signals, and the shift toward remote work. However, synthesized speech can also be exploited for malicious purposes, such as fabricating speech signals and falsely attributing them to individuals who did not speak the content. Therefore, developing reliable methods for detecting whether a speech signal is synthesized is essential. In this study, we examine speech signals represented as spectrograms using a Compact Convolutional Transformer (CCT) to identify synthesized speech. The CCT incorporates convolutional layers that embed inductive biases and shared weights into the model, enabling effective performance with fewer training samples. It employs an attention mechanism to analyze and integrate information from all segments of the signal. By training the model on both authentic human speech and artificially generated speech, we demonstrate that our CCT-based approach can accurately distinguish between genuine and synthesized speech signals.

This paper introduces the adaptation of Recurrent Neural Networks with Stochastic Layers—currently at the forefront for generating text, music, and speech—to the task of acoustic novelty detection. By incorporating uncertainty into the hidden states, this approach enables the network to learn the probability distribution of complex sequences. Consequently, it can explicitly compute the likelihood of observations and identify low-probability events as novel. The model is robust, highly unsupervised, end-to-end, and requires minimal preprocessing, feature engineering, or hyperparameter tuning. Experimental results on a benchmark dataset demonstrate that our method surpasses existing state-of-the-art acoustic novelty detection techniques.

Machine Learning (ML) models trained on data from diverse demographic groups can inherit existing representation disparities (Hashimoto et al., 2018), where the model may favor groups that contribute more to the training data. This can lead to decreased retention of underrepresented groups over time, ultimately intensifying long-term disparities. In this research, we explore the dynamic relationship between ML decision-making and the underlying group representation, examining how these interactions evolve within a sequential framework and the role fairness criteria play in shaping these outcomes. Our findings indicate that, under realistic user dynamics involving arrivals and departures, representation disparities can intensify over time when decisions are guided by standard objectives and fairness measures. This can even result in certain groups disappearing entirely from the sample pool in the long run. These results underscore the importance of designing fairness criteria that account for user dynamics, and we demonstrate how to select appropriate fairness measures based on a comprehensive model of user behavior.

The vast amount of data produced by human activities such as online shopping, health record management, and spatial movement is typically stored as a series of events occurring over continuous time. Applying deep learning techniques to these sequences presents significant challenges, as it requires modeling the continuously increasing event timestamps, inter-event intervals, event types, and the complex interactions both within and across different sequences. These challenges are intensified by practical constraints like limited data availability, incomplete sequences, and privacy considerations. In this research, we aim to explore the characteristics of continuous-time event sequences (CTES) and develop robust, scalable neural network models to address these issues. Specifically, we utilize marked temporal point processes (MTPP) to represent the underlying generative distribution of events, enabling us to tackle a variety of real-world problems. Additionally, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed methods compared to existing state-of-the-art approaches and discuss ongoing research challenges.

In the task of predicting edge signs within a directed graph that models a social network, our goal is to determine the binary labels of edges—specifically, whether social relationships are positive or negative. Existing heuristics often rely on troll-trust features, which estimate at each node the proportion of outgoing and incoming edges that are positive or negative. We demonstrate that these heuristics can be rigorously interpreted and analyzed as approximate solutions to the Bayes optimal classifier under a simple probabilistic model of edge labels. Furthermore, we establish that the maximum likelihood estimator derived from this model closely aligns with the predictions generated by a Label Propagation algorithm applied to a transformed version of the original social graph. Extensive experiments across multiple real-world datasets reveal that this approach performs competitively with state-of-the-art classifiers in both accuracy and scalability. Lastly, we illustrate that troll-trust features can also be employed to develop online learning algorithms with strong theoretical guarantees, even in adversarial labeling scenarios.

Flow-based generative models are highly effective exact likelihood models that enable efficient sampling and inference. However, despite their computational advantages, these models often underperform compared to the leading autoregressive approaches in density estimation. In this study, we examine and enhance three critical design choices from previous flow-based models: the use of uniform noise for dequantization, the employment of simplistic affine flows, and the reliance solely on convolutional conditioning networks within coupling layers. Building on our insights, we introduce Flow++, a novel flow-based model that currently sets the benchmark as the top non-autoregressive method for unconditional density estimation on standard image datasets. Our advancements help bridge much of the gap in performance that has historically separated autoregressive and flow-based models. The implementation of our model is accessible at https://github.com/aravindsrinivas/flowpp

We present MIDI-VAE, a neural network model built on Variational Autoencoders designed to process polyphonic music with multiple instrument tracks and to capture musical dynamics through note durations and velocities. MIDI-VAE enables style transfer on symbolic music by automatically modifying pitches, dynamics, and instrumentation to transform a piece from, for example, a Classical to a Jazz style. The effectiveness of the style transfer is validated using dedicated style classification models. Additionally, our model can interpolate between short musical segments, generate medleys, and blend entire songs, with smooth transitions in pitch, dynamics, and instrumentation that create cohesive bridges between different pieces. To our knowledge, this is the first successful application of neural style transfer to complete musical compositions.

We analyze the Minimum Description Length (MDL) principle in the context of online sequence prediction. When the model class is discrete, the total expected squared loss serves as a particularly meaningful performance metric: (a) it remains bounded, ensuring convergence with probability one, and (b) it offers a quantified rate of convergence. Typically, MDL yields exponential bounds on loss, unlike the linear bounds seen with Bayesian mixtures. This holds even when the model class is limited to Bernoulli distributions. We establish a novel upper bound on the prediction error for countable Bernoulli classes, which in turn guarantees a relatively small bound—similar to that of Bayesian mixtures—in certain significant cases. Our findings are applicable to numerous machine learning tasks, such as classification and hypothesis testing, and we argue that our theorems extend naturally to countable sets of i.i.d. models.

Sliced inverse regression is a widely used technique for sufficient dimension reduction, which simplifies covariates into a minimal set of linear combinations without losing information about the conditional distribution of the response given the covariates. However, the resulting linear combinations typically involve all covariates, making the interpretation complex and possibly introducing unnecessary variability, especially when dealing with a large number of covariates. In this paper, we introduce a convex framework for implementing sparse sliced inverse regression in high-dimensional contexts. Our approach directly estimates the subspace spanned by the relevant linear combinations of covariates while simultaneously performing variable selection. We solve the resulting convex optimization problem using the linearized alternating direction method of multipliers, and provide a theoretical bound on the subspace distance between our estimated subspace and the true one. Numerical experiments demonstrate that our method effectively identifies the relevant covariates in high-dimensional scenarios.

Leveraging knowledge acquired from large-scale datasets such as ImageNet through fine-tuning provides an effective approach for tackling domain-specific fine-grained visual categorization (FGVC) tasks, including identifying bird species or distinguishing car makes and models.
