While extensive research has focused on data augmentation to enhance the accuracy and robustness of classifiers, its application in improving GAN-based image synthesis has received less attention. In this study, we conduct a comprehensive evaluation of various existing augmentation techniques for GAN training across multiple scenarios. Our findings offer valuable insights and practical guidelines for augmenting images in both standard GANs and those incorporating regularizations, leading to significant enhancements in the realism of generated images. Interestingly, we discover that vanilla GANs can achieve generation quality comparable to current state-of-the-art models when augmentations are applied to both real and fake images. Furthermore, integrating these augmentations with other regularization strategies—such as contrastive loss and consistency regularization—further elevates the quality of generated outputs. Notably, we establish new state-of-the-art results for conditional image generation on CIFAR-10 by combining consistency and contrastive losses with augmentation techniques.

We investigate sequential decision-making problems focused on maximizing the expected total reward while adhering to a constraint on the expected total utility. To address the discounted infinite-horizon optimal control problem in Constrained Markov Decision Processes (constrained MDPs), we utilize the natural policy gradient approach. In particular, we introduce a novel Natural Policy Gradient Primal-Dual (NPG-PD) method that updates the primal variable through natural policy gradient ascent and the dual variable via projected sub-gradient descent. Despite the nonconcave nature of the objective function and the nonconvexity of the constraint set, we demonstrate that, under a softmax policy parametrization, our method guarantees global convergence with sublinear rates concerning both the optimality gap and constraint violation. Notably, this convergence performance is dimension-free, remaining unaffected by the size of the state-action space. Additionally, for log-linear and more general smooth policy parametrizations, we establish sublinear convergence rates that account for approximation errors introduced by limited policy representations. We further provide convergence analysis and finite-sample complexity bounds for two sample-based implementations of the NPG-PD algorithm. Ultimately, computational experiments highlight the effectiveness and advantages of our proposed approach.

High-throughput mRNA sequencing (RNA-Seq) is a widely used method for quantifying gene isoform transcripts. However, relying solely on RNA-Seq data often falls short in precisely determining the origins of reads from specific isoforms. To address this challenge, we propose utilizing protein domain-domain interactions as prior knowledge to enhance integrative analysis with RNA-Seq data. We developed a network-based approach called Net-RSTQ (Network-based RNA-Seq Transcript Quantification), which combines protein domain interaction networks with short read alignments to improve transcript abundance estimation. Our approach is founded on the observation that isoforms connected through domain-domain interactions tend to have positively correlated expression levels. Net-RSTQ models the expression of neighboring transcripts as Dirichlet priors, influencing the likelihood of observed read alignments for transcripts within each gene. The overall transcript abundances across multiple genes are then jointly estimated through an iterative process involving the alternating optimization of multiple EM algorithms. Simulation studies demonstrated that Net-RSTQ significantly enhances isoform quantification accuracy, especially when co-expression patterns align with interaction networks. Experimental validation using qRT-PCR on 25 multi-isoform genes across stem cell, ovarian cancer, and breast cancer cell lines further confirmed that Net-RSTQ produced more consistent isoform proportion estimates in agreement with RNA-Seq data. Reinforcement Learning (RL) can be viewed as a sequence modeling task, where a model autoregressively predicts future actions based on a sequence of past state-action-reward experiences. Recently, Transformers have been successfully employed to address this challenge. In this paper, we introduce the State-Action-Reward Transformer (StARformer), a novel approach that explicitly captures local causal relationships to enhance action prediction over long sequences. StARformer begins by extracting local representations—referred to as StAR-representations—from small groups of state-action-reward tokens within brief time windows. These local representations, combined with the overall state information, are then utilized to forecast actions across extended time horizons. Our experimental results demonstrate that StARformer surpasses current leading Transformer-based methods on Atari (image-based) and Gym (state vector-based) benchmarks, excelling in both offline RL and imitation learning scenarios. Additionally, StARformer maintains robust performance with longer input sequences compared to the baseline. The implementation code is accessible at https://github.com/elicassion/StARformer.

This paper introduces a novel convolutional layer called Perturbed Convolution (PConv), designed to achieve two main objectives: enhance the performance of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) and mitigate the issue of discriminator memorization, where the model memorizes all training images over time. PConv works by generating perturbed features through random disturbances applied to the input tensor prior to convolution. Although simple, this method proves to be highly effective. Firstly, to generate consistent outputs despite the perturbations, each discriminator layer must learn robust features characterized by small local Lipschitz constants. Secondly, because the input tensors are randomly perturbed during training—similar to dropout—the approach helps reduce the discriminator’s tendency to memorize training data. To evaluate the generalization capabilities of PConv, we conducted extensive experiments across various loss functions and datasets, including CIFAR-10, CelebA, CelebA-HQ, LSUN, and tiny-ImageNet. The results, measured by the Frechet Inception Distance (FID), demonstrate that PConv significantly improves GAN and conditional GAN performance.

Approximate Bayesian computation (ABC) is a well-established and widely used approach for likelihood-free inference across various fields. Its success largely depends on the availability of effective summary statistics. Selecting appropriate summaries often relies heavily on domain expertise and carefully crafted features, making the process labor-intensive and time-consuming. Because ABC is sensitive to data dimensionality, choosing summary statistics involves balancing the inclusion of informative features with maintaining manageable dimensionality of the feature space. 

This paper introduces a novel approach by framing the selection of an appropriate summary statistic from a pool of candidates as a multi-armed bandit problem. This strategy enables ABC rejection sampling to adaptively focus on a distribution over well-performing summaries rather than relying on a fixed subset. Our method is distinctive in that it requires no prior data preprocessing and is scalable to large collections of candidate statistics. This allows for efficient utilization of extensive libraries of time series summaries without the need for extensive feature engineering upfront. We evaluate the proposed approach against state-of-the-art techniques for summary statistic selection, using a challenging test case from the systems biology domain.

The typical assumption regarding code smells is that they cause poor code quality: detecting a smell, eliminating it, and thereby enhancing the code. In this study, we empirically examine the validity of this assumption. We outline a set of properties that code smells should possess if they truly lead to reduced quality. Our evaluation involved 31,687 Java files from 677 GitHub repositories, all with over 200 commits in 2019. We assessed the impact of smells on four key metrics related to quality, productivity, and bug detection efficiency. Of the 151 code smells identified by the CheckStyle detector, fewer than 20% appeared to be potentially causal, and only a few demonstrated robustness. The most significant smells relate to simplicity, defensive programming, and abstraction. Files lacking these potentially causal smells are 50% more likely to be of high quality. Unfortunately, most smells remain unremoved, as developers tend to eliminate only the easiest ones rather than the most impactful.

We introduce an efficient computational framework designed to accelerate multiple machine learning algorithms with minimal impact on their accuracy. This framework leverages projections through structured matrices, which we term Structured Spinners. These matrices are constructed as products of three structured matrix-blocks incorporating rotations. The approach is highly versatile: i) the structured matrices can be either fully randomized or learned; ii) our family of structured matrices encompasses all previously studied structured schemes as special cases; iii) the framework extends naturally to nonlinear settings where the projections are followed by nonlinear functions; and iv) it has a wide range of applications, including kernel approximation using random feature maps, dimensionality reduction techniques, novel fast cross-polytope Locality-Sensitive Hashing (LSH) methods, deep learning, convex optimization via Newton sketches, quantization through random projection trees, among others. Our framework is supported by theoretical guarantees that relate the model’s capacity to its unstructured counterpart, based on a broad theoretical foundation described in the paper. As a result of our analysis, we present the first theoretical assurances for one of the most effective existing LSH algorithms utilizing the HD3HD2HD1 structured matrix [Andoni et al., 2015]. Extensive experimental evaluations validate the effectiveness and efficiency of our approach.

We introduce any-precision deep neural networks (DNNs), trained using a novel approach that enables the learned models to adapt their numerical precision during inference. The same model can be dynamically configured at runtime to different bit-widths by truncating the least significant bits, allowing for a flexible balance between speed and accuracy. When all layers are set to low-bit modes, our results show that the model maintains accuracy comparable to dedicated models trained at those specific precisions. This desirable property greatly enhances the practical deployment of deep learning models, where trade-offs between accuracy and efficiency are often necessary. Existing methods typically focus on training separate models for fixed efficiency/accuracy points, but achieving a single model capable of adjusting its precision on-the-fly has been largely unexplored. Such flexibility is especially valuable when efficiency and accuracy demands fluctuate over time or change dynamically during runtime, making retraining or storing multiple models impractical. Our framework provides this adaptability without sacrificing performance. Moreover, we demonstrate that this approach is architecture-agnostic and effective across various vision tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/SHI-Labs/Any-Precision-DNNs.

We analyze a population divided into multiple communities and address the challenge of identifying the largest community through sequential, random sampling of individuals. The population is also partitioned into several sampling domains, called \emph{boxes}, which further segment the population. Each box may contain individuals from various communities, and each community may span multiple boxes. The learning agent can, at any point, sample an individual with replacement from any selected box; upon sampling, the agent learns the individual's community affiliation and whether this individual has been previously sampled. The primary objective is to minimize the probability of incorrectly identifying the largest community within a fixed sampling budget, by strategically choosing sampling methods and decision rules. We develop and analyze innovative algorithms for this task and establish information-theoretic lower bounds on the error probability achievable by any algorithm. For several relevant scenarios, we demonstrate that the error decay rates achieved by our algorithms are optimal up to constant factors. Additionally, we validate our approaches through simulations using real-world datasets.

Rectified Linear Units, or ReLUs, have emerged as the standard activation function in artificial neural networks. In this study, we examine two fundamental learning challenges grounded in a generative model based on ReLU networks—a neural network utilizing ReLU activations. Focusing primarily on theoretical insights, we restrict our analysis to a single-layer network. The first challenge pertains to dictionary learning in the context of nonlinearity introduced by ReLU functions. Given a set of observation vectors \(\mathbf{y}^i \in \mathbb{R}^d\) for \(i = 1, 2, \dots, n\), our goal is to recover the matrix \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times k}\) and the corresponding latent vectors \(\{\mathbf{c}^i\} \subset \mathbb{R}^k\) under the model

\[
\mathbf{y}^i = \mathrm{ReLU}(A\mathbf{c}^i + \mathbf{b}),
\]

where \(\mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{R}^d\) is a random bias. We demonstrate that, under certain conditions on the distribution of \(\mathbf{b}\), it is feasible to approximate the column space of \(A\) with an error bounded by \(O(d)\) in Frobenius norm. The second challenge addresses the robust recovery of signals amid sparse, large-magnitude noise or outliers. Here, the focus is on reconstructing the latent vector \(\mathbf{c}\) from its noisy, nonlinear measurements of the form

\[

\]

We explore a data-driven methodology for constructing uncertainty sets in robust optimization, where the uncertain parameters are modeled as random variables with an unknown joint distribution. Using only independent samples from this distribution, we develop a nonparametric technique to estimate uncertainty sets that probabilistically approximate a specified target mass within a predefined margin, with high confidence. Our nonparametric estimators are also demonstrated to satisfy distribution-free finite-sample performance bounds, ensuring their convergence in probability to the desired target mass. Besides their computational efficiency, these estimators produce uncertainty sets that lead to robust optimization problems—applicable to a broad class of constraint functions—that are computationally manageable.

Inspired by the learned iterative soft thresholding algorithm (LISTA), we propose a broad class of neural networks designed for sparse reconstruction from limited linear measurements. By permitting a flexible degree of weight-sharing across layers, our framework facilitates a unified analysis encompassing various neural network architectures, from recurrent models to conventional feedforward networks. Using training data and empirical risk minimization, our goal is to identify the optimal network parameters that best reconstruct signals from their low-dimensional linear observations. We establish generalization bounds by examining the Rademacher complexity of the hypothesis classes formed by these deep networks, incorporating the influence of thresholding parameters. Our analysis yields sample complexity estimates that scale approximately linearly with the number of parameters and the network depth. Furthermore, we demonstrate the applicability of our main findings by deriving specific generalization guarantees for several practical scenarios, including different approaches to (implicit) dictionary learning and convolutional neural networks.

Comparing the top \(k\) elements across two or more ranked lists is a common task in various fields and contexts. Several measures have been proposed to evaluate the similarity of top \(k\) lists, each exhibiting appealing mathematical properties. However, these methods often encounter practical limitations and shortcomings. In this work, we introduce a novel measure for comparing any two top \(k\) lists based on the information they convey. Our approach examines the lists' compressibility, with the length of a lossless encoding serving as a natural and robust indicator of their variability. This information-theoretic measure objectively encompasses key aspects of list comparison, including the degree of non-overlapping elements in each list, the level of disorder among shared elements, and the displacement of their actual ranks.

Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) is commonly employed to optimize non-convex functions; however, traditional convergence analyses in smooth non-convex scenarios typically indicate a slow, sublinear rate toward a stationary point. In this paper, we establish several convergence theorems demonstrating that SGD can achieve convergence to a global minimum under certain additional structural assumptions on the problem. We concentrate on two prominent classes of structured non-convex functions: (i) Quasar (Strongly) Convex functions, which extend the concept of convexity, and (ii) functions satisfying the Polyak-Lojasiewicz condition, a broader generalization of strong convexity. Our approach hinges on an Expected Residual condition, which we prove to be strictly weaker than previously utilized growth conditions, expected smoothness, or bounded variance assumptions. We derive theoretical guarantees for SGD convergence employing various step-size strategies, including constant, diminishing, and the recently introduced stochastic Polyak step-size. Furthermore, our analysis is valid under the arbitrary sampling framework, providing valuable insights into minibatch complexity and enabling the determination of an optimal minibatch size. Lastly, for models that interpolate the training data, we demonstrate that the Expected Residual condition can be omitted, leading to state-of-the-art convergence results in this setting.

The issue of data imbalance often hampers the classification accuracy of neural networks. In this study, we introduce a novel supervised discriminative feature generation (DFG) approach tailored for datasets with minority classes. DFG leverages an enhanced generative adversarial network architecture composed of four separate components: a generator, a discriminator, a feature extractor, and a classifier. To enrich the discriminative features of the minority class, we incorporate an attention mechanism into the training process, which guides the generator in producing more relevant features for the imbalanced target task. Furthermore, the feature extractor and classifier are regularized using pre-trained features derived from a large, balanced source dataset. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that the DFG generator effectively augments label-preserving and diverse features, leading to a marked improvement in classification performance on the target dataset. This feature generation framework significantly advances data augmentation techniques by combining discriminative feature synthesis with supervised attention mechanisms.

We investigate the challenge of identifying the optimal arm in a stochastic multi-armed bandit setting. Consider a collection of \( n \) arms labeled from 1 to \( n \), each associated with an unknown reward distribution supported on the interval \([0,1]\), characterized by mean \(\theta_i\) and variance \(\sigma_i^2\). We assume that the means satisfy \(\theta_1 > \theta_2 \geq \cdots \geq \theta_n\). We introduce an adaptive algorithm that dynamically explores the gaps \(\Delta_i\) and variances \(\sigma_i^2\) of the arms, making informed decisions based on accumulated data through a novel \textit{grouped median elimination} technique. This method guarantees identification of the best arm with probability at least \( 1 - \delta \), using no more than
\[ O \left( \sum_{i=1}^n \left( \frac{\sigma_i^2}{\Delta_i^2} + \frac{1}{\Delta_i} \right) (\ln \delta^{-1} + \ln \ln \Delta_i^{-1}) \right) \]
samples, where \(\Delta_i\) for \( i \geq 2 \) denotes the reward gap between arm \( i \) and the optimal arm, and \(\Delta_1 = \Delta_2\). This approach offers notable improvements over variance-agnostic algorithms in certain favorable conditions and marks the first result to eliminate the additional \(\ln n\) factor on the best arm when compared to existing leading methods. Furthermore, we establish that any algorithm aiming for the same goal must utilize at least
