Time series data frequently contain outliers or other types of anomalies that can distort analysis. Detecting these unusual points can be valuable in itself (anomaly detection) or serve to enhance the accuracy of other tasks such as forecasting. Recent deep learning methods for anomaly detection and forecasting often assume that the proportion of anomalies in training data is minimal and therefore treat all unlabeled data as normal, representing the typical data distribution. 

We propose a straightforward yet powerful approach to enhance existing time series models by explicitly incorporating the presence of anomalies in the training process. This is achieved by introducing a latent anomaly indicator variable into the training data, whose distribution is inferred during model training through Monte Carlo Expectation-Maximization (EM). Our technique enables the simultaneous identification of anomalous points and improves the model’s performance on nominal data. 

To demonstrate the effectiveness of this method, we integrate it with a simple feed-forward forecasting model. We also examine how anomalies in the training set impact the training of forecasting models used for time series anomaly detection, showing that our approach leads to better model training and reliability.

Accurate blood cell counts are essential for diagnosing conditions like leukemia and anemia. Typically, hematologists manually annotate and count cells in microscopy images. However, differentiating cells at various maturation stages can be challenging due to image noise and subjective judgment, leading to labeling errors. These inaccuracies often lack reproducibility and can adversely impact diagnosis accuracy. To address this issue, we present TIMELY, a probabilistic model that integrates pseudotime inference with inhomogeneous hidden Markov trees to tackle label inconsistencies. Our initial tests on simulated data demonstrate that TIMELY outperforms baseline correction methods by more accurately identifying and rectifying incorrect labels. We further validate our approach on two real-world blood cell datasets, where TIMELY effectively detects inconsistent labels and enhances the overall quality of human annotations.

Bayesian optimization is commonly applied to the tuning of black-box or highly complex functions, particularly those representing intricate real-world systems in industrial environments. Although these functions may have explicit formulations, traditional optimization methods often struggle to deliver validated solutions or assurance of correctness. In this paper, we propose an approach that integrates Bayesian optimization with SMT-based constraint solving, enabling the attainment of safe, reliable solutions with provable optimality guarantees.

In this paper, we introduce an innovative approach to address the challenge of monocular 3D lane detection by harnessing the underlying geometric structure involved in the process of converting 2D to 3D lane reconstructions. Building on previous techniques, we begin by examining the geometric relationships between 3D lanes and their 2D ground representations, and we propose to incorporate explicit supervision based on these structural priors. This enables the establishment of inter-lane and intra-lane relationships, thereby enhancing the accuracy of 3D lane reconstruction from local details to a global perspective. Additionally, to mitigate structural inaccuracies in 2D lane representations, we extract top-view lane information directly from front-view images, significantly reducing confusion caused by distant lane features that hinder previous methods. Furthermore, we introduce a novel, task-specific data augmentation strategy that synthesizes new training samples for both segmentation and reconstruction tasks. This approach addresses the imbalance in camera pose and ground slope data, thereby boosting the model's generalization capabilities on unseen scenarios. Our work pioneers the integration of geometric prior information into deep neural network-based 3D lane detection, enabling the system to detect lanes at twice the original distance. The proposed method can be seamlessly integrated into other frameworks, paving the way for more robust long-range lane detection.

Word embeddings enhance NLP system performance by uncovering the hidden structural relationships between words. Although they have achieved notable success across various applications, their use in computational social science NLP tasks remains limited, likely due to their dependence on large datasets and challenges in interpretability. I introduce a probabilistic, model-based approach to word embeddings that can produce interpretable representations without requiring extensive data. The core idea involves leveraging mixed membership modeling, where global representations are shared across words, but each individual word can utilize these representations to varying degrees uniquely. The model is trained using a combination of cutting-edge techniques from both word embedding and topic modeling research. Experimental results indicate a significant improvement in predictive language modeling, with up to 63% higher mean reciprocal rank (MRR) compared to the skip-gram model, and demonstrate that these representations are advantageous for supervised learning tasks. To showcase the interpretability of the model, I present case studies analyzing State of the Union addresses and NIPS articles within the context of computational social science.

Exploring large-scale pretrained foundation models is highly valuable in computer vision, as these models facilitate rapid transfer to a variety of downstream applications. This paper introduces Contrastive Captioner (CoCa), a streamlined architecture designed to pretrain an image-text encoder-decoder foundation model using combined contrastive and captioning losses. This approach integrates the strengths of contrastive methods like CLIP and generative techniques such as SimVLM. Unlike conventional encoder-decoder transformers where all decoder layers attend to the encoder output, CoCa strategically omits cross-attention in the initial half of the decoder layers to develop unimodal text representations, while the remaining layers perform cross-attention with the image encoder to generate rich multimodal image-text representations. We incorporate a contrastive loss between unimodal image and text embeddings alongside a captioning loss on the decoder outputs, which autoregressively predicts text tokens. Both objectives share the same computational graph, enabling efficient training with minimal overhead. CoCa is trained end-to-end from scratch on large-scale web-based alt-text data and annotated images by representing all labels as text, effectively unifying natural language supervision for representation learning. Empirical results demonstrate that CoCa achieves state-of-the-art performance in zero-shot transfer and requires little task-specific adaptation across a wide range of downstream visual recognition tasks.

The exchange algorithm stands as one of the most widely used extensions of the Metropolis–Hastings method for sampling from doubly-intractable distributions. Despite its popularity, there has been limited theoretical investigation into its properties. Key questions—such as whether the exchange algorithm converges at a geometric rate or whether it satisfies a Central Limit Theorem—remain open. In this work, we explore the theoretical characteristics of the exchange algorithm with a focus on its asymptotic variance and convergence rate. We compare it to the original Metropolis–Hastings algorithm and establish necessary and sufficient conditions for its geometric ergodicity. Additionally, we demonstrate that our findings are applicable to a variety of practical models, including location models, Gaussian models, Poisson models, and a broad class of exponential families, encompassing most scenarios where the exchange algorithm is employed. We also prove a Central Limit Theorem for the exchange algorithm. Our results provide a solid theoretical foundation that affirms the algorithm’s validity and usefulness.

The automated classification of texts into predefined categories has experienced a significant surge in interest over the past decade, driven by the rising availability of digital documents and the growing need for efficient organization. Within the research community, the prevailing method for tackling this challenge is centered on machine learning techniques, which utilize an inductive process to automatically develop classifiers. This process involves learning from a set of pre-labeled documents to identify the features characteristic of each category. Compared to knowledge engineering—where domain experts manually define classifiers—this machine learning approach offers high effectiveness, substantial reductions in expert effort, and easy adaptability across different fields. This survey explores the primary machine learning-based strategies for text categorization, with a particular focus on three key issues: how documents are represented, how classifiers are built, and how their performance is evaluated.

In this paper, we revisit the often-overlooked classical Semi-Supervised Distance Metric Learning (SSDML) problem through the lens of Riemannian geometry, enabling the integration of stochastic optimization within a comprehensive end-to-end deep learning framework. Our motivation stems from the observation that, aside from a few classical approaches focused on learning linear Mahalanobis metrics, the exploration of deep SSDML remains largely unexplored. We first adapt existing SSDML techniques to their deep variants, then introduce a novel method designed to address their inherent limitations. Given the constraints on our metric parameters, we employ Riemannian optimization techniques. Our proposed deep SSDML approach, featuring a unique affinity propagation-based triplet mining strategy, significantly outperforms existing methods.

This paper introduces a novel framework for anomaly detection. The core concept involves reducing the data to a two-dimensional space and ranking each point within this reduced representation. Our approach estimates the level of anomaly by analyzing both the spatial and density characteristics of the data. Specifically, we convert data points into a density space and measure the distances between each point and its k-nearest neighbors in the spatial domain within this density context. Subsequently, an anomaly coordinate system is constructed by capturing two unilateral anomalies from the k-nearest neighbors of each point. Additionally, we propose two methods to model the correlation between these anomalies and combine them to derive a comprehensive anomaly score. Experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that our method performs effectively and achieves the highest average accuracy. We also highlight that our approach facilitates straightforward visualization and classification of anomalies. Given the complexity of anomaly patterns, no single existing method excels across all benchmark datasets. Our framework considers both spatial and density domains and can be tailored to different datasets by fine-tuning a few parameters.

We introduce a novel approach to the classical problem of dictionary learning, also known as "sparse coding," which involves recovering an unknown \( n \times m \) matrix \( A \) (where \( m \geq n \)) from observed examples of the form \[ y = Ax + e, \] with \( x \) being a random vector in \(\mathbb{R}^m\) that has at most \(\tau m \) nonzero entries, and \( e \) a random noise vector in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) with bounded magnitude. For scenarios where \( m = O(n) \), our method can recover each column of \( A \) with arbitrarily close constant accuracy in time \( m^{O(\log m / \log(\tau^{-1}))} \). This means that, in particular, the algorithm runs in polynomial time when \(\tau = m^{-\delta}\) for any \(\delta > 0\), and in time \( m^{O(\log m)} \) if \(\tau\) is a sufficiently small constant. Previous algorithms under similar distributional assumptions demanded that \( x \) be significantly sparser—containing at most \(\sqrt{n}\) nonzero entries—and faced fundamental limitations preventing their extension to denser vectors \( x \). Our breakthrough stems from developing an algorithm for noisy tensor decomposition capable of approximately extracting rank-one components of a tensor \( T \), given access to a tensor \( T' \) that is within \(\tau \) spectral norm distance of \( T \) (viewed as a matrix). To our knowledge, this represents the first algorithmic result for tensor decomposition under such general noisy conditions.

The recent deployment of Google TPU-v3 Pods in the industry-standard MLPerf v0.6 training benchmark showcases the scalability of a broad range of relevant ML models. MLPerf provides a comprehensive set of models, datasets, and guidelines to ensure fair and comparable benchmarking across different hardware, frameworks, and organizations. Utilizing this benchmark suite, we explore various optimizations and techniques—including the selection of optimizers, spatial partitioning strategies, and weight update sharding—necessary to achieve scaling across 1024 TPU chips. Additionally, we highlight model characteristics that pose scalability challenges, such as limited data parallelism and unscaled weights. These optimization efforts have enabled record-breaking performance for transformer models, ResNet-50, and SSD within Google’s MLPerf v0.6 submission.

Clustering serves as a fundamental component of contemporary statistical analysis workflows. In recent years, fair clustering has garnered significant attention within the machine learning community. Our work is among the first to explore fairness in the realm of hierarchical clustering, building upon the foundational results of Ahmadian et al. presented at NeurIPS 2020. We assess our methods using Dasgupta's cost function, a widely adopted theoretical metric for hierarchical clustering evaluation. Our approach significantly advances prior work by improving the fair approximation of cost from the previous \( O(n^{5/6} \, poly\log(n)) \) to a near-polylogarithmic \( O(n^\delta \, poly\log(n)) \) for any constant \(\delta \in (0,1)\). This breakthrough reveals a fundamental cost-fairness tradeoff and broadens the scope to include more comprehensive fairness constraints than previously considered. Additionally, we demonstrate techniques to modify existing hierarchical clusterings to ensure fairness and maintain balanced clusters at any level within the hierarchy.

Set functions are functions (or signals) indexed by the powerset—the collection of all subsets—of a finite set N. They are essential and widely applied across numerous fields, serving as formal tools to describe or measure aspects such as loss functions in semantic image segmentation, the informativeness of sensors within sensor networks, the utility of item collections in recommender systems, cooperative game analyses in game theory, and bidding strategies in combinatorial auctions. Notably, the subclass of submodular functions plays a significant role in optimization and machine learning challenges. 

In this paper, we introduce discrete-set signal processing (SP), a new shift-invariant linear framework tailored for set functions. This approach defines different types of shifts based on set union and difference operations. For each shift type, we establish corresponding concepts of shift-invariant filters, convolution, Fourier transform, and frequency response. To illustrate our framework, we introduce the generalized coverage function and demonstrate how multivariate mutual information emerges as a particular case of a discrete-set spectrum. We also explore the concept of frequency ordering within this context.

Our work provides a fresh set of analytical and processing tools for set functions, especially addressing their exponential complexity. We illustrate two preliminary applications and experiments, including compression techniques for submodular functions.

Community detection in networks serves as a vital exploratory tool across various domains, including uncovering social and biological communities and spotting link farms on the Web. The challenge of identifying communities or clusters within a network has garnered significant interest from fields such as statistics, physics, and computer science. Nonetheless, many clustering methods rely on knowing the number of clusters, k, in advance. In this work, we introduce a method to automatically determine k for graphs generated by a Stochastic Blockmodel. Our primary contributions are twofold: first, we rigorously derive the asymptotic distribution of the leading eigenvalue of the appropriately centered and scaled adjacency matrix, leveraging this for a hypothesis testing framework; second, we develop a recursive bipartitioning procedure based on this test. Through quantitative assessments on real-world networks with known ground truth, we demonstrate that our approach surpasses existing probabilistic models in detecting overlapping communities and, in the absence of labels, reveals nested community structures.

Classifiers are frequently evaluated using relatively small datasets, which can result in uncertain performance metrics. Despite this, these metrics are often accepted without question. We propose a method to quantify the uncertainty in classification performance metrics by employing a probabilistic model of the confusion matrix. Applying our approach to classifiers from scientific studies and a classification competition reveals that uncertainties can be unexpectedly large, thereby constraining the reliability of performance assessments. In some cases, published classifiers may be misleading due to these uncertainties. Our method is straightforward to implement, requiring only the confusion matrix, and is independent of the specific classifier used. Additionally, it can be utilized to determine the necessary sample size to achieve a desired level of precision in a performance metric.

A novel variational autoencoder (VAE) framework is introduced, designed to learn a compact shared representation of two interrelated data variables for both conditional and joint generation tasks. The Wyner VAE is grounded in two fundamental information-theoretic challenges—distributed simulation and channel synthesis—where Wyner’s common information defines the core limit on how concise the shared representation can be. This model decomposes a pair of correlated data variables into their common component (such as a shared concept) and individual local features that account for the remaining variability (like texture or style). It achieves this by incorporating a regularization term that constrains the mutual information between each data variable and the shared representation. The effectiveness of the Wyner VAE is validated through experiments involving both synthetic and real image data, demonstrating its capability for joint and conditional generation, with or without style modulation. Results indicate that learning a concise common representation enhances generative quality and that the proposed model surpasses existing VAE variants and the variational information bottleneck approach.

Research into model-free learning for multi-agent stochastic games is an ongoing and vibrant field. However, most current reinforcement learning methods are mainly limited to zero-sum scenarios and are effective only within small state-action spaces or simplified environments. In this work, we introduce a novel, data-efficient Deep-Q-learning approach designed to learn Nash equilibria in general-sum stochastic games without relying on a model. Our method employs a local linear-quadratic expansion of the stochastic game, enabling the derivation of analytically solvable optimal actions. This expansion is parameterized by deep neural networks, providing the flexibility needed to adapt to the environment without requiring comprehensive exploration of all state-action combinations. Additionally, we explore symmetry properties of the algorithm that arise from label-invariant stochastic games. As a demonstration, we apply our approach to develop optimal trading strategies in competitive electronic markets.

With the rapid expansion of information technology, multi-view graph data has become increasingly widespread and valuable. Most current multi-view clustering methods either concentrate on multiple graphs or multi-view attributes separately. In this paper, we introduce a versatile framework for clustering multi-view attributed graph data. Drawing inspiration from the success of contrastive learning, we present the Multi-View Contrastive Graph Clustering (MCGC) technique, designed to learn a unified consensus graph, as the original graph may be noisy or incomplete and thus unsuitable for direct use. Our approach involves two primary steps: first, we eliminate undesirable high-frequency noise while maintaining the graph’s geometric features through graph filtering, resulting in a smooth node representation; second, we learn a consensus graph guided by a graph contrastive loss. Experimental results on several benchmark datasets demonstrate our method’s superiority over existing state-of-the-art approaches. Notably, our straightforward approach surpasses current deep learning-based methods in performance.

Radio-frequency dosimetry plays a crucial role in ensuring human safety and verifying compliance of related devices. Recently, computational human models derived from medical imaging have become increasingly popular for such evaluations, particularly to account for individual variability among subjects. However, creating personalized models is often time-consuming due to the extensive segmentation of multiple biological tissue components, which hampers the ability to efficiently assess radiation safety on a personalized basis. Leveraging the strengths of deep learning, known for excellent pattern recognition and signal analysis capabilities, offers a promising solution. Convolutional neural networks with deep architectures have demonstrated robustness in extracting features and mapping images across various biomedical applications. In this work, we introduce a learning-based method for rapid and precise estimation of tissue dielectric properties and density directly from magnetic resonance images in a single step. This approach produces smoothly distributed dielectric properties in head models without requiring tissue segmentation, resulting in a more uniform specific absorption rate (SAR) distribution compared to traditional methods. The SAR distributions estimated by our method, including the average over a 10-gram tissue cube, show a high degree of consistency with established reference data.

Human behavior expression and experience are inherently multi-modal, exhibiting significant individual and contextual variability. To facilitate effective human-computer and human-robot interactions, it is essential to develop multi-modal models that accurately capture user states, such as engagement. Existing approaches to building classifiers for these states typically assume fully labeled training data, but data annotation is costly, time-consuming, and often subject to human biases—especially when dealing with multi-modal data, where some users may express themselves more through facial cues while others rely more on vocal cues. Consequently, creating models capable of reliably estimating user states during interactions remains a complex challenge. 

To address this, we introduce a novel multi-modal active learning (AL) framework that leverages deep reinforcement learning (RL) to optimize the selection of user data required for training modality-specific models. We explore various strategies for combining multi-modal data, demonstrating that model-level fusion integrated with RL surpasses feature-level fusion, modality-specific approaches, as well as traditional AL techniques like random sampling and heuristic methods such as uncertainty sampling. Our results highlight the advantages of this approach in enhancing model performance and efficiency.

Community detection plays a vital role in enhancing our understanding of the functions and structures within complex networks. Consequently, the methods employed to evaluate community detection must be designed to minimize bias and prevent inaccuracies that could compromise subsequent analysis or practical applications relying on these communities. Typically, two principal evaluation strategies are employed: structural and functional. The structural approach involves identifying and analyzing communities through various algorithms and structural metrics. Conversely, the functional approach is applicable when ground truth data are available, allowing for direct assessment of the detected communities. Nonetheless, evaluations based on these strategies are often conducted within experimental setups that are highly vulnerable to biases stemming from the algorithms, metrics, and network data utilized. Moreover, these strategies are rarely integrated systematically, hindering the identification and correction of biases across different components to achieve more reliable results. Against this backdrop, the primary contribution of this paper is the development of a robust framework for quality assessment in community detection within real-world networks. We address the challenge of creating rankings in recommender systems that are fair to both users and content creators. Our scope includes traditional recommendations such as music and movies, as well as reciprocal recommendations like dating. Drawing on principles of distributive justice from welfare economics, our definition of fairness focuses on improving the well-being of the least advantaged individuals. We formalize this idea through Lorenz efficiency, which ensures that rankings are Pareto optimal and maximize utility redistribution from those better off to those worse off without sacrificing total utility. Our method involves optimizing concave welfare functions to generate fairer rankings, employing an efficient inference technique based on the Frank-Wolfe algorithm. We demonstrate that, unlike existing fairness approaches constrained by fixed criteria, our framework consistently produces fair rankings. Furthermore, our experimental results indicate that our approach enhances the welfare of the most disadvantaged users while incurring lower costs in terms of the overall utility.

Most existing methods in deep reinforcement learning (DRL) focus on mastering a single task at a time. Consequently, current research benchmarks typically consist of individual games or groups of games with standardized interfaces but minimal overlap in perceptual features, objectives, or reward structures. To advance research in knowledge transfer among trained agents—such as through multi-task and meta-learning—there is a pressing need for more versatile environment suites that offer configurable tasks sharing enough commonality for collective study. In this paper, we introduce Meta Arcade, a tool designed for easy creation and customization of 2D arcade games that share visual styles, state and action spaces, game components, and scoring systems. Unlike previous environments, Meta Arcade emphasizes both task commonality and flexibility: entire sets of games can be built from shared elements, which are adjustable via user-defined parameters. We showcase a collection of 24 predefined games that demonstrate the framework's capabilities and discuss how these games can be tailored for various research purposes. Additionally, we present several experiments illustrating potential applications, including single-task benchmarks, curriculum-based approaches that progressively modify game parameters, and exploratory studies into...

Recent research has increasingly focused on utilizing deep learning models to forecast resource consumption patterns of SQL queries. As many organizations rely on cloud platforms to support their data lakes for extensive analytics, these models play a crucial role in managing cloud resource provisioning. Although they have shown promising levels of accuracy, training these models on large-scale industry workloads remains costly. The inefficiencies in encoding techniques—such as the extensive padding required to standardize the shapes of diverse query plans—lead to longer training times and necessitate high-cost, scaled-up infrastructure for batch processing. To address these challenges, we introduced Prestroid, a data science pipeline built on tree convolution that accurately predicts query trace resource consumption at a significantly reduced cost. We tested our pipeline on 19,000 Presto OLAP queries from Grab, utilizing a data lake exceeding 20 petabytes. The results indicate that Prestroid surpasses existing benchmarks in predictive accuracy, enabling more precise resource management for large workloads. Furthermore, it reduces per-batch memory usage by 13.5 times and cuts per-epoch training time by 3.45 times, ultimately leading to substantial cost savings.

To develop effective sequential recommenders, we introduce a series of sequence representation learning (SRL) techniques designed to model users' historical behaviors. Existing SRL methods predominantly depend on explicit item IDs to construct sequence models, thereby capturing user preferences. While effective to a degree, these approaches face challenges when applied to new recommendation environments, as their reliance on specific item IDs limits their transferability. To address this, we propose a novel universal sequence representation learning framework called UniSRec. This method leverages the descriptive texts associated with items to learn representations that are transferable across diverse recommendation scenarios. For universal item representation learning, we implement a compact encoding architecture that combines parametric whitening with a mixture-of-experts enhanced adaptor. To achieve universal sequence representations, we incorporate two contrastive pre-training tasks that sample multi-domain negatives. Equipped with this pre-trained universal sequence model, our approach can be efficiently adapted to new recommendation domains or platforms, whether in inductive or transductive settings, with minimal parameter overhead. Extensive evaluations on real-world datasets validate the effectiveness of our approach, highlighting its superior performance and demonstrating its strong transferability across different platforms.

Distributional word representations, commonly known as word vectors, have become essential in modern natural language processing due to their extensive applications. Recently, there has been a surge in postprocessing algorithms aimed at enhancing the quality of pre-existing word vectors. Building on these developments, we propose a novel postprocessing approach grounded in a causal inference framework. Specifically, our method employs Half-Sibling Regression (HSR) to identify and eliminate confounding noise within word vectors. Unlike prior techniques, our approach offers greater interpretability and transparency through its causal inference foundation. When evaluated across various standard lexical tasks and downstream sentiment analysis applications, our method achieves state-of-the-art results.

Understanding how to acquire innate skills from environments without relying on external rewards or supervision, similar to human learning, remains a significant challenge. In response, we introduce a novel unsupervised skill discovery approach called Information Bottleneck Option Learning (IBOL). By leveraging environment linearization techniques that facilitate broader and more distant state transitions, IBOL promotes the emergence of a diverse range of skills. It abstracts these skills within an information bottleneck framework, enhancing stability and fostering disentanglement of learned options. Empirical results demonstrate that IBOL surpasses several leading unsupervised skill discovery methods in both information-theoretic assessments and downstream tasks across MuJoCo environments, including Ant, HalfCheetah, Hopper, and D'Kitty.

In this study, we investigate various Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) architectures and their variants for binary fire detection and localization in both video and still images, without considering temporal information. We examine the performance of simplified, experimentally designed deep CNN models tailored for this task and analyze the impact of different optimization and normalization techniques across several architectures, including Inception, ResNet, and EfficientNet. Contrary to current trends, our results demonstrate a maximum overall accuracy of 0.96 for full-frame binary fire detection and 0.94 for superpixel-based localization, achieved with an experimentally optimized InceptionV4-inspired CNN architecture. Additionally, we attain a notably low false positive rate of 0.06, surpassing previous methods, and provide an efficient, robust, and real-time solution for fire region detection.

Parameterized actions in reinforcement learning consist of discrete choices accompanied by continuous action parameters. This framework enables the solution of complex tasks that require integrating high-level decisions with precise control. The recent P-DQN algorithm extends deep Q-networks to operate within such action spaces; however, it consolidates all action-parameters into a single joint input for the Q-network, undermining its theoretical validity. We examine the shortcomings of this method and introduce a novel approach called Multi-Pass Deep Q-Networks (MP-DQN) to address these issues. Empirical results show that MP-DQN substantially surpasses P-DQN and other prior algorithms in data efficiency and policy performance across the Platform, Robot Soccer Goal, and Half Field Offense environments.

We explore how to imitate tasks across different domains that exhibit discrepancies such as differences in embodiment, viewpoint, and dynamics. Many existing methods depend on paired, aligned demonstrations and incorporate additional reinforcement learning (RL) steps that require environment interactions, which are often costly and difficult to obtain. To address these challenges, we formalize the Domain Adaptive Imitation Learning (DAIL) problem, a comprehensive framework for imitation learning amid variations in embodiment, viewpoint, and dynamics. In essence, DAIL focuses on learning to perform a specified task optimally when only demonstrations from a different domain are available. 

Our approach to DAIL involves two key phases: alignment followed by adaptation. During the alignment phase, we introduce a novel unsupervised Markov Decision Process (MDP) alignment technique called Generative Adversarial MDP Alignment (GAMA), which discovers correspondences between states and actions from unpaired, unaligned demonstrations. In the adaptation phase, these correspondences are utilized to enable zero-shot task imitation across domains. 

Furthermore, we establish a theoretical framework called MDP alignability to determine when DAIL is achievable through alignment and adaptation. Our experiments evaluate GAMA against various baseline methods in scenarios involving embodiment, viewpoint, and dynamics mismatches, particularly where aligned demonstrations are unavailable. The results demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of our approach.

Recent interest in learning differential equation models from time series has grown, yet existing methods often struggle with highly noisy data. We address this challenge by dividing the problem into two parts: (i) approximating the unknown vector field (or right-hand side) of the differential equation, and (ii) managing noise. To tackle (i), we introduce a neural network architecture built from tensor products of one-dimensional neural shape functions. For (ii), we develop an alternating minimization approach that oscillates between training the vector field and applying filtering techniques, utilizing multiple trajectories of training data. Our results show that the neural shape function architecture preserves the approximation capabilities of dense neural networks, facilitates precise computation of vector field errors, and offers visual interpretability, applicable to systems in any finite dimension \(d\). Additionally, we explore combining our neural shape function method or other existing differential equation learning techniques with the alternating minimization scheme and multiple trajectories. This combination significantly enhances robustness to noise; while the original methods face difficulties with 1% Gaussian noise, their retrofitted versions successfully learn accurate vector fields from data contaminated with up to 10% Gaussian noise.

Unlike the traditional classification approach where each training example is labeled with its true class, complementary-label learning assigns each sample a label indicating one class it does not belong to. This paper aims to establish a new framework for complementary-label learning that provides an unbiased estimation of the classification risk applicable to arbitrary loss functions and models—an achievement that previous methods have not accomplished. This advancement not only enhances the training process but also enables model and hyperparameter selection via cross-validation without relying on normally labeled validation data, regardless of whether linear or nonlinear models and convex or non-convex loss functions are used. Additionally, we refine the risk estimator with a non-negative correction and a gradient ascent technique, demonstrating its effectiveness through comprehensive experiments.

Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are fundamental to many deep learning applications. Nonetheless, their substantial storage requirements and high computational demands pose challenges for hardware accelerators. Computing-in-memory (CIM) architectures have shown significant promise in efficiently executing large-scale matrix-vector multiplications. Despite this progress, the intensive multiply-accumulate (MAC) operations within crossbar arrays and the limited capacity of CIM macros serve as barriers to further enhancing energy efficiency and throughput. To mitigate computation costs, techniques such as network pruning and quantization are commonly employed to reduce model size. However, most of these model compression methods are primarily designed for digital CNN accelerators and do not account for hardware constraints inherent to SRAM-based CIM systems. Implementing these methods on SRAM CIM accelerators requires careful consideration of factors like the number of word lines and bit lines accessible simultaneously, as well as effective strategies for mapping weights onto SRAM macros. In this work, we introduce a combined software-hardware co-design framework to develop an SRAM CIM-based CNN accelerator alongside a CIM-aware model compression algorithm. We introduce an oracle-efficient algorithm designed to enhance the adversarial robustness of barely robust learners. These learners typically develop predictors that are only adversarially robust on a small portion \(\beta \ll 1\) of the data distribution. Our new concept of barely robust learning demands robustness against a "larger" perturbation set; we demonstrate that this requirement is essential for achieving strong robustness and that weaker relaxations do not suffice for fully robust learning. Our findings establish both a qualitative and quantitative equivalence between two seemingly distinct problems: strongly robust learning and barely robust learning.

Interactive machine learning (IML) is an emerging research domain focused on integrating human insights and computational capabilities to enhance decision-making systems. It involves a collaborative effort between diverse human and machine intelligence systems, each bringing their distinct strengths and constraints to the table. This collaboration can occur through simultaneous actions or sequential processes. Key open questions in IML include: "How can we design systems that continuously improve their decision-making through human interaction?" and "What are the best methods to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of these systems?" Neglecting proper consideration of human participants can lead to undesirable behaviors and raise concerns around fairness, accountability, and transparency. Therefore, this work aims to provide a human-centered framework for designing and assessing IML systems, aiming to minimize associated risks. This guide is intended for machine learning practitioners tasked with ensuring the safety, wellbeing, and ethical integrity of human interactions. Upholding principles of honesty, fairness, and legal compliance is essential in responsible public engagement. Guided by these values, we as a machine learning community...

Takagi-Sugeno-Kang (TSK) fuzzy systems are highly effective machine learning models for regression tasks. However, to date, no training algorithm has demonstrated both efficiency and robustness in ensuring their generalization capabilities while handling large-scale data. Drawing from the parallels between TSK fuzzy systems and neural networks, we have adapted three advanced neural network optimization techniques—mini-batch gradient descent, regularization, and AdaBound—to TSK fuzzy systems. Additionally, we introduce three novel methods tailored specifically for training TSK fuzzy systems: DropRule, DropMembership, and DropMF. Our comprehensive training approach, termed MBGD-RDA—combining mini-batch gradient descent with regularization, DropRule, and AdaBound—facilitates rapid convergence and improved generalization during testing. This method is versatile and applicable to datasets of any size, with particular advantages for large datasets where existing training algorithms fall short in efficiency.

Neural implicit fields are rapidly gaining popularity as an effective representation for learning-based approaches. However, leveraging them for 3D shape modeling and editing presents significant challenges. In response, we propose a novel method called SPAGHETTI—short for E—diting I—mportant S—hapes T—hrough P—art Aware G—eneration. Our framework facilitates the manipulation of implicit shapes through transforming, interpolating, and combining shape segments, all without the need for explicit part annotations. SPAGHETTI separates shape parts into extrinsic and intrinsic geometric features, enabling a generative system with fine-grained, part-level control. We demonstrate the effectiveness of SPAGHETTI through an interactive graphical interface that allows users to directly edit neural implicit shapes with ease.

Accurate house price prediction holds significant importance for various real estate stakeholders including homeowners, prospective buyers, investors, and agents. We introduce a location-centric prediction framework that distinguishes itself from existing approaches through innovative data profiling and modeling techniques. For data profiling, we establish a detailed and granular location profile leveraging diverse sources such as transportation data (e.g., proximity to the nearest train station), educational information (e.g., school zones and rankings), neighborhood demographics based on census data, and local facilities (e.g., nearby hospitals and supermarkets). Regarding prediction models, we observe that many existing methods either utilize the entire housing dataset for modeling or divide the data into segments and build separate models for each, overlooking the relationships between segments. The latter approach often suffers from insufficient training samples per partition. To overcome this, we explore the application of Multi-Task Learning (MTL), aligning data partitioning strategies with task definitions in MTL—each partition corresponds to a distinct task. We further evaluate various MTL-based methods with different regularization techniques to enhance prediction accuracy and leverage inter-partition relatedness.

We address the challenge of operating within an unknown finite and discrete Markov Decision Process (MDP), where the expected shortest path between any two states is bounded by a known finite value \( D \). An MDP is characterized by \( S \) states and \( A \) possible actions at each state. At each time step \( t \), selecting action \( a_t \) in state \( s_t \) yields a reward \( r_t \), then transitions the process to a new state \( s_{t+1} \). The reward \( r_t \) is drawn from a fixed distribution conditioned solely on \( (s_t, a_t) \), and the next state \( s_{t+1} \) is determined by a fixed transition distribution also depending only on \( (s_t, a_t) \). Our goal is to maximize the cumulative rewards over \( T \) steps. In this work, we consider the scenario where the reward distributions, transition dynamics, as well as the horizon \( T \) and diameter \( D \), are unknown. We introduce BUCRL, the first polynomial-time Bayesian algorithm that, up to logarithmic factors, achieves a regret—defined as the gap between the rewards of the optimal policy and our method—on the order of \( \tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{D S A T}) \). Crucially, our guarantees hold with high probability in a worst-case (frequentist) sense, rather than relying on the weaker Bayesian regret framework. We validate our approach through experiments across diverse environments, demonstrating...

Variational inference (VI) is a vital technique in approximate Bayesian inference owing to its computational efficiency and wide-ranging applicability. A key factor influencing VI's effectiveness is the choice of divergence measure, as VI seeks to approximate intractable distributions by minimizing this divergence. In this paper, we introduce a meta-learning framework designed to automatically identify the most suitable divergence metric for a given task, thereby streamlining the development of VI methods. Additionally, our approach learns optimal initializations for the variational parameters without incurring extra costs, particularly beneficial in few-shot learning scenarios. We demonstrate that our method surpasses traditional VI in tasks such as Gaussian mixture distribution approximation, Bayesian neural network regression, image generation with variational autoencoders, and recommender systems leveraging partial variational autoencoders.

Deep learning techniques are celebrated for their high performance; however, their lack of interpretability limits their applicability in high-stakes environments. Recent model-agnostic methods attempt to address this issue by offering post-hoc explanations through reverse-engineering the model's internal processes. Nonetheless, in heavily regulated sectors, interpretability should be integrated from the outset, rendering post-hoc methods useful primarily as validation tools after model development. Achieving interpretability from the beginning involves imposing soft constraints on the model's behavior by incorporating domain knowledge and minimizing potential biases within an abstract framework. 

We introduce a multi-criteria approach that enables control over feature effects on the model's predictions by embedding knowledge directly into the objective function. This method is further extended to include a non-linear knowledge function, accommodating more intricate effects and areas of limited knowledge locally. The outcome is a deep learning model that is inherently interpretable from the start, aligning with contemporary regulatory standards. An empirical demonstration using credit risk data shows that our approach produces models that are both highly effective and robust, capable of mitigating biases stemming from limited data availability.

A key challenge in data acquisition for mineral and energy resource exploration is optimizing the integration of diverse sensor types while minimizing overall costs. We introduce a probabilistic framework for multi-objective optimization and inverse problems, specifically designed to handle expensive cost functions associated with deploying new measurements. This innovative approach concurrently addresses multi-linear forward models for 2D sensor data and 3D geophysical properties by leveraging sparse Gaussian Process kernels, effectively incorporating the cross-variances among different parameters. Various optimization strategies are explored and assessed using both synthetic and real-world geophysical datasets. We showcase the benefits of our method through a specific joint inverse problem, illustrating how to determine optimal locations for new drill-core measurements based on 2D gravity and magnetic data. This approach is versatile and can be adapted to a wide range of remote sensing challenges involving linear forward models—such as navigating surface access constraints for data collection or implementing adaptive multi-sensor positioning systems.

In recent decades, biomedical signals have played a vital role in communication within Human-Computer Interfaces (HCI) for medical applications. One notable example is myoelectric signals (MES), which are generated in the muscles of the human body as unidimensional patterns. Consequently, pattern recognition methods and algorithms developed for signal analysis can be effectively applied once these signals are sampled and converted into electromyographic (EMG) signals. In recent years, numerous researchers have focused on prosthetic control through EMG signal classification, involving recording MES within specific frequency ranges to categorize the corresponding EMG signals. Feature extraction and classification can be performed in various domains, including the time domain, frequency (spectral) domain, time scale, and time-frequency domain. A prominent method used for pattern recognition in myoelectric signals is Support Vector Machines (SVM), which functions by identifying an n-dimensional hyperplane to separate different classes of input features. This approach is capable of recognizing complex patterns and has frequently demonstrated its effectiveness in diverse applications.

The drive to develop sophisticated machine learning algorithms and enhance statistical power in neuroimaging association studies encourages the use of increasingly large datasets. While pooling scans from multiple independent studies appears to be the most straightforward strategy to boost sample size, this approach often introduces biases related to selection, measurement, and confounding factors, risking the emergence of false correlations. In this study, we analyze a combined dataset of 35,320 brain magnetic resonance images from 17 different sources to investigate bias in neuroimaging. Our first experiment, titled "Name That Dataset," provides empirical evidence of bias by demonstrating that scans can be accurately classified into their original datasets with a 71.5% success rate. Recognizing this, we focus on confounding bias, commonly regarded as a significant challenge in observational research. Since it is typically impossible to identify all potential confounders or obtain data on them, we conceptualize these confounders as unknown, latent variables. To determine whether the confounded or the causal model offers a more parsimonious explanation, we employ Kolmogorov complexity to assess which model results in the simplest factorization of the graphical structure. This study examines the expressive capabilities of multi-layer Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) in comparison to a streamlined alternative termed Graph-Augmented Multi-Layer Perceptrons (GA-MLPs). GA-MLPs enhance node features by applying specific multi-hop operators on the graph before processing each node independently with an MLP. In assessing their ability to distinguish between non-isomorphic graphs, we demonstrate both theoretically and empirically that GA-MLPs equipped with appropriate operators can differentiate nearly all such graph pairs, matching the effectiveness of the Weisfeiler-Lehman (WL) test. However, by analyzing these models as functions at the node level and considering the equivalence classes they form on rooted graphs, we establish that the difference in expressive power between GA-MLPs and GNNs expands exponentially with increasing depth. Notably, unlike GNNs, GA-MLPs cannot perform counting of attributed walks. Additionally, community detection experiments reveal that the performance of GA-MLPs may be restricted by the specific operator set employed, whereas GNNs offer greater flexibility and adaptability through learned representations.

Recent years have seen growing interest in understanding the convergence behavior of asynchronous stochastic gradient descent (Async-SGD), given its fundamental importance in machine learning. However, most existing research has focused on scenarios with either bounded gradient delays or convex objectives. In this work, we examine Async-SGD and its variant, Async-SGDI—which employs increasing batch sizes—for non-convex optimization problems characterized by unbounded gradient delays. We establish an $o(1/\sqrt{k})$ convergence rate for Async-SGD and an improved $o(1/k)$ rate for Async-SGDI. Additionally, we present a comprehensive sufficient condition for the convergence of Async-SGD, unifying two prominent delay models found in current literature as special cases and introducing a novel delay model that has not been explored before.

This study introduces an automated three-dimensional (3D) deep segmentation method for identifying gliomas in pre-operative MRI scans. Additionally, a random forest-based classification algorithm is proposed to predict patient survival. The primary goal is to accurately segment the glioma region and delineate its various sub-regions, including the necrotic and non-enhancing tumor core, peri-tumoral edema, and enhancing tumor. The segmentation framework employs a dual-stream deep architecture featuring two different resolutions: one deep convolutional neural network focuses on capturing local features of the input data, while the other provides a global perspective across the entire image. These complementary streams' outputs are integrated to form an ensemble, enabling comprehensive learning of the input image. Unlike traditional patch-based methods, the network processes the entire image to leverage semantic features throughout the full volume. The algorithm was trained on the BraTS 2019 dataset, comprising 335 cases, and validated on 127 unseen cases using a blind testing protocol. We introduce a framework for Gaussian process regression that incorporates boundary value problem constraints. This approach can be used to infer solutions to well-posed boundary value problems characterized by a known second-order differential operator and specific boundary conditions, even when only scattered observations of the source term are available. Additionally, scattered data of the solution itself can be integrated into the regression process. The framework merges co-kriging with linear transformations of Gaussian processes and employs kernels derived from spectral expansions in the eigenfunctions associated with the boundary value problem. This methodology leverages the reduced-rank structure of covariance matrices to enhance computational efficiency. Our results demonstrate that this framework provides more precise and stable solution estimates compared to traditional physics-informed Gaussian process regression methods that do not enforce boundary condition constraints.

This paper introduces a comprehensive Arabic Sentiment Analysis Benchmark Dataset (ASAD) based on Twitter, developed for a competition sponsored by KAUST, which offers prize money of $10,000, $5,000, and $2,000 to the top three winners. Unlike other publicly available Arabic datasets, ASAD is a sizable, high-quality annotated resource comprising 95,000 tweets, classified into three sentiment categories: positive, negative, and neutral. The paper details the data collection and annotation processes, and presents several baseline models designed for the competition task, along with their results, to serve as reference points for participants.

Cardinal scores—numeric ratings gathered from individuals—are well known to suffer from calibration issues. A common method to address this involves assuming simple miscalibration models, such as linear biases, in order to correct the scores. However, this approach often performs poorly because human miscalibrations are typically more complex and poorly understood. Without relying on simplifying assumptions about miscalibration, many in the crowdsourcing community believe that the only valuable information in cardinal scores is the ranking they produce. Challenging this widespread belief, our paper draws inspiration from Stein's shrinkage, empirical Bayes methods, and the classic two-envelope problem. We examine cardinal scores with arbitrary, even adversarial, miscalibrations that are only required to be consistent with the induced ranking. We develop estimators that, without any assumptions about miscalibration, consistently outperform all estimators based solely on rank information. These estimators are versatile and can serve as plug-ins across various applications; in particular, we demonstrate their potential in A/B testing and ranking scenarios. Our findings offer new perspectives in the ongoing debate between leveraging cardinal versus ordinal data.

A ReLU neural network functions as a continuous piecewise linear transformation from the input space to the output space. The network's weights define a partition of the input space into convex polytopes, with each polytope corresponding to a unique affine mapping. By examining the arrangement of these polytopes and their associated affine functions, one can analyze the network's behavior and understand how it processes information.

We introduce an extensive extension of the latent position network model, known as the random dot product graph, to handle multiple graphs—both undirected and directed—that share a common subset of nodes. Additionally, we propose a joint embedding technique for the corresponding adjacency matrices, or their submatrices, into an appropriate latent space. We establish theoretical results on the asymptotic behavior of the resulting node representations, demonstrating that, after applying a linear transformation, they converge uniformly in the Euclidean norm to the true latent positions, with Gaussian error bounds. Within this framework, we also generalize the stochastic block model to various multi-graph scenarios and showcase the effectiveness of our joint embedding approach through several statistical inference tasks. Our method achieves results that are comparable to or better than existing spectral techniques. Furthermore, in a cybersecurity application, we observe empirical improvements in link prediction performance over single-graph embeddings.

Real-world electricity consumption forecasting often involves multiple tasks, such as predicting consumption at various future time points or across different geographical locations. Traditionally, these tasks are addressed separately, missing out on the potential benefits of shared knowledge that could enhance overall performance. In this study, we introduce a multi-task optimization (MTO) based co-training framework, termed MTO-CT, which enables simultaneous training of models tailored to different tasks. This approach allows each task to benefit from insights gained through others, thereby improving their solution accuracy. MTO-CT employs an LSTM-based predictor, where knowledge is embedded within connection weights and biases. An inter-task knowledge transfer module is incorporated to facilitate the sharing process, selecting the most relevant source tasks using probability matching and stochastic universal sampling. Additionally, genetic operations such as mutation and crossover are applied to effectively reuse knowledge from these source tasks within target tasks. We utilized electricity consumption data from five Australian states to formulate two task sets at different scales: (a) one-step ahead predictions for each state (five tasks), and (b) six-step ahead predictions, demonstrating the framework's applicability across various prediction horizons.

Unsupervised learning has long captivated machine learning researchers and practitioners by enabling them to bypass the costly and intricate process of data labeling. Despite its appeal, learning complex patterns without supervision remains a formidable challenge, with current methods often underperforming compared to supervised approaches. Self-supervised deep learning has emerged as a powerful tool for representation learning in computer vision; however, its evaluation has largely been limited to semi-supervised or downstream tasks, rather than in a fully unsupervised context. In this work, we introduce a straightforward framework for unsupervised classification that leverages self-supervised representations. Our experiments, conducted with several state-of-the-art self-supervised techniques, demonstrate that the approach yields competitive results on ImageNet—achieving 39% accuracy with 1000 clusters and 46% with overclustering. We advocate for including unsupervised evaluation metrics alongside traditional benchmarks in self-supervised learning. The implementation code is accessible at https://github.com/Randl/kmeans_selfsuper

We conceptualize infinitesimal gradient boosting as the limiting form of the well-known tree-based gradient boosting algorithm in machine learning. This limit is examined under the vanishing learning rate regime, where the learning rate approaches zero and the number of gradient boosting trees is scaled accordingly. To facilitate this, we introduce a novel category of randomized regression trees that connect fully randomized trees and Extra Trees, employing a softmax distribution for binary splitting. Our primary finding is the proof of convergence of the associated stochastic process and the characterization of the limit as the unique solution to a nonlinear ordinary differential equation set in an infinite-dimensional function space. Infinitesimal gradient boosting thus traces a smooth trajectory within the space of continuous functions, during which the training error steadily diminishes, residuals remain centered, and total variation stays effectively controlled.

As machine learning (ML) models become increasingly integrated into decision-making processes, the importance of interpretability has gained prominence in research. Current explanation techniques primarily rely on feature importance scores to highlight which features matter for individual predictions. However, systematically summarizing and interpreting these sample-specific importance scores remains a significant challenge. In this work, we introduce guiding principles and desirable criteria for concept-based explanations, aiming to move beyond per-sample feature attributions toward identifying higher-level, human-understandable concepts that are consistent across the entire dataset. We present ACE, a novel algorithm designed to automatically extract visual concepts. Through comprehensive experiments, we demonstrate that ACE uncovers concepts that are meaningful to humans, coherent, and crucial for understanding the neural network's predictions.

Predicting future outcomes and quantifying associated uncertainties in sequential data pose fundamental challenges in machine learning, increasingly drawing research interest. In response, we introduce SigGPDE, a scalable and sparse variational inference framework tailored for Gaussian Processes (GPs) operating on sequential inputs. Our work offers two key advances: firstly, we design inducing variables that form the basis of our sparse approximation, ensuring that the evidence lower bound (ELBO) can be computed without any matrix inversions. secondly, we demonstrate that the gradients of the GP signature kernel satisfy a hyperbolic partial differential equation (PDE). This theoretical revelation enables us to develop an efficient back-propagation algorithm for ELBO optimization. Empirical results highlight SigGPDE's substantial computational improvements over existing methods, while delivering state-of-the-art classification performance on large-scale datasets containing up to one million multivariate time series.

Attention guidance is a strategy for mitigating dataset bias in deep learning by steering the model away from relying on misleading features. In the context of image classification, we introduce an efficient human-in-the-loop system that enables users to interactively direct the model’s focus toward specific regions within images. This approach helps diminish the effects of co-occurrence bias and enhances the transferability and interpretability of deep neural networks. Unlike previous methods that depend on detailed pixel-level annotations and lack interactivity, our technique allows users to simply click on images to annotate regions of interest. We also develop a novel active learning strategy to minimize the number of annotations required. Through both quantitative evaluations and user studies across multiple datasets, we demonstrate that our system outperforms existing non-active learning approaches, which typically demand extensive polygonal segmentation masks for training or fine-tuning. Our method significantly reduces labor and costs while producing more effective, bias-robust models. Experimental results affirm that our system is efficient, practical, and dependable.

Anomaly detection in attributed networks focuses on identifying nodes whose patterns significantly deviate from those of most reference nodes, a task crucial in applications like network intrusion detection and social spammer identification. Existing approaches often overlook the intricate cross-modality interactions between network topology and node attributes. In this paper, we introduce a deep joint representation learning framework for anomaly detection called AnomalyDAE, which employs a dual autoencoder architecture to effectively capture the complex interplay between network structure and node attributes, resulting in high-quality embeddings. Specifically, AnomalyDAE integrates a structure autoencoder and an attribute autoencoder to jointly learn node and attribute embeddings within a latent space. An attention mechanism is incorporated into the structure encoder to assess the significance of each neighbor, enhancing the model's ability to discern structural patterns vital for anomaly detection. Additionally, by inputting both node embeddings and attribute embeddings into the attribute decoder, the model learns cross-modality interactions between network structure and node attributes during the attribute reconstruction process. Anomalies are then identified based on the reconstruction errors from both structural and attitudinal perspectives. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets validate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

The widespread empirical approach of employing factor models to account for shared, unobserved confounders, denoted as $\mathbf{Z}$, in observational studies involving multiple treatments, $\mathbf{A}$, spans disciplines such as genetics, network analysis, medicine, and political science. Wang and Blei (2019, WB) formalized this approach by introducing the "deconfounder," a causal inference technique that utilizes factor models of $\mathbf{A}$ to estimate "substitute confounders" $\hat{\mathbf{Z}}$, subsequently estimating treatment effects through regression of the outcome $\mathbf{Y}$ on a subset of treatments while controlling for $\hat{\mathbf{Z}}$. They assert that the deconfounder provides unbiased estimates under the conditions that there are no single-cause confounders and that $\hat{\mathbf{Z}}$ is accurately "pinpointed." We clarify that achieving pinpointing requires each confounder to influence an infinite number of treatments. Under these assumptions, we demonstrate that a naive semiparametric regression of $\mathbf{Y}$ on $\mathbf{A}$ is asymptotically unbiased. Consequently, variants of the deconfounder that incorporate this regression are also asymptotically unbiased; however, those that depend on $\hat{\mathbf{Z}}$ and subsets of causes demand additional, untestable assumptions. We replicate each available deconfounder analysis with the corresponding data and find that they do not consistently outperform naive regression. In practical applications, the deconfounder can yield implausible estimates, as seen in WB's case study on movie earnings, where it suggests that comic creator Stan Lee's cameo appearances causally contributed \$15.5 billion—most of Marvel's movie revenue. We conclude that neither approach reliably substitutes for meticulous research design.

We investigate a fair machine learning (ML) scenario in which an 'upstream' model developer is responsible for creating a fair ML model intended for deployment by multiple, similar yet distinct 'downstream' users. This context presents unique challenges that are not adequately addressed by many existing fairness interventions, highlighting critiques that current methods lack broad applicability across the diverse needs of real-world fair ML applications. To tackle this, we adopt a distributional perspective on fair classification, proposing a new fairness criterion called distributional parity. This measure assesses disparities in outcome distributions across protected groups. We also introduce a post-processing technique rooted in optimal transport to minimize this disparity. Our approach is capable of producing fairer outcomes for all downstream users, accommodating various fairness definitions, and operates effectively at inference time on unlabeled data. We validate these claims through experiments comparing our method against several alternatives across four benchmark tasks. Ultimately, we contend that developing setting-specific interventions can lead to more equitable classification results.

Fairness in machine learning has garnered significant attention, yet most research has concentrated on either supervised or unsupervised learning, with limited exploration of semi-supervised approaches. In practical applications, however, most datasets comprise both labeled and unlabeled data, highlighting the importance of semi-supervised methods. A central challenge in fair learning is balancing fairness and accuracy, with prior studies suggesting that enlarging the training set can improve this trade-off. We propose that incorporating unlabeled data into the training set may yield similar benefits. To this end, we introduce a framework for fair semi-supervised learning formulated as an optimization problem that integrates classifier loss to enhance accuracy, label propagation loss for predicting unlabeled data, and fairness constraints applied to both labeled and unlabeled samples to ensure fairness. Our approach is implemented within logistic regression and support vector machines, evaluated through fairness metrics such as disparate impact and disparate mistreatment. We also provide a theoretical analysis of the sources of discrimination in semi-supervised learning, decomposing bias, variance, and noise. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method effectively achieves fair semi-supervised learning and offers a superior balance between accuracy and fairness compared to methods solely based on supervised learning.

Accurate prediction of firm earnings is crucial for informing investment choices, dividend forecasts, and share price movements. This task often involves integrating multiple tensor-compatible datasets characterized by complex non-linear multi-way relationships, spatiotemporal structures, and varying degrees of sparsity. Existing non-linear tensor completion methods frequently learn noisy embeddings and tend to overfit. 

This paper centers on enhancing the embedding learning process within tensor completion by introducing a novel multi-layer neural network architecture called MLCTR for tensor factorization and completion. The proposed network offers several key advantages: it employs multiple low-rank matrix factorization (MF) modules to reduce overfitting, incorporates interleaved nonlinear transfer functions at each layer to capture complex relationships, and utilizes skip connections to mitigate gradient vanishing problems and enable deeper networks. 

Additionally, the model leverages Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) for efficient optimization and rapid convergence during training. Our approach proves highly effective in imputing missing data within EPS datasets. Experimental results demonstrate that integrating non-linearity into the factor matrices significantly enhances embedding learning and end-to-end tensor modeling, outperforming methods that introduce non-linearity only during tensor reconstruction from factor matrices.

Bike sharing has become an increasingly integral component of urban transit networks. Precise demand forecasting is essential for effective rebalancing and maintaining service quality. Most current models rely solely on historical bike-sharing data, treating the system as isolated and overlooking interactions with other transportation modes. This approach fails to capture the interconnected nature of multimodal travel, where bike sharing often serves as a complement to public transit and other modes. Although some recent studies have made progress, there is still a lack of methods that effectively utilize spatiotemporal data across different modes and diverse spatial units. To fill this gap, we propose a graph-based deep learning model, termed B-MRGNN, which leverages multimodal historical data for demand prediction. The model encodes spatial dependencies within and between modes through multiple intra- and inter-modal graphs. A multi-relational graph neural network (MRGNN) is employed to learn correlations between spatial entities such as bike stations, subway stations, and ride-hailing zones. We validate our approach with extensive experiments using real-world data from New York City, including bike sharing, subway, and ride-hailing datasets. The results demonstrate that our model significantly outperforms existing methods, highlighting its effectiveness in multimodal demand prediction.

The Gaussian-smoothed optimal transport (GOT) framework, introduced by Goldfeld et al. (2020) and further developed in subsequent studies, has rapidly gained interest among researchers in statistics, machine learning, information theory, and related disciplines. A crucial insight from this work is that, by adopting the GOT framework instead of its unsmoothed version, the curse of dimensionality associated with approximating the true underlying distribution via the empirical measure can be mitigated. In this paper, we demonstrate that a similar principle applies to the estimation of nonparametric mixing distributions within discrete exponential family models, where utilizing the GOT cost enables the nonparametric maximum likelihood estimator (MLE) to achieve a convergence rate that is polynomial. This markedly contrasts with the traditional sub-polynomial rates associated with unsmoothed metrics, which are fundamentally hard to improve from an information-theoretic standpoint. A pivotal component of our analysis is the development of a novel Jackson-type approximation bound for Gaussian-convoluted Lipschitz functions. This advancement serves to connect existing techniques for analyzing nonparametric MLEs with the innovative GOT framework.

Machine Learning (ML) has attracted significant interest from researchers and practitioners as a versatile and emerging tool for disease diagnosis. As ML technology advances and the volume of related literature grows, a comprehensive review of Machine Learning-Based Disease Diagnosis (MLBDD) is essential. From a bibliometric perspective, this study thoroughly analyzes MLBDD publications from 2012 to 2021. A total of 1,710 relevant papers, along with associated metadata, were retrieved using specific keywords from the Scopus and Web of Science (WOS) databases and compiled into an Excel dataset for detailed examination. The analysis begins with an exploration of publication trends over the years and identifies the most prolific countries, regions, institutions, and authors. Next, co-citation networks among countries, institutions, authors, and articles are visualized utilizing R-studio software, allowing for insights into citation patterns and identifying the most influential contributors. This paper offers a comprehensive overview of MLBDD, serving as a valuable resource for researchers interested in this domain and providing a thorough foundation for future investigations in the field.

We present a novel inference technique for stochastic epidemic models that employs recursive multinomial approximations to integrate over unobserved variables, thereby overcoming the challenge of intractable likelihoods. This approach is suited for a class of discrete-time, finite-population compartmental models with partial, randomly under-reported, or missing count data. Unlike advanced methods such as Approximate Bayesian Computation, our method does not require forward simulation of the model and involves no tuning parameters. It approximates the marginal likelihood of model parameters through a straightforward filtering recursion, ensuring computational efficiency. The accuracy of this approximation is validated using both real and simulated datasets, including a model of the 1995 Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo. Additionally, we demonstrate how this approach can be integrated within a Sequential Monte Carlo framework to estimate the time-varying reproduction number of COVID-19 in Wuhan, China, as recently described by Kucharski et al. in 2020.

Machine learning has experienced remarkable growth recently, leading to broader adoption in areas such as educational assessments, credit risk analysis, healthcare, employment screening, and criminal justice. Ensuring the reliability and fairness of ML and NLP systems is essential, necessitating guarantees that their decisions are both equitable and robust. In pursuit of this, we introduce GYC, a framework designed to generate a set of counterfactual text samples crucial for testing these systems. Our key contributions are: (a) the development of GYC, a method for producing counterfactual samples that are plausible, diverse, goal-oriented, and effective, and (b) the capability of GYC to generate counterfactuals conditioned on specific attributes such as named-entity tags, semantic role labels, or sentiment. Experimental results across multiple domains demonstrate that GYC reliably produces counterfactual texts embodying these four properties. These counterfactual samples serve as valuable test cases for evaluating model performance and assessing the effectiveness of text debiasing algorithms.

Generating long-range, skeleton-based human actions remains a challenging task, as minor deviations in a single frame can lead to distorted action sequences.
