Many existing approaches draw inspiration from video generation techniques, treating skeleton nodes or joints as pixels in images without considering the complex inter-frame and intra-frame structural information, which often results in flawed action representations. Graph convolutional networks (GCNs) offer a promising solution by leveraging structural information to learn meaningful representations. However, applying GCNs directly to continuous action sequences across both spatial and temporal domains poses difficulties, primarily because the resulting action graph can become extremely large. To address this challenge, we introduce a modified GCN architecture that utilizes a powerful self-attention mechanism to selectively sparsify the complete action graph along the temporal dimension. Our approach dynamically focuses on important past frames, constructing a sparse graph that facilitates effective GCN processing and preserves the structural nuances of action sequences. Extensive experiments on two widely used human action datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms existing techniques, showcasing its superior capability in modeling long-range skeleton-based actions.

In this paper, we explore deep multimodal learning techniques for integrating speech and visual data in Audio-Visual Automatic Speech Recognition (AV-ASR). Initially, we examine a method where individual unimodal deep networks are trained separately, and their final hidden layers are combined to create a shared feature space. A subsequent deep network is then trained on this fused representation. For example, the audio-only network achieves a phone error rate (PER) of 41% under clean conditions on the IBM large vocabulary audio-visual studio dataset. In contrast, the fusion model reduces the PER to 35.83%, highlighting the significant contribution of the visual modality in phoneme classification, even with clear audio signals. Additionally, we introduce a novel deep network architecture featuring a bilinear softmax layer, which captures class-specific correlations between modalities. Combining the posterior outputs from these bilinear networks with those from the fusion model results in a further substantial PER reduction, reaching 34.03%.

We introduce effective pre-training approaches for neural machine translation (NMT) that utilize parallel corpora involving a pivot language—specifically, source-pivot and pivot-target pairs—to significantly enhance source-target translation quality. Our strategies for strengthening the connections among source, pivot, and target languages during pre-training include: 1) step-by-step training of a single model across different language pairs; 2) incorporating an additional adapter component to facilitate seamless integration between pre-trained encoder and decoder; and 3) conducting cross-lingual encoder training through autoencoding of the pivot language. These methods substantially outperform traditional multilingual models, achieving up to +2.6% BLEU score improvements on the WMT 2019 French-German and German-Czech translation tasks. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our techniques remain effective even in zero-shot and low-resource scenarios.

Event generators are crucial tools in high-energy nuclear and particle physics for advancing the understanding of particle interactions. In this review, we examine the latest developments in applying machine learning (ML) techniques to construct physics event generators. We analyze the types of ML generative models employed in these ML-based event generators, highlight their unique challenges, and discuss strategies for integrating physical principles into model architectures to address these issues. Additionally, we consider open questions related to enhancing resolution, accuracy, and extrapolation capabilities of ML-driven physics event generation.

An asynchronous Brain-Computer Interface (BCI) based on imagined speech is a device that enables users to control external systems or send messages at will by decoding EEG signals associated with imagined speech. To effectively implement such BCIs, it is essential to accurately identify the moments when a user begins to imagine words from a continuous EEG signal. In this study, we introduce five feature extraction techniques—wavelet decomposition, empirical mode decomposition, frequency energy analysis, fractal dimension calculation, and chaos theory features—to detect segments of imagined speech within continuous EEG data. These methods serve as a preliminary step toward developing an asynchronous BCI driven by imagined speech. We evaluated these techniques across three datasets using four different classifiers. The highest F1 scores achieved were 0.73, 0.79, and 0.68 for each dataset, respectively. These promising results suggest the potential to build systems capable of automatic segmentation of imagined speech segments, paving the way for more advanced classification and control applications.

Pixelizations of Platonic solids, such as the cube and icosahedron, have been extensively employed to represent spherical data, including climate records and Cosmic Microwave Background maps. These solids are characterized by well-known global symmetries. When each face of a solid is pixelized, that face also exhibits local symmetries in the form of Euclidean isometries. A common approach to integrating these symmetries involves constructing a hierarchy; however, this method often fails to accurately capture the dynamic interaction between the two symmetry levels. In this work, we demonstrate how to model this interaction utilizing principles from group theory, identify equivariant linear maps, and develop equivariant padding that preserves these symmetries. Deep neural networks built upon these maps extend the concept of gauge equivariant CNNs to pixelized spherical domains. These networks achieve state-of-the-art performance in semantic segmentation tasks for climate data and omnidirectional image analysis. The implementation code is accessible at https://git.io/JGiZA.

Commonsense reasoning systems should be capable of generalizing across a wide range of reasoning scenarios. However, most current leading methods rely heavily on costly data annotations and tend to overfit to specific benchmarks, failing to develop true semantic reasoning abilities. To address these limitations, zero-shot question-answering (QA) systems have emerged as a promising approach, leveraging the transformation of commonsense knowledge graphs (KGs) into synthetic QA samples for training models. Given the growing diversity of commonsense KGs, this paper seeks to expand the zero-shot transfer learning framework to accommodate multiple knowledge sources, allowing different KGs to be utilized collaboratively. To achieve this, we introduce a modular knowledge aggregation method designed to prevent knowledge loss and interference among the various sources, forming a new zero-shot commonsense reasoning paradigm. Experiments conducted on five benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, showing improved performance when multiple KGs are employed.

This paper introduces a novel fusion strategy for multistream convolutional networks, termed Lattice Cross Fusion. This method integrates signals from convolutional layers through mathematical operation-based fusions implemented immediately prior to pooling layers. Experiments conducted on a deliberately challenging version of CIFAR-10, a widely used image classification dataset, using a modified AlexNet-LCNN architecture demonstrate that Lattice Cross Fusion surpasses the baseline single-stream network by 46%. Additionally, it achieves faster convergence, enhanced stability, and greater robustness.

Understanding and predicting chemical reactions are essential challenges in studying complex chemical systems. Reactive molecular dynamics (MD) simulation has become a widely adopted tool for this purpose, providing detailed atomic insights and enabling a deeper understanding of reaction mechanisms. In this research, two reference datasets were created, and corresponding neural network (NN) potentials were trained based on them. These NN potentials can accurately forecast potential energy and atomic forces with DFT-level precision, while being vastly more efficient—by several orders of magnitude—than traditional DFT calculations. Utilizing these models, reactive MD simulations were conducted to investigate the combustion processes of hydrogen and methane. Thanks to the high computational efficiency of the NN approach, nanosecond-scale MD trajectories for large systems containing hundreds of atoms were generated, revealing comprehensive combustion mechanisms. The algorithms developed in this study hold potential for broader application, enabling the exploration and discovery of reaction pathways in diverse complex systems such as combustion, synthesis, and heterogeneous catalysis—without relying on predefined reaction coordinates or elementary steps.

Due to the opaque nature of deep learning models, developing techniques to explain their outputs is essential for building human trust and facilitating collaboration between humans and AI. In this paper, we explore several explanation methods, both model-agnostic and model-specific, tailored for convolutional neural networks used in text classification. We perform three human-centered evaluations, each targeting a different goal of explanations: (1) uncovering the model’s behavior, (2) providing justifications for predictions, and (3) assisting humans in examining uncertain outcomes. Our findings reveal distinct strengths and characteristics among the various explanation techniques and demonstrate how effectively each can fulfill its respective purpose.

Over the past decade, many fields have experienced a surge in data volumes and increasing complexity of computational tasks, prompting a heightened need for highly data-parallel computing within distributed systems. Managing these systems effectively becomes particularly challenging when uncertainties about job and task performance under different resource configurations arise, impacting scheduling and resource allocation decisions. This survey explores predictive performance modeling (PPM) methods designed to estimate key performance indicators—such as execution time, memory requirements, and wait times—for future jobs and tasks based on previous performance data. Our focus is on non-intrusive approaches, which can be applied universally across workloads without modification, given that workloads are typically treated as black boxes by system managers. We categorize and analyze sources of performance variability, the performance metrics predicted, the types of training data needed, application scenarios, and the underlying prediction techniques. The survey concludes with an outline of remaining open challenges and urgent research priorities in this domain.

Since the operation of autonomous systems often impacts multiple users simultaneously, it is essential to incorporate fairness considerations into their design. Unlike standard (deep) reinforcement learning (RL), our focus is on developing a policy that ensures equitable treatment for all users. In this paper, we introduce this novel RL challenge, where the goal is to optimize an objective function that captures a formally defined concept of fairness. We present a comprehensive theoretical analysis of this problem, examining both discounted and average reward frameworks. Notably, our analysis yields a new and significant result in the traditional RL setting: a novel bound on the approximation error between the optimal average reward and the reward achieved by a policy optimized for discounted rewards. Given that learning with discounted rewards is generally more straightforward, this finding provides a solid justification for deriving fair policies for the average reward by first learning them within the discounted reward paradigm. We also illustrate how several established deep RL algorithms can be modified to address this fairness-driven optimization problem and demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through extensive experiments across three distinct domains.

The increasing prevalence of network datasets—such as social, biological, and informational networks—has elevated the importance of relational data representations, especially with the growing application of statistical relational learning (SRL) algorithms across these fields. In this paper, we explore various issues related to representing relational data in graph-based formats. Recognizing that the way nodes, links, and features are represented can significantly influence the effectiveness of SRL algorithms, we review different methods and opportunities for transforming relational representations to enhance their performance. To organize these concepts, we propose a clear taxonomy for data transformation in relational domains, treating link and node transformations as symmetric tasks. Specifically, these tasks include (i) predicting the existence of nodes and links, (ii) determining their labels or types, (iii) estimating their weights or significance, and (iv) systematically generating relevant features for both nodes and links. We illustrate our taxonomy with detailed examples and compare various approaches for each task. Additionally, we examine the general conditions necessary for transforming links, nodes, and features. Finally, we identify ongoing challenges and open questions in this area.

Bayesian nonparametric (BNP) models offer elegant approaches for uncovering latent features within data, yet inference in these models often tends to be slow. We leverage the fact that completely random measures—such as those underlying models like the Dirichlet process and the beta-Bernoulli process—can be decomposed into independent sub-measures. This decomposition allows us to split the latent measure into a finite measure containing only the instantiated components and an infinite measure encompassing all remaining parts. Different inference methods are then employed for each component: uncollapsed samplers efficiently mix on the finite measure, while collapsed samplers perform well on the infinite tail, which is sparsely populated. This hybrid algorithm is broadly applicable across various models and can be easily parallelized to facilitate scalable inference, all while maintaining asymptotic convergence guarantees.

We investigate the cross-entropy method (CEM) for the non-convex optimization of continuous, parameterized objective functions, and we propose a differentiable variant that allows for the computation of gradients of CEM outputs with respect to the parameters of the objective function. This development integrates CEM into end-to-end learning frameworks, which was previously unattainable. Our approach is demonstrated through applications in a synthetic energy-based structured prediction task and in non-convex continuous control problems. In the control domain, we illustrate how to embed optimal action sequences into a lower-dimensional representation. The differentiable CEM (DCEM) enables the fine-tuning of CEM-based controllers via policy optimization techniques.

This paper introduces an efficient variational inference framework for deriving a family of structured Gaussian process regression network (SGPRN) models. The core concept involves incorporating auxiliary inducing variables within latent functions and jointly optimizing both the distributions of these inducing variables and the hyperparameters as variational parameters. We propose structured variational distributions and marginalize over latent variables, which facilitates a decomposable, tractable variational lower bound and enables stochastic optimization. Our inference method is capable of modeling data where outputs do not share a common input set, with computational complexity independent of the sizes of inputs and outputs, making it well-suited for datasets with missing values. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on synthetic and real-world datasets, showing that our model consistently outperforms the current state-of-the-art in imputing missing data. Additionally, we introduce a visualization technique for analyzing time-varying correlations across outputs in electrocorticography data, providing valuable insights into neural population dynamics.

When analyzing literary texts like novels or short stories, extracting structured information in the form of a knowledge graph can be challenging due to the vast number of potential relationships among characters and the difficulty in gathering supervised data for these relations. To address this issue, an unsupervised approach utilizing transformers is proposed. Relational sentences from the original text are embedded using SBERT and grouped into clusters based on their semantic similarity. These clusters are then summarized with BART, and a descriptive label is derived from each summary. Initial results indicate that this clustering effectively identifies similar relations and serves as a useful preprocessing step for semi-supervised methods.

Manifold learning is employed for dimensionality reduction, aiming to identify a projection subspace that enhances interclass variance while reducing intraclass variance. However, the high dimensionality of datasets often presents a bottleneck for subspace learning techniques. In this study, we propose a hierarchical framework to scale subspace learning methods, with the objective of boosting classification performance on large datasets by approximately 3% to 10%. Various combinations of methods are explored. We evaluate the proposed approach using five publicly available large datasets across multiple eigenvalue-based subspace learning techniques, including linear discriminant analysis, principal component analysis, generalized discriminant analysis, and reconstruction independent component analysis. To further analyze the impact of our method on different classifiers, the resulting features are fed into linear discriminant analysis, quadratic discriminant analysis, k-nearest neighbors, and random forest classifiers. The classification results demonstrate an average improvement of around 5%, underscoring the effectiveness of the hierarchical approach.

Recent advances in deep learning have markedly enhanced the precision of brain tumor segmentation. Nevertheless, fully supervised approaches demand extensive manually annotated masks, which are labor-intensive and require specialized expertise. Weakly supervised learning using scribbles offers an effective compromise between model performance and annotation effort. Yet, when dealing with the hierarchical complexity of brain tumor structures, annotating scribbles for each subregion remains laborious. In this study, we propose a method that leverages only two types of weak labels: scribbles covering the entire tumor and healthy brain tissue, along with global indicators of the presence of each substructure, to train a deep learning model capable of segmenting all sub-regions. Our approach involves a two-phase training process: initially, we train a whole tumor (WT) segmentation network solely with scribbles on the whole tumor, producing an approximate WT mask; subsequently, we cluster the WT region guided by the global labels. This coarse substructure segmentation obtained via clustering serves as weak supervision to train a second network. To enhance segmentation accuracy, a dense CRF loss is employed for refinement. We evaluate our method on the BraTS2017 dataset, achieving competitive Dice scores for WT segmentation and comparable results for substructure delineation.

In this study, we investigate adversarial attacks targeting Variational Autoencoders (VAEs). We demonstrate methods to manipulate data points to produce a specific latent representation (supervised attack) or to generate a significantly altered latent code (unsupervised attack). Additionally, we analyze how model variations such as $\beta$-VAE and NVAE affect the robustness of VAEs and propose metrics to evaluate this robustness.

A recently introduced SLOPE estimator (arXiv:1407.3824) has been demonstrated to adaptively attain the minimax \(\ell_2\) estimation rate in high-dimensional sparse linear regression models (arXiv:1503.08393). This minimax optimality is valid in regimes where the sparsity level \(k\), sample size \(n\), and dimension \(p\) satisfy the conditions \(k/p \to 0\) and \(k \log p / n \to 0\). In this work, we examine the estimation error of SLOPE in the complementary regime where both \(k\) and \(n\) grow linearly with \(p\), offering new perspectives on the performance of SLOPE estimators. We begin by establishing a concentration inequality for the finite-sample mean squared error (MSE) of SLOPE. The concentration center of this MSE is defined by a complex, implicit quantity. Through careful analysis, we show that, among all SLOPE estimators, LASSO is optimal for estimating \(k\)-sparse vectors without tied non-zero entries in low-noise conditions. Conversely, in high-noise settings, the SLOPE family is sub-optimal compared to bridge regression methods such as Ridge regression.

This paper presents two key contributions. First, it introduces mixed compositional kernels and mixed neural network Gaussian processes (NGGPs). These mixed compositional kernels are formed through the composition of probability generating functions (PGFs). A mixed NNGP is a Gaussian process (GP) characterized by a mixed compositional kernel, which emerges as the infinite-width limit of multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) that employ different activation functions at each layer. Second, the paper proposes $\theta$ activation functions for neural networks and $\theta$ compositional kernels, building upon the theory of branching processes and, more specifically, $\theta$ PGFs. Although $\theta$ compositional kernels are recursive by nature, they can be expressed in closed form. It is demonstrated that, under certain conditions, these kernels exhibit non-degenerate asymptotic behavior. Consequently, Gaussian processes equipped with $\theta$ compositional kernels do not depend on explicit recursive kernel computations and possess manageable asymptotic properties as depth approaches infinity. An open question for future research is whether GPs with $\theta$ compositional kernels can be regarded as limits of infinitely-wide MLPs employing $\theta$ activation functions.

Early detection of sacroiliitis is crucial, as it enables preventive treatment that can markedly enhance a patient's long-term quality of life. Typically, a CT scan of the lower back or abdomen is performed when back pain is suspected. However, because early-stage inflamed sacroiliac joints often exhibit subtle differences from healthy joints, the condition can be easily overlooked. To address this challenge, we have developed an innovative automatic algorithm designed to diagnose and grade sacroiliitis from CT scans, identified incidentally during scans performed for lower back pain assessment. This approach leverages supervised machine learning and deep learning techniques. The system takes as input a pelvic CT scan and outputs a diagnostic assessment for each sacroiliac joint. The process involves four key steps: 1) identifying the initial region of interest (ROI) encompassing the pelvic joints using heuristic methods and a U-Net classifier; 2) refining the ROI to accurately locate both sacroiliac joints with a four-tree random forest; 3) grading sacroiliitis for each joint across individual CT slices using a specialized slice-based CNN classifier; and 4) synthesizing these slice grades to provide a comprehensive diagnosis and grading of sacroiliitis, utilizing a random approach for final evaluation.

Automated segmentation in medical image analysis presents numerous challenges, primarily due to the extensive manual labeling required. Most current learning-based methods, however, are hindered by scarce annotated medical data, creating significant obstacles to achieving accurate and robust segmentation. Additionally, existing semi-supervised approaches often lack robustness compared to fully supervised techniques and do not explicitly incorporate geometric structure and semantic context, which further limits their effectiveness. In this work, we introduce SimCVD, a straightforward contrastive distillation framework that markedly advances voxel-wise representation learning. Our approach begins with an unsupervised training strategy that leverages two different views of an input volume to predict signed distance maps of object boundaries through a contrastive objective, utilizing only two independent dropout masks as perturbations. Remarkably, this simple method performs comparably to fully supervised models despite requiring significantly less labeled data. We theorize that dropout functions as a minimal form of data augmentation, enhancing the network's resilience against representation collapse. Furthermore, we implement structural distillation by transferring pairwise similarity relationships. We evaluate SimCVD on two well-known datasets: the Left Atrial Segmentation Challenge (LA) dataset and another prominent benchmark, demonstrating its effectiveness and potential for advancing medical image segmentation.

We present the Convolutional Conditional Neural Process (ConvCNP), a novel addition to the Neural Process family designed to incorporate translation equivariance into data modeling. This property is a crucial inductive bias for various learning tasks, such as time series analysis, spatial data interpretation, and image processing. Unlike traditional models that embed data into finite-dimensional vectors, ConvCNPs embed datasets into an infinite-dimensional function space. To formalize this approach, we extend the neural set representation framework to include functional embeddings and show that any translation-equivariant embedding can be realized through a convolutional deep set architecture. Our experiments across multiple scenarios demonstrate that ConvCNPs achieve state-of-the-art results compared to existing Neural Processes. Moreover, leveraging translation equivariance allows the model to generalize zero-shot to complex, out-of-domain tasks.

Max-cut, clustering, and numerous other partitioning challenges that are crucial to machine learning and various scientific disciplines are classified as NP-hard problems. This complexity has driven researchers to develop a wide array of approximation algorithms and heuristics. Although the optimal algorithm often depends on the specific application context, traditional comparisons rely on worst-case analysis. However, this approach can be misleading if such worst-case scenarios are rare. Consequently, there is a growing need for optimization methods that identify the algorithm configuration best suited to typical inputs encountered in real-world applications. We address this challenge for clustering, max-cut, and related partitioning problems—including integer quadratic programming—by creating computationally efficient and sample-efficient learning algorithms. These algorithms utilize samples drawn from an application-specific distribution over problem instances to learn a partitioning strategy with high expected performance. Our methods focus on well-known families such as SDP rounding algorithms and agglomerative clustering techniques enhanced with dynamic programming. In our analysis of sample complexity, we establish tight bounds on the pseudodimension of these algorithm classes and reveal, intriguingly, that even classes of algorithms parameterized by a single variable can have a superconstant pseudodimension. Through this work, we make significant contributions to the theoretical foundations of adaptive algorithm selection in complex partitioning problems.

Although deep learning models and techniques have achieved remarkable empirical success, our understanding of the fundamental reasons behind this success remains limited. To address this gap, we examine the decision boundary of a standard deep learning architecture under minimal assumptions about the training data and the model itself. We establish both theoretically and empirically that the final weight layer of a neural network converges to a linear SVM trained on the outputs of the last hidden layer, applicable to both binary and multi-class classification tasks with the commonly used cross-entropy loss. Additionally, our empirical findings suggest that training the entire neural network, rather than just fine-tuning the last layer, can lead to a more favorable bias constant for the final weights, which is crucial for better generalization. Beyond deepening the understanding of neural networks, our results have practical implications for addressing issues such as catastrophic forgetting and adversarial attacks. The code for our experiments is available at https://github.com/lykaust15/NN_decision_boundary

Recently, end-to-end learning frameworks have become increasingly popular in the field of robot control. These systems take input states or images and directly predict the necessary torques or action parameters. However, they often face criticism for their substantial data requirements to successfully learn a task. The challenge of scalability across multiple tasks is well-founded, as training each task typically demands hundreds or thousands of examples. But is it necessary for end-to-end approaches to develop a separate model for every individual task? Intuitively, sharing knowledge across tasks should be advantageous, since all tasks involve some common understanding of the environment. In this paper, we take a step further in data-driven end-to-end learning: shifting from models dedicated to single tasks to joint learning of multiple robot tasks. Remarkably, our results demonstrate that multi-task learning models often outperform task-specific models trained with the same data volume. For instance, a deep network trained with 2,500 grasp examples and 2,500 push examples shows improved grasping performance compared to a network trained solely on 5,000 grasp examples.

A set of transition probability functions constitute a Shannon's channel, while a set of truth functions define a semantic channel. Label learning aims to align semantic channels with Shannon's channels, whereas label selection seeks to match Shannon's channels to semantic channels. The Channel Matching (CM) algorithm is designed for multi-label classification, operating under the maximum semantic information criterion, which is compatible with the maximum likelihood and regularized least squares criteria. When dealing with very large samples, Shannon's channels can be directly transformed into semantic channels using the third kind of Bayes' theorem; if not, truth functions can be trained with parameters based on sampled distributions. A label may be expressed as a Boolean function of certain atomic labels. To simplify the learning process, we may focus on deriving truth functions for only some atomic labels. For a specific label, instances are categorized into three types—positive, negative, and unclear—in contrast to the conventional binary approach, thereby avoiding issues associated with binary relevance. For each instance, the classifier selects a compound label that carries the most semantic information or the richest connotation. As a predictive model, the semantic channel remains unaffected by the prior probability distribution (source) of instances and continues to function even when the source is

Interactive reinforcement learning agents leverage human feedback or instructions to facilitate learning in complex environments. Typically, this feedback appears as a discrete signal—positive or negative—that provides guidance. However, such binary signals can be limited in scope and challenging to generalize. In this study, we investigate how natural language advice can serve as a more informative feedback mechanism, enhancing traditional policy shaping techniques—a well-established method in interactive reinforcement learning. Conventionally, policy shaping involves using human feedback policies to guide the agent toward its goals. Here, we substitute human feedback with policies derived from natural language advice. Our goal is to determine whether the reasoning embedded in natural language can aid a deep reinforcement learning agent in making effective decisions across diverse environments. To achieve this, we design a model comprising three networks: an experience-driven network, an advice generator, and an advice-driven network. While the experience-driven component selects actions based on environmental rewards, the advice generator produces natural language guidance, which then influences the advice-driven neural network’s decision-making in new situations.

We introduce a novel algorithm designed to minimize the sum of functions by integrating the computational speed of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with the second-order curvature insights provided by quasi-Newton methods. This approach unifies these strategies by maintaining a separate Hessian approximation for each individual function contributing to the sum. To ensure computational efficiency and manageable memory usage in high-dimensional optimization tasks, we store and update these quadratic approximations within a shared, low-dimensional, dynamically evolving subspace. Each iteration involves evaluating only a single function or mini-batch, mirroring SGD's efficiency, and updates are scaled using an approximate inverse Hessian. Unlike traditional quasi-Newton techniques, this method requires minimal hyperparameter tuning. Departing from earlier stochastic second-order methods that treat each function’s Hessian as a noisy estimate of the full Hessian, our approach directly targets the individual Hessians for precise approximation. We demonstrate superior convergence across seven diverse optimization challenges and provide the implementation as open-source Python and MATLAB packages.

This paper addresses a learning algorithm for a probabilistic model of spiking neural networks (SNNs). Rezende and Gerstner (2014) introduced a stochastic variational inference method for training SNNs with hidden neurons. Their approach updates the variational distribution using a score function gradient estimator, which often suffers from high variance, hampering the efficiency of the learning process. In contrast, this work proposes an alternative gradient estimator for SNNs based on the path-wise gradient method. The primary technical challenge lies in the absence of a general technique for differentiating realizations of arbitrary point processes, a crucial step in deriving the path-wise gradient estimator. To address this, we develop a differentiable point process—a key contribution of this paper—and utilize it to formulate the path-wise gradient estimator for SNNs. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated through numerical simulations.

Traditional clustering methods primarily rely on analyzing the feature space. However, many real-world datasets contain supplementary spatial information and have ground truth labels that are spatially coherent, which standard clustering techniques may fail to accurately recover. Inspired by applications in hyperspectral imaging, we propose novel clustering models based on orthogonal nonnegative matrix factorization, enhanced with a total variation (TV) regularization applied to the cluster membership matrix to promote spatial coherence. We develop several approaches utilizing different optimization strategies, where the TV regularization is either implemented as a postprocessing step or integrated directly into the clustering process. Finally, we evaluate all the proposed methods numerically on a hyperspectral dataset obtained through matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization imaging, demonstrating significantly improved clustering performance over conventional models.

We introduce a novel memory-based tracking approach utilizing part-level dense memory and a voting-driven retrieval mechanism, termed DMV. With the advent of deep learning in the tracking domain, Siamese trackers have gained popularity due to their favorable balance of speed and accuracy. Nonetheless, most of these methods rely on single-template matching, which constrains performance by limiting access to only the initial target features. To address this, our approach maintains an external memory that records tracking history, enabling the tracker to access richer information. Part-level retrieval from this memory decouples the process from the original template, enhancing robustness against challenges like appearance variations and occlusions. Additionally, by updating the memory throughout tracking, we bolster the target’s representation without the need for online learning. We also introduce an innovative voting mechanism for memory reading, effectively filtering out unreliable data. Extensive evaluations on OTB-100, TrackingNet, GOT-10k, LaSOT, and UAV123 demonstrate that our method achieves results comparable to state-of-the-art trackers.

Given the ubiquity and significance of online payment platforms, detecting fraudulent transactions has become crucial to safeguarding user accounts and maintaining platform security. In this study, we introduce a novel approach to fraud detection that integrates patterns from both users' static profiles and their dynamic behaviors within a unified framework. To effectively capture behavioral information in continuous time, we employ time attention-based recurrent layers that encode detailed temporal data—such as action durations, time gaps between actions, and sequential behavioral patterns—into a shared latent space. We then fuse these learned embeddings with users' static profile information within a comprehensive model. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques across various evaluation metrics, notably excelling in recall at top percentages—a vital measure balancing user experience and potential financial risk.

This paper examines the qualitative distinctions between evolutionary strategies and reinforcement learning algorithms by focusing on two leading methods: the OpenAI-ES evolutionary strategy and the Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) reinforcement learning algorithm—two closely related approaches within their respective families. We compare these methods across several dimensions: (i) overall effectiveness, (ii) robustness in handling sparse rewards, (iii) tendency and capacity to identify minimal solutions, (iv) reliance on reward shaping, and (v) adaptability to changes in environmental conditions. Through an analysis of their performance and the behavioral strategies exhibited by agents trained with each approach on standard benchmark tasks, we reveal nuanced qualitative differences previously unrecognized. Our findings identify specific weaknesses inherent to each method and suggest potential improvements. Additionally, we demonstrate that the nature of the reward function plays a crucial role, influencing results differently not only between OpenAI-ES and PPO but also across other reinforcement learning algorithms. This underscores the importance of tailoring reward function design to the particular algorithm to optimize performance.

Adversarial Training (AT) and Virtual Adversarial Training (VAT) are regularization methods that enhance Deep Neural Network (DNN) robustness by incorporating adversarial examples created through small, worst-case perturbations to input data. In this paper, we introduce xAT and xVAT, novel adversarial training algorithms that generate *multiplicative* perturbations for more effective and resilient DNN training. Unlike the *additive* perturbations used in AT and VAT, these multiplicative modifications are more perceptible and easier to interpret. Additionally, they can be generated both transductively and inductively, whereas traditional AT and VAT primarily support transductive approaches. Through a series of experiments, we examine the properties of these multiplicative perturbations and demonstrate that xAT and xVAT achieve comparable or superior accuracy on various standard benchmarks, often outperforming existing methods by around 30% in training speed. The resulting DNNs also exhibit notably different weight distributions.

Given the joint probabilities of a pair of random variables, it is possible to compute relevant quantities such as mutual information. The Bayesian approach to unknown probabilities involves deriving a posterior distribution from a second-order prior and the observed data likelihood. In dealing with incomplete data, a common strategy is to assume ignorability and apply the Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm to estimate the probabilities. Traditionally, these two methods—Bayesian inference and EM—are treated separately. This paper integrates both approaches specifically for Dirichlet priors, developing efficient approximations for the mean, mode, and (co)variance of the probabilities and mutual information. Additionally, we establish the unimodality of the posterior distribution, ensuring that the EM algorithm converges to the global maximum within this framework. These findings are applied to feature selection in incremental learning and naive Bayes classification. We introduce a rapid filtering method based on the distribution of mutual information, which consistently outperforms the conventional filter relying on empirical mutual information across various incomplete real-world datasets.

We present a versatile family of fairness regularizers applicable to both linear and logistic regression tasks. These regularizers are convex, enabling efficient optimization, and they encompass a spectrum ranging from group fairness to robust individual fairness. By adjusting the regularizer's weight, we can determine the optimal balance between accuracy and fairness—the so-called efficiency frontier—on any dataset. To quantify this balance, we introduce the concept of the Price of Fairness (PoF). Our main contribution is a comprehensive comparative analysis of the PoF across six datasets where fairness plays a central role.

Recent advancements in point-cloud-based 3D object detection have been substantial. Nonetheless, most research primarily focuses on enhancing deep learning architectures to boost accuracy alone. In this paper, we introduce an autoencoder-inspired framework that employs channel-wise compression and decompression through interchange transfer for effective knowledge distillation. To capture the map-view features of a teacher network, features from both teacher and student models are independently processed through a shared autoencoder. We incorporate a compressed representation loss that aligns the channel-wise compressed knowledge from both networks, serving as a form of regularization. The decompressed features are then exchanged bidirectionally to minimize reconstruction discrepancies. Additionally, we propose an attentive head loss to accurately match key detection information extracted via a multi-head self-attention mechanism. Extensive experiments confirm that our approach effectively trains lightweight models tailored for 3D point cloud detection, demonstrating superior performance on renowned public datasets such as Waymo and nuScenes.

This brief overview introduces an image classification dataset comprising 10 types of executable code and nearly 50,000 virus samples. The malicious categories include nine distinct virus families along with a benign class. The dataset's format converts the first 1024 bytes of Portable Executable (PE) files into images, similar to the MNIST handwritten digit dataset, allowing most existing image processing algorithms to be adapted with minimal adjustments. The nine virus families were identified through unsupervised learning, specifically KMeans clustering that excluded non-malicious samples. Using deep learning techniques such as MobileNetV2 as a benchmark, the model achieved approximately 80% accuracy in classifying viruses by family when including benign files. Notably, after initial malware detection via signatures or heuristics, transforming the first 1024 bytes into a thumbnail image enables virus type classification with 87% accuracy. This approach extends prior research demonstrating that convolutional neural networks—originally designed for image recognition—can be effectively applied to the domain of executable byte data. The dataset is publicly accessible on Kaggle and Github.

Width-based planning has demonstrated notable success in Atari 2600 games using pixel inputs, achieving this with significantly fewer environment interactions compared to reinforcement learning. Recent advancements in width-based methods involve generating feature vectors for each screen via either a handcrafted feature set or a variational autoencoder trained on game images (VAE-IW), then pruning screens lacking novel features during search. We introduce Olive (Online-VAE-IW), which dynamically updates VAE features through active learning to enhance the informativeness of screens encountered during planning. Experiments across 55 Atari titles show that Olive surpasses Rollout-IW by a ratio of 42:11 and VAE-IW by 32:20. Additionally, Olive outperforms existing policy-learning approaches such as $\pi$-IW and DQN—trained with 100 times the budget—by margins of 30:22 and 31:17, respectively. It also exceeds the performance of the state-of-the-art data-efficient reinforcement learning method, EfficientZero, which was trained with the same budget and executed with 1.8 times more planning steps, achieving scores of 18:7 on the Atari 100k benchmark—all without any policy learning. The source code is publicly available at github.com/ibm/atari-active-learning.

Most industrial recommender systems predominantly utilize collaborative filtering (CF) techniques to deliver personalized recommendations. However, CF inherently conflicts with user privacy, as it requires users to disclose their preferences to facilitate grouping with similar users and enhance recommendation accuracy. Although previous privacy-preserving methods have managed to obscure user preferences from centralized systems to some degree, they often involve notable compromises in privacy, scalability, and accuracy, and remain susceptible to malicious breaches. Addressing these challenges, we introduce the innovative Selective Privacy Preserving (SP2) paradigm, empowering users to specify their privacy preferences by categorizing their ratings as either public—shareable with the system—or private—kept exclusively on their device and never disclosed. The SP2 framework operates in two phases: (i) it initially constructs a recommendation model using all publicly shared ratings, and (ii) it further personalizes this model on each user’s device by incorporating their private ratings, ensuring tailored recommendations without compromising individual privacy.

We perform an extensive investigation into the relationship between out-of-sample performance and Bayesian evidence (marginal likelihood) in Bayesian neural networks (BNNs), along with an examination of ensemble approaches of BNNs, leveraging the Boston housing dataset. Utilizing advanced nested sampling techniques, we numerically explore the entire network posterior space, capturing its non-Gaussian and multimodal characteristics, and derive estimates of the Bayesian evidence for models with up to 156 trainable parameters. These models feature between zero and four hidden layers, employ either \(\tanh\) or ReLU activation functions, and include configurations with and without hierarchical priors. Ensembles are constructed by sampling from the posterior distribution over networks, re-weighted by their Bayesian evidence, to derive a combined posterior. Our results reveal a strong correlation between out-of-sample performance and Bayesian evidence, alongside an intriguing symmetry between how evidence scales with model size and how performance varies with model size. Networks utilizing ReLU activation functions generally exhibit higher evidence scores than those with \(\tanh\), which correlates with improved out-of-sample results. Furthermore, ensemble methods across different architectures further enhance predictive performance beyond that of individual BNNs.

Many real-world prediction tasks require modeling multi-order feature interactions within user event sequences to enhance detection accuracy. However, current popular approaches often encounter two main challenges: 1) they primarily focus on feature interactions without accounting for the influence of sequence context; 2) they emphasize sequence information but overlook the internal relationships among features within each event, limiting the quality of event representations. In this paper, we propose a hierarchical two-level framework to capture the layered information in user event sequences: 1) learning robust feature interactions to construct effective event representations; 2) modeling the overall sequence representation of a user's historical events. Experimental results on both industrial and public datasets clearly demonstrate that our model significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines.

This paper explores various methods for time series modeling. It discusses forecasting techniques employing linear models, the ARIMA algorithm, and the XGBoost machine learning algorithm. The results of different model combinations are presented. Additionally, the paper examines probabilistic modeling approaches based on copulas and Bayesian inference.

The primary goal of Privacy-Preserving Machine Learning (PPML) is to safeguard data privacy and ensure security during the development of Machine Learning models. PPML encompasses a range of techniques, including Secure Multi-Party Computation, Differential Privacy, and Homomorphic Encryption (HE). These methods are integrated with various Machine Learning and Deep Learning architectures to both protect user identity and maintain data confidentiality. In this paper, we introduce a fully homomorphically encrypted wavelet neural network designed to preserve privacy without sacrificing model performance. We evaluated our approach using seven datasets from the finance and healthcare sectors. The results demonstrate that our proposed model achieves performance comparable to that of unencrypted models.

Most existing graph neural networks (GNNs) utilize message passing and aggregation frameworks to learn node embeddings but lack the ability to capture the relative positions of nodes within a graph. To address this limitation, some methods incorporate anchor nodes, using distances from each node to these anchors to infer relative positioning. However, P-GNNs often select anchors arbitrarily, which undermines both position-awareness and feature extraction quality. We argue that selecting anchors that are evenly distributed and asymmetrically positioned is crucial for effective position encoding. Additionally, we demonstrate that choosing anchors capable of aggregating embeddings for all nodes in a graph is NP-hard, making the design of optimal deterministic algorithms practically infeasible. To overcome these challenges and avoid NP-completeness, we introduce Position-Sensing Graph Neural Networks (PSGNNs), which learn to select anchors in a differentiable, backpropagation-compatible manner. Experimental results confirm that PSGNNs outperform current state-of-the-art GNNs, significantly enhancing performance across various synthetic and real-world graph datasets while maintaining stable scalability. Specifically, PSGNNs achieve an average increase of over 14% in AUC for pairwise node classification and more than 18% for link prediction compared to existing position-aware methods. Our source code is publicly available.

We address the challenge of certifying individual fairness (IF) in feed-forward neural networks (NNs). Specifically, we focus on the $\epsilon$-$\delta$-IF framework, which, given a neural network and a data-driven similarity metric, mandates that the output difference between any pair of individuals deemed $\epsilon$-similar remains within a maximum decision tolerance $\delta \geq 0$. To handle a variety of metrics, including the Mahalanobis distance, we introduce a technique to overapproximate the resulting optimization problem using piecewise-linear functions, providing global bounds on the NN’s non-linearities across the entire input space. This approach is formulated as a Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) problem, enabling the computation of IF guarantees on four widely used fairness benchmark datasets. Additionally, we demonstrate how this formulation can guide fairness-aware training by adjusting the neural network’s loss function. Empirical results confirm that our method produces neural networks that are significantly more fair—by orders of magnitude—compared to existing state-of-the-art approaches.

Recent advancements have demonstrated remarkable success of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) across various computer vision applications. Nonetheless, their deployment in tasks involving high-dimensional inputs and outputs—such as high-resolution image and video segmentation or 3D medical imaging—remains challenging due to several limitations. A key obstacle during training is the need to store intermediate activations for backpropagation, which can demand memory capacities beyond current hardware capabilities, especially in 3D contexts. Inspired by signal propagation in physical networks described by the hyperbolic Telegraph equation, this work presents a fully conservative hyperbolic network tailored for high-dimensional data problems. We incorporate a coarsening mechanism that enables fully reversible CNNs through a learnable Discrete Wavelet Transform and its inverse, facilitating both the coarsening and interpolation of network states and allowing dynamic adjustment of channel numbers. Our results demonstrate that these fully reversible networks can match state-of-the-art performance in 4D time-lapse hyperspectral image segmentation and comprehensive 3D video segmentation, all while maintaining a memory footprint that remains constant regardless of network depth. Additionally, we explore further extensions of this approach.

It is well established that Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) are susceptible to adversarial attacks, and enhancing their adversarial robustness typically involves incorporating adversarial noise into training data, such as through standard adversarial training (SAT). However, the addition of inappropriate noise levels can impair a model's performance, leading to a trade-off between accuracy and robustness. While this issue has been extensively examined in the context of whole-image classification, it remains underexplored in medical image analysis tasks—including image segmentation, landmark detection, and object detection. In this work, we demonstrate that the traditional SAT approach encounters a significant limitation in these medical applications: it applies a uniform, fixed noise level across all training samples, which hampers effective robust training. Excessive noise can cause substantial performance degradation, whereas insufficient noise may fail to enhance robustness. To address this challenge, we propose an adaptive-margin adversarial training (AMAT) method that generates sample-specific adversarial noise tailored to each training instance. Unlike conventional, classification-focused adversarial training techniques, our AMAT approach employs a loss-based margin strategy, enabling more effective and flexible robust training for medical image analysis.

In the medical field, the scarcity of extensive training datasets and benchmarks often hampers the effective development of deep neural networks. While manual annotation is costly and time-consuming, computer simulations offer a promising alternative by generating large, fully labeled datasets with minimal manual effort. However, models trained solely on simulated data frequently struggle to perform well on real-world images. To address this domain gap between simulated and actual laparoscopic images, we leverage recent advancements in unpaired image-to-image translation. We enhance an image translation technique to produce a wide variety of realistically appearing synthetic images derived from simple laparoscopic simulations. By implementing mechanisms that preserve the original image content during translation, we ensure that the labels assigned to simulated images remain applicable to their realistically rendered counterparts. Consequently, we create a substantial, fully annotated synthetic dataset of laparoscopic images that closely resemble real visuals. Our experiments demonstrate that this dataset effectively trains models for liver segmentation in laparoscopic imagery, achieving average Dice scores up to 0.89 in some patients—all without manually annotating a single real laparoscopic image.

Typically, fair machine learning research centers on a single decision-maker and presumes a stationary population. In contrast, many critical areas motivating this work involve competitive markets with numerous decision-makers. Realistically, only a subset of these actors may choose to implement non-compulsory, fairness-focused policies—a scenario known as partial compliance in political philosophy. This raises important questions: How does the strategic behavior of decision-makers in partial compliance contexts influence allocation outcomes? If a certain percentage of employers (say, k%) voluntarily adopt fairness-promoting measures, should we expect that same percentage of progress toward universal fairness benefits? Or might the dynamics of partial compliance negate the anticipated gains? Additionally, how would adopting a global perspective, as opposed to a local one, alter an auditor’s conclusions? In this paper, we introduce a straightforward model of an employment market, utilizing simulation to examine how interaction effects and incentives shape outcomes and auditing metrics. Our primary findings indicate that at equilibrium: (1) partial compliance—where only a fraction k% of employers adopt fairness policies—often yields significantly less than proportional progress toward full compliance; and (2) this disparity becomes even more pronounced when fair employers align with global, rather than local, strategies.

In this study, we demonstrate that metric learning encounters significant inseparability issues in the absence of informative sample mining. Since inseparable samples are often indistinguishable from hard samples, existing strategies for informative sample mining aimed at addressing inseparability may introduce side effects, such as instability in the objective function. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel distance metric learning approach called Adaptive Neighborhood Metric Learning (ANML). In ANML, we implement two thresholds that dynamically identify inseparable similar and dissimilar samples during training, enabling simultaneous inseparable sample removal and metric parameter optimization. Given the non-continuous nature of ANML, we propose an innovative function named the \emph{log-exp mean function} to create a continuous surrogate formulation, which can be efficiently optimized through gradient descent. Similar to Triplet loss, ANML can be employed to learn both linear and deep embeddings. Further analysis reveals several interesting properties; for instance, when used for linear embedding learning, ANML encompasses well-known metric learning algorithms such as Large Margin Nearest Neighbor (LMNN) and Neighborhood Components Analysis (NCA) as special cases.

Explainable AI has become a crucial element for black-box machine learning methods, especially in fields where reliability and transparency are paramount. Examples include medical support systems and applications governed by the European Union's General Data Protection Regulation, which emphasizes transparency as a fundamental principle. These requirements necessitate the ability to scrutinize the reasons behind a classifier's decisions. Although visualizations are commonly used as explanation tools, they often lack sufficient expressiveness: they cannot effectively differentiate between various attribute manifestations of visual features (such as an open versus closed eye) or accurately convey the impact of the presence or absence of features and their interrelations. An alternative approach involves using more expressive symbolic surrogate models, but these typically require symbolic inputs, which are seldom available in most computer vision tasks. In this paper, we explore how to address this challenge by leveraging the inherent features learned by neural networks to generate comprehensive, verbal explanations of a feed-forward convolutional deep neural network (DNN). The semantic meanings of these features are extracted through a concept analysis method trained on a set of human-understandable visual concepts. The explanation itself is derived using an Inductive Logic Programming (ILP) approach.

This paper investigates vehicle re-identification through the comparison of image distances within CNN latent spaces. Initially, we examine the influence of various distance metrics, evaluating their performance with different measures: minimal Euclidean distance (MED), minimal cosine distance (MCD), and the residuals from sparse coding reconstruction (RSCR). These metrics are applied to features extracted from five distinct CNN architectures—ResNet18, AlexNet, VGG16, InceptionV3, and DenseNet201. Using the VeRi dataset, a specialized vehicle re-identification benchmark, we fine-tune the CNNs and assess their performance. Across all CNNs, MCD consistently outperforms MED, which is predominantly used in existing literature. These findings are validated on additional vehicle retrieval datasets. Next, we extend the existing image-to-track process (I2TP) to a track-to-track process (T2TP), allowing for distance measurement between entire tracks rather than individual images. The three distance metrics are adapted accordingly for track comparison, enabling the T2TP framework. Comparative analysis shows that T2TP surpasses I2TP in performance when using MCD and RSCR metrics. The combination of DenseNet201 with MCD-based metrics within T2TP yields the best results, exceeding current state-of-the-art I2TP models. Ultimately, our experiments underscore two key insights: first, the selection of the distance metric significantly affects vehicle re-identification accuracy; second, T2TP provides improved performance over I2TP, particularly when paired with MCD-based metrics.

In hardware-aware Differentiable Neural Architecture Search (DNAS), calculating gradients of hardware metrics for architecture optimization remains a significant challenge. Current approaches primarily rely on linear approximations that have limited applicability to customized hardware accelerators. To address this, we introduce End-to-end Hardware-aware DNAS (EH-DNAS), a comprehensive framework that seamlessly combines end-to-end hardware benchmarking with fully automated DNAS to produce hardware-efficient deep neural networks across diverse platforms, including Edge GPUs, Edge TPUs, mobile CPUs, and specialized accelerators. Given a target hardware platform, our method involves learning a differentiable model that predicts the end-to-end hardware performance of neural network architectures within the DNAS process. Additionally, we present E2E-Perf, an end-to-end hardware benchmarking tool tailored for customized accelerators. Experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet demonstrate that EH-DNAS enhances hardware performance by an average of 1.4× on customized accelerators and 1.6× on existing hardware processors, all while preserving classification accuracy.

This paper introduces an innovative method for distributed linear filtering and prediction. The problem involves a random dynamical system observed by a sparse multi-agent sensor network. Drawing inspiration from consensus plus innovations strategies in distributed estimation, the study proposes a new algorithm that integrates the principles of consensus and innovation-based updates. Additionally, the paper defines a concept of distributed observability, a requirement for the algorithm that is less stringent than the combined assumptions of global observability and network connectivity. Using foundational principles, the optimal gain matrices are designed to minimize the mean-squared estimation error at each agent, and a distributed form of the algebraic Riccati equation is formulated to compute these gains effectively.

This paper reviews previous approaches to utilizing deep learning frameworks for analyzing complex sequential datasets characterized by discrete, irregular patterns. An illustrative example of such data is financial time series, where specific events can cause abrupt, unpredictable changes in the sequence. Traditional deep learning techniques often struggle or fail to effectively analyze these datasets. A comprehensive review of the literature highlights the predominance of recurrent neural network-based frameworks. The evaluation of these frameworks typically relies on accuracy metrics such as mean absolute error and root mean square error. Key challenges identified include limited robustness of performance, lack of interpretability, and issues related to internal and external architectural design and configuration. These challenges present opportunities for advancing frameworks tailored to complex, irregular-patterned sequential data.

Recently, a series of studies have yielded promising theoretical insights into training over-parameterized neural networks—networks whose sizes exceed the minimum needed for low-error performance. The central idea is that, with ample over-parameterization, gradient-based training methods tend to leave certain components of the network largely unchanged, causing the optimization to behave as if these parts are effectively fixed at their initial random values. This phenomenon underpins the well-known approach of learning through random features. Essentially, these findings suggest that successful training of neural networks hinges on their ability to learn features akin to random ones. In this paper, we first review these methods, offering a straightforward and self-contained analysis for networks with one hidden layer. We then highlight a fundamental limitation: despite these encouraging results, the random feature framework cannot fully account for neural network learning. Specifically, we rigorously demonstrate that random features cannot be used to learn even a single ReLU neuron with standard Gaussian inputs unless the network size or weight magnitudes grow exponentially. Since such a single neuron can indeed be learned via gradient-based methods, we conclude that a comprehensive, general explanation for the empirical success of neural networks remains an open challenge.

Word vector representations play a crucial role in deep learning models for natural language processing. Various forms of these vectors, collectively called embeddings—such as word2vec and GloVe—are trained on extensive corpora to capture how words are used within context, thereby encoding semantic relationships between words. However, these embeddings typically operate at the level of word types, which can lead to ambiguities—for instance, distinguishing whether a word functions as a noun or a verb. In tasks like question answering, recognizing parts of speech and named entity types is vital, but incorporating these attributes directly into neural models often increases the input complexity and size. This study utilizes holographic compression techniques on pre-trained embeddings to simultaneously encode a token, its part-of-speech, and its named entity type within a single vector dimension—matching the original size used for token-only representations. Implemented within an adapted recurrent deep learning question answering system, this approach maintains semantic integrity and demonstrates strong performance.

Training machine learning models on sensitive user data has raised growing privacy concerns across various sectors. Federated learning offers a promising privacy-preserving approach by exchanging only local gradient information instead of raw data. To ensure rigorous privacy protection, integrating local differential privacy into federated learning is a viable strategy. However, existing methods face three key challenges: first, the added noise often remains close to the original data with high probability, increasing the risk of information leakage; second, the substantial variance introduced during averaging leads to diminished accuracy; and third, the high dimensionality of deep learning model weights causes the privacy budget to escalate rapidly. In this study, we introduce a novel local differential privacy mechanism tailored for federated learning to overcome these hurdles. Our design enhances data obscurity beyond the original values, reduces variance in estimates, and mitigates the curse of dimensionality by partitioning and shuffling model updates. Extensive experiments on three widely used datasets—MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR-10—demonstrate that our method not only delivers superior deep learning performance but also ensures robust privacy guarantees.

Deep learning algorithms have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in the field of Computer Vision. In recent years, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have been employed to address challenges in image generation, finding widespread use in areas such as photo editing, image design, computer animation, real-time rendering of large scenes, and visual effects for movies. However, current state-of-the-art CNNs face limitations in texture synthesis, particularly in capturing the spatial arrangement of textures within images, often resulting in significant distortions post-synthesis. To address this issue, we propose a novel image generation approach that incorporates a semantic segmentation step as a pre-processing stage within the deep learning framework, followed by analysis of the generated results.

This paper introduces the baseline methodology for the organized 2nd Covid-19 Competition, held within the framework of the AIMIA Workshop at ECCV 2022. It details the COV19-CT-DB database, which is annotated for COVID-19 detection and comprises approximately 7,700 three-dimensional CT scans. A subset of the database containing COVID-19 cases is further labeled with four severity levels of the disease. The database has been partitioned into training, validation, and test sets, with the first two used for model development and tuning, and the test set reserved for evaluation purposes. The proposed baseline employs a deep learning model based on a CNN-RNN architecture, and its performance on the COVID19-CT-DB dataset is reported.

Optimal Transport (OT) frequently appears in numerous machine learning tasks; however, its significant computational demands hinder widespread adoption. To overcome this scalability challenge, we introduce SPOT (Scalable Push-forward of Optimal Transport), an implicit generative learning framework. Our approach approximates the optimal transport plan by transforming a reference distribution via a pushforward operation, reformulating the OT problem as a minimax optimization. This enables us to efficiently solve OT problems using primal-dual stochastic gradient algorithms. Furthermore, we demonstrate how neural ordinary differential equations can be employed to recover the density of the optimal transport plan. Numerical experiments on both synthetic and real datasets confirm that SPOT is robust and exhibits favorable convergence properties. Additionally, SPOT facilitates efficient sampling from the optimal transport plan, enhancing downstream tasks such as domain adaptation.

Machine learning models are frequently integrated into workflows alongside human experts, with the models having the option to defer to domain specialists when their confidence in an inference is low. Our objective is to develop strategies that ensure accuracy and fairness in such hybrid prediction systems that combine machine-generated inferences with expert judgments. Previous research on "deferral systems" in classification has primarily focused on scenarios involving a single expert, aiming to account for the expert's inaccuracies and biases to concurrently train an inference model and a deferral mechanism. We expand this approach to environments featuring multiple experts, each with distinct areas of expertise and bias profiles. We introduce a framework that jointly trains a classifier and a deferral system, where the deferral mechanism can choose to delegate uncertain inputs to one or more human experts. We evaluate our framework using both a synthetic dataset and a content moderation dataset containing biased synthetic experts, demonstrating that it significantly enhances the accuracy and fairness of the final predictions in comparison to baseline methods. Additionally, we gather crowdsourced labels to further validate our approach.

This paper presents a novel loss function, the One-Sided Margin (OSM), designed to effectively address maximum-margin classification challenges. Unlike the traditional hinge loss, OSM explicitly sets the margin using specific hyperparameters before solving the classification problem. Experimental results demonstrate that employing OSM accelerates training and achieves higher accuracy compared to binary and categorical cross-entropy across various deep models used for classification and optical character recognition tasks. OSM consistently outperforms cross-entropy and hinge losses in classification accuracy across neural networks of different sizes, while also enabling more efficient training processes. Our approach has achieved state-of-the-art results on several benchmark datasets, including CIFAR-10 (98.82%), CIFAR-100 (91.56%), Flowers (98.04%), and Stanford Cars (93.91%), surpassing other loss functions significantly. Furthermore, OSM's superior performance extends to larger networks, often yielding better results than both cross-entropy and hinge loss. We are confident that OSM offers a robust alternative to traditional loss functions like hinge and cross-entropy for training deep neural networks on classification tasks.

Given a dataset, biclustering seeks to simultaneously partition both the samples and the features used to represent them into biclusters. Consistent biclustering results enable accurate classification of samples based on known feature classifications, and vice versa, making it highly valuable for supervised classification tasks. The challenge of identifying consistent biclusters can be viewed as a feature selection problem, where irrelevant features are eliminated to improve classification accuracy, while aiming to retain as many features as possible to preserve informational richness. This feature selection task can be modeled as a linear fractional 0-1 optimization problem. We introduce a reformulation of this problem as a bilevel optimization problem and develop a heuristic algorithm to efficiently solve it. Computational experiments demonstrate that our algorithm outperforms existing heuristic methods, providing improved solutions.

In this study, we introduce a Discourse-Aware Semantic Self-Attention encoder that leverages linguistic annotations to improve reading comprehension on lengthy narrative texts. By utilizing existing annotation tools, we identify relationships among discourse units, events and their arguments, as well as coreferential mentions. Our empirical results demonstrate that incorporating these structures enhances overall performance, particularly in capturing intra-sentential and cross-sentential discourse relations, semantic roles within sentences, and long-distance coreference links. We find that allocating self-attention heads to model intra-sentential relations and connections between adjacent sentences significantly aids in extracting answers from extended contexts. These insights highlight the value of discourse-semantic annotations in boosting the generalization abilities of self-attention models for reading comprehension tasks.

Forecasting particulate matter (PM) concentrations in South Korea has become critically important due to its severe adverse effects on human health. Traditional statistical and machine learning approaches often assume that data are independent and identically distributed, such as following a Gaussian distribution; however, air pollution and weather data are time series that do not satisfy these assumptions. In this research, the maximum correntropy criterion for regression (MCCR) loss was employed to analyze the statistical properties of air pollution and weather datasets. Given their intricate seasonal patterns and the heavy-tailed nature of the data even after deseasonalization, thorough seasonality adjustments were conducted. The MCCR loss function was utilized across various models, including both conventional statistical methods and cutting-edge machine learning techniques. The findings indicate that the MCCR loss outperforms the traditional mean squared error loss, particularly in predicting extreme pollution events.

Support Vector Machine (SVM) is a reliable machine learning technique that delivers high accuracy across diverse classification tasks and is extensively employed in various embedded systems. However, deploying embedded SVM classifiers poses challenges due to the complex computational demands involved. This has driven efforts to implement SVMs on hardware platforms to attain high-performance processing with reduced cost and power consumption. Melanoma, the most aggressive skin cancer, significantly increases mortality risks. Our goal is to create an optimized embedded SVM classifier tailored for low-cost portable devices to facilitate early melanoma detection in primary healthcare settings. In this study, we introduce a hardware/software co-design approach to implement the SVM classifier on an FPGA, enabling on-chip melanoma detection. Utilizing a modern hybrid FPGA (Zynq) platform and advanced UltraFast High-Level Synthesis techniques, our design efficiently classifies melanoma directly on the chip. The hardware implementation achieves a classification accuracy of 97.9%, along with a hardware acceleration factor of 21, utilizing only 3% of resources and consuming 1.69W of power. These results demonstrate that our system on chip effectively balances high performance with minimal resource utilization, low power consumption, and affordability, making it suitable for embedded medical diagnostic applications.

Most machine learning systems that engage with humans attempt to construct some concept of a person's "identity." However, the prevailing approach in AI research tends to view identity as composed of fixed, discrete attributes. In contrast, critical theory offers a perspective that sees identity as fluid and constructed through ongoing interactions—more of a process of doing than a static being. In this paper, we translate some of these ideas for machine learning practitioners and propose a theory of identity based on autopoiesis—cyclical processes of formation and function.
