This study represents an initial experimental effort to examine the spectrum of performance bottlenecks that can occur in 5G mobile networks. Utilizing a comprehensive set of measurements collected from a prototype testbed that emulates the core features of a cloud-enabled mobile network, we assess the effectiveness of various metrics and methods for detecting bottlenecks efficiently and accurately across different network locations and system layers. Our results underscore the complexity inherent in monitoring such multi-layered architectures and emphasize the necessity for innovative approaches that intelligently integrate metrics from multiple network layers and functions. Notably, our analysis shows that distributed analytics offers a promising balance, achieving satisfactory accuracy in bottleneck detection while maintaining manageable computational and communication costs.

Distillation is a powerful technique for transferring knowledge, where soft targets derived from a sophisticated teacher model's predicted distributions are used to train a smaller student model. However, a pre-trained high-capacity teacher is not always accessible. Recent online methods address this by utilizing the combined intermediate predictions of multiple student models as targets, enabling teacher-free distillation. While this approach improves flexibility, the group members tend to converge quickly into similar solutions due to simple aggregation methods, leading to early saturation. 

In this work, we introduce Online Knowledge Distillation with Diverse peers (OKDDip), a dual-level distillation framework involving multiple auxiliary peers and a single group leader. During the first level, each auxiliary peer employs an attention-based mechanism to assign unique aggregation weights, generating individualized targets based on the predictions of other peers. This diversity in target distributions encourages greater heterogeneity among peers, enhancing the effectiveness of group-based distillation. The second level involves distilling the combined knowledge of all auxiliary peers into the group leader model, which serves as the inference model. Experimental results demonstrate that OKDDip consistently outperforms current state-of-the-art methods without increasing training or inference complexity, underscoring its effectiveness.

We introduced a model based on flocking behavior within a complex network framework and subsequently developed two clustering algorithms derived from this model. The algorithms begin by constructing a weighted, directed \textit{k}-nearest neighbor (knn) graph among all data points in the dataset, with each point treated as an agent capable of moving in space. Next, a dynamic, time-evolving network is generated by adding long-range links for each data point. Moreover, each point interacts not only with its \textit{k} nearest neighbors but also with \textit{r} long-range neighbors through spatial fields established by these neighbors. The point then moves in the direction of the vector sum of all these fields. Importantly, these long-range links provide hidden information that influences each point’s movement and help accelerate convergence toward a central position. As the data points move according to this model, those belonging to the same class gradually cluster together, while points from different classes tend to separate. Experimental results confirm that the data points are effectively grouped into meaningful clusters within the datasets.

Metal artifacts in computed tomography (CT) result from discrepancies between the physical principles of image formation and the simplified assumptions made during tomographic reconstruction. These artifacts are especially prominent around metal implants, limiting the widespread use of 3D cone-beam CT (CBCT) despite its potential for intraoperative verification of implant placement, such as in spinal fusion procedures. Using both synthetic and real datasets, we show that much of these artifacts can be mitigated by acquiring higher-quality data tailored to the specific task and patient. We also introduce the initial step toward a future task-aware CBCT protocol. Traditional short-scan CBCT paths are confined to a planar trajectory, offering limited flexibility for scene-specific adjustments. To address this, we autonomously modify the out-of-plane angulation, creating scene-adapted C-arm source trajectories that avoid capturing low-quality images affected by beam hardening, photon starvation, and noise. The optimal out-of-plane angulation is determined in real-time through a deep convolutional neural network, which predicts a detectability ranking derived from the physics of the imaging process.

We introduce semi-random features for nonlinear function approximation, offering a versatile middle ground between fully adjustable units in deep learning and the purely random features employed in kernel methods. For models with a single hidden layer utilizing semi-random features, we demonstrate—under realistic assumptions—that as the width increases, the model class can approximate any target function arbitrarily well (universality). Despite the non-convex nature of the optimization landscape, we establish that finding such an optimal function is feasible (optimization theory), and that the learned model can generalize effectively to unseen data (generalization bounds). Extending to deep models, we prove they possess universal approximation capabilities, provide a lower bound on approximation error, offer partial guarantees on optimization success, and derive robustness in generalization performance. Remarkably, depending on the application, the generalization bounds for deep semi-random features can be exponentially tighter than those for deep ReLU networks; our bounds are also independent of depth, the number of trainable parameters, and input dimensionality. Empirical results show that semi-random features can match neural network performance with only a modest increase in units, and significantly outperform random features while utilizing far fewer units. Additionally, we propose a novel implicit ensemble approach based on semi-random features.

We present a novel class of lower bounds for the log partition function in Markov random fields, grounded in a reversed form of Jensen's inequality. Our approach approximates the intractable distribution by a linear combination of spanning trees assigned negative weights. This method serves as a lower-bound equivalent to the tree-reweighted belief propagation algorithm, which employs a convex combination of spanning trees with positive weights to establish upper bounds. We also propose algorithms to optimize and tighten these lower bounds across the non-convex space of valid parameters. Our framework extends traditional mean field techniques—including both naive and structured mean field approximations—and encompasses them as special cases in the limit.

We investigate efficient algorithms for statistical regression under the strong contamination model, where the objective is to approximately optimize a generalized linear model (GLM) in the presence of adversarially corrupted data. Previous approaches in this area include the robust gradient descent method developed by Prasad et al., a first-order technique utilizing biased gradient queries, and the Sever framework introduced by Diakonikolas et al., which employs iterative outlier removal coupled with stationary point identification. We propose algorithms that operate in nearly-linear time, offering enhanced runtime performance and improved estimation guarantees relative to existing methods. Specifically, for smooth GLMs such as logistic regression, we demonstrate that the robust gradient descent technique can be accelerated. Furthermore, our framework extends to the optimization of Moreau envelopes of Lipschitz GLMs, including support vector machines, thereby addressing several open questions in the literature. In the well-understood setting of robust linear regression, we introduce an alternative strategy that achieves superior estimation accuracy within nearly-linear time constraints. Notably, our approach begins with an identifiability argument originally developed within the sum-of-squares framework by Bakshi and Prasad—an approach that attains optimal error bounds but at the cost of higher polynomial runtime and sample requirements. We reinterpret their proof within our broader context, leading to improved efficiency and guarantees.

Reinforcement learning has demonstrated remarkable success across a range of applications. However, developing an effective policy typically necessitates extensive interaction with the environment, which can be computationally intensive and time-consuming. To address this challenge, the framework known as Reinforcement Learning with Expert Demonstrations (RLED) was introduced to leverage supervision from expert data. While RLED methods can reduce the number of learning iterations, they generally assume that the demonstrations are perfect, making them vulnerable to misleading noise in real-world scenarios. In this paper, we present a novel framework that adaptively learns policies by concurrently interacting with the environment and utilizing expert demonstrations. Specifically, each step in a demonstration trajectory is treated as an individual instance. We define a joint loss function designed to maximize the expected reward while minimizing the discrepancy between the agent’s behavior and the demonstrations. Crucially, by evaluating the expected gain from the value function, we assign each instance a weight reflecting its potential utility, enabling the model to prioritize more informative demonstrations and filter out noisy data. Experimental results across various environments, employing multiple popular reinforcement learning algorithms, demonstrate that our proposed approach significantly improves learning efficiency and robustness.

Most artificial neural networks employed for object detection and recognition are trained using fully supervised methods. This approach is not only highly resource-intensive, requiring extensive datasets of labeled examples, but it also diverges significantly from human learning processes. We propose a different framework in which an artificial agent initially explores and learns within a simulated environment through self-supervised interactions. Subsequently, the representations acquired through these interactions enable the agent to associate semantic concepts, such as various types of doors. To achieve this, we introduce a technique called rapid concept mapping, which leverages correlated neural firing patterns to define and identify semantic categories. Remarkably, this method allows for immediate recognition of objects with as few as a single labeled example, mirroring the human phenomenon known as fast mapping. This demonstrates the high quality of the encoded information obtained through self-supervised, embodiment-driven curiosity exploration. Therefore, our approach offers a promising pathway for concept learning with minimal supervision, illustrating that meaningful environmental representations can be learned solely through active interaction with the world.

The Box-Cox transformation is a distinctive member of the power transformation family. It is a mathematical technique designed to identify the optimal lambda (λ) value that maximizes the log-likelihood function, thereby transforming data into a more normally distributed form and reducing heteroscedasticity. In data analytics, the assumption of normality is fundamental to numerous statistical testing methods. While this technique is primarily recognized for its application to one-dimensional data in statistical analysis, this paper explores its utility as a preprocessing step for two-dimensional data, specifically digital images, to examine its impact. Additionally, to enhance computational efficiency, the approach involves estimating the lambda parameter in real-time for large two-dimensional matrices by leveraging their probability density functions as a basis for statistical inference of the underlying data distribution. We evaluate the performance of this lightweight Box-Cox transformation against established state-of-the-art low-light image enhancement techniques. Furthermore, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through various test datasets, focusing on overall visual quality improvements and enhancing the accuracy of a color pattern classification algorithm as a representative application. Comparative results, with and without the implementation of our approach, are presented and analyzed.

Hottopixx, introduced by Bittorf et al. at NIPS 2012, is an algorithm designed to solve nonnegative matrix factorization (NMF) problems under the separability assumption. Separable NMFs are particularly valuable in applications such as extracting topics from text documents and decomposing hyperspectral images. In these contexts, the ability of the algorithm to handle noise effectively is crucial for its success. Hottopixx has demonstrated strong robustness to noise, which can be further improved through postprocessing techniques. However, a significant limitation is that both Hottopixx and its postprocessing require an estimate of the noise level in the input matrix beforehand, since this estimate influences the algorithm's parameters. Obtaining an accurate noise-level estimate is often challenging. In this paper, we address this limitation by proposing a refined version of Hottopixx and its postprocessing that operate without prior knowledge of the noise level. We prove that this refinement maintains nearly the same level of noise robustness as the original algorithm.

With the rapid expansion of mobile applications and cloud computing technologies, mobile cloud computing has garnered significant attention from both academia and industry. Nonetheless, mobile cloud applications are vulnerable to security challenges such as data integrity breaches, user confidentiality violations, and service disruptions. A proactive strategy to address these issues involves early detection and isolation of cyber threats before they can severely impact the system. In this paper, we introduce a novel framework that utilizes deep learning techniques to identify cyberattacks within mobile cloud environments. Experimental results demonstrate that our framework not only detects a wide range of cyber threats but also achieves a high detection accuracy of up to 97.11%. Additionally, we compare our approach with existing machine learning-based methods to highlight its effectiveness and advantages.

Creating new combinations of images and text is a challenge that merges computer vision with natural language processing. In this paper, we introduce methods for generating novel image-caption pairs using existing caption datasets. Our approach leverages recent breakthroughs in generative adversarial networks and sequence-to-sequence models. We extend these techniques to produce paired samples across various domains. Additionally, we explore cycle-based generation—transforming images into text and back into images, as well as its relationship with autoencoders.

Diabetes is one of the most prevalent, hazardous, and costly diseases worldwide, resulting from elevated blood sugar levels or insufficient insulin production. If diagnosed late, it can severely impact individuals' health. Today, diabetes presents a significant challenge for healthcare systems and policymakers. Prevention has become a top priority, emphasizing the importance of safeguarding health while maintaining comfort. This study employs an ensemble training approach based on genetic algorithms to enhance the accuracy of diabetes diagnosis and prognosis. The data utilized includes real-world information on Indian diabetic patients sourced from the University of California's online database. Advances in information and communication technology, such as the Internet of Things, machine learning, and data mining, enable more intelligent health management strategies—facilitating precise disease outcome predictions in everyday life and clinical settings. These technologies aid in preventing disease progression and reducing complications. The results demonstrate the high effectiveness of the proposed method, achieving a diagnostic accuracy of 98.8% and an overall prediction accuracy of 99%.

We analyze vector-valued nonlinear dynamical systems defined by the recurrence relation \(X_{t+1} = \phi(A^* X_t) + \eta_t\), where \(\eta_t\) represents unbiased noise and \(\phi : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\) is a known link function satisfying specific {\em expansivity} conditions. Our objective is to recover the unknown matrix \(A^*\) from a single, dependent, and potentially correlated trajectory \(X_1, \dots, X_T\). While the linear case—where \(\phi\) is the identity—has been extensively studied, with optimal error bounds even for non-mixing systems, current results for the nonlinear setting are limited to systems exhibiting mixing properties. 

In this work, we make several advances: (a) we introduce the first offline algorithm capable of learning nonlinear dynamical systems without relying on the mixing assumption; (b) we significantly reduce the sample complexity required for systems that do satisfy mixing conditions; (c) recognizing the challenges of streaming and one-pass scenarios, we propose a stochastic gradient descent method with Reverse Experience Replay (\(\mathsf{SGD\text{-}RER}\)), demonstrating that for mixing systems, it attains the same sample complexity as our offline approach; (d) we substantiate the expansivity assumption by examining the popular ReLU activation function—a non-expansive but easily learnable link function—and show that, under i.i.d. sampling, any learning method would necessitate...

We analyze a scenario where a seller manages a large portfolio of \( N \) products over a time span of \( T \) periods. The seller lacks prior knowledge of the parameters governing the linear demand model but can dynamically adjust product prices to learn demand patterns through sales data. The objective is to minimize pseudo-regret, defined as the expected revenue shortfall compared to an omniscient dealer who knows the true demand model. To characterize various connectivity structures within the product network, we consider a sparse demand relationship framework. Specifically, we explore three sparsity models: (1) \( L_0 \) sparsity, which limits the number of connections in the network; (2) off-diagonal sparsity, which restricts the magnitude of cross-product price sensitivities; and (3) a novel spectral sparsity, which bounds the rate at which a similarity metric among network nodes decays asymptotically. We introduce a dynamic pricing and learning strategy that integrates optimism in the face of uncertainty with PAC-Bayesian techniques, achieving near-optimal performance asymptotically in terms of \( N \) and \( T \). Furthermore, we demonstrate that under spectral and off-diagonal sparsity conditions, the seller can attain a pseudo-regret that scales linearly with \( N \), even when the network is densely connected.

We demonstrate that language models pre-trained on codified (discretely-encoded) music audio develop representations that are highly effective for downstream Music Information Retrieval (MIR) tasks. In particular, we examine the features derived from Jukebox (Dhariwal et al., 2020), a music generation system equipped with a language model trained on codified audio from one million songs. To assess whether Jukebox's representations contain valuable information for MIR, we use them as input features to train simple, shallow models across several MIR tasks. Compared to traditional MIR representations pre-trained on tagging, Jukebox's features deliver an average performance increase of 30% across four tasks: tagging, genre classification, emotion recognition, and key detection. Notably, in key detection, Jukebox’s representations outperform those from models pre-trained solely on tagging by a significant margin, indicating that pre-training through codified audio language modeling can address limitations inherent in conventional methods. We interpret these findings as evidence that modeling audio directly—rather than relying on tags—yields richer and more informative representations for MIR applications.

In this paper, we present Symplectic ODE-Net (SymODEN), a deep learning approach designed to infer the dynamics of physical systems described by ordinary differential equations (ODEs) from observed state trajectories. To enhance generalization while using fewer training samples, SymODEN leverages a physics-informed computation graph that incorporates suitable inductive biases. Specifically, we embed Hamiltonian dynamics with control into the model to explicitly learn the system's underlying behavior, facilitating insights into key physical properties such as mass and potential energy. Furthermore, we introduce a parametrization approach that maintains the Hamiltonian structure even when the data is embedded in high-dimensional spaces or when only velocity measurements are available instead of generalized momentum. By providing interpretable and physically consistent models of dynamical systems, this framework paves the way for advanced model-based control strategies.

We present the Chi-Square Test Neural Network, a single hidden layer backpropagation neural network that employs the chi-square test theorem to redefine both the cost and error functions. The weights and thresholds are adjusted through the standard backpropagation algorithm. This approach offers the benefit of maintaining consistent data distribution between training and testing sets. It is suitable for binary classification tasks. Experimental results on real-world datasets demonstrate that our proposed algorithm can substantially enhance classification accuracy compared to existing methods.

Traditional machine translation systems, whether phrase-based or neural, have predominantly depended on word-level modeling with explicit segmentation. In this study, we pose a core question: Is it possible for neural machine translation to produce a sequence of characters without relying on any explicit segmentation? To explore this, we assess an attention-based encoder-decoder architecture that employs a subword-level encoder and a character-level decoder across four language pairs—English-Czech, English-German, English-Russian, and English-Finnish—using the WMT'15 parallel corpora. Our results demonstrate that models featuring a character-level decoder consistently outperform those with a subword-level decoder across all four language pairs. Additionally, ensembles of neural models utilizing a character-level decoder surpass the current leading non-neural machine translation systems for En-Cs, En-De, and En-Fi, and achieve comparable performance on En-Ru.

Random feature maps are a fundamental component of contemporary statistical machine learning, extending random projections through sophisticated nonlinear operators that are often challenging to analyze. In this work, we utilize the "concentration" phenomenon predicted by random matrix theory to conduct a spectral analysis of the Gram matrix formed by these random feature maps, focusing on Gaussian mixture models with both high dimension and large sample size. Our findings provide valuable insights into how nonlinearity interacts with data statistics, ultimately enabling more effective calibration of random feature-based methods.

The partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) provides a rigorous framework for robot decision-making under uncertainty. However, planning within POMDPs becomes computationally demanding when long-term strategies are needed. Employing temporally-extended macro-actions can reduce the effective planning horizon and enhance computational efficiency, but the challenge remains: how can we effectively learn these macro-actions? This paper introduces the Macro-Action Generator-Critic (MAGIC), a method that performs offline learning of macro-actions tailored for online POMDP planning. MAGIC trains a macro-action generator end-to-end, using the performance of an online planner as feedback. During real-time operation, the generator produces context-aware, situation-dependent macro-actions based on the robot’s current belief and environment. We tested MAGIC across multiple long-horizon planning scenarios both in simulation and on a physical robot. The results demonstrate that the learned macro-actions substantially improve online planning efficiency and effectiveness compared to primitive actions and manually designed macro-actions.

Generating textual descriptions from structured data, such as tables, is a key task in natural language processing applications like question answering and dialogue systems. Recent research has employed neural language models and encoder-decoder architectures for table-to-text generation. However, these neural approaches often overlook the importance of content ordering during text creation. Human summarization, for instance, typically reflects an inherent order—such as mentioning nationality before occupation in a biography. To address this, we introduce an order-planning-based text generation model that explicitly captures the relationships between different data fields, enhancing the fluency and coherence of the produced text. Experiments on the WikiBio dataset demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms previous approaches, achieving higher scores in BLEU, ROUGE, and NIST metrics.

This paper introduces the Pressure Ulcers Online Website, an initial step toward a pioneering platform designed to assist individuals in detecting, understanding, and managing pressure ulcers. It explains the motivations behind the project's development and serves as a central hub for pressure ulcer analysis and ongoing research. Leveraging cutting-edge technologies such as convolutional neural networks, transfer learning, and comprehensive web development, this platform enables the analysis of pressure ulcers and the reporting of findings. As it develops through collaborative partnerships, future iterations will incorporate decision support features to detail the complex attributes of pressure ulcers and provide wound care information across diverse user groups. Ultimately, this initiative aims to raise awareness and offer support to those affected by or caring for individuals with pressure ulcers.

This paper introduces the Grounded Language-Image Pre-Training (GLIP) model, designed to develop object-level, language-aware, and semantically rich visual representations. GLIP combines object detection and phrase grounding into a unified pre-training framework, yielding two key advantages: (1) it enables learning from both detection and grounding datasets to enhance performance on both tasks and to bootstrap an effective grounding model; (2) it harnesses a vast number of image-text pairs by generating grounding boxes through self-training, thereby enriching the semantic content of the learned representations. In our experiments, we pre-train GLIP using 27 million grounding annotations, comprising 3 million human-annotated and 24 million web-crawled image-text pairs. The resulting representations exhibit strong zero-shot and few-shot transfer capabilities across various object recognition benchmarks. Specifically, when evaluated directly on COCO and LVIS without prior exposure during pre-training, GLIP achieves 49.8 AP and 26.9 AP, respectively, outperforming many supervised methods. Fine-tuning on COCO yields 60.8 AP on the validation set and 61.5 AP on the test-dev set, surpassing previous state-of-the-art results. Additionally, when applied to 13 downstream object detection tasks, a one-shot GLIP matches the performance of fully supervised models like Dynamic Head. The code will be available at https://github.com/microsoft/GLIP.

The automation of condition monitoring and workpiece inspection is crucial for ensuring both high quality and efficient throughput in manufacturing processes. Recent advancements in machine learning have significantly enhanced autonomous process oversight. However, as these models grow more complex and powerful, they often become less transparent and harder to interpret. A key challenge lies in effectively monitoring live deployments of these systems and issuing alerts when events occur that could compromise model performance. Supervised classifiers, for instance, usually assume that the data distribution remains stable over time—an assumption known as stationarity. In practice, systems like visual inspectors trained on specific defect types may fail to adapt to gradual changes, such as the appearance of new defect classes—a phenomenon known as "data drift." This can result in serious misclassifications, where novel defect types are incorrectly identified as non-defective. Therefore, implementing real-time performance monitoring of classifiers is essential to detect early signs of errors, including the emergence of new defect categories.

Are machine learning recommendation models easily deceived? While the vulnerability of hand-crafted fake user profiles has been addressed, the realm of machine-learned adversarial attacks remains largely unexplored. This study aims to fill that gap. We introduce a framework for creating synthetic user profiles that, when integrated into the training process of a recommendation system, can serve an adversarial purpose while appearing indistinguishable from authentic user data. The approach is modeled as an iterative general-sum game involving two participants: an unaware recommendation system, denoted as \( R \), and an adversarial fake user generator, \( A \). \( A \) pursues two objectives: (G1) ensuring the fake user rating distribution closely matches that of real users, and (G2) optimizing a specific attack function \( f_A \), such as undermining the system's top-K recommendations for certain user segments. We develop a learning framework to simultaneously achieve these goals and conduct comprehensive experiments with various attack types, demonstrating the inherent vulnerabilities of recommendation systems.

Acoustic monitoring for machine fault detection is a rapidly evolving research area that has shown promising results across various industries. However, collecting sufficient data to identify all possible faults remains a significant challenge. Consequently, new unsupervised anomaly detection algorithms have been developed, trained solely on data from healthy conditions. A major challenge in these methods is managing noise within the signals, which can impair detection accuracy. In this study, we introduce a robust, data-driven, and quasi non-parametric denoising approach for spectral data utilizing tensor decomposition techniques—specifically, the Non-negative Canonical Polyadic (CP) decomposition. This approach is particularly suitable for machines producing stationary sound signals. Through a case study using the Malfunctioning Industrial Machine Investigation and Inspection (MIMII) benchmark, we demonstrate that our denoising strategy significantly enhances the performance of unsupervised anomaly detection. Such methods hold great potential for making sound-based industrial process monitoring more dependable.

Deep learning classifiers play a vital role in assisting humans with decision-making, making user trust in these models critically important. Trust often hinges on consistent behavior; in AI terms, this means that given the same input, users expect the model to produce the same output—ideally correct—every time. This paper explores model behavior in the context of periodic retraining of deployed models, where outputs from successive versions may sometimes differ on the same input. We introduce formal definitions of consistency and correct-consistency for learning models. Our findings demonstrate that the consistency and correct-consistency of an ensemble learner are at least as high as the average of those measures across individual models. Additionally, correct-consistency can be probabilistically improved by combining learners whose accuracy is at or above the ensemble's average accuracy. To empirically validate our theoretical insights, we analyze three datasets using two state-of-the-art deep learning classifiers and propose an efficient dynamic snapshot ensemble method, confirming its effectiveness through experiments.

Modern large-scale data analysis often requires prioritizing samples for manual review, such as identifying misclassified critical data points or uncovering vulnerabilities that could be exploited by adversaries. To address the challenge of selecting the most impactful samples—the proverbial "needle in a haystack"—we introduce a scalable adaptation of Cook’s distance, a traditional statistical measure used to pinpoint data points that significantly influence a regression model's fit and subsequent predictions. 

To extend this approach to massive, high-dimensional datasets, we propose "influence sketching," an innovative algorithm that incorporates random projections into the influence calculation. Specifically, the influence score is derived using a pseudo-dataset generated through random projections of the post-convergence Generalized Linear Model (GLM). We demonstrate the effectiveness of influence sketching through application to a malware detection dataset comprising over 2 million executable files with nearly 100,000 features each. The results show that randomly removing about 10% of training samples barely impacts predictive accuracy—dropping from 99.47% to 99.45%—whereas eliminating the same proportion of samples with high influence scores significantly degrades model performance, confirming the method's ability to reliably identify truly influential data points.

Machine learning techniques for network traffic classification have been extensively explored. Most existing methods classify entire traffic flows, but these approaches face significant practical limitations. In a network router, packets must be processed with minimal delay, preventing classifiers from waiting until the end of a flow to determine its category. Additionally, complex machine learning models may be too computationally demanding to run directly on routers. In this paper, we propose a flow-packet hybrid traffic classification (FPHTC) approach, where the router makes per-packet decisions based on a routing policy derived from transferring knowledge learned by a flow-based classifier located outside the router. We analyze the generalization bounds of FPHTC and demonstrate its superiority over traditional packet-based classification methods. Experimental results on real-world traffic datasets showcase FPHTC's effective performance, robustness to changing traffic patterns, and suitability for deployment on systems with limited computational resources.

In this work, we introduce a novel method for reconstructing multivariate functions from training data by simultaneously identifying an appropriate network architecture and initializing it with polynomial-based approximations. Training deep neural networks through gradient descent can be viewed as navigating the loss landscape to minimize the loss functional. The choice of initial parameters plays a crucial role in iterative descent-based training methods. Our approach results in a network whose initial parameters represent a polynomial approximation of the training data. The primary benefit of this technique is that from this informed starting point, the network can be further refined using standard training procedures. Since the network already closely approximates the data initially, subsequent training is more likely to converge to a desirable local minimum. We detail the theoretical framework needed to construct such networks and present several numerical examples demonstrating that our method ultimately yields networks that can be effectively trained from the initialized state to achieve enhanced approximation accuracy for a broad class of target functions.

In biological perception, attention mechanisms are believed to selectively focus on certain subsets of perceptual information to enable more advanced processing, which would be unmanageable if all sensory inputs were processed equally. In contrast, computer vision research has largely overlooked the concept of hard attention—where specific information is intentionally ignored—despite the notable success of soft attention techniques that re-weight and combine information without eliminating any features. Here, we present a novel approach to hard attention that demonstrates highly competitive results on a recent visual question answering dataset, matching or even exceeding the performance of comparable soft attention models while completely disregarding some features. Although hard attention is often considered non-differentiable, we observe that the magnitudes of features correlate with their semantic importance, providing a valuable signal for guiding our attention mechanism. Since hard attention emphasizes the most relevant input features, it can also offer greater efficiency than soft attention methods, particularly in recent models that rely on non-local pairwise operations, which tend to have quadratic computational and memory costs relative to the number of features.

We investigate the optimization of finite sums of geodesically smooth functions on Riemannian manifolds. While variance reduction techniques for finite-sum problems have gained significant attention in recent years, existing research primarily focuses on vector space settings. In response, we propose Riemannian SVRG (RSVRG), a novel variance-reduced optimization algorithm tailored for Riemannian manifolds. We provide a comprehensive analysis of RSVRG for both geodesically convex and nonconvex (smooth) functions. Our findings demonstrate that RSVRG retains the benefits of the traditional SVRG method, with convergence factors influenced by the curvature of the manifold. To the best of our knowledge, RSVRG is the first stochastic Riemannian method with proven acceleration guarantees. Additionally, our work presents the first non-asymptotic complexity analysis for nonconvex Riemannian optimization, a breakthrough even in the batch setting. These results have broad implications, including offering a Riemannian perspective on variance-reduced PCA, which enables concise and clear convergence analyses.

In this paper, we address the problem of identifying cluster heads within a two-tier unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) swarm network (USNET) comprising multiple UAV clusters. The challenge lies in the fact that the inherent follow strategy (IFS) of low-level follower UAVs (FUAVs) relative to high-level cluster head UAVs (HUAVs) remains unknown. To tackle this, we initially introduce a graph attention self-supervised learning algorithm (GASSL) designed to identify the HUAVs within a single UAV cluster, effectively capturing the IFS simultaneously. Building upon GASSL, we then propose a multi-cluster graph attention self-supervised learning algorithm (MC-GASSL) to detect HUAVs across multiple clusters in the USNET. This approach employs a gated recurrent unit (GRU)-based metric learning scheme to perform clustering, enabling the GASSL to accurately locate HUAVs in each cluster. Numerical experiments demonstrate that GASSL achieves over 98% average accuracy in detecting HUAVs within single UAV clusters, regardless of various IFS types. Simulation results further indicate that the clustering purity of the USNET using MC-GASSL surpasses that of traditional algorithms by at least 10% on average. Additionally, MC-GASSL efficiently detects all HUAVs across diverse IFS configurations and cluster counts, with minimal detection redundancy.

Machine learning models are frequently employed to analyze human brain imaging data to link neural structure or function with behavior, health, or other individual traits. These models typically depend on low-dimensional representations created through intricate processing pipelines. However, inherent numerical instabilities within these pipelines can compromise the accuracy of these maps and introduce computational biases. To address this issue, Monte Carlo Arithmetic—a method that injects controlled amounts of numerical noise—was used to perturb a structural connectome estimation pipeline. This approach generated a spectrum of plausible brain networks for each sample. The resulting variability was incorporated into an expanded dataset, which was then used for an age classification task. Our results demonstrated that resampling brain networks across multiple numerically perturbed outcomes consistently enhanced classifier performance, regardless of the specific algorithms, preprocessing methods, or dimensionality reduction techniques employed. Notably, this improvement was achieved without requiring extensive perturbations, indicating that even minimal numerical variations can introduce valuable diversity that can be effectively leveraged in model development.

Variable selection plays a crucial role in analyzing high-dimensional data, prompting the development of numerous algorithms. Ideally, an effective variable selection method should be flexible, scalable, and supported by strong theoretical guarantees. However, most existing approaches struggle to achieve all these qualities simultaneously. In this paper, we introduce a novel three-step variable selection algorithm that leverages kernel-based estimation of the regression function and its gradients, combined with a hard thresholding procedure. The main strengths of our approach are its model-free nature, accommodating diverse predictor effects, computational scalability, and proven asymptotic sparsistency. This algorithm can be adapted to any reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) with various kernel functions and can be extended to include interaction effects with minimal modifications. Its computational complexity grows linearly with the data dimension and can be further optimized via parallel processing. We establish the sparsistency of our method under mild conditions for general RKHS, including special cases such as linear and Gaussian kernels. The effectiveness of the proposed approach is demonstrated through extensive simulations and real-world data applications.

While convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have shown exceptional skill in extracting discriminative features, they often struggle with poor generalization to unseen domains. Domain generalization seeks to overcome this challenge by training a model on multiple source domains that can perform well on any unfamiliar domain. In this paper, we introduce a novel technique that probabilistically blends instance-level feature statistics across source domains. Our approach, called MixStyle, is inspired by the insight that visual domains are closely linked to image style—such as distinguishing between photographs and sketches. This style information is captured in the lower layers of a CNN, where our style-mixing operation occurs. By combining styles from different training instances, MixStyle implicitly synthesizes new domains, thereby enhancing the diversity of source domain styles and improving the model's generalization capabilities. The method integrates seamlessly with mini-batch training and is straightforward to implement. We demonstrate the effectiveness of MixStyle across various tasks, including category classification, instance retrieval, and reinforcement learning.

In computed tomography (CT), automatic exposure control (AEC) is commonly employed to minimize patient radiation exposure. For organ-specific AEC, an initial CT reconstruction is required to estimate organ boundaries for dose optimization, which involves limited projection data for real-time processing. In this study, we evaluate the effectiveness of AUTOMAP (automated transform by manifold approximation) in such scenarios. As a proof of concept, we first test its performance on the MNIST dataset, which comprises all ten handwritten digits randomly divided into training and testing subsets. We train the AUTOMAP model to reconstruct images from either 2 or 4 projections. The results show that AUTOMAP can accurately reconstruct most digits, with error rates of 1.6% and 6.8%, respectively. In a subsequent experiment, we partition the dataset so that the training set contains nine digits, while the test set includes only a specific excluded digit—such as "2." When reconstructing with just 2 projections, the digit "2" is frequently misclassified as "3" or "5," yielding a false rate of 94.4%. For medical imaging applications, AUTOMAP is also trained on patient data to further assess its practical utility.

Deep learning holds great promise for medical imaging applications. However, the wide variation in disease incidence results in imbalanced datasets, with certain classes occurring infrequently and consequently reducing classification accuracy for these rare conditions. One approach to address this challenge is to augment data for underrepresented classes using synthetic images generated by Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). Nonetheless, traditional GANs typically require a sufficient number of images to learn effectively. To overcome this limitation, we introduce the General-to-Detailed GAN (GDGAN), a sequential model composed of two connected GANs: one focusing on general labels and the other on detailed labels. GDGAN generates diverse medical images, and when trained on this augmented dataset, it surpasses existing methods in classification performance, as evidenced by higher Area-Under-Curve (AUC) metrics on the Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve.

Deep convolutional networks commonly incorporate additive constant ("bias") terms into their convolutional operations, enhancing their capacity to model complex functions. These biases also aid training processes, such as by subtracting mean responses over batches (a technique known as "batch normalization"). Recent leading-edge blind denoising models, like DnCNN, appear to rely heavily on these bias terms for optimal performance. However, we demonstrate that such networks tend to overfit to the specific noise levels encountered during training: when applied to images with noise levels outside the training scope, their effectiveness drops significantly. Conversely, a bias-free architecture—created by eliminating constant terms in every layer, including those within batch normalization—exhibits strong generalization across various noise levels, maintaining state-of-the-art results within the training range. At a local level, the bias-free network behaves as a linear operator on the noisy input, allowing for straightforward analysis using conventional linear algebra techniques. These insights interpret the network's function as a form of nonlinear adaptive filtering and projection onto a union of low-dimensional subspaces, thereby bridging learning-based approaches with traditional denoising strategies.

Recent advances in the theory of overparameterized learning have aimed to establish generalization guarantees within the interpolating regime. While such results have been achieved for several common classes of methods, ensemble techniques have yet to be thoroughly addressed. In response, we introduce an ensemble classification approach that not only perfectly interpolates the training data but also maintains consistency across a wide range of data distributions. To achieve this, we define the manifold-Hilbert kernel for data residing on a Riemannian manifold. We demonstrate that kernel smoothing regression utilizing the manifold-Hilbert kernel exhibits weak consistency in the framework described by Devroye et al. (1998). Specifically, on the sphere, we establish that the manifold-Hilbert kernel can be expressed as a weighted random partition kernel, which can be interpreted as an infinite ensemble of classifiers based on partitions.

This paper addresses the challenge of constrained robust (min-max) optimization in a black-box environment, where the optimizer can only query function values without access to gradients. We propose a comprehensive optimization framework that combines a zeroth-order (ZO) gradient estimator with an alternating projected stochastic gradient descent-ascent approach. The ZO component requires only a small number of function evaluations, while the descent/ascent step involves a single update. We demonstrate that our framework, named ZO-Min-Max, achieves a sub-linear convergence rate under mild assumptions and maintains scalability as problem dimensions grow. Additionally, we explore a significant application connection between black-box min-max optimization and black-box evasion and poisoning attacks in adversarial machine learning. Our experiments on these scenarios confirm the effectiveness of our method and its ability to handle high-dimensional problems that challenge existing black-box solvers.

In response to the rapid increase in available data, there has been a growing focus on enhancing the efficiency of data analysis and machine learning libraries. While substantial progress has been made in traditional array-based computations, these methods are often constrained by the limited resources of a single computational node. Therefore, innovative strategies are needed to leverage distributed resources, such as distributed memory architectures. 

To address this, we present HeAT, an array-oriented numerical programming framework designed for large-scale parallel processing with an intuitive, NumPy-like API. HeAT leverages PyTorch as a node-local eager execution engine and employs MPI to distribute workloads across extensive high-performance computing systems. It supports both fundamental array operations and a variety of higher-level algorithms. With HeAT, NumPy users can fully utilize their available resources, making distributed data analysis more accessible. When benchmarked against similar frameworks, HeAT demonstrates speed improvements of up to two orders of magnitude.

This paper aims to compare several commonly used Bayesian model selection techniques within practical modeling contexts, highlight their key differences, and offer recommendations for the most effective approaches. Our focus is on selecting variable subsets for regression and classification tasks, supported by multiple numerical experiments conducted on both simulated and real-world datasets. The findings indicate that optimizing utility estimates—such as the cross-validation (CV) score—tends to favor overfitted models when data is limited, primarily due to the high variance associated with utility estimates under these conditions. Consequently, this can induce significant selection bias and overly optimistic assessments of model performance. From a predictive standpoint, the most reliable results are achieved by embracing model uncertainty through the use of comprehensive models, like Bayesian model averaging over candidate models. When such encompassing models are overly complex, they can be effectively simplified via the projection method, which transfers information from the full model to submodels. This strategy is notably less susceptible to overfitting compared to CV-based selection. Overall, the projection approach not only surpasses the maximum a posteriori (MAP) model but also outperforms selecting the most probable model alone.

Learning features directly from data has proven more effective than relying on manually crafted features in many machine learning applications. In the realm of music information retrieval (MIR), features derived from windowed spectrograms tend to vary significantly under transformations such as transposition or time-shifting, which is undesirable when these variations are irrelevant to the specific MIR task. To address this, we introduce the Complex Autoencoder (CAE), an architecture designed to learn features invariant to orthogonal transformations. By projecting signals onto complex basis functions learned by the CAE, we obtain a "magnitude space" that remains unaffected by transformations, alongside a "phase space" that captures the specific transformations between data pairs. The phase information is particularly useful for inferring the nature of these transformations. Leveraging the invariance of the magnitude space, our approach sets new benchmarks in tasks such as audio-to-score alignment and repeated section detection. A PyTorch implementation of the CAE and the repeated section discovery method is available online for further use.

This paper tackles the challenge of estimating real-time occupancy levels in dynamic environments and forecasting future occupancy states. Given the complexity of real-world scenarios like urban streets and crowded spaces, effectively integrating temporal dependencies into static occupancy models poses significant difficulties. We introduce a novel approach to model the spatial uncertainty associated with moving objects and embed this uncertainty into a continuous occupancy map within a high-dimensional feature space. Experimental results utilizing LIDAR data demonstrate the algorithm’s capability to operate in real time.

This paper presents a method for learning control policies for dynamical systems that ensure both safety and goal achievement. Safety is defined as preventing the system's state from entering unsafe regions, while goal-reaching requires the system's trajectory to asymptotically approach a designated target area—a broad extension of stability. The approach involves simultaneously training two auxiliary certificate functions: a barrier function to certify safety and a Lyapunov-like function to ensure convergence to the goal. Both functions are modeled using neural networks. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in deriving policies that are both safe and goal-oriented across various systems, including pendulums, cart-poles, and UAVs.

In this paper, we introduce a more realistic and challenging variant of the intent detection problem in natural language understanding, called Generalized Few-Shot Intent Detection (GFSID). GFSID involves distinguishing among a combined label space that includes both well-established intents with ample labeled data and new intents with only a few examples per class. To address this task, we propose a novel approach: Conditional Text Generation with BERT (CG-BERT). CG-BERT utilizes a large pre-trained language model to generate text conditioned on specific intent labels. By employing variational inference to model the distribution of utterances, CG-BERT can produce diverse samples for new intents, even when only a limited number of examples are available. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that CG-BERT sets new state-of-the-art results in GFSID, outperforming existing methods in 1-shot and 5-shot scenarios across two real-world datasets.

Customers are typically exposed to various online digital advertising channels, including email marketing, display ads, and paid search, during their journey toward purchasing or subscribing to products (i.e., conversion). Marketers continuously analyze all customer interaction data to evaluate the effectiveness of each advertising channel. Insights into each channel's influence are crucial for informed decisions on budget allocation and pricing strategies. While traditional approaches rely on simple rule-based methods or basic data-driven algorithms, these often fail to capture complexities such as channel interactions, time-dependent effects, and user-specific factors. 

In this paper, we introduce a novel deep learning-based attribution algorithm designed to accurately assess the contribution of each advertising channel. Our proposed model, the Deep Neural Network with Attention for Multi-Touch Attribution (DNAMTA), employs supervised learning to predict whether a sequence of events results in conversion. This approach provides a comprehensive understanding of the dynamic interactions among media channels. Additionally, DNAMTA incorporates user-context information—such as demographics and behavioral data—as control variables, helping to mitigate biases in media effect estimation. 

We validated our model through computational experiments on large-scale real-world marketing datasets, demonstrating that our approach outperforms existing methods in capturing the true impact of advertising channels.

Spatial clustering techniques can effectively reduce multi-channel noise across a wide range of microphone configurations but often struggle to incorporate detailed speech and noise models. Conversely, LSTM neural networks have demonstrated success in recognizing speech from noise using single-channel inputs but face challenges in leveraging the full potential of multi-channel recordings. This paper proposes a hybrid approach by training LSTM-based speech models to enhance the masks generated by the Model-based EM Source Separation and Localization (MESSL) spatial clustering method. This integration combines the spatial separation and robustness of multi-channel clustering with the detailed signal modeling capabilities of multiple parallel single-channel LSTM speech enhancers. Experimental results on the CHiME-3 dataset of noisy tablet recordings show that our system improves speech quality, as measured by the Perceptual Evaluation of Speech Quality (PESQ), and reduces the word error rate of the baseline CHiME-3 speech recognizer compared to the standard BeamformIt beamformer.

Noise is a significant factor contributing to the low quality of Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) images. Convolutional Neural Network (CNN)-based models have shown excellent performance in image denoising tasks. However, OCT image denoising remains challenging due to the reliance of many existing neural network algorithms on large amounts of labeled data, which can be costly and time-consuming to obtain. Additionally, these CNN-based methods often require numerous parameters and complex tuning, leading to high hardware resource consumption. To address these issues, we propose a novel Cycle-Consistent Generative Adversarial Network called Dual-Merged Cycle-WGAN for retinal OCT image denoising, which delivers outstanding results with fewer unlabeled training samples. Our model incorporates two CycleGANs with enhanced generators, discriminators, and Wasserstein loss to improve training stability and performance. By employing a merging technique between the two CycleGAN networks, our model captures more detailed information, resulting in superior training outcomes. The effectiveness and versatility of our approach have been validated through ablation and comparative experiments. When compared to other state-of-the-art methods, our unsupervised approach achieves the best subjective visual quality and higher objective evaluation metrics.

A neural network operating in real-world environments may be tasked with making predictions on inputs originating from distributions different from its training data. Numerous studies have shown that it is relatively easy to identify or generate inputs on which a neural network exhibits high confidence despite being incorrect. Generative models are generally considered more robust against such overconfidence because modeling the density of input features can help detect out-of-distribution or novel inputs. However, in this paper, we question this assumption. Our findings reveal that the densities learned by flow-based models, Variational Autoencoders (VAEs), and PixelCNNs fail to effectively distinguish images of common objects like dogs, trucks, and horses (e.g., CIFAR-10) from images of house numbers (e.g., SVHN), often assigning higher likelihoods to SVHN when trained on CIFAR-10. We observe similar phenomena when comparing several popular datasets: FashionMNIST versus MNIST, CelebA versus SVHN, and ImageNet versus CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, or SVHN. To understand this peculiar behavior, we focus our analysis mainly on flow-based generative models, as they are trained and evaluated based on exact marginal likelihoods.
