End-to-end (E2E) models are frequently enhanced with language models (LMs) through shallow fusion to improve overall performance and improve recognition of rare words. However, prior research indicates that LMs can inadvertently memorize rare or unique sequences present in their training data. In this study, we introduce a framework for identifying memorization of random textual sequences, which we term canaries, within LM training data using only black-box (query-based) access to a fused speech recognition system—without direct access to the LM itself. Specifically, we demonstrate that it is feasible to detect whether a Conformer RNN-T E2E model, fused with a Transformer LM and deployed in a production environment, has memorized single-occurrence canaries from a training set of 300 million examples. To address privacy concerns, we further show that implementing per-example gradient clipping during LM training significantly reduces memorization of these canaries without sacrificing overall recognition quality.

We investigate the universal approximation capabilities of two-layer neural networks with randomly initialized weights that are "nearly Gaussian" in the sense of Kullback-Leibler divergence. This inquiry is inspired by recent studies on lazy training, where stochastic gradient descent (SGD) updates cause weights to remain close to their i.i.d. Gaussian initialization. We first analyze the mean-field limit, replacing the finite set of hidden-layer neurons with a continuous ensemble, and demonstrate that the problem reduces to the global minimization of a free-energy functional defined over the space of probability measures on the weights. This functional balances the squared $L^2$ approximation error against the KL divergence relative to a centered Gaussian prior. We identify the unique global minimizer and then develop a controlled nonlinear evolution in the space of probability measures that solves a McKean–Vlasov optimal control problem. This control framework is intimately connected to the Schrödinger bridge (entropic optimal transport) problem, with its minimized value proportional to the free energy's minimum. Finally, we establish that in the lazy training regime—achievable through joint tuning of the Gaussian prior's variance and the entropic regularization—SGD effectively approximates this optimal control dynamics.

A key implicit objective in research on deep generative models is their ability to produce novel samples that were not part of the training data. In this study, we examine the extent to which this capability applies to widely used variational autoencoder (VAE) architectures. VAEs optimize a lower bound on the log marginal likelihood, which suggests they may tend to overfit the training data when equipped with a highly expressive decoder. In the limit of an infinitely capable decoder, the optimal generative model becomes a uniform mixture over the training examples. More generally, the ideal decoder should generate a weighted average of training samples, with the weights influenced by the proximity of their latent representations. This reasoning leads us to hypothesize that, given a sufficiently capable encoder and decoder, the VAE decoder effectively performs nearest-neighbor matching in the latent space. To evaluate this hypothesis, we analyze the model's generalization on the MNIST dataset, focusing on both its ability to generalize to unseen examples within known classes and to entirely new classes excluded during training. Our results show that in both scenarios, the reconstructions closely resemble the original data, supporting the idea that VAEs primarily rely on local neighborhood information in the latent space.

In this article, we introduce CANDIES (Combined Approach for Novelty Detection in Intelligent Embedded Systems), a novel method for identifying novelties within technical systems. We consider that multiple processes operate and interact within these systems. By employing sensors to monitor these processes, we can model the collected observations—or samples—using a probabilistic framework, ideally ensuring that the components of the parametric mixture density model align with real-world processes. Over time, unforeseen processes, such as unpredictable failures, may appear in the system. These events generate new sample types, necessitating an update to the existing model. CANDIES employs Gaussian mixture models, which are also useful for classification tasks. New processes can manifest in regions of the input space characterized by either sparse data (low-density areas) or dense data (high-density regions). Detecting novelties in high-density regions is particularly challenging, as most existing methods tend to focus on low-density areas. Effective novelty detection must therefore adapt strategies for both scenarios. With CANDIES, we propose an innovative approach to identify new processes within high-density regions efficiently and in real-time.

Mini-batch SGD with momentum is a core algorithm for training large-scale predictive models. In this work, we introduce a novel analytical framework to examine mini-batch SGD applied to linear models across various momentum parameters and batch sizes. Our central approach involves representing the sequence of loss values through its generating function, which simplifies to a concise form when assuming a diagonal approximation of the second moments of model weights. By investigating this generating function, we derive several insights into the conditions for convergence, the phase structure of the learning process, and strategies for optimal training. Specifically, we demonstrate that: 1) the optimization trajectory can typically transition from a "signal-driven" phase to a "noise-driven" phase, with the timing of this shift being analytically predictable; 2) during the "signal-dominated" stage (prior to the noise dominance), employing a larger effective learning rate is advantageous, though it must be carefully regulated for finite batch sizes to prevent divergence; and 3) the fastest convergence rate is achievable with a negative momentum. Our theoretical findings are validated through extensive experiments on MNIST and synthetic datasets, showing strong quantitative agreement.

We present a model-free relax-and-round algorithm for k-means clustering, building upon the semidefinite relaxation developed by Peng and Wei. This approach treats the SDP solution as a denoised version of the original data, subsequently rounding it to produce a definitive clustering. Additionally, we introduce a versatile framework for establishing performance guarantees for this algorithm and evaluate its effectiveness within the setting of subgaussian mixture models. Furthermore, we examine the fundamental limits of Gaussian center estimation via k-means clustering to compare our approximation guarantees against the theoretically optimal k-means clustering solution.

Supervised learning-based segmentation techniques generally depend on large volumes of annotated data to achieve robust performance during testing. In medical contexts, assembling such datasets is often impractical due to the time-consuming and costly nature of expert annotations. As a result, many studies have explored methods for effective learning from limited annotated samples. However, these approaches have yet to demonstrate substantial improvements over simple random data augmentation, which itself offers only modest accuracy gains. In this paper, we introduce a novel task-specific data augmentation strategy designed for scenarios with scarce labeled data. The core of our approach is a synthetic data generator optimized specifically for the segmentation task. It captures intensity and shape variations through two transformation sets: additive intensity adjustments and deformation fields. These transformations are refined using both labeled and unlabeled data within a semi-supervised framework. Evaluation on three medical datasets—cardiac, prostate, and pancreatic—shows that our method significantly surpasses standard augmentation techniques and existing semi-supervised methods in limited annotation settings. The implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/krishnabits001/task$\_$driven$\_$data$\_$augmentation.

In recent years, the application of machine learning techniques has gained significant traction within the realm of lattice field theories. Central to these theories are symmetries, which, when incorporated into neural network architectures, can substantially enhance both performance and generalization capabilities. A key symmetry commonly present in physical systems on a lattice with periodic boundary conditions is equivariance under spacetime translations. In this study, we explore the benefits of employing translationally equivariant neural networks compared to their non-equivariant counterparts. Our focus is on a complex scalar field with quartic interactions defined on a two-dimensional lattice in the flux representation, where the networks perform various regression and classification tasks. Through a systematic search, we identify promising architectures for both equivariant and non-equivariant models. Our results show that, across most tasks, the best equivariant networks consistently outperform and generalize more effectively than non-equivariant models—both for physical parameters outside the training set and across different lattice sizes.

This paper illustrates the application of a Transformer Neural Network to develop a generative model from a single path-based example image. Additionally, it showcases methods for creating a dataset derived from the example, and demonstrates how the model can produce a substantial collection of varied images that retain the original image's style and underlying concept.

The recently introduced "generalized min-max" (GMM) kernel can be effectively linearized, enabling its application in large-scale statistical learning and rapid near-neighbor searches. When compared to linearized radial basis function (RBF) kernels across numerous classification tasks, the tuning-free GMM kernel surprisingly performs on par with optimally tuned RBF kernels. However, it is natural to consider whether introducing tunable parameters could further enhance the GMM kernel's performance. In this work, we explore three straightforward tunable variants of the GMM kernel: (i) the exponentiated-GMM (eGMM) kernel, (ii) the powered-GMM (pGMM) kernel, and (iii) the exponentiated-powered-GMM (epGMM) kernel. The pGMM kernel remains efficiently linearizable through modifications to the existing hashing method used for the original GMM kernel. Experiments on approximately 60 publicly available classification datasets demonstrate that these tunable GMM kernels generally outperform the original GMM kernel, with some cases exhibiting notably significant improvements. For instance, on 11 well-known datasets previously utilized for testing deep learning models and tree-based methods, our results indicate that the proposed tunable GMM kernels are competitive with, and in some cases rival, decision trees and deep neural networks. Prior research has also developed tree-based approaches such as "abc-robust-logitboost" and demonstrated their effectiveness.

Research is a tertiary concern within the EHR system, where the primary focuses are patient care and billing. As a result, the data is often unstandardized and not formatted in a way that readily supports machine learning methods. Missing data occurs for various reasons, including differences in individual input styles and clinical decision-making processes, such as which laboratory tests to order. Only a small subset of patient data is annotated at research quality, limiting sample sizes and creating a constantly shifting gold standard. Understanding patient progression over time is crucial for many disease insights; however, many machine learning algorithms require data snapshots at single time points to generate usable vector representations. Additionally, algorithms that operate as black boxes lack the interpretability necessary for clinical decision-making. This chapter explores these challenges and others related to applying machine learning to structured EHR data—such as patient demographics, family history, medication records, vital signs, lab results, and genetic tests. While it does not address feature extraction from external sources like imaging or free-text notes, the discussed approaches can incorporate features derived from these additional data types.

Chemical kinetics and reaction engineering provide a phenomenological framework for unraveling reaction mechanisms, optimizing reaction performance, and designing chemical processes intelligently. In this work, we employ feed-forward artificial neural networks as basis functions to solve ordinary differential equations (ODEs) governed by differential algebraic equations (DAEs) that represent microkinetic models (MKMs). We introduce an algebraic framework for mathematically describing and classifying reaction networks, elementary reaction types, and chemical species. Within this framework, we demonstrate that joint training of neural networks and kinetic model parameters in a regularized multi-objective optimization setting enables solving the inverse problem—estimating kinetic parameters from synthetic experimental data. We investigate various scenarios to determine how effectively kinetic parameters can be recovered from transient kinetic data and evaluate the robustness of the approach in the presence of statistical noise. This methodology for inverse kinetic ODEs offers a valuable tool for elucidating reaction mechanisms based on transient datasets.

Currently, Learning Management Systems (LMS) are extensively utilized across educational levels—from primary schools to universities—for managing student records, maintaining documentation, monitoring progress, generating reports, and delivering educational content, training modules, or professional development programs. As the focus shifts toward effective assessment of learning outcomes, the challenge of automatically generating exam scripts has garnered increasing interest and has been the subject of recent research. However, this field remains in its infancy, offering significant opportunities to enhance the quality of generated exam scripts in various ways. Notably, two critical issues have largely been overlooked by existing approaches. First, when provided with a course, it remains unclear how to produce an exam script that yields a desirable distribution of student scores within a class or across multiple classes. Second, although generating multiple assessment-equivalent exam scripts with diverse question sets is a common practical need, current methods have not addressed how to produce pairs of high-quality exams that are comparable in their evaluation but differ substantially in their questions. To address these challenges, this paper introduces ExamGAN (Exam Script Generative Adversarial Network), a model designed to generate high-quality exam scripts. Furthermore, it extends this framework to T-ExamGAN (Twin-ExamGAN) to facilitate the creation of such exam pairs.

Collaborative personalization methods, such as learned user representations (embeddings), can markedly enhance the prediction accuracy of neural network-based models. We introduce Federated User Representation Learning (FURL), a straightforward, scalable, privacy-conscious, and resource-efficient approach for applying existing neural personalization techniques within the Federated Learning (FL) framework. FURL partitions model parameters into federated and private segments. Private parameters, including individual user embeddings, are trained locally and are not transmitted to or averaged on the server, unlike federated parameters. Our theoretical analysis confirms that this division of parameters does not compromise training effectiveness for most personalization strategies. By storing user embeddings locally, we not only safeguard user privacy but also boost memory locality during personalization compared to server-side training. Experimental results on two datasets reveal substantial gains in model performance, with improvements of 8% and 51%, and performance levels comparable to centralized training with only 0% and 4% reductions. Additionally, the learned user embeddings in FL closely resemble those obtained centrally, demonstrating that FURL can effectively learn shared representations collaboratively while maintaining user privacy.

Rural electrification requires cost-effective technologies such as single wire earth return (SWER) systems. As remote communities' energy needs continue to grow, existing infrastructure may soon prove insufficient. Additionally, high impedance arcing faults (HIF) on SWER lines can trigger devastating bushfires, exemplified by the 2009 Black Saturday inferno. To address these challenges, a reliable remote power network can be achieved by dividing current systems into microgrids interconnected via existing SWER lines. Developing such resilient networks with improved demand management hinges on implementing comprehensive, system-wide condition monitoring. 

This thesis introduces a distributed online monitoring platform capable of power quality assessment, real-time HIF detection, and transient classification within SWER networks. Advanced AI techniques are employed to accurately identify faults and transient events, achieving a HIF detection accuracy of 98.67% and a detection latency of just 115.2 milliseconds. Additionally, a methodology for remote load identification is developed, enabling the determination of load types based on transient signatures. An edge computing architecture is proposed to perform high-frequency data analysis essential for load detection, and this approach is validated in real-time scenarios.

The effectiveness of semi-supervised learning heavily depends on its ability to handle vast amounts of unlabeled data, which are essential for capturing the underlying manifold structure and enhancing classification performance. However, calculating pairwise similarity between training samples is computationally prohibitive for most data types, and currently, there are no widely available semi-supervised methods or tools capable of processing tens of millions or more data points. In this study, we leveraged two low-rank label propagation techniques—Global Linear Neighborhood Propagation (GLNP) and Kernel Nyström Approximation—and developed a parallelized implementation of these algorithms, accelerated using Nesterov's accelerated projected gradient descent, dubbed BigLP (Big-data Label Propagation). We evaluated the parallel algorithms on five real-world datasets ranging from 7,000 to 10 million samples, as well as a synthetic dataset containing 100 million samples. Our experiments demonstrated that the scalable implementation could handle datasets with up to 100 million samples and numerous features, significantly improving prediction accuracy even when only a small fraction of the data was labeled. These findings confirm that BigLP is highly scalable for large-scale data and effective in leveraging unlabeled data to enhance semi-supervised learning outcomes.

High-dimensional integration is a common challenge across various scientific disciplines. To address this, numerous numerical methods have been developed to evaluate these complex integrals. Here, we present i-flow, a Python package designed for high-dimensional numerical integration using normalizing flows. Normalizing flows are machine learning models that establish bijective mappings between two probability distributions. In addition to integration, i-flow can efficiently generate samples from intricate, high-dimensional distributions. We compare the performance of i-flow with other existing algorithms for high-dimensional integration and demonstrate its superior efficiency, particularly for correlated integrals in high dimensions. The i-flow package is openly accessible on GitLab at https://gitlab.com/i-flow/i-flow.

In machine learning, likelihood-free inference involves conducting analyses based on data rather than relying on explicit analytical formulas. Here, we explore the use of Neural Spline Flows, a neural density estimation technique, for the likelihood-free inference of neutrino oscillation parameters in Long Baseline neutrino experiments. We develop a specialized method tailored to physics parameter estimation and apply it to the disappearance of muon neutrinos in the T2K experiment.

We introduce a unified framework that extends various well-known loss functions, including Cauchy/Lorentzian, Geman-McClure, Welsch/Leclerc, generalized Charbonnier, Charbonnier/pseudo-Huber/L1-L2, and L2 losses. By incorporating a continuous robustness parameter, our approach enables the adaptation of algorithms based on robust loss minimization, leading to enhanced performance in fundamental vision tasks such as registration and clustering. Viewing our loss as the negative logarithm of a univariate probability density function, we derive a comprehensive distribution family that encompasses both normal and Cauchy distributions as special cases. This probabilistic perspective allows for the automatic adjustment of loss robustness during neural network training, resulting in improved outcomes for tasks like generative image synthesis and unsupervised monocular depth estimation, all without the need for manual parameter tuning.

We introduce Sparse Sinkhorn Attention, an innovative, efficient, and sparse approach for learning to attend. This technique leverages differentiable sorting of internal representations by employing a meta sorting network that learns to produce latent permutations over sequences. Once sequences are sorted, we can perform quasi-global attention utilizing only local windows, thereby enhancing the memory efficiency of the attention mechanism. Key algorithmic contributions include Causal Sinkhorn Balancing and SortCut, a dynamic sequence truncation method designed to adapt Sinkhorn Attention for encoding and decoding tasks. Through comprehensive experiments spanning algorithmic sequence-to-sequence sorting, language modeling, pixel-level image generation, document classification, and natural language inference, we demonstrate that our memory-efficient Sinkhorn Attention rivals standard attention mechanisms and consistently surpasses recent efficient Transformer variants such as Sparse Transformers.

Sum-Product Networks featuring complex probability distributions at their leaves are established as powerful and computationally efficient probabilistic models. While significant research has focused on optimizing their internal parameters, effectively learning complex distributions at the leaves remains an open challenge, with only limited solutions available for specialized cases. In this paper, we introduce an efficient approach to learn a broad class of leaf distributions using Expectation-Maximization. The EM updates simplify to weighted maximum likelihood problems, enabling the use of any distribution that can be estimated through maximum likelihood, even approximately. Our algorithm operates with linear complexity relative to the model size and guarantees convergence even with partial optimization steps. We validate our method through experiments on twenty real-world datasets for density estimation, employing tree-structured graphical models as leaves. Our approach surpasses current leading methods for parameter learning, achieving superior performance with significantly fewer parameters in the SPN models.

Deep reinforcement learning has proven to be an effective framework for developing policies from complex, high-dimensional sensory inputs to actions in intricate tasks, such as those encountered in the Atari environment. In this study, we investigate output representation modeling through temporal abstraction to enhance the convergence rate and reliability of deep reinforcement learning methods. Our focus is on macro-actions, which we evaluate across various Atari 2600 games, demonstrating that they significantly accelerate the learning process. Furthermore, we find that these methods can surpass DQN in performance scores. We provide an in-depth analysis and explanation of both the convergence behavior and the final outcomes, highlighting a key challenge faced by deep RL approaches: handling sparse reward signals.

This paper provides an overview of physics- and data-driven reconstruction methods for integrated positron emission tomography (PET) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) systems, highlighting their significant benefits for clinical diagnosis of cancer, neurological conditions, and cardiovascular diseases. These reconstruction techniques incorporate priors—either structural or statistical—alongside a physics-based model of the PET system response. Due to the layered nature of the forward problem, direct PET/MRI reconstruction is inherently nonlinear. We explore how a comprehensive approach leverages hybrid data- and physics-guided machine learning to facilitate 3D PET/MRI reconstruction, summarizing key deep learning advancements from the past five years that address challenges such as attenuation correction, scattering, limited photon counts, and data consistency. Additionally, we discuss how these multi-modality methods extend beyond PET/MRI to enhance precision in radiation therapy planning. The paper concludes with insights into future opportunities for advancing the field, driven by emerging trends in physics-informed deep learning, computational imaging, and next-generation detector technologies.

Addressing inverse problems, such as parameter estimation and optimal control, is essential in scientific research. Many experiments involve repeated data collection and the use of machine learning algorithms to rapidly infer solutions to these inverse challenges. We observe that current state-of-the-art training methods often struggle with problems involving physical processes, as the size and direction of gradients can vary dramatically. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a novel hybrid training strategy that integrates higher-order optimization techniques with machine learning. Our approach involves replacing the traditional gradient of the physical process with a new construct called the physical gradient, which enables the incorporation of domain knowledge by embedding prior information about the solution space into the gradients. We showcase the effectiveness of our method across several fundamental physical systems, demonstrating that leveraging physical gradients leads to substantial improvements across a broad spectrum of optimization and learning tasks.

In the field of optimization, it is well understood that when objective functions are strictly convex and well-conditioned, gradient-based methods can be highly effective, often achieving exponential convergence rates. Conversely, the standard Lasso-type estimators generally fail to reach optimal rates due to the non-smooth behavior of the absolute value function at zero. A homotopic approach addresses this issue by employing a sequence of surrogate functions to approximate the \(\ell_1\) penalty used in Lasso estimators. These surrogate functions gradually converge to the \(\ell_1\) penalty, while each remains strictly convex, thereby enabling provably faster convergence rates. In this study, we demonstrate that carefully designing these surrogate functions allows us to establish a convergence rate surpassing that of existing methods for Lasso-type estimators. Specifically, while current algorithms are limited to guarantees of \(O(1/\epsilon)\) or \(O(1/\sqrt{\epsilon})\) convergence, our proposed approach achieves an \(O([\log(1/\epsilon)]^2)\) rate. Numerical experiments confirm that our method not only offers theoretical improvements but also exhibits superior practical performance.

A novel approach for training variational autoencoders (VAEs) has been introduced, utilizing Stein variational gradient descent. This method's primary benefit is that it eliminates the need for parametric assumptions regarding the encoder distribution's form. Its effectiveness is further improved by combining the proposed encoder with importance sampling techniques. The approach exhibits outstanding performance across various unsupervised and semi-supervised tasks, including semi-supervised analysis of the ImageNet dataset, showcasing its scalability to large-scale data.

We develop a low-complexity decentralized learning algorithm to train a recently proposed large neural network across distributed processing nodes (workers). Our setup assumes a synchronized communication network between the workers, represented by a doubly-stochastic mixing matrix, with no central master node. The training data is partitioned among the workers and remains private throughout the process to ensure security. By leveraging the alternating-direction method of multipliers (ADMM) in conjunction with a layer-wise convex optimization strategy, we construct a decentralized algorithm that minimizes both computational and communication overhead among the workers. We demonstrate that this approach can achieve learning performance comparable to that of a centralized system where all data is consolidated. Finally, we provide experimental results to illustrate the algorithm’s time complexity and convergence characteristics.

Maillard's 2013 doctoral thesis introduces a somewhat obscure algorithm for the $K$-armed bandit problem. This lesser-known method, which we refer to as Maillard sampling (MS), uniquely computes the probability of selecting each arm in a \textit{closed-form} expression—something that does not hold for Thompson sampling, a widely-used bandit algorithm in industry. This closed-form property allows bandit-logged data from MS to be directly utilized for counterfactual evaluation, a significant advantage over Thompson sampling. Inspired by this benefit, we revisit MS and provide an improved analysis demonstrating that it attains both asymptotic optimality and a minimax regret bound of $\sqrt{KT \log T}$, where $T$ is the time horizon. This matches the known bounds for asymptotically optimal UCB algorithms. Additionally, we introduce a variant called MS$^+$, which enhances the minimax bound to $\sqrt{KT \log K}$. MS$^+$ can also be tuned to become more aggressive—reducing exploration—without sacrificing asymptotic optimality, a feature not available in existing bandit algorithms. Our numerical experiments confirm the effectiveness of MS$^+$.

Modeling units and model architecture are two crucial components of Recurrent Neural Network Transducer (RNN-T) in end-to-end speech recognition. To enhance RNN-T performance for Mandarin speech recognition tasks, a novel transformer transducer that combines self-attention transformer architecture with RNN has been proposed. Additionally, we investigate the impact of different modeling units for the transformer transducer. Furthermore, we introduce a new mixed-bandwidth training approach to develop a versatile model capable of accurately recognizing Mandarin speech across various sampling rates simultaneously. All experiments were conducted on approximately 12,000 hours of Mandarin speech sampled at 8kHz and 16kHz. The results demonstrate that the Mandarin transformer transducer utilizing syllables with tone achieves the best performance, with an average relative Word Error Rate (WER) reduction of 14.4% compared to models using syllables' initials/finals with tone and a 44.1% reduction compared to models based on Chinese characters. It also surpasses syllable initial/final with tone-based models, achieving an average of 13.5% relative reduction in Character Error Rate (CER).

Patent data offers extensive insights into technical inventions but lacks information about the ethnic backgrounds of inventors. In this study, I employ supervised learning methods to infer this demographic detail. I compile a dataset of 95,202 labeled names and train a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) recurrent neural network to predict ethnic origins from names. The model achieves an overall accuracy of 91% across 17 ethnic categories. Using this tool, I classify and analyze the ethnic composition of 2.68 million inventors, providing new descriptive evidence on how their ethnic backgrounds have evolved over time, across different countries, and within various technological sectors. The global diversity of inventors' ethnic origins has increased in recent decades, primarily driven by a significant rise in Asian-origin inventors. Moreover, the presence of foreign-origin inventors is notably high in the United States but has also grown in other affluent nations. This trend is mainly due to an influx of non-Western inventors entering emerging high-tech fields in the US, a pattern not observed similarly in other high-income countries.

In the universal hypothesis testing framework, where the objective is to differentiate between a known null distribution and an unknown alternative, Hoeffding introduced a universal testing methodology in the 1960s. His test statistic is based on the Kullback-Leibler (K-L) divergence between the empirical distribution of observed data and the null hypothesis distribution. This paper explores a modified version of Hoeffding's test that relaxes the K-L divergence measure, leading to what is called the mismatched divergence. The resulting mismatched test can be interpreted as a generalized likelihood-ratio test (GLRT) tailored for cases where the alternative hypothesis belongs to a parametric family defined by a finite set of parameters. This setup effectively addresses a composite hypothesis testing problem. For specific choices of the alternative distribution, it is demonstrated that both Hoeffding's original test and the mismatched test achieve identical asymptotic error exponents. Consequently, the GLRT proves to be optimal in distinguishing a particular distribution within an exponential family from others. Additionally, it is shown that the mismatched test offers notable advantages over Hoeffding's test in finite-sample scenarios.

Dual decomposition offers a manageable framework for developing algorithms to identify the most probable (MAP) configurations in graphical models. Nonetheless, in many practical inference scenarios, the standard decomposition often results in a large integrality gap caused by frustrated cycles. To improve the relaxation, one can incorporate additional constraints that explicitly enforce cycle consistency. Prior research demonstrated that cluster-pursuit algorithms—iteratively adding cycle and higher-order consistency constraints—can precisely solve many challenging inference problems. However, these methods typically require enumerating candidate clusters, restricting them to short cycles like triplets. We address this limitation by developing a search algorithm for cycle constraints that efficiently identifies the most frustrated cycle of any length in nearly linear time. We then integrate this search method within the dual decomposition framework and cluster-pursuit approach. The resulting algorithm precisely solves MAP inference problems relevant to relational classification and stereo vision tasks.

We focus on a supervised training approach for deriving task-specific word embeddings. Starting with initial embeddings obtained from unlabeled data, we refine these embeddings during supervised training to capture task-specific nuances. However, for unseen words in the test set, we rely either on their original embeddings or a generic unknown token, which can often introduce errors. To mitigate this, we propose training a neural network that maps initial embeddings to the task-specific embedding space, optimized through a multi-loss function. Although this method is broadly applicable, we demonstrate its effectiveness in enhancing dependency parsing—particularly for sentences containing out-of-vocabulary words—and in achieving downstream improvements in sentiment analysis.

The National Football League (NFL) partnered with Amazon Web Services (AWS) to create a leading sports injury surveillance and mitigation program through a Kaggle competition. The NFL aims to assign unique identifiers to each helmet, enabling precise tracking of players' exposures during gameplay. Our project focuses on developing computer vision-based machine learning algorithms to accurately match helmet impacts to the correct players using tracking data. In our paper, we will detail the methodology for automatically tracking player helmets and analyzing their collisions. This system will also facilitate review of past plays and allow for the examination of exposure trends over time.

In this study, we introduce DiCOVA-Net, a deep residual network-based approach designed to detect COVID-19 infection from acoustic recordings of coughs. Given the significant class imbalance—with considerably more healthy individuals than infected patients—our method addresses this challenge by incorporating data augmentation and cost-sensitive learning techniques to enhance the recognition of the minority class. Additionally, we apply fine-tuning strategies to adapt the pre-trained ResNet50 model specifically for this task. To bolster the model's robustness and generalizability, we employ ensemble learning by combining predictions from multiple base classifiers trained with different random seeds. We evaluated the performance of DiCOVA-Net using the DiCOVA challenge dataset, achieving an AUC of 85.43%, placing our method among the top performers in the competition.

Phase retrieval involves reconstructing images solely from magnitude measurements. In many practical scenarios, this problem is underdetermined. When training data is accessible, generative models offer a promising approach to restrict the solution space. However, not all potential solutions lie within the generator's range, leading to some approximation error. To address this in phase retrieval, we first employ a novel variation of intermediate layer optimization (ILO) that broadens the generator's range while ensuring consistency with training data. Next, we develop new initialization strategies that further enhance reconstruction quality. Through comprehensive experiments on Fourier and Gaussian phase retrieval tasks, along with detailed ablation studies, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our modified ILO and the improved initialization methods.

As smartphone usage continues to grow, mobile malware has become more widespread and sophisticated. Android has overtaken other mobile platforms to become the most popular, coinciding with a significant rise in malware targeting it. A concerning development is the increasing complexity of Android malware, enabling it to bypass traditional signature-based detection methods. Consequently, Android app marketplaces remain vulnerable to malicious apps that can evade detection before users download them. In this paper, we propose an effective solution to address this issue, utilizing Bayesian classification models derived from static code analysis. These models are built using various code and app characteristics that serve as indicators of potential malicious activity. We evaluate the models with real-world malware samples, and the experimental results demonstrate the robustness and effectiveness of our approach.

Kernel ridge regression (KRR) is a widely used approach for non-linear, non-parametric learning tasks. However, traditional implementations of KRR necessitate storing the entire dataset in main memory, severely restricting its applicability in scenarios where data volume vastly exceeds available memory resources. Such situations are increasingly prevalent in fields like data mining, bioinformatics, and control systems. To address this challenge, the streaming model of computation offers a powerful solution, enabling processing of data samples sequentially—handling one at a time and discarding each after processing before moving to the next. In this work, we introduce StreaMRAK, a streaming adaptation of KRR. This method enhances existing KRR techniques by employing a multi-resolution framework, allowing incremental refinement of predictions over time. It minimizes memory usage by efficiently incorporating new samples into the model as they arrive. Additionally, through a novel sub-sampling strategy, StreaMRAK constructs a compact data sketch—adjusting sampling density based on the kernel bandwidth and local data dimensionality—to reduce both memory and computational demands. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach with case studies involving two synthetic datasets and the prediction of trajectory patterns.

We introduce a novel estimation approach for topic models that diverges from traditional simplex-finding algorithms and actively estimates the number of topics, K, directly from the observed data. Our work establishes new finite-sample minimax lower bounds for the estimation of the matrix A, alongside corresponding upper bounds for our proposed estimator. We identify conditions under which our estimator achieves minimax adaptivity. The finite-sample analysis applies universally across any number of documents (n), individual document lengths (N_i), dictionary size (p), and number of topics (K), with both p and K permitted to grow with n—an aspect inadequately addressed by prior studies. To support our theoretical findings, we conduct an extensive simulation study demonstrating that our algorithm outperforms existing methods in both speed and accuracy. Notably, while our approach does not require prior knowledge of the true number of topics K—unlike the competing methods tested with known K—we still achieve superior performance.

Considering the worst-case scenario, the junction tree algorithm remains the most versatile method for exact MAP inference, offering polynomial time guarantees. However, its primary tractability constraint—limiting the treewidth of the associated Markov Random Field (MRF)—significantly narrows its range of practical applications. In reality, many real-world structured prediction problems involve modeling global dependencies, either by incorporating global factors directly or by imposing global constraints on prediction variables. Such requirements inevitably lead to fully connected graphs, rendering exact inference with this algorithm computationally infeasible. Prior research [1]-[4] addressing loss-augmented inference has shown that efficient inference can be achieved in models containing specific global factors representing non-decomposable loss functions within the Structured Support Vector Machine (SSVM) training framework. In this work, we expand upon the inference efficiency framework introduced in [3], enabling more detailed interactions between the core model’s energy function and the global terms’ sufficient statistics, without incurring additional computational costs. We illustrate the effectiveness of our approach through several applications, including one that surpasses the capabilities of existing methods. Accurate electricity demand forecasting is essential for developing sustainable power systems. To support more informed decision-making—particularly regarding end-user demand flexibility—it is important to deliver forecasts that are not only precise but also transparent and actionable. Global Forecasting Models (GFMs), which utilize training across multiple time series, have recently demonstrated superior performance in numerous demand forecasting competitions and real-world applications compared to univariate methods. Our goal is to bridge the gap between accuracy and interpretability in global forecasting approaches. To elucidate the predictions of these global models, we introduce LIMREF—Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Rule-based Explanations for Forecasting. This framework generates k-optimal impact rules tailored to specific forecasts, treating the global model as a black box in a model-agnostic manner. LIMREF provides diverse rule types that explain the global model’s predictions, including counterfactual rules that reveal actionable insights for achieving different outcomes under specific conditions. We validate our approach using a comprehensive electricity demand dataset that incorporates external factors such as temperature and calendar effects. Our experiments assess the explanatory quality of LIMREF’s outputs through both qualitative and quantitative metrics, demonstrating its effectiveness in improving interpretability without sacrificing accuracy.

This paper investigates multi-UAV enabled mobile edge computing (UAVE), where multiple UAVs serve as flying MEC platforms to provide computing resources to ground user equipments (UEs). Compared to traditional fixed-location MEC, UAVE offers significant advantages in scenarios such as temporary events, emergency situations, and on-demand services, owing to its high flexibility, cost-effectiveness, and ease of deployment. Nonetheless, operating UAVE presents several challenges, particularly in managing the association between multiple UEs and UAVs, as well as allocating resources from UAVs to UEs—all while minimizing the overall energy consumption. To address these issues, we formulate the problem as a mixed-integer nonlinear programming (MINLP) model, which is notably difficult to solve, especially at large scales. We then introduce a Reinforcement Learning (RL)-based user association and resource allocation (RLAA) algorithm designed to solve the problem efficiently and effectively. Numerical results demonstrate that RLAA achieves near-optimal performance comparable to exhaustive search in small-scale scenarios and significantly outperforms other conventional algorithms in large-scale environments.

Promptly and accurately responding to product inquiries is essential for e-commerce platforms. Manual responses, such as those on community question-and-answer sites, are often slow and do not scale effectively. Recent research indicates that product reviews serve as a valuable resource for real-time, automated product question answering (PQA). In the literature, PQA is typically approached as a retrieval task, aiming to identify the most relevant reviews to address a specific question. This paper concentrates on two critical aspects of PQA using reviews: answerability and answer reliability. Our premise is that many questions cannot be answered fully with a limited set of reviews. When a question is unanswerable, the system should return a null response rather than irrelevant reviews, thereby preventing negative impacts on user experience. Conversely, for answerable questions, only the most pertinent reviews that truly address the query should be included in the results. We introduce a conformal prediction-based framework designed to enhance the dependability of PQA systems by filtering out unreliable answers. This approach ensures that the system returns concise and accurate responses, including nil answers for questions that cannot be answered based on available reviews. Experiments

We introduce a novel neural topic model within the Wasserstein autoencoder (WAE) framework. Unlike traditional variational autoencoder-based approaches, our model directly imposes a Dirichlet prior on the latent document-topic representations. By leveraging the structure of the latent space, we apply an appropriate kernel in minimizing the Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) to effectively match distributions. Our findings reveal that MMD outperforms Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) in matching high-dimensional Dirichlet distributions. Additionally, we observe that injecting randomness into the encoder outputs during training substantially enhances topic coherence. To assess the diversity of generated topics, we propose a straightforward topic uniqueness metric. When combined with the widely used NPMI coherence measure, this provides a more comprehensive evaluation of topic quality. Experiments on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate that our approach yields significantly superior topics compared to existing models.

Variational methods for Gaussian processes (GPs) often rely on a limited set of inducing points to create a low-rank approximation of the covariance matrix. In contrast, this work leverages a sparse approximation of the precision matrix. We introduce the variational nearest neighbor Gaussian process (VNNGP), which incorporates a prior that preserves only the correlations among the K nearest neighbors, resulting in a sparse precision structure. Within a variational framework, the VNNGP objective can be decomposed over both the observations and the inducing points, allowing for stochastic optimization with a computational complexity of O($K^3$). This approach enables us to scale the number of inducing points arbitrarily, even to the extent of placing an inducing point at every observed location. Through various experiments comparing VNNGP to other scalable Gaussian process methods, we show that (1) VNNGP can significantly outperform low-rank approaches, and (2) it is less susceptible to overfitting than alternative nearest neighbor techniques.

Online meta-learning is increasingly recognized as a vital technique for enabling edge intelligence within the Internet of Things (IoT) ecosystem. However, effectively learning a robust meta-model that allows rapid adaptation to new tasks often requires a single agent to train over numerous tasks, leading to the well-known 'cold-start' challenge. Noticing that in a network of multiple agents, the tasks they encounter frequently share underlying similarities, we pose a fundamental question: "Can limited communication among agents accelerate online meta-learning, and if so, what level of improvement can be achieved?" To explore this, we introduce a multi-agent online meta-learning framework formulated as an equivalent two-tier nested online convex optimization (OCO) problem. By analyzing the upper bounds of the average regret across agents and tasks, we demonstrate that the effectiveness of multi-agent online meta-learning heavily relies on how much each agent can leverage the collective network—via constrained communication—to update its meta-model. This aspect, however, remains insufficiently understood. To address this, we develop a distributed online gradient descent algorithm with gradient tracking, enabling each agent to estimate the global gradient through a single communication step with its neighbors per iteration. This approach results in an average regret bound of $O(\sqrt{T/N})$ per agent, highlighting the potential benefits of cooperative learning in multi-agent meta-learning systems.

Answer-agnostic question generation is a complex and demanding task that involves automatically creating questions from a given sentence without specifying an answer. In this paper, we introduce two innovative strategies to address this challenge: question type prediction and a copy loss mechanism. The question type prediction module determines the categories of questions to be generated, enabling our model to produce diverse question types from the same source sentence. The copy loss mechanism enhances the standard copy process, ensuring that all key words in the source are accurately incorporated into the generated questions. Our comprehensive model surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods in answer-agnostic question generation, achieving a BLEU-4 score of 13.9 on the SQuAD dataset. Human assessments also confirm the high quality of our questions. We plan to release our code publicly to facilitate further research.

Langevin diffusion is an effective technique for tackling nonconvex optimization problems, facilitating escape from local minima by introducing stochastic noise into the gradient. The temperature parameter, which governs the noise intensity, balances the tradeoff between “global exploration” at high temperatures and “local exploitation” at low temperatures. To leverage the benefits of both regimes, we propose employing replica exchange, a method that alternates between two Langevin diffusions operating at different temperatures. We provide a theoretical analysis of the acceleration benefits of replica exchange from two viewpoints: (i) convergence in \(\chi^2\)-divergence and (ii) large deviation principles. This acceleration enables a faster convergence toward the global minimum. Additionally, by discretizing the replica exchange Langevin process, we develop a discrete-time algorithm. We rigorously assess its discretization error and demonstrate its practical acceleration effects through empirical results.

Complex time-varying systems are frequently examined by abstracting away from the individual components' dynamics to develop a model focusing on population-level behavior. However, this approach can sometimes obscure the contribution of each individual within the larger system. In this study, we introduce a novel transformer-based architecture designed to learn from time-dependent data, capturing both the behavior of individual elements and the collective dynamics of the population. Unlike traditional models that integrate all data upfront, our separable architecture processes each individual's time series independently before combining the information, ensuring permutation invariance and enabling transferability across systems of varying sizes and complexities. We first demonstrate the efficacy of our model in recovering complex interactions and dynamics in many-body systems. Subsequently, we apply it to neural populations within the nervous system. On neural activity datasets, our multi-scale transformer not only achieves robust decoding performance but also exhibits remarkable transfer capabilities. These findings suggest that it is feasible to learn from neurons in one animal’s brain and successfully adapt the model to neurons in another.

Deep learning models trained through fully supervised methods have been found to depend heavily on what are known as "shortcut" features—inputs that correlate with the target outcome in the training data but become irrelevant or absent in testing or deployment environments. In our experiments, we demonstrate that recent self-supervised models trained on images and text generate more robust image representations and lessen reliance on visual shortcut features, using a realistic medical imaging scenario. Moreover, we observe that these self-supervised models tend to forget shortcut features more rapidly than their fully supervised counterparts when fine-tuned with labeled data. While this approach is not a complete fix, our findings provide strong evidence that self-supervised models trained on visual and textual data offer increased resistance to the influence of shortcut features.

Multi-agent reinforcement learning often encounters challenges due to the exponentially expanding action space resulting from numerous agents. In this paper, we introduce HAVEN, a novel value decomposition framework grounded in hierarchical reinforcement learning, designed for fully cooperative multi-agent tasks. To mitigate instability caused by the simultaneous optimization of high-level and low-level policies, as well as the concurrent learning of multiple agents, we implement a dual coordination mechanism that manages inter-layer and inter-agent strategies. HAVEN requires no domain expertise or pretraining and is compatible with any variant of value decomposition methods. Our approach demonstrates strong performance across various decentralized partially observable Markov decision process domains and provides an efficient, implicit partitioning of the decision space.

This paper focuses solely on the efficiency of AIS-INMACA. Developed by Pokkuluri Kiran Sree in 2014, AIS-INMACA has demonstrated significant success in addressing critical bioinformatics challenges such as protein region identification and promoter region prediction, achieving these results in less time. Since its inception, various modifications of AIS-INMACA have been introduced to enhance its potential as a versatile tool for solving diverse problems within bioinformatics. Consequently, this study will prove highly valuable to researchers working in bioinformatics, particularly those utilizing cellular automata.

In many academic environments, medical students commence their scientific endeavors early in their training. At our institution, they often collaborate within interdisciplinary teams alongside postgraduate researchers from pharmaceutical sciences, natural sciences, or biostatistics. Ensuring all these students are educated in robust research practices, particularly regarding statistical analysis, is essential. Central to this is the concept of reproducibility, a cornerstone of contemporary scientific inquiry. Recognizing that even educators may be unfamiliar with all aspects of a fully reproducible workflow, I agreed to deliver a series of lectures on reproducible research (RR) tailored for medical students and postgraduate pharmacists engaged in various facets of clinical research. I structured this pilot lecture series to explore the definitions of RR, its importance, potential benefits, and practical implementation methods. During an attempt to replicate a published analysis, I encountered several real-world challenges. This article uses that experience to illustrate the diverse aspects of RR, offers explanations and potential solutions, and advocates for the inclusion of RR principles in standardized curricula for quantitative clinical researchers. I hope these insights will help raise awareness among educators and students about the importance of adopting reproducible research practices.

Robust reinforcement learning (RL) aims to identify a policy that maximizes performance in the worst-case scenarios within an uncertainty set of Markov Decision Processes (MDPs). In this study, we concentrate on model-free robust RL, where the uncertainty set is centered around a potentially misspecified MDP that produces a single sample trajectory sequentially and is considered unknown. We propose a sampling-based method to estimate the unknown uncertainty set and introduce robust algorithms suitable for different settings: a robust Q-learning algorithm for the tabular case and a robust TDC algorithm for scenarios involving function approximation. Both algorithms are designed for online, incremental implementation. We establish that the robust Q-learning algorithm converges to the optimal robust Q-function, while the robust TDC algorithm converges asymptotically to stationary points. Unlike previous results [Roy et al., 2017], our methods do not require additional conditions on the discount factor to ensure convergence. Additionally, we derive finite-time error bounds for both algorithms, demonstrating that their convergence rates are comparable to those of their standard counterparts, within a constant factor. Numerical experiments further validate the robustness of our approaches. Our framework can also be adapted to enhance the robustness of numerous other RL algorithms.

Contextual bandit algorithms—an advanced subclass of multi-armed bandit techniques that leverage contextual information—have demonstrated significant effectiveness in tackling sequential decision-making tasks under uncertainty. Typically, these models assume that the true reward associated with an action is observed by the learner at no expense. However, this assumption often falls short in real-world applications where acquiring the ground truth reward incurs costs. When observing the true reward is costly, a major challenge is for the learner to strategically determine when and how to acquire this information, weighing the benefits against the costs to optimize learning efficiency while minimizing expenses. From an information-theoretic standpoint, an intriguing question arises: how much potential loss in learning efficiency occurs due to these observation costs? In this work, we propose a novel contextual bandit learning algorithm equipped with active learning capabilities. A distinguishing feature of our method is that, alongside querying an annotator for the true reward, the algorithm also transmits prior learned information about the ground truth, thereby reducing the number of costly queries. We demonstrate that, by appropriately tuning the algorithm’s parameters, the regret of our proposed approach can be effectively bounded, ensuring robust performance despite the costs associated with reward observation.

Twenty-three machine learning algorithms were trained and evaluated to establish baseline comparison metrics and identify an image classification model suitable for integration into mission-critical satellite imaging systems. The Overhead-MNIST dataset, comprising satellite images resembling the well-known MNIST handwritten digits, served as the test bed. Among the models tested, CatBoost, Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM), and Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) achieved the highest accuracies, Areas Under the Curve (AUC), and F1 scores during a comprehensive PyCaret comparison. Separate analyses indicated that a deep convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture showed the greatest promise. The results for the top-performing model, intended as a reference point for edge deployment and ongoing enhancement, feature a CNN achieving a 0.965 categorical accuracy on unseen test data.

Accurately predicting the completion time of business process instances is crucial for effectively managing processes under service level agreement (SLA) constraints. Foreseeing the likely trajectory of ongoing processes enables managers to take timely actions to prevent delays or adverse outcomes. Nonetheless, making precise predictions is challenging due to numerous factors that can influence the duration of a process instance. In this paper, we introduce a novel approach utilizing deep Recurrent Neural Networks, specifically Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) models, which can leverage diverse information associated with individual events to generate highly accurate estimates of process completion times. Experiments conducted on real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and reliability of our method.

The extensive data requirements of DNNs often lead practitioners to collect internet data without thorough inspection due to high costs, which introduces potential risks of backdoor attacks. A backdoored model consistently predicts a specific target class when a predefined trigger pattern is present, and such triggers can be easily embedded by poisoning a small portion of the training data. Generally, adversarial training is considered a potential defense against backdoor attacks because it helps maintain the model’s predictions even when inputs are slightly perturbed within certain limits. However, prior research has shown limited success in achieving this robustness. To evaluate whether adversarial training can effectively defend against backdoor threats, we conducted extensive experiments across various threat scenarios and perturbation budgets, discovering that the effectiveness depends heavily on the specific threat model used. For example, adversarial training with spatial adversarial examples offers significant resilience against common patch-based backdoor attacks. Additionally, we introduce a hybrid approach that achieves satisfactory robustness against a range of backdoor attack methods.

Identifying groups of similar objects within data is crucial across numerous applications. As a representative problem in clustering, we examine the densest k-disjoint-clique problem, which aims to find k disjoint cliques in a weighted complete graph that maximize the total density of the subgraphs induced by these cliques. In this study, we derive conditions under which the exact identification of the densest k cliques can be achieved through the solution of a specific semidefinite program. Notably, this semidefinite relaxation precisely recovers the true cliques when the input graph models data containing k prominent, well-separated clusters alongside a smaller set of outliers. Our methodology also provides a semidefinite relaxation for the biclustering problem, with similar guarantees for accurate recovery. Biclustering involves simultaneously grouping objects and their features based on expression levels, which can be formulated as partitioning the nodes of a weighted bipartite complete graph to maximize the sum of densities of the resulting bipartite subgraphs. As with our analysis of the densest k-disjoint-clique problem, we demonstrate that the correct partitioning can be reliably recovered under certain conditions.

Clustering is a fundamental technique in data analysis, including the study of time series data. It is inherently subjective, as different users may prefer various clustering solutions for the same dataset. Semi-supervised clustering mitigates this subjectivity by enabling users to specify examples of instances that should (or should not) be grouped together. This paper explores semi-supervised clustering within the realm of time series analysis. We demonstrate that COBRAS, a leading semi-supervised clustering algorithm, can be effectively adapted to this context. We call this adaptation COBRAS-TS. Through comprehensive experiments, we establish the following findings: (1) COBRAS-TS significantly surpasses existing methods in semi-supervised time series clustering and sets a new performance benchmark; (2) COBRAS-TS effectively detects clusters comprised of separated components; (3) it successfully identifies clusters defined by subtle local patterns; (4) even minimal semi-supervision can markedly enhance clustering quality for time series data; (5) the selection of the clustering algorithm is crucial, challenging previous assumptions in the literature.

The growing proliferation of machine learning applications has made reusable model design increasingly valuable. In this paper, we concentrate on the reusability of pre-trained deep convolutional models. Unlike approaches that use pre-trained models merely as feature extractors, we uncover additional potentials within the convolutional layers—specifically, that convolutional activations can serve as detectors for common objects in image co-localization tasks. We introduce a straightforward yet powerful method called Deep Descriptor Transforming (DDT), which assesses the relationships among descriptors to identify category-consistent regions, thereby accurately locating shared objects across a set of images. Extensive experiments confirm the effectiveness of DDT, showing that it consistently surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods on standard image co-localization benchmarks. Additionally, DDT exhibits strong generalization to unseen categories and maintains robustness when handling noisy data.

Crypto-ransomware inflicts damage through encryption, which is often irreversible and leads to data loss. This paper introduces a machine learning (ML) classifier designed to detect crypto-ransomware early by analyzing program behavior. While signature-based detection may fail at times, a behavior-based approach serves as a crucial last line of defense to identify and mitigate potential damage. Our research highlights that ransomware exhibits distinctive input/output activities and file-content entropy, which are effective indicators for detection. Additionally, a deep learning (DL) classifier demonstrated high accuracy and a low false positive rate in identifying ransomware. To assess the model's robustness, we conducted adversarial testing using simulated ransomware programs in a gray-box analysis, revealing vulnerabilities and guiding improvements. Beyond accuracy and resilience, trustworthiness is essential for a reliable detector—ensuring the integrity of inference data is vital in security contexts. We employed the Integrated Gradient method to interpret the deep learning model’s decisions and to understand why some false negatives evade detection. The paper discusses the development and evaluation of a practical, real-world ransomware detector, emphasizing both its effectiveness and security considerations.

When data stores and users are spread across different geographical regions, it becomes crucial to strategically position distributed data caches at optimal locations to reduce data transfer costs. In response, we are creating an adaptive distributed data caching framework capable of determining which data chunks to cache and dynamically relocating them within a network of community cache nodes.

Bibliographic reference parsers aim to convert reference strings into structured, machine-readable metadata—including author names, titles, journal names, and publication years. These parsers utilize heuristics or machine learning techniques to perform the extraction. Nonetheless, no single parser or algorithm consistently outperforms others across all scenarios. For example, one tool might excel at extracting titles formatted in ACM style but perform only modestly with APA citations. Conversely, certain tools may be superior at identifying English author names or handling noisy data with inconsistent citation formats. In this extended version of our recent RecSys poster, we explore reference parsing from the perspectives of recommender systems and meta-learning. We introduce ParsRec, a meta-learning-based recommender system designed to suggest the most suitable parser for a specific reference string. ParsRec evaluates ten open-source parsers: Anystyle-Parser, Biblio, CERMINE, Citation, Citation-Parser, GROBID, ParsCit, PDFSSA4MET, Reference Tagger, and Science Parse. Our evaluation, conducted on a dataset of 105,000 references from the field of chemistry, considers two meta-learning strategies: one that recommends the optimal parser for the entire reference string, and another that selects the best parser for each individual metadata type within the reference. The second approach demonstrated superior performance in our experiments.

Recommendation challenges involving vast sets of discrete items—such as products, web pages, or videos—are prevalent across the technology sector. To address these, deep neural networks are increasingly being employed, utilizing embeddings to convert discrete items into continuous vector representations. While the sizes of these vocabularies and embedding dimensions significantly impact model performance, they are often selected manually through heuristic methods. In this work, we introduce Neural Input Search (NIS), a method designed to learn optimal vocabulary sizes and embedding dimensions for categorical features. The primary objective is to maximize prediction accuracy while respecting a total memory budget for all embeddings. Additionally, we critique the conventional Single-size Embedding (SE), which assigns a uniform embedding dimension to all feature values, highlighting its inefficiency in utilizing model capacity and training data. To overcome this, we propose Multi-size Embedding (ME), a flexible approach that assigns different embedding dimensions to different feature values. During training, reinforcement learning is employed to determine the best vocabulary size for each feature and the optimal embedding dimension for each value.
