As the demand for training DNN models directly on end-user devices like smartphones grows—driven by concerns over data privacy and communication costs—it becomes increasingly important to address the unique hardware constraints of these devices. Unlike data center servers equipped with high-performance CPUs and GPUs, modern smartphones utilize a diverse array of specialized cores within a system-on-a-chip (SoC) architecture, designed to handle multiple functions efficiently. Training deep neural networks on such SoCs without carefully managing their limited resources can result in poor training efficiency and negatively impact user experience. In this paper, we introduce Swan, a neural engine designed to optimize DNN training on smartphone SoCs while maintaining a seamless user experience. Our extensive large-scale evaluations demonstrate that Swan can enhance training performance by a factor of 1.2 to 23.3 times compared to the current state-of-the-art solutions.

This paper proposes the development of stochastic hard thresholding algorithms tailored for maximizing the Area Under the Curve (AUC) in imbalanced classification scenarios. The primary difficulty lies in handling the pairwise loss function intrinsic to AUC maximization. To address this, we reformulate the U-statistics objective into an empirical risk minimization (ERM) framework, enabling the creation of a stochastic hard thresholding algorithm named \texttt{SHT-AUC}. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first approach to introduce stochastic hard thresholding algorithms for AUC maximization that operate with a per-iteration complexity of $\O(b d)$, where $d$ represents the data dimension and $b$ the minibatch size. We demonstrate that the proposed method achieves linear convergence up to a specified tolerance level. Notably, in the case where data is generated from a Gaussian distribution, the convergence rate diminishes as class imbalance increases. Extensive experiments confirm the efficiency and effectiveness of our algorithms.

Adaptive control challenges are notoriously complex, even when plant-specific controllers are available. One approach to circumvent the computational difficulty of identifying the optimal policy is to reformulate the problem as minimizing the relative entropy between a controller that disregards the true plant dynamics and an informed controller. This leads to the Bayesian control rule—a set of equations that define a stochastic adaptive controller capable of handling a range of possible plant models. Applying the Bayesian control rule, we develop BCR-MDP, a controller designed to solve undiscounted Markov decision processes with finite state and action spaces, where the system dynamics are unknown. Notably, we establish a non-parametric conjugate prior distribution over the policy space that integrates the agent's entire relevant history, and we implement a Gibbs sampler to generate random policies from this distribution. Initial results indicate that BCR-MDP effectively avoids sub-optimal limit cycles, thanks to its intrinsic mechanism that balances exploration and exploitation.

Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) are advanced machine learning techniques widely applied across numerous innovative and significant fields. In imaging science, GANs are highly effective in generating diverse image datasets, creating realistic human face photographs, captioning images and videos, translating images between different styles, converting text to images, predicting video sequences, and producing three-dimensional objects, among other uses. In this paper, we explore how GANs can be employed to construct artificial environments. Specifically, we examine how GANs facilitate image description through captioning methods and enable the transformation of one image into another within a desired thematic style using image-to-image translation frameworks. We highlight the role of GANs in shaping and customizing virtual worlds.

Motivation: Protein-protein interactions (PPIs) are essential for the proper functioning of proteins within both healthy and diseased cells, with many key protein roles being facilitated through such interactions. Understanding the specific nature of these interactions is vital for constructing biological networks and analyzing experimental data. However, only a small fraction of PPIs documented in interaction databases are annotated with functional information—just about 4% in the case of the IntAct database. To address this gap, our goal is to assign functional labels to PPIs by extracting relevant relationship information from PubMed abstracts.

Method: We develop a weakly supervised dataset derived from the IntAct PPI database, comprising protein pairs with known functions and their corresponding PubMed abstracts. Utilizing BioBERT, a cutting-edge deep learning model tailored for biomedical natural language processing, we build PPI-BioBERT—an approach designed to classify the function types of PPIs. To ensure high-quality function extraction on a large scale, we employ an ensemble of PPI-BioBERT models to enhance uncertainty assessment and implement interaction type-specific thresholds—these help to mitigate the impact of varying amounts of training data across different interaction types.

Results: Our approach enabled the scanning of 18 million PubMed abstracts, leading to the automatic identification of 3,253 previously unannotated PPIs with assigned functional types.

Understanding the extent to which neural networks memorize training data poses a fascinating question with significant practical and theoretical consequences. In this study, we demonstrate that, in certain scenarios, a considerable portion of the training data can be reconstructed solely from the parameters of a trained neural network classifier. We introduce a novel reconstruction approach, inspired by recent theoretical insights into the implicit bias of gradient-based training methods for neural networks. To our knowledge, these findings are the first to establish that it is generally feasible to recover a large subset of the original training samples from a trained neural network classifier. This raises specific privacy concerns, as such techniques could be exploited to extract sensitive training information. We validate our approach using binary MLP classifiers across several standard computer vision datasets.

In complex networks, nodes exhibiting similar structural traits often perform analogous roles, such as particular user types in a social network or hierarchical positions within an organization. To capitalize on this correlation, recent research has introduced latent representations aimed at identifying structurally equivalent nodes. However, many existing techniques tend to be computationally intensive, requiring significant time and storage resources. In this paper, we introduce VNEstruct, a straightforward method for generating low-dimensional structural node embeddings that is both computationally efficient and resilient to changes in the network's structure. Our approach concentrates on each node’s local neighborhood and utilizes Von Neumann entropy, an information-theoretic measure, to extract features that effectively encode the neighborhood’s topology. Additionally, for graph classification tasks, we propose leveraging these structural embeddings to transform attribute-rich graph structures into enhanced node feature sets. Empirical results demonstrate that VNEstruct is robust in identifying structural roles and delivers state-of-the-art performance in graph classification, all while maintaining exceptional speed in computation.

Consider the challenge of approximating the optimal policy in a Markov decision process (MDP) through sampling of state transitions. Unlike traditional reinforcement learning approaches that rely on iterative approximations of the nonlinear Bellman equation, we introduce a Primal-Dual π-Learning methodology rooted in the linear duality between value functions and policies. This π-Learning algorithm is model-free and iteratively updates both the policy and value vectors as new data becomes available. For infinite-horizon, undiscounted MDPs with finite state space \( S \) and action space \( A \), our method achieves an \(\epsilon\)-optimal policy with a number of sampled transitions bounded by

\[
\tilde{O}\left( \frac{(\tau \cdot t_{mix}^*)^2 \, |S| \, |A|}{\epsilon^2} \right),
\]

where \( t_{mix}^* \) is an upper limit on the mixing times across all policies, and \( \tau \) characterizes the variation in stationary distributions among policies. The π-Learning framework is also applicable to computational scenarios where transition probabilities and rewards are explicitly provided. When each state transition can be sampled in approximately constant time \(\tilde{O}(1)\), this approach yields a sublinear-time algorithm for solving average-reward MDPs.

Over the past decade, there has been a remarkable surge in the volume of digital information stored within electronic health records (EHR). Originally created to archive patient clinical data and facilitate administrative healthcare functions, these records have increasingly been repurposed for various clinical informatics applications by researchers. Concurrently, the field of machine learning has experienced significant advancements in deep learning methodologies, which have been effectively utilized to analyze the extensive EHR datasets. This paper provides a comprehensive review of these deep EHR systems, focusing on their architectures, technical details, and clinical applications. Additionally, we discuss the current limitations of existing approaches and explore potential directions for future research in EHR-based deep learning.

Many open-domain conversation applications in the real world serve specific objectives during open-ended interactions, such as providing recommendations, offering psychotherapy, or facilitating education. This study addresses the challenge of integrating conversational goals into open-domain chat agents. Our goal is to enable a conversational system to engage naturally with users while proactively steering the dialogue toward a predetermined topic. This task is particularly complex due to the lack of publicly available data tailored to learn such goal-oriented strategies. To tackle this, we propose a structured methodology that employs coarse-grained keywords to guide the content of system responses. We ensure seamless conversational flow through turn-level supervised learning and direct the dialogue toward the target topic using discourse-level constraints. Additionally, we create a keyword-augmented conversation dataset specifically for this purpose. Experimental results, including both quantitative metrics and human assessments, demonstrate that our system can generate coherent and purposeful conversations, substantially outperforming existing methods.

Automated algorithm selection aims to assist users in choosing the most appropriate algorithm for a specific problem. A key component of these machine learning techniques involves regression models that estimate an algorithm’s performance on previously unseen problem instances. In numerical black-box optimization, these regression models often rely on exploratory landscape analysis (ELA), which measures various problem characteristics. These measures serve as features to train supervised performance regression models. Initial efforts in ELA-based performance prediction have focused on fixed-target scenarios. However, many real-world applications require selecting an algorithm that performs optimally within a limited evaluation budget. In this fixed-budget context, we show that high-quality performance predictions can be achieved with standard supervised learning methods by effectively combining two differently trained regression models. We evaluate this approach on a particularly challenging task: selecting the best algorithm from a portfolio of highly similar algorithms, specifically from the modular CMA-ES family.

The Information Bottleneck (IB) approach facilitates balancing data compression with the predictive accuracy of learned representations and has been effectively and reliably applied to both supervised and unsupervised learning tasks. Nonetheless, the IB framework faces several challenges. Firstly, optimizing the IB objective is inherently difficult. The IB Lagrangian, defined as \(\mathcal{L}_{IB} := I(X;Z) - \beta I(Y;Z)\), is non-convex, and existing algorithms typically guarantee only local convergence, making the solutions sensitive to initial conditions. Secondly, assessing the quality of a solution presents its own difficulties. Traditionally, this involves analyzing the information plane by plotting \(I(Y;Z)\) against \(I(X;Z)\) across solutions obtained from various initializations. Additionally, the IB Lagrangian exhibits phase transitions as the multiplier \(\beta\) varies. During these transitions, both \(I(X;Z)\) and \(I(Y;Z)\) increase abruptly, and convergence rates slow considerably for current methods. Recent advancements have employed variational surrogate bounds to approximate the IB Lagrangian, enabling more efficient optimization; however, the fidelity of these surrogates relative to the original Lagrangian remains uncertain. In this work, we address these issues by solving the IB Lagrangian through augmented Lagrangian techniques. The growing deployment of machine-learning (ML) systems in critical applications intensifies the need for innovative verification and validation methods rooted in established system assurance principles. Traditionally, model-based techniques have been extensively used in system development, relying on the premise that abstract models of the system offer a reliable foundation for evaluating implementation quality. We propose a similar methodology for ML systems, utilizing an ML approach that derives a low-dimensional manifold—a core structure—from the high-dimensional training data that implicitly characterizes the system. This manifold serves as a tool for various quality assurance activities, including measuring test coverage, generating test inputs, and monitoring system performance during runtime. Our approach is based on variational autoencoders, an unsupervised learning technique that discovers a pair of nearly inverse functions between the high-dimensional data and its low-dimensional representation. Early experiments demonstrate that this manifold-based strategy enhances test diversity, produces fault-revealing yet realistic test cases, and offers an independent means to evaluate the trustworthiness of the system's outputs during operation.

Recent studies on adversarial attack and defense methods indicate that PGD is a universal first-order attack under the $l_\infty$ norm, and that PGD-based adversarial training significantly enhances neural network robustness against a broad spectrum of first-order $l_\infty$-bounded attacks, establishing it as the current state-of-the-art defense technique. Nonetheless, a notable drawback of PGD adversarial training is its high computational cost in generating adversarial examples, rendering it impractical for large-scale, high-resolution datasets such as ImageNet. Furthermore, recent research has proposed a straightforward "closed-form" solution for achieving robustness on MNIST, raising the question of whether PGD adversarial training is truly essential for robust defense. In this paper, we provide a negative answer by introducing a training paradigm that matches the effectiveness of PGD adversarial training across several standard datasets, but only requires noisy-natural samples. Specifically, we reformulate the min-max problem in PGD adversarial training as one that minimizes the original loss plus the $l_1$ norms of the network’s input gradients. For the $l_1$-norm component, we develop a computationally efficient solution by incorporating a differentiable soft-quantization layer after the input layer. We formally demonstrate that training this soft-quantization layer with noisy-natural samples serves as an alternative approach to minimizing the $l_1$-norms of input gradients.

Adversarial imitation learning has emerged as a widely adopted approach for continuous control imitation tasks. Over time, numerous variations in its components have been proposed to improve policy performance and reduce sample complexity. However, these design choices are rarely tested comprehensively in rigorous empirical studies, making it difficult to identify which high-level algorithmic options and low-level implementation details truly influence outcomes. To address this, we developed a versatile adversarial imitation learning framework incorporating over 50 different choices and conducted an extensive large-scale investigation involving more than 500,000 trained agents. This study utilized both synthetic and human-generated demonstrations. While many of our findings reinforce established best practices, some results were unexpected or even contradicted previous research. Notably, we found that artificial demonstrations do not serve as reliable proxies for human data, and that the common practice of evaluating imitation algorithms solely with synthetic data may result in solutions that underperform in more realistic settings involving human demonstrations.

Federated learning (FL) offers a promising approach for enabling numerous AI applications by allowing the collaborative training of a global model using sensitive data distributed across multiple clients, all without sharing their local datasets. In FL, clients participate in the training process under the coordination of a central server, which manages the aggregation of model updates while preserving data privacy. A major challenge in FL is the communication overhead, as clients must transmit their model updates to the server during each global training round. Recently, over-the-air computation (AirComp) has been introduced to mitigate this bottleneck by enabling simultaneous transmission of updates over the multiple-access channel. However, relying solely on simple averaging through AirComp makes the system susceptible to malicious or erroneous updates from Byzantine clients, which can compromise learning. In this work, we introduce a transmission and aggregation framework designed to mitigate the impact of such attacks while maintaining the efficiency benefits of AirComp for FL. Our robust method involves the central server randomly grouping clients and assigning specific transmission time slots to each group. The server then performs a resilient aggregation of the received updates from different groups. We further extend our framework to address scenarios involving non-independent and identically distributed (non-i.i.d.) data across clients.

This paper explores stochastic optimization problems within a broad class of objective functions, including convex and continuous submodular functions. While stochastic proximal gradient methods have been commonly employed to address these problems, their effectiveness diminishes in high-dimensional settings where projections onto convex sets are computationally expensive. As an alternative, we introduce stochastic conditional gradient methods that leverage: (i) a simple averaging technique to approximate gradients, requiring only a single stochastic gradient evaluation per iteration; and (ii) linear programming to determine descent or ascent directions. The averaging process progressively reduces gradient noise over time, and substituting the projection step with linear programming decreases the computational burden per iteration. Under assumptions of convexity and smoothness, we demonstrate that our approach converges to the optimal objective value at a sublinear rate of \(O(1/t^{1/3})\). Prescriptive process monitoring methods utilize historical data to recommend timely interventions during process execution, aiming to prevent undesirable outcomes or enhance overall performance. A key component of these methods is the intervention policy—a decision rule that determines when and whether to intervene in an ongoing case. Prior approaches typically base their policies solely on the current state of a case, neglecting the tradeoff between acting immediately—despite uncertainty in predictive models—and postponing intervention to potentially achieve better results later. Additionally, these methods often assume unlimited resources are available for interventions, overlooking resource constraints. This paper presents a novel prescriptive process monitoring technique that addresses these limitations by filtering and prioritizing active cases based on prediction scores, uncertainty levels, and the causal impact of interventions. It then triggers interventions strategically to maximize a predefined gain function, given resource limitations. The method is tested on real-world event log data, demonstrating superior performance in maximizing total gain compared to existing baseline approaches.

Offline handwritten mathematical expression recognition presents significant challenges, primarily due to two key issues encountered during the recognition process. The first involves accurately identifying a wide variety of mathematical symbols, while the second pertains to deciphering the complex two-dimensional structures inherent in mathematical expressions. Inspired by recent advancements in deep learning, this work introduces a novel neural network architecture that integrates a Multi-Scale Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) with an Attention-based Recurrent Neural Network (RNN). This combination enables the system to convert two-dimensional handwritten mathematical expressions into linear LaTeX sequences effectively. Consequently, the proposed model achieves a Word Error Rate (WER) of 25.715% and an Expression Recognition Rate (ExpRate) of 28.216%.

The co-evolution of time series manifests across various domains such as environmental monitoring, financial analysis, and intelligent transportation systems. This study addresses key challenges, namely (C1) how to explicitly incorporate relationship networks among time series, and (C2) how to effectively model the implicit dynamics within these series. To this end, we introduce a novel framework called the Network of Tensor Time Series, composed of two core components: the Tensor Graph Convolutional Network (TGCN) and the Tensor Recurrent Neural Network (TRNN). TGCN extends traditional Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) from simple graphs to tensor graphs, enabling the capture of interactions across multiple interconnected graphs associated with the data tensors. Meanwhile, TRNN employs tensor decomposition techniques to uncover and model the latent, implicit relationships inherent in the co-evolving time series. Extensive experiments on five real-world datasets validate the superior performance and effectiveness of our proposed approach.

Crowdsourcing has emerged as a popular approach for obtaining labeled data across various tasks where humans tend to outperform computers, such as image annotation, object recognition, and sentiment analysis. Nonetheless, relying exclusively on crowdsourcing can be impractical, even for datasets comprising thousands of items, due to the time and expense involved in collecting human annotations—costing only pennies and minutes per label. In this paper, we introduce algorithms designed to integrate machine learning techniques into crowdsourced databases, aiming to enable these systems to scale efficiently by managing larger datasets at reduced costs. Our core insight is that, for many of these tasks, humans and machine learning models can work in tandem: humans offer higher accuracy but are slower and more costly, whereas algorithms provide faster, cheaper, yet somewhat less accurate predictions. Leveraging this synergy, we propose two active learning algorithms that combine human input and machine learning within a crowdsourcing framework. These algorithms are grounded in the principles of non-parametric bootstrap theory, ensuring broad applicability across diverse machine learning models. Our experiments, conducted on three real-world datasets collected via Amazon Mechanical Turk and complemented by tests on 15 well-known UCI datasets, demonstrate that our methods significantly enhance performance and scalability.
